title: German A1
description: German from your first word to CEFR level A1, the level of the Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1. Grammar lessons cover sounds and spelling, greetings, numbers, the present tense, articles and plurals, the accusative and a first look at the dative, modal and separable verbs, the imperative and the perfect tense. About 700 everyday words are learned through typed vocabulary reviews with pronunciation, and a reading list points to graded readers you can try on your own.
author: Erudior
changelog: Honors lessons with longer texts and culture, pictures and diagrams in every lesson, new question types and vocabulary; corrections from a second full review.

lessons.title: Sounds, letters and spelling
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

German is spelled far more regularly than English. Once you know how the letters sound, you can
read almost any German word out loud, and you can usually write a word you hear. This lesson
gives you that key: the alphabet and its letter names, the vowels (including the three with
dots), the letter ß, the letter groups that trip up English speakers, and where the stress
falls. Along the way you'll learn the first words everyone needs: *ja*, *nein*, *bitte*,
*danke* and the everyday greetings, and how to spell your name when someone asks.

Read every example aloud: pronunciation is learned with your mouth, not your eyes.

## The alphabet

German uses the same 26 letters as English, plus *ä*, *ö*, *ü* and *ß*. The letter names are
different, and you need them to spell your name on the phone or at a counter. The respellings
below are approximate English sounds.

| Letter | Name | Letter | Name | Letter | Name |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | ah | J | yot | S | ess |
| B | bay | K | kah | T | tay |
| C | tsay | L | ell | U | oo |
| D | day | M | emm | V | fow (rhymes with *cow*) |
| E | ay | N | enn | W | vay |
| F | eff | O | oh | X | iks |
| G | gay (hard g) | P | pay | Y | üpsilon |
| H | hah | Q | koo | Z | tset |
| I | ee | R | air (roughly) | ß | ess-tset |

The letters English speakers mix up most are A (ah), E (ay), I (ee) and J (yot). English
"ay" is the German name of E, and English "ee" is the German name of I, so if you spell *Jane*
the English way ("jay, ay, en, ee"), a German writes down something like "?, E, N, I".
Practise your own name until the German letter names come without thinking.

## Vowels: long and short

Every German **[[vowel]]** (a, e, i, o, u) can be long or short, and the difference can change the
meaning of a word. Some rough rules for spotting a long vowel:

- a vowel followed by *h* is long: *Jahr*, *wohnen*, *sehr*;
- a doubled vowel is long: *Tee* (tea), *Boot* (boat);
- *ie* is a long "ee": *sie*, *wie*, *vier*.

A vowel before a double **[[consonant]]** (*ll*, *mm*, *ss*, *tt*…) is short: *Hallo*, *kommen*,
*bitte*. Short vowels are clipped, as in English *bit* or *hot*; long vowels are held, with no
glide at the end. Long *e* in *Tee* is a pure, steady "ay" that doesn't slide into "ee" the way English
"ay" does.

| Short | Long |
|---|---|
| *Stadt* (city) | *Tag* (day) |
| *bitte* (please) | *sie* (she) |
| *Wort* (word) | *wohnen* (to live) |

An unstressed *e* at the end of a word is never silent. *Name* has two syllables: "NAH-meh".
*Danke* is "DAHN-keh". 

## The umlauts ä, ö, ü

The two dots are called an **[[umlaut]]**. They change the sound of the vowel:

- *ä* sounds like *e* in English *bed* (long *ä* as in *Käse* is a longer version of that);
- *ö*: say "ay", then round your lips as if to whistle, keeping your tongue where it is;
- *ü*: say "ee", then round your lips the same way.

You know *Tschüss* (bye). Try *Österreich* (Austria) and *Grüß Gott* (hello, in the south). The
umlaut is part of the spelling, not decoration: *schon* (already) and *schön* (beautiful) are
different words.

Typing them: in this app, use the buttons under the answer box. On a Windows US keyboard,
hold Alt and type 0228 (ä), 0246 (ö), 0252 (ü), 0223 (ß) on the number pad, or switch to the
US-International layout. On a Mac, press Option+u and then the vowel; Option+s gives ß. On a
phone, press and hold the vowel. Germans write *ae*, *oe*, *ue* (*Oesterreich*) only when
they can't type the real letter.

## ß and ss

The letter *ß* is called *Eszett* (ess-tset) or *scharfes S*. It always sounds like a
sharp *s* as in *kiss*. The rule for when to use it:

- after a long vowel or a **[[diphthong]]** (two vowels gliding together, like *ei* or *au*),
  write *ß*: *Straße*, *heißen*, *Grüß Gott*;
- after a short vowel, write *ss*: *Tschüss*, *dass*, *Wasser*.

The same decision as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Writing ß or ss
  accDescr: When you hear a sharp s sound inside a word, look at the sound just before it. After a long vowel or a diphthong such as ei, au or eu, write ß, as in Straße, heißen and Grüß Gott. After a short vowel, write ss, as in Tschüss, Wasser and dass. In Switzerland, ss is written in both cases.
  A["You hear a sharp s, as in kiss"] --> B{"What comes just before it?"}
  B -- "a long vowel or ei, au, eu" --> C["Write ß: Straße, heißen, Grüß Gott"]
  B -- "a short vowel" --> D["Write ss: Tschüss, Wasser, dass"]
  C --> E["In Switzerland: always ss"]
  D --> E
```

Switzerland doesn't use *ß* at all and writes *ss* everywhere. No German word begins with
*ß*, so you never need it as a capital at the start of a word; in text written all in capitals,
*ß* becomes *SS* (*STRASSE*).

## Vowel pairs: ei, ie, eu, äu, au

These are the pairs English speakers swap most often.

| Spelling | Sounds like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *ei* | English *eye* | *nein* (no), *heißen* (to be called) |
| *ie* | English *ee* | *Wie bitte?* (pardon?), *Wiedersehen* |
| *eu*, *äu* | *oy* as in *boy* | *Deutschland*, *Häuser* (houses) |
| *au* | *ow* as in *cow* | *auf*, *Frau* |

Memory hook: in *ei* and *ie*, say the English name of the second letter. *Nein* ends in
*i*, so you say "eye"; *wie* ends in *e*, so you say "ee". *Wein* (wine) and *Wien* (Vienna)
are a good pair to practise.

## Consonants that differ from English

| Spelling | Sound | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *w* | English *v* | *wie*, *Wort*, *wohnen* |
| *v* | usually English *f* | *Vorname*, *vier* |
| *j* | English *y* | *ja*, *Jahr* |
| *z* | *ts* as in *cats* | *zehn* (ten), *zwei* (two) |
| *s* before a vowel | English *z* | *sie*, *Sonne* (sun), *langsam* |
| *sch* | English *sh* | *schreiben*, *schön* |
| *sp*, *st* at the start of a word or part | *shp*, *sht* | *sprechen*, *Stadt*, *buchstabieren* |
| *ch* after a, o, u, au | rough sound at the back of the throat | *Nacht* (night), *noch* (still), *Buchstabe* (letter) |
| *ch* after other letters | soft hiss, like the *h* in *huge* | *ich*, *nicht* (not) |
| *-ig* at the end | like *ich* | *zwanzig* (twenty) |
| *qu* | *kv* | *Quatsch* (nonsense) |
| *th* | plain *t* | *Theater* |

The two *ch* sounds deserve practice. After *a*, *o*, *u* and *au* (*Nacht*, *noch*, *auch*),
it's the scraping sound in Scottish *loch*. After everything else (*ich*, *nicht*, *Milch*),
it's softer, made at the front of the mouth: say "hue" and stretch the h. (*Milch* means milk.) Never turn either
into an English *k* or *ch* as in *church*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which ch sound?
  accDescr: To choose the ch sound, look at the letter just before ch. After a, o, u or au, say the rough sound at the back of the mouth, as in Nacht, noch and auch. After any other letter, such as e, i, ä, ö, ü, ei, eu, l, n or r, say the soft hiss at the front of the mouth, as in ich, nicht and Milch. The ending -ig, as in zwanzig, is also said with the soft sound.
  A["You see ch in a word"] --> B{"Which letter comes just before it?"}
  B -- "a, o, u or au" --> C["Back of the mouth, rough: Nacht, noch, auch"]
  B -- "any other letter" --> D["Front of the mouth, soft hiss: ich, nicht, Milch"]
  D --> E["Same soft sound for -ig at the end: zwanzig"]
```

The picture shows where in the mouth these sounds are made. The soft *ch* of *ich* is made with
the middle of the tongue raised close to the hard palate, the rough *ch* of *ach* with the back
of the tongue near the soft palate, and the throat *r* even further back, near the uvula. For
*ü* and *ö*, the work is done by the lips, which round and push forward. (This is a simplified
picture; your mouth will find the exact spot as you practise.)

![A simplified side view of the mouth. The hard palate, the bony roof just behind the top teeth, is where the soft ch of ich and nicht is made. The soft palate, further back, is where the rough ch of ach and Nacht is made. The uvula, hanging at the very back, is used for the German r as in richtig. The lips are rounded for ü and ö.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

At the end of a word or syllable, *b*, *d* and *g* lose their voice and
sound like *p*, *t* and *k*. This is called **[[final devoicing]]**: *Tag* sounds like "tahk", *und* like "oont", *gelb* (yellow) like
"gelp". The spelling doesn't change.

The German *r*: at the start of a syllable, *r* is made at the back of the throat, close to a
light gargle: *richtig* (right), *Grüß Gott*. After a vowel, it mostly melts into a short
"uh": *der* (the) sounds close to "dare-uh", and the *r* in *Wort* is barely heard. If the throat *r* is hard at first, a
rolled *r* is understood everywhere, and many southern speakers use one.

## Where the stress falls

**[[Word stress]]** in German is usually on the first syllable: *DAN-ke*, *BIT-te*, *SCHREI-ben*,
*VOR-na-me*. Important exceptions:

- words beginning with *be-*, *ent-*, *ver-* and a few other short prefixes stress the next
  syllable: *Ent-SCHUL-di-gung*, *ver-STE-hen*;
- verbs ending in *-ieren* stress the *ie*: *buch-sta-BIE-ren*;
- many words borrowed from other languages stress the end: *Al-pha-BET*, *Ad-RES-se*;
- *Auf Wiedersehen* is stressed on *WIE*, and *Tschüss* has one syllable.

## Nouns have capital letters

Every German **[[noun]]** starts with a capital letter, wherever it is in the sentence: *der Name*,
*das Wort*, *mein Vorname*. That's a gift for readers: you can spot the nouns at a glance. Other
words are lowercase unless they start a sentence. The pronoun *ich* (I) is always lowercase,
unlike English *I*.

*Mein Name ist Lena.* — My name is Lena.
*Wie ist Ihr Familienname?* — What is your surname?
*Das Wort ist neu.* — The word is new.

## Spelling your name

When you give your name in Germany, people will often ask you to spell it. The question is *Wie
schreibt man das?* (literally "How does one write that?"), and the answer is the letters,
said one by one with the verb *buchstabieren* (to spell):

*Wie schreibt man das?* — How do you spell that?
*Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?* — Could you spell that, please?
*M – Ü – Double-L – E – R.* In German: *em, ü, zwei el* or *doppel-el, e, er.*

A double letter is often said as *zwei* (two) or *Doppel-* plus the letter.

## Polite words and greetings

Greetings change with the time of day. *Guten Morgen* is used until about 10 or 11 o'clock,
*Guten Tag* through the day, *Guten Abend* from about 6 p.m. *Gute Nacht* is only for going to
bed. *Hallo* is friendly and works almost anywhere; *Grüß Gott* is the standard greeting in
Bavaria and Austria. For goodbye, *Auf Wiedersehen* is polite and *Tschüss* is casual.

*Danke!* — *Bitte!* is the everyday exchange: thanks, you're welcome. *Bitte* also means
"please" and "here you are". *Danke schön* and *Bitte schön* are a little warmer.
*Entschuldigung* means "excuse me" (to get attention) and "sorry". *Wie bitte?* asks someone
to repeat what they said: "pardon?". If you need it again and slower, say *Noch einmal,
bitte. Langsam, bitte.*

## Dialogue: at a reception desk

> Frau Brandt: Guten Morgen!
>
> Tom: Guten Morgen. Mein Name ist Tom Weaver.
>
> Frau Brandt: Wie bitte? Noch einmal, bitte. Langsam, bitte.
>
> Tom: Tom Weaver. Mein Vorname ist Tom, mein Familienname ist Weaver.
>
> Frau Brandt: Danke. Wie schreibt man das?
>
> Tom: W – E – A – V – E – R.
>
> Frau Brandt: W, E, A, V wie Vogel, E, R?
>
> Tom: Ja, richtig.
>
> Frau Brandt: Danke schön, Herr Weaver.
>
> Tom: Bitte schön. Auf Wiedersehen!

Good morning! — Good morning. My name is Tom Weaver. — Pardon? Again, please. Slowly, please.
— Tom Weaver. My first name is Tom, my surname is Weaver. — Thank you. How do you spell that? —
W-E-A-V-E-R. — W, E, A, V as in *Vogel* (bird), E, R? — Yes, right. — Thank you very much, Mr
Weaver. — You're welcome. Goodbye!

Notice that Tom says the letter names the German way: *vay, ay, ah, fow, ay, air*.
Germans clarify a letter with a word that starts with it ("V as in Vogel"), much like "B as
in Bravo".

## Pronunciation

- *Entschuldigung*: stress on *SCHUL*; *-ung* is a short "oo" plus the *ng* of English *sing*,
  with no hard g: "oong".
- *Tschüss*: one syllable; start with "ch" as in *church*, then *ü*.
- *Wiedersehen*: "VEE-der-zay-en", with *w* as v and *s* as z.
- *buchstabieren*: *ch* at the back (after *u*), *st* as "sht", stress on *BIE*.
- *schreiben*: "SHRY-ben", *ei* as in *eye*.
- *Familienname*: stress on *MI*; *-lien* is one syllable, "lyen": "fa-MEE-lyen-nah-meh".

## Common mistakes

- Reading *w* as English w. *Wie* is "vee", *Wort* is "vort".
- Swapping *ei* and *ie*. *nein* is "nine", *sie* is "zee". Use the second-letter hook.
- A silent final *e*. *Danke*, *bitte*, *Name*: always pronounce the last *e*.
- Using *Gute Nacht* as a greeting in the evening. It means goodbye at bedtime; say *Guten
  Abend* when you arrive.
- Leaving off the umlaut. *schon* and *schön* are different words; write the dots.
- Lowercase nouns. *das wort* is wrong; nouns are always capitalized: *das Wort*.
- Spelling with English letter names. Practise *E* = ay, *I* = ee, *J* = yot, *V* = fow,
  *W* = vay.

## Key points

- German spelling is regular: learn the sounds of the letters once and you can read aloud.
- *w* = v, *v* = f, *j* = y, *z* = ts, *s* before a vowel = z, *sp/st* = shp/sht.
- *ei* = "eye", *ie* = "ee", *eu/äu* = "oy"; two *ch* sounds; final *b/d/g* sound like *p/t/k*.
- *ä, ö, ü* are separate sounds; write *ß* after long vowels and diphthongs, *ss* after short ones.
- Stress is usually on the first syllable, except after *be-, ent-, ver-*, in *-ieren* verbs
  and in many borrowed words.
- All nouns start with a capital letter.
- *Wie schreibt man das?* — answer with German letter names.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Greetings and introductions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson you learned to say hello, thank you and goodbye, and to spell your name. Now
you'll hold a first real conversation: say who you are, where you're from and where you live,
ask the same of someone else, and ask how they are. To do that you need four verbs (*sein*,
*heißen*, *kommen*, *wohnen*), four question words, and one decision German makes you take in
every conversation: *du* or *Sie*?

## du or Sie?

English has one word for "you". German has two for talking to one person:

| | Use it with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *du* | friends, family, children, classmates, people your age in casual settings, pets | *Wie heißt du?* |
| *Sie* | adults you don't know, shop and office staff, your boss, older people, anyone you call *Herr* or *Frau* | *Wie heißen Sie?* |

*du* is the **[[informal]]** "you"; *Sie* is the **[[formal]]** "you". *Sie* is always written with a
capital S, even in the middle of a sentence; that's how you tell it apart from *sie* (she,
they), which you'll meet in Lesson 4.

The two go with different ways of naming people. With *du*, people use first names: *Hallo,
Lena!* With *Sie*, they use *Herr* (Mr) or *Frau* (Mrs or Ms) and the surname: *Guten Tag,
Frau Schulz.* *Frau* is used for every adult woman, married or not; there's no German
equivalent of "Miss" in everyday use.

When in doubt, start with *Sie*. Switching from *Sie* to *du* is a small social step, and
usually the older person or the one in a senior position offers it: *Wir können gern du
sagen.* (We can say *du* to each other, if you like.) Among students, young people and in many workplaces, *du* is normal from
the first minute.

The chart sums up the choice for one person (customs vary by region, age and workplace, so
treat it as a guide, not a law):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: du or Sie with one person
  accDescr: If you are talking to a friend, a family member, a child or a fellow student, say du. If not, ask whether the person has offered du, for example with Wir können gern du sagen. If they have, say du with first names. If they have not, say Sie with Herr or Frau and the surname. When in doubt, start with Sie.
  A["You are talking to one person"] --> B{"Friend, family, child or fellow student?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["du + first name: Wie heißt du?"]
  B -- "no" --> D{"Has the person offered du?"}
  D -- "yes" --> C
  D -- "no, or not sure" --> E["Sie + Herr or Frau and surname: Wie heißen Sie?"]
```

You learned the greetings for each time of day in Lesson 1. Here they are on a clock; the
borders are rough, and *Hallo* works at any time of day with people you'd say *du* to, and in
many casual places with *Sie* too.

![A timeline from 6:00 to 24:00. Guten Morgen covers the early morning until about 10 or 11 o'clock, Guten Tag covers the middle of the day until about 18:00, and Guten Abend covers the evening. Gute Nacht, shown with a bed, is only for when someone is going to bed.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The verb sein (to be)

A **[[verb]]** is a word for an action or state, like *to be*, *to live* or *to come*. The form
you find in a dictionary is the **[[infinitive]]**: *sein* (to be), *wohnen* (to live). In a
sentence, the verb changes its ending to match its **[[subject]]**, the person or thing doing it.
*sein* is irregular, as "to be" is in English, so learn these forms by heart:

| | sein |
|---|---|
| ich (I) | *bin* |
| du (you, informal) | *bist* |
| Sie (you, formal) | *sind* |
| er (he) / sie (she) | *ist* |

*Ich bin Paul.* — I'm Paul.
*Bist du Lena?* — Are you Lena?
*Sind Sie Herr Fischer?* — Are you Mr Fischer?
*Frau Ahmadi ist sehr nett.* — Ms Ahmadi is very nice.

You'll see the full table (we, you all, they) in Lesson 4.

## heißen, kommen, wohnen

Most German verbs are regular. You take the infinitive, remove *-en* to get the stem, and add
an ending. For now you need three forms:

| | heißen (to be called) | kommen (to come) | wohnen (to live) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | *heiße* | *komme* | *wohne* |
| du | *heißt* | *kommst* | *wohnst* |
| Sie | *heißen* | *kommen* | *wohnen* |

The *du* form ends in *-st*. *heißen* is the exception you can already see: its stem ends in
*ß*, so *du* adds only *-t* (*du heißt*, not *du heißst*). The *Sie* form is always the same as
the infinitive, which makes formal German easy.

*heißen* is how Germans give their name. Literally *Ich heiße Anna* is "I am called Anna". You
can also say *Ich bin Anna* or *Mein Name ist Anna* (my name is Anna).

*kommen* goes with *aus* (from) for where you come from:
*Ich komme aus Deutschland.* — I'm from Germany.
*Kommst du aus Österreich?* — Are you from Austria?
*Herr Meier kommt aus der Schweiz.* — Mr Meier is from Switzerland.

*wohnen* goes with *in* for where you live now:
*Ich wohne in Hamburg.* — I live in Hamburg.
*Wohnen Sie in der Stadt?* — Do you live in the city?

Most country names, like *Deutschland* and *Österreich*, have no article. A few do, and *die
Schweiz* is the one you need now: say *aus der Schweiz* and *in der Schweiz* as fixed chunks.
The *der* is explained when you learn the dative in Lesson 18.

One more verb is useful straight away, *sprechen* (to speak), though you'll study it properly
in Lesson 7. Notice the *du* form changes its vowel: *Ich spreche Englisch. Sprichst du
Deutsch? Sprechen Sie Englisch?*

## Asking questions with wer, wie, woher, wo

A **[[W-question]]** starts with a question word, and in German almost all of them begin with *w*.
The verb comes straight after the question word, and the subject follows the verb:

| Question word | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *wer* | who | *Wer ist das?* — Who is that? |
| *wie* | how; what (with names) | *Wie heißt du?* — What's your name? |
| *woher* | where from | *Woher kommen Sie?* — Where are you from? |
| *wo* | where | *Wo wohnst du?* — Where do you live? |

Careful: *wer* means "who" and *wo* means "where". English speakers constantly swap them
because *wer* looks like "where". And *wie* is "how", even where English uses "what": *Wie
heißen Sie?* is "What's your name?", literally "How are you called?"

*woher* asks about origin and needs *aus* in the answer; *wo* asks about location and needs
*in*:
*Woher kommst du? — Aus Kanada.* — Where are you from? — From Canada.
*Wo wohnst du? — In Berlin.* — Where do you live? — In Berlin.

## How are you?

| Informal | Formal |
|---|---|
| *Wie geht's?* | *Wie geht es Ihnen?* |
| *Gut, danke. Und dir?* | *Gut, danke. Und Ihnen?* |

*Wie geht's?* is short for *Wie geht es?* (literally "How goes it?"). *Ihnen* and *dir* mean
"to you"; for now, learn the questions and answers as whole chunks. Possible answers, from
best to worst:

*Sehr gut, danke!* — Very well, thanks!
*Gut.* — Fine / good.
*Auch gut.* — Fine too (after the other person has said they're fine and asked *Und dir?*).
*Es geht.* — So-so.
*Nicht so gut.* — Not so good.

*Wie geht's?* is a real question between friends, not just "hi": Germans may tell you how
they actually are. In a shop or with strangers, people say *Guten Tag* and skip it.

When you meet someone, say *Freut mich* (nice to meet you), literally "pleases me". The other
person often answers *Mich auch* (me too).

## Introducing someone else

Use *Das ist …* (this is …) to introduce a third person: *Das ist Jonas. Er kommt aus Bremen.*
(This is Jonas. He's from Bremen.) *er* means he, *sie* means she; both take *ist*, *kommt*,
*wohnt*, *heißt*. Lesson 4 covers these forms in full.

## Dialogue 1: at a language course (du)

> Mia: Hallo! Ich bin Mia. Wie heißt du?
>
> Ben: Hallo, Mia. Ich heiße Ben. Freut mich!
>
> Mia: Freut mich auch. Woher kommst du, Ben?
>
> Ben: Ich komme aus Irland. Und du?
>
> Mia: Ich komme aus Österreich, aus Graz. Aber ich wohne jetzt in Leipzig.
>
> Ben: Leipzig ist eine schöne Stadt!

Hi! I'm Mia. What's your name? — Hi, Mia. I'm Ben. Nice to meet you! — Nice to meet you too.
Where are you from, Ben? — I'm from Ireland. And you? — I'm from Austria, from Graz. But I live
in Leipzig now. — Leipzig is a beautiful city!

## Dialogue 2: at a hotel (Sie)

> Herr Wolf: Guten Abend! Wie geht es Ihnen, Frau Novak?
>
> Frau Novak: Danke, sehr gut. Und Ihnen, Herr Wolf?
>
> Herr Wolf: Auch gut, danke. Wer ist das?
>
> Frau Novak: Das ist Herr Costa. Er kommt aus Portugal.
>
> Herr Wolf: Guten Abend, Herr Costa. Freut mich. Wo wohnen Sie?
>
> Herr Costa: In Lissabon. Lissabon ist eine Stadt in Portugal.

Good evening! How are you, Ms Novak? — Very well, thank you. And you, Mr Wolf? — Fine too,
thanks. Who is that? — This is Mr Costa. He's from Portugal. — Good evening, Mr Costa. Pleased
to meet you. Where do you live? — In Lisbon. Lisbon is a city in Portugal.

(*aber* means "but", *jetzt* means "now", *schön* means "beautiful" and *eine* means "a"; you'll
learn these properly later.)

## Countries and places

*das Land* (country) and *die Stadt* (city, town) are your first two nouns with articles. Every
German noun has one of three articles, *der*, *die* or *das*, and you'll learn why in Lesson 5.
For now, learn each noun together with its article as one unit.

*Deutschland ist ein Land.* — Germany is a country.
*Wien ist eine Stadt in Österreich.* — Vienna is a city in Austria.
*Die Schweiz ist klein.* — Switzerland is small.

## Pronunciation

- *heißen*: *ei* as in "eye", *ß* as a sharp *s*: "HY-sen".
- *wohnen*: *w* = v, long *o*, silent *h*: "VOH-nen".
- *woher*: stress on the second syllable, "vo-HAIR".
- *Österreich*: stress on *Ö*; *eich* ends with the soft *ch* of *ich*.
- *die Schweiz*: "shvites", one syllable, *z* = ts.
- *Wie geht's?*: "vee gates".

## Common mistakes

- Mixing *du* and *Sie* in one conversation (*Wie heißen du?*). Pick one and keep its forms:
  *Wie heißt du?* or *Wie heißen Sie?*
- *Wer* for "where". *Wer* is who, *wo* is where.
- *Wie ist dein Name?* is fine, but *Was ist dein Name?* sounds like a translation from English.
- *Ich komme von Deutschland.* Origin takes *aus*: *Ich komme aus Deutschland.*
- *Ich bin gut* for "I'm fine". Say *Mir geht's gut* or just *Gut, danke*. *Ich bin gut* means
  "I'm good at something" or "I'm a good person".
- Writing the formal *Sie* in lowercase. It's always *Sie*.
- *Du heißst*. The stem ends in *ß*, so it's *du heißt*.

## Key points

- *du* for friends, family and children; *Sie* (capital S) for adults you don't know and
  anyone you call *Herr* or *Frau*.
- *sein*: *ich bin, du bist, Sie sind, er/sie ist*.
- Regular verbs: *ich -e, du -st, Sie -en*; *du heißt* is the exception.
- *kommen aus* for origin, *wohnen in* for where you live now.
- *wer* = who, *wie* = how, *woher* = where from, *wo* = where; the verb follows the question word.
- *Wie geht's?* (informal), *Wie geht es Ihnen?* (formal); *Freut mich* when you meet someone.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers, age and phone numbers
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can now say who you are and where you're from. The next things people ask are how old you
are, your phone number and your address, and the answers are all numbers. This lesson teaches
the numbers from 0 to 100, the one big surprise in how German says them, and how to give your
age, phone number, postcode and e-mail address. You'll also meet a second key verb, *haben*
(to have).

## 0 to 12

These have to be learned one by one, as in English.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 *null* | 1 *eins* | 2 *zwei* | 3 *drei* |
| 4 *vier* | 5 *fünf* | 6 *sechs* | 7 *sieben* |
| 8 *acht* | 9 *neun* | 10 *zehn* | 11 *elf* |
| 12 *zwölf* | | | |

Watch the sounds from Lesson 1: *zwei* and *zehn* start with "ts", *vier* starts with "f",
*neun* rhymes with "coin", and *sechs* sounds like "zex". *elf* looks
like the English creature, but it's eleven.

On the phone and in announcements, people often say *zwo* instead of *zwei*, so it can't be
confused with *drei*. You'll hear *zwo* at train stations and in phone numbers; both are correct.

## 13 to 19

Like English "-teen", German adds *-zehn* (ten) to the unit:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 13 *dreizehn* | 14 *vierzehn* | 15 *fünfzehn* |
| 16 *sechzehn* | 17 *siebzehn* | 18 *achtzehn* |
| 19 *neunzehn* | | |

Two spelling traps: *sechzehn* drops the *s* of *sechs*, and *siebzehn* drops the *-en* of
*sieben*.

## The tens

The tens end in *-zig*, which is pronounced like "-tsich" with the soft *ch* of *ich*. (In
southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland you'll hear "-tsik".)

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 20 *zwanzig* | 30 *dreißig* | 40 *vierzig* |
| 50 *fünfzig* | 60 *sechzig* | 70 *siebzig* |
| 80 *achtzig* | 90 *neunzig* | 100 *hundert* |

*dreißig* is the odd one: it ends in *-ßig*, not *-zig*. *sechzig* and *siebzig* lose letters,
just like 16 and 17. *hundert* can also be *einhundert*.

## 21 to 99: the units come first

This is the big difference from English. German says the unit first, then *und* (and), then
the ten, all as one word:

| Number | German | Literally |
|---|---|---|
| 21 | *einundzwanzig* | one-and-twenty |
| 34 | *vierunddreißig* | four-and-thirty |
| 47 | *siebenundvierzig* | seven-and-forty |
| 58 | *achtundfünfzig* | eight-and-fifty |
| 66 | *sechsundsechzig* | six-and-sixty |
| 99 | *neunundneunzig* | nine-and-ninety |

Memory hook: think of the old English nursery rhyme "four-and-twenty blackbirds". German
always counts this way. When you hear a number, hold the first part in your head until the
ten arrives: *dreiundsiebzig* — you hear 3, then 70, and you write 73.

![The number 73 with two crossing arrows: the 3 is read first as drei, then comes und, then the 7 is read as siebzig, giving dreiundsiebzig as one word.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Practise by reading numbers off
car number plates or prices until you stop reversing them.

*eins* becomes *ein* inside a longer number: *einundzwanzig*, *einunddreißig*. On its own, or
at the end, it's *eins*: *hunderteins* (101). And *sechs* keeps its *s* in *sechsundzwanzig*,
*sechsundsechzig*; only 16 and 60 drop it.

## How old are you?

*alt* means "old". To ask someone's age:

*Wie alt bist du?* — How old are you? (informal)
*Wie alt sind Sie?* — How old are you? (formal)
*Ich bin 29 Jahre alt.* — I'm 29 years old.
*Ich bin 29.* — I'm 29.

*das Jahr* is "the year", and its plural is *die Jahre*: *ein Jahr*, *zwei Jahre*. German
uses *sein* (to be) for age, just like English, so *Ich habe 29 Jahre* is wrong. The opposite
of *alt* is *jung* (young): *Das Kind ist sehr jung.* (The child is very young.)

## The verb haben (to have)

*haben* is the second most important German verb. Like *sein*, it's slightly irregular:

| | haben |
|---|---|
| ich | *habe* |
| du | *hast* |
| Sie | *haben* |
| er / sie | *hat* |

The *du* and *er/sie* forms drop the *b*: *du hast*, *er hat*. You'll see *haben* in full
in Lesson 6.

*Hast du eine Telefonnummer?* — Do you have a phone number?
*Ich habe eine Handynummer.* — I have a mobile number.
*Haben Sie eine E-Mail-Adresse?* — Do you have an e-mail address?

(*eine* means "a" here; more on that in Lesson 5.)

## Phone numbers

*die Telefonnummer* is a phone number in general; *die Handynummer* is a mobile number (*das
Handy* is the German word for a mobile phone). *die Nummer* is a number used as a label, like
a phone, room or house number; *die Zahl* is a number as a quantity or figure: *Sieben ist eine
Zahl.*

Germans usually say phone numbers digit by digit, or in pairs: 0176 48 25 93 can be *null eins
sieben sechs, achtundvierzig, fünfundzwanzig, dreiundneunzig*. Asking someone to repeat is
normal: *Noch einmal, bitte. Langsam, bitte.*

*Wie ist deine Telefonnummer?* — What's your phone number? (informal)
*Wie ist Ihre Handynummer?* — What's your mobile number? (formal)
*Meine Nummer ist 0151 23 40 17.* — My number is 0151 23 40 17.

*deine*, *Ihre* and *meine* mean "your" and "my"; Lesson 6 explains them.

## Addresses and e-mail

A German address puts the street first and the house number after it, then the postcode
before the town:

> Lisa Krämer
>
> Lindenstraße 14
>
> 04107 Leipzig

*die Adresse* is the address, *die Hausnummer* the house number, *die Postleitzahl* the postcode
(often shortened to *PLZ*). German postcodes have five digits; Austrian and Swiss ones have four.

On an envelope, the parts of the address sit like this (*die Straße* is the street; you'll
learn the word properly in Lesson 17):

![An envelope with a stamp and a small sender line at the top. The address reads Lisa Krämer, Lindenstraße 14, 04107 Leipzig. Labels point to Lisa (Vorname), Krämer (Familienname), Lindenstraße (Straße), 14 (Hausnummer), 04107 (Postleitzahl) and Leipzig (Stadt).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Wie ist Ihre Adresse? — Lindenstraße 14, 04107 Leipzig.*
*Die Hausnummer ist vierzehn.* — The house number is fourteen.
*Die Postleitzahl ist null-vier-eins-null-sieben.* — The postcode is 04107.

For an e-mail address, @ is said like English "at", the dot is *Punkt*, and the hyphen is
*Bindestrich*. *die E-Mail* is both "the e-mail" (the message) and,
in everyday speech, short for *die E-Mail-Adresse*.

*Meine E-Mail ist lisa.kraemer@post.de.* — "lisa Punkt kraemer at post Punkt de"

Notice the address uses *ae* for *ä*, because many e-mail addresses can't contain umlauts.

## Dialogue: signing up at a gym

> Mitarbeiter: Guten Tag! Wie ist Ihr Name, bitte?
>
> Frau Okafor: Okafor, Grace Okafor.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Und wie alt sind Sie, Frau Okafor?
>
> Frau Okafor: Ich bin 34 Jahre alt.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Wie ist Ihre Adresse?
>
> Frau Okafor: Bergstraße 72, 50667 Köln.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Zweiundsiebzig oder siebenundzwanzig?
>
> Frau Okafor: Zweiundsiebzig. Sieben, zwei.
>
> Mitarbeiter: Danke. Haben Sie eine Handynummer?
>
> Frau Okafor: Ja, die Nummer ist 0172 58 39 61.

Hello! What's your name, please? — Okafor, Grace Okafor. — And how old are you, Ms Okafor? —
I'm 34 years old. — What's your address? — Bergstraße 72, 50667 Cologne. — Seventy-two or
twenty-seven? — Seventy-two. Seven, two. — Thank you. Do you have a mobile number? — Yes, the
number is 0172 58 39 61.

(*der Mitarbeiter* is the employee; *oder* means "or".) The question "72 or 27?" is exactly the
confusion German numbers cause, even among Germans: saying the digits separately settles it.

## Pronunciation

- *zwanzig*, *dreißig*, *vierzig*: stress on the first syllable; *-ig* like *ich*.
- *dreißig*: *ei* as in "eye", then a sharp *s*: "DRY-sich".
- *sieben*: "ZEE-ben" (*s* before a vowel is z; *ie* is ee).
- *fünf*: round your lips for *ü*; don't say "funf".
- *zwölf*: *ö* with rounded lips, *z* = ts: "tsvölf".
- *Postleitzahl*: *st* in the middle of a word is a plain "st"; stress on *POST*.
- *achtzig*: the *ch* is the throaty one, as in *Nacht*.

## Common mistakes

- Reversing two-digit numbers: writing 52 for *fünfundzwanzig* (25). Units first, then tens.
- Writing *dreizig* or *dreissig*. It's *dreißig* (or *dreissig* only in Switzerland).
- Writing *sechszehn*, *siebenzehn*, *sechszig*, *siebenzig*. Correct: *sechzehn*, *siebzehn*,
  *sechzig*, *siebzig*.
- *eins und zwanzig* as separate words. Numbers under a million are one word: *einundzwanzig*.
- *Ich habe 30 Jahre.* German uses *sein* for age: *Ich bin 30 Jahre alt.*
- *du habst*, *er habt*. The forms are *du hast*, *er hat*.

## Key points

- Learn 0–12 by heart; 13–19 add *-zehn*; tens end in *-zig*, except *dreißig*.
- *sechzehn, sechzig, siebzehn, siebzig* drop letters.
- 21–99: unit + *und* + ten, written as one word: *vierundfünfzig* = 54.
- *zwo* is an alternative to *zwei*, common on the phone.
- Age: *Wie alt bist du? Ich bin … Jahre alt.*
- *haben*: *ich habe, du hast, Sie haben, er/sie hat*.
- Addresses: street + number, then postcode + town.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The present tense and asking questions
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far you've used verbs with *ich*, *du* and *Sie*, plus *er/sie ist*. This lesson completes
the picture: all the people a verb can go with, the endings for every one of them, the full
forms of *sein*, and the two rules of German word order that you'll use in every sentence
from now on: the verb comes second in a statement, and first in a yes/no question. Once you
have these, you can talk about what people do, and ask about it.

## Personal pronouns

A **[[personal pronoun]]** is a short word that stands for a person or thing: I, you, she, we…

| | Singular | | Plural | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st person | *ich* | I | *wir* | we |
| 2nd person | *du* | you (informal, one person) | *ihr* | you (informal, two or more) |
| 3rd person | *er* / *sie* / *es* | he / she / it | *sie* | they |
| formal | *Sie* | you (formal, one or more) | *Sie* | you (formal) |

Three things to notice:

- German has a separate plural "you": *ihr* is what you say to two or more friends, like
  "you guys" or "y'all". Formal *Sie* is the same for one person or many.
- *sie* has three jobs. Lowercase *sie* means "she" or "they"; capital *Sie* means formal
  "you". The verb ending tells "she" apart from "they": *sie wohnt* (she lives), *sie wohnen*
  (they live).
- *er*, *sie* and *es* also mean "it", depending on the noun's gender (Lesson 5). For people,
  *er* is he and *sie* is she.

## Regular verb endings

To use a verb in a sentence you **[[conjugate]]** it: you take its **[[stem]]** (the infinitive minus
*-en*) and add the **[[ending]]** that matches the subject. *machen* (to do, to make) has the stem
*mach-*:

| | Ending | machen | wohnen | spielen (to play) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | -e | *mache* | *wohne* | *spiele* |
| du | -st | *machst* | *wohnst* | *spielst* |
| er / sie / es | -t | *macht* | *wohnt* | *spielt* |
| wir | -en | *machen* | *wohnen* | *spielen* |
| ihr | -t | *macht* | *wohnt* | *spielt* |
| sie / Sie | -en | *machen* | *wohnen* | *spielen* |

Memory hook: say the endings as a chant, *e, st, t, en, t, en*. Two pairs look the same: the
*wir* and *sie/Sie* forms are both the infinitive, and the *er* and *ihr* forms both end in
*-t*. The pronoun tells you which one you mean.

The **[[present tense]]** covers all of English "I play", "I'm playing" and "I do play". There's no
"-ing" form in German: *Ich lerne Deutsch* is both "I learn German" and "I'm learning German".
With a time word it can also mean the future: *Heute spielen wir Tennis.* (We're playing tennis
today.)

## Stems ending in -t or -d

If the stem ends in *-t* or *-d*, German adds an *e* before *-st* and *-t*, because *arbeitt*
or *antwortst* can't be pronounced clearly:

| | arbeiten (to work) | antworten (to answer) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | *arbeite* | *antworte* |
| du | *arbeitest* | *antwortest* |
| er / sie / es | *arbeitet* | *antwortet* |
| wir | *arbeiten* | *antworten* |
| ihr | *arbeitet* | *antwortet* |
| sie / Sie | *arbeiten* | *antworten* |

*Er arbeitet hier.* — He works here.
*Antwortest du?* — Are you answering?

## Stems ending in -s, -ß or -z

If the stem ends in an *s* sound (*-s*, *-ß*, *-z*), the *du* form adds only *-t*, so it looks
like the *er* form: *du heißt*, *er heißt*. The same happens with *tanzen* (to dance): *du
tanzt*.

Put together, the three stem rules make one short check:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing the du and er endings
  accDescr: Start with the stem, the infinitive minus -en. If the stem ends in -t or -d, add an extra e before -st and -t, as in du arbeitest and er arbeitet. Otherwise, if the stem ends in -s, -ß or -z, the du form adds only -t, as in du heißt and du tanzt. Otherwise use the regular endings, du -st and er -t, as in du machst and er macht.
  A["Take the stem: infinitive minus -en"] --> B{"Does the stem end in -t or -d?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Add e: du arbeitest, er arbeitet"]
  B -- "no" --> D{"Does it end in -s, -ß or -z?"}
  D -- "yes" --> E["du adds only -t: du heißt, du tanzt"]
  D -- "no" --> F["Regular: du machst, er macht"]
```

## sein in full

| | sein (to be) |
|---|---|
| ich | *bin* |
| du | *bist* |
| er / sie / es | *ist* |
| wir | *sind* |
| ihr | *seid* |
| sie / Sie | *sind* |

Don't confuse *ihr seid* (you are) with *seit* (since), which sounds the same. *ist* is easy to
remember: it's English "is" with a *t*.

*Wir sind hier.* — We're here.
*Seid ihr aus Berlin?* — Are you (all) from Berlin?
*Sie sind jetzt in Wien.* — They're in Vienna now. / You're in Vienna now.

## A few verbs to know

*gehen* (to go, on foot), *kommen* (to come), *hören* (to hear, to listen to), *fragen* (to
ask), *sagen* (to say), *lernen* (to learn), *studieren* (to study at university), *leben*
(to live, to be alive) and *verstehen* (to understand) are all regular in the present tense.

*lernen* vs *studieren*: *lernen* is learning anything, including revising for a test;
*studieren* is studying a subject at a university. *Ich studiere Biologie* (I'm a biology
student), but *Ich lerne Deutsch* (I'm learning German).

*wohnen* vs *leben*: *wohnen* is where your home is (*Ich wohne in der Goethestraße*), *leben*
is living in a wider sense (*Wir leben in Deutschland. Er lebt allein.* — He lives alone).

## Rule 1: the verb comes second

In a German **[[statement]]**, the conjugated verb is always the second element. The first element
can be the subject, but it can also be a time word, a place or an object. When something else
comes first, the subject moves to just after the verb:

| 1 | 2 (verb) | rest |
|---|---|---|
| *Ich* | *arbeite* | *heute in Köln.* |
| *Heute* | *arbeite* | *ich in Köln.* |
| *In Köln* | *arbeite* | *ich heute.* |

All three mean "I'm working in Cologne today". This is the **[[verb-second rule]]**, and it's the
biggest difference from English word order. English says "Today I work"; German must say
*Heute arbeite ich*. Starting with a time word is very common and sounds natural:

*Jetzt lernen wir.* — Now we're studying.
*Oft hört sie Musik.* — She often listens to music.
*Hier wohnt Familie Klein.* — The Klein family lives here.

Adverbs such as *oft* (often), *immer* (always) and *gern* usually come right after the verb:
*Ich spiele oft Tennis. Er arbeitet immer.* *gern* is how German says "like doing": *Ich lerne
gern Deutsch.* (I like learning German.) *Wir spielen gern.* (We like playing.)

## Rule 2: questions

For a **[[yes/no question]]**, put the verb first and the subject second:

*Du wohnst hier.* → *Wohnst du hier?* — Do you live here?
*Er arbeitet heute.* → *Arbeitet er heute?* — Is he working today?
*Ihr versteht das.* → *Versteht ihr das?* — Do you (all) understand that?

There's no "do" in German questions. Just swap the verb to the front.

For a W-question, the question word comes first and the verb second, exactly as in Lesson 2.
Three new question words:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| *was* | what | *Was machst du heute?* — What are you doing today? |
| *warum* | why | *Warum lernst du Deutsch?* — Why are you learning German? |
| *wann* | when | *Wann arbeitet Lara?* — When does Lara work? |

The picture puts the two rules side by side. In statements and W-questions the verb is in
position 2; only in a yes/no question does it move to position 1.

![Four sentences split into position 1, position 2 and the rest, with the conjugated verb highlighted. Statement: Ich, arbeite, heute in Köln. Time word first: Heute, arbeite, ich in Köln. W-question: Wo, arbeitest, du heute? Yes/no question: Arbeitest, du, heute in Köln? Only in the yes/no question is the verb in position 1.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*wann* only asks questions about time. It looks like English "when" but isn't used for
"when I was young"; that's a different word you'll meet later.

*hier* (here), *dort* (there), *jetzt* (now) and *heute* (today) are useful in answers:
*Wo ist Max? — Dort.* *Wann lernst du? — Jetzt.*

## Dialogue: a new flatmate

> Lukas: Hallo! Bist du Sara? Ich bin Lukas. Ich wohne hier.
>
> Sara: Hallo, Lukas! Ja, ich bin Sara. Was machst du? Studierst du?
>
> Lukas: Nein, ich arbeite. Ich bin Koch. Und du?
>
> Sara: Ich studiere Musik. Ich spiele Klavier.
>
> Lukas: Toll! Spielst du oft?
>
> Sara: Ja, immer. Heute spiele ich auch. Warum fragst du?
>
> Lukas: Ich höre gern Musik. Und Jonas und Mira, sie spielen Gitarre.
>
> Sara: Wann sind Jonas und Mira hier?
>
> Lukas: Jetzt sind sie dort, im Park. Gehen wir?

Hi! Are you Sara? I'm Lukas. I live here. — Hi, Lukas! Yes, I'm Sara. What do you do? Are you a
student? — No, I work. I'm a cook. And you? — I study music. I play the piano. — Great! Do you
play often? — Yes, all the time. I'm playing today too. Why do you ask? — I like listening to
music. And Jonas and Mira, they play the guitar. — When are Jonas and Mira here? — Right now
they're over there, in the park. Shall we go?

(*der Koch* is a cook, *das Klavier* a piano, *die Gitarre* a guitar, *toll* means "great", and
*im Park* "in the park". Notice: no article before a job: *Ich bin Koch*.)

## Pronunciation

- *arbeiten*: "AR-by-ten"; *ei* as in "eye".
- *verstehen*: stress on *STE*; *st* = "sht" because it starts the root.
- *studieren*: "shtoo-DEE-ren"; *-ieren* verbs are stressed on *ie*.
- *warum*: stress on *RUM*: "va-ROOM".
- *ihr seid*: "eer zite"; same sound as *seit*.
- *jetzt*: *j* = y, *tzt* is one quick "tst": "yetst".

## Common mistakes

- English word order after a time word: *Heute ich arbeite.* Correct: *Heute arbeite ich.*
- Adding a helper verb the way English adds "do": *Tust du hier wohnen?* Just put the verb
  first: *Wohnst du hier?*
- Using *-st* with *ihr*: *ihr wohnst*. The *ihr* ending is *-t*: *ihr wohnt*.
- Forgetting the extra *e*: *er arbeitt*, *du antwortst*. Correct: *er arbeitet*, *du
  antwortest*.
- *ihr sind*, *wir seid*. Correct: *wir sind*, *ihr seid*.
- Translating "I am learning" word for word: *Ich bin lernen.* German uses one verb: *Ich lerne.*
- Using *studieren* for school homework. Say *Ich lerne* for revising.

## Key points

- Pronouns: *ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie*.
- Endings: *-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en*; stems in *-t/-d* add *e* (*arbeitest*); stems in
  *-s/-ß/-z* take only *-t* with *du* (*heißt*).
- *sein*: *bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind*.
- One German present form covers "I play", "I'm playing" and "I do play".
- Statements: the verb is second; if something else comes first, the subject follows the verb.
- Yes/no questions: the verb comes first. W-questions: question word, then verb.
- *gern* after the verb means "like doing".

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Sounds in depth: vowel length, the glottal stop and sentence melody
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 1 gave you the sounds of the German letters. This honors lesson goes one step further,
to the things that make the difference between "readable" and "sounds
German": how to tell long and short vowels apart from the spelling alone, what happens to *-e*
and *-er* at the end of a word, the small catch in the throat that Germans put before words
starting with a vowel, how a sentence rises and falls, and how the sounds differ between
regions. At the end you'll see why *daß* became *dass* in 1996.

The new words for talking about pronunciation are *die Aussprache* (pronunciation), *aussprechen* (to pronounce), *der Laut*
(a sound of speech), *die Silbe* (syllable) and *der Akzent* (accent).

## Long or short? Reading vowel length from the spelling

Lesson 1 said a vowel is long before *h*, when doubled, and in *ie*, and short before a double
consonant. Two more patterns cover most of the rest.

First, a vowel at the end of a syllable is usually long. Such a syllable is called an
**[[open syllable]]**: *Na-me*, *ha-ben*, *le-ben*, *Ta-ge*. A syllable that ends in a consonant is closed,
and the vowel there is often short: *Stadt*, *Wort*, *jetzt*.

Second, a one-syllable word often "borrows" its length from a longer form of the same word.
*Tag* is closed, but its plural *Tage* has an open syllable *Ta-*, so the *a* is long in both.
The same goes for *Weg* (way, plural *Wege*) and *gut* (good, *gute*). This is why you can't
always tell from one form: you need to know the family.

Short everyday words are the exception you just have to learn. These have short vowels even
though only one consonant follows: *das*, *was*, *es*, *in*, *mit*, *an*, *um*, *bis*, *man*,
*hat*. A few others look short but are long: *der*, *wir*, *mir*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Long or short vowel?
  accDescr: To guess whether a stressed vowel is long or short, first check for a doubled vowel, a following h, or ie; these are long, as in Tee, Jahr and sie. If not, check for a double consonant, ck or tz after it; these make it short, as in Hallo, bitte and jetzt. If not, check whether the vowel ends its syllable, as in Na-me; then it is usually long. If none of these applies, the spelling does not decide, so learn the word, as with long Tag and short das.
  A["A stressed vowel"] --> B{"Doubled, followed by h, or ie?"}
  B -- "yes" --> L1["Long: Tee, Jahr, sie"]
  B -- "no" --> C{"Followed by a double consonant, ck or tz?"}
  C -- "yes" --> S1["Short: Hallo, bitte, jetzt"]
  C -- "no" --> D{"Does the vowel end the syllable?"}
  D -- "yes, as in Na-me" --> L2["Usually long: Name, haben, leben"]
  D -- "no" --> E["Spelling does not decide: learn it. Tag is long, das is short"]
```

### Example 1: Name, Stadt, Bett, Boot, Jahr, das

Work through the chart for each word.

1. *Name*: no doubling, no *h*, no double consonant. Split it: *Na-me*. The *a* ends the
   syllable, so it's long: "NAH-meh".
2. *Stadt*: *dt* is two different consonants, not a double one, and the *a* doesn't end a
   syllable. The chart says "learn it": it's short, as Lesson 1's table showed.
3. *Bett* (bed): double *t*, so short.
4. *Boot* (boat): doubled vowel, so long.
5. *Jahr*: vowel plus *h*, so long; the *h* is silent.
6. *das*: one of the short everyday words; the *a* is short and clipped.

## The schwa and the vocalic r

An unstressed *e*, as in *bitte*, *Name* or the ending *-en*, is a weak, relaxed sound called
**[[schwa]]**. Your mouth is half open and nothing is tense: it sounds like the *a* in English
*about*. Lesson 1 said a final *e* is never silent; the schwa is what you say.

The letters *-er* at the end of a word sound different again. The *r* doesn't appear as an
*r* at all; *-er* becomes a short, open sound close to the *u* in English *but*. This is
called the **[[vocalic r]]**. Compare:

| schwa (-e) | vocalic r (-er) |
|---|---|
| *bitte* (please) | *bitter* (bitter) |
| *Lehre* (training, apprenticeship) | *Lehrer* (teacher) |
| *eine* (a) | *einer* (one of them) |

Words like *bitte* and *bitter* that differ in a single sound are a **[[minimal pair]]**, and they
are the best way to train your ear. The same melting happens after a long vowel: *der*, *wir*,
*hier* (here) and *Bier* (beer) end in a short "uh" glide, and *aber* (but) and *oder* (or)
end like *Lehrer*. A hard English *r* here is the clearest sign of an English accent.

## The glottal stop: the catch before a vowel

Say English "uh-oh". The tiny break in the middle, where your throat closes for a moment, is a
**[[glottal stop]]**. In English it's rare; in German it's everywhere. In careful standard German
of Germany, a word or word part that begins with a vowel usually starts with this small catch
instead of being joined to the word before it.

English links words: "an egg" can sound like "a-negg". German keeps them apart: *ein Ei* (an
egg) is said "ein | Ei", with a fresh start on *Ei*. That's part of why German sounds "choppy"
to English ears.

The glottal stop also works inside words, at the border between two parts:

- *das Spiegelei* (fried egg) is *Spiegel* (mirror) + *Ei*, said "SHPEE-gel | ei". Without the
  catch it would sound like *Spie-ge-lei*, which isn't a word.
- *verreisen* (to go away on a trip) is *ver-* + *reisen* (to travel): "fer-RY-zen", with an
  *r* sound. *vereisen* (to ice over) is *ver-* + *eisen*: "fer | EYE-zen", with a catch and no
  *r*. Only the glottal stop tells them apart.
- *beantworten* (to answer something) is *be-* + *antworten*: "be | ANT-vor-ten".

In the south, in Austria and in Switzerland the catch is often softer or left out, so take it
as a feature of northern and careful speech rather than a strict rule.

## More letter groups

Lesson 1 covered the groups you meet every day. These come up as your vocabulary grows:

| Spelling | Sound | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *pf* | both letters: *p* then *f* | *der Apfel* (apple), *der Kopf* (head) |
| *chs* | usually *ks* | *sechs*, *der Fuchs* (fox) |
| *ng* | *ng* as in *singer*, never *ng-g* | *singen* (to sing), *Entschuldigung*, *der Finger* |
| *-tion* | *tsion*, stressed | *die Information* (in-for-ma-TSION) |
| *v* in borrowed words | English *v* | *das Klavier*, *die Universität*, *November* |
| *y* in Greek words | like *ü* | *der Typ* (type, guy) |
| *y* in English words | as in English | *das Handy* ("HEN-dee") |

A **[[loanword]]** is a word taken from another language, and loanwords often keep some of their
old pronunciation and stress. That's why *v* is an *f* in old German words (*Vater*, *vier*,
*Vogel*) but a *v* in *Klavier* and *Universität*, and why *Information* and *Universität* are
stressed at the end. *Finger* is a nice trap: in English the *g* is heard, in German it isn't.

## Sentence melody

**[[Intonation]]** is the rise and fall of your voice across a sentence. German uses it much as
English does, which makes it one of the easier parts:

- A statement falls at the end: *Du wohnst in Berlin.*
- A yes/no question usually rises at the end: *Wohnst du in Berlin?*
- A W-question usually falls, because the question word already marks it as a question:
  *Wo wohnst du?* A rising W-question sounds extra friendly or surprised.

![Three sentences with arrows showing their melody. Du wohnst in Berlin: the arrow falls at the end. Wohnst du in Berlin?: the arrow rises at the end. Wo wohnst du?: the arrow usually falls at the end.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: Reading a long word aloud

Take *das Mittagessen* (lunch), a word you'll meet in Lesson 9, and apply everything so far.

1. Find the parts: *Mittag* (midday) + *Essen* (food, meal). In a compound, the first part
   carries the main stress: "MIT-tag-essen".
2. *Mit-*: double *t*, so the *i* is short.
3. *-tag*: the *g* ends the syllable, so final devoicing makes it a *k*: "-tahk".
4. *essen* starts with a vowel and is a new part, so put a glottal stop before it: "MIT-tahk |
   es-sen". Double *s*: short *e*.
5. *-en* at the end is a schwa plus *n*, very light.

Result: "MIT-tahk | ess-en", with the stress at the start and a clean catch in the middle.

### Example 3: A tongue twister

Germans practise sounds with tongue twisters (*Zungenbrecher*, literally "tongue
breakers"). This one is traditional:

> Fischers Fritz fischt frische Fische, frische Fische fischt Fischers Fritz.

(Fisher's Fritz fishes fresh fish.) Go through it slowly. Every *sch* is English *sh*. Every *i*
before *sch* or *tz* is short. *Fritz* ends in *tz*, one quick "ts". *fischt* has *sch* and
then *t* at once: "fisht". The *-e* in *frische* and *Fische* is a schwa, not silent. Say it
slowly three times, then faster.

## One language, many accents

German has several standard forms (you'll learn more about this in the next honors lesson),
and the pronunciation of educated speakers differs by region. None of these is "wrong":

- The ending *-ig*: *zwanzig* ends with the *ich* sound in most of Germany, but with a *k*
  ("-tsik") in the south, in Austria and in Switzerland, where that counts as standard.
- *ch* at the start of a word, as in *China*: in standard German of Germany it's the soft *ich*
  sound, in the south and in Austria and Switzerland it's a *k* ("Kina"), and in everyday
  speech in much of central and northern Germany you'll often hear "Schina".
- The *r*: the throat *r* is usual in most of Germany, but many speakers in the south, in
  Austria and in Switzerland roll it with the tip of the tongue.

For your own speaking, pick one model and stay with it; this course follows the standard of
Germany.

## Spelling reform: dass, Fluss and the capital ẞ

In 1996 Germany, Austria and Switzerland agreed on a **[[spelling reform]]**, which came into
schools in 1998 and was revised in 2004 and 2006. Its best-known change is the rule you learned
in Lesson 1: *ß* after a long vowel or diphthong, *ss* after a short one. Before the reform,
*ß* was also written after short vowels at the end of a word or before a consonant. So:

| Before 1996 | Now | Why |
|---|---|---|
| *daß* | *dass* (that) | short *a* |
| *Fluß* | *Fluss* (river) | short *u* |
| *muß* | *muss* (must) | short *u* |
| *Straße* | *Straße* (no change) | long *a* |
| *heißen* | *heißen* (no change) | diphthong *ei* |

You'll still see *daß* on old signs and in older books. Now the spelling tells you the vowel
length, which helps when reading aloud.

Text in capitals used to be a problem: *ß* had no capital, so *STRASSE* was written with *SS*.
Since 2017 the official rules also allow a capital *ẞ* (*STRAẞE*), though *SS* is still the
usual choice. Swiss Standard German has done without *ß* for decades and writes *Strasse*.

## Reading: a voice message

Kemal, a learner, sends a voice message to his tandem partner Jana. Read it aloud, using
everything in this lesson.

> Hallo Jana, hier ist Kemal! Ich lerne jetzt jeden Tag Aussprache. Das ist nicht leicht! Mein
> "r" in "Bier" ist noch sehr englisch. Und "Spiegelei" ist ein Problem: ich sage
> "Spie-ge-lei". Mein Lehrer sagt: "Ei" ist ein Wort, und ein Wort mit Vokal am Anfang beginnt
> neu, mit Stopp. Wir machen jetzt oft Zungenbrecher. "Fischers Fritz" mache ich schon gut! Aber
> "Blaukraut bleibt Blaukraut" ist sehr schwer. Verreist du im Sommer? Ich verreise nicht, ich
> lerne. Bis bald!

Hi Jana, it's Kemal! I'm practising pronunciation every day now. It isn't easy! My "r" in
*Bier* is still very English. And *Spiegelei* is a problem: I say "Spie-ge-lei". My teacher
says: *Ei* is a word, and a word with a vowel at the beginning starts fresh, with a stop. We
often do tongue twisters now. I can already do "Fischers Fritz" well! But "Blaukraut bleibt
Blaukraut" is very hard. Are you going away in the summer? I'm not going away, I'm studying.
See you soon!

(*jeden Tag* means every day, *leicht* easy, *noch* still, *schwer* hard, *am Anfang* at the
beginning and *im Sommer* in the summer. The full twister *Blaukraut bleibt Blaukraut und Brautkleid bleibt
Brautkleid* means "red cabbage stays red cabbage and a wedding dress stays a wedding dress".)


## Common mistakes

- Saying the *r* in *-er* like English *r*. *Lehrer*, *aber*, *oder* end in a short "uh".
- Joining words the English way: *ein Ei* as "ei-nei". Make a clean new start on the vowel.
- Treating every single-consonant vowel as long. *das*, *was*, *mit*, *in*, *hat* are short.
- Hearing *g* in *ng*: *Finger* is "FING-uh", *singen* is "ZING-en", with no hard *g*.
- Reading *v* as *f* in borrowed words: *Klavier* and *Universität* have a real *v*.
- Raising the voice at the end of every question. W-questions usually fall.
- Writing *daß* or *muß*. Since the reform it's *dass* and *muss*.

## Key points

- A vowel that ends its syllable is usually long (*Na-me*); short everyday words like *das,
  mit, in* are short.
- Unstressed *-e* is a schwa; final *-er* is a vocalic *r*, close to a short "uh".
- Germans put a glottal stop before a word or word part that starts with a vowel: *ein | Ei*,
  *Spiegel | ei*, *ver | eisen*.
- *pf* = both letters, *chs* = ks, *ng* has no *g*, *-tion* = tsion, *v* = v in many loanwords.
- Statements and W-questions usually fall; yes/no questions rise.
- Regional standards differ (*-ig* as *-ik*, rolled *r*), and all are correct where they're used.
- Since the 1996 reform: *ss* after a short vowel (*dass*), *ß* after a long one (*Straße*); a
  capital *ẞ* has been allowed since 2017.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: du, Sie and the German-speaking world
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In Lesson 2 you learned to greet people, to choose between *du* and *Sie*, and to say where
you're from. That's enough for a first conversation, but real conversations happen in real
places: a bakery in Hamburg, an office in Vienna, a train in Zurich. This honors lesson shows
you where German is spoken, why a Swiss and a Bavarian may greet you with words you've never
seen, and how *du* and *Sie* work in everyday life, including how people switch from one to the
other. You'll also learn two useful verbs, *duzen* and *siezen*, and practise the present tense
from Lesson 4 with them.

## Where German is spoken

German is the main language of Germany, Austria and Liechtenstein, and of most of Switzerland.
It's an **[[official language]]**, a language the state uses for laws, schools and offices, in
several more places:

| Country or region | German there |
|---|---|
| *Deutschland* | the official language |
| *Österreich* | the official language |
| *die Schweiz* | one of four national languages, with French, Italian and Romansh; the language of most of the population |
| *Liechtenstein* | the only official language |
| *Luxemburg* | one of three official languages, with Luxembourgish and French |
| *Belgien* (Belgium) | one of three official languages; spoken in a small area in the east, home to about 80,000 people |
| *Südtirol* (South Tyrol, Italy) | official alongside Italian; the first language of most people there |

![A simplified map of central Europe showing Deutschland with Berlin, Österreich with Wien, die Schweiz with Bern, the small dot of Liechtenstein between Switzerland and Austria, Luxemburg and Ostbelgien on Germany's western border, and Südtirol in Italy just south of Austria.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

German is the most widely spoken first language (*Muttersprache*, literally "mother language")
in the European Union. You'll also hear the
short form *DACH* for the three big German-speaking countries: *D* (Deutschland), *A*
(Austria, from its Latin name) and *CH* (Switzerland, from Latin *Confoederatio Helvetica*).
Those letters are also the countries' international car codes.

## Standard German and dialects

When you learn German, you learn **[[standard German]]**, in German *Hochdeutsch*. The word means
"High German", but "high" is about geography, not quality: the standard grew mainly out of the
dialects of the higher, hilly middle and south of the German-speaking area, as opposed to the
flat north (where *Plattdeutsch*, "Low German", is spoken). Standard German is what you read in
newspapers, hear on the news and use in school and at work.

Alongside it, many people speak a **[[dialect]]**, a regional form of the language with its own
sounds, words and some grammar. Bavarian, Swabian and Low German are well-known examples (Low German is so different that
many linguists count it as a language of its own). Most
Germans and Austrians can switch between their dialect and standard German, and the standard is
always understood.

Switzerland is a special case. In everyday speech, German-speaking Swiss people of every
background use **[[Swiss German]]** (*Schweizerdeutsch*), a family of dialects that can be hard for
Germans to follow. In writing, at school and on the news, they use Swiss Standard German. As a
learner, you speak standard German in Switzerland too, and people will answer you in it.

German is a **[[pluricentric language]]**: it has more than one standard. Germany, Austria and
Switzerland each have their own standard form, with small differences in words, spelling and
pronunciation. A few examples:

| Germany | Austria | Switzerland | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Januar* | *Jänner* | *Januar* | January |
| *Fahrrad* | *Fahrrad* | *Velo* | bicycle |
| *Straße* | *Straße* | *Strasse* | street |
| *Tschüss* | *Servus*, *Baba* (casual) | *Tschüss*, *Ciao* | bye |

None of these is "better German". If you live in Vienna, *Jänner* is correct; on a German exam,
either is accepted.

## Hello and goodbye around the region

Lessons 1 and 2 gave you *Hallo*, *Guten Tag* and *Tschüss*, which work everywhere. Here are
greetings you'll hear in particular regions:

| Greeting | Where | How it's used |
|---|---|---|
| *Moin* | northern Germany | hello, at any time of day, even in the evening |
| *Grüß Gott* | southern Germany, Austria | hello; polite, fine with *Sie* |
| *Grüß dich* | southern Germany, Austria | hello to one person you say *du* to |
| *Servus* | Bavaria, Austria | hello and goodbye, informal |
| *Grüezi* | Switzerland | hello to people you say *Sie* to |
| *Hoi* | Switzerland | hi, informal |

Most experts trace *Moin* to a Low German word for "nice" rather than to *Morgen* (the origin
is debated), and either way it works in the evening too. *Grüß dich* literally means "(God) greet you", and its *dich* is the *du* form, so it's
only for people you'd say *du* to. In Switzerland, *Grüezi* is the safe choice in shops and
offices. You don't have to use these greetings yourself, but you should recognise them. A
learner who answers *Moin!* in Hamburg or *Servus!* among friends in Munich is doing well.

## du and Sie in real life

Two verbs name the choice: *duzen* (to say *du* to someone) and *siezen* (to say *Sie*). They're
regular, and their stems end in *-z*, so they follow the rule from Lesson 4: the *du* form adds
only *-t*.

| | duzen | siezen |
|---|---|---|
| ich | *duze* | *sieze* |
| du | *duzt* | *siezt* |
| er / sie / es | *duzt* | *siezt* |
| wir | *duzen* | *siezen* |
| ihr | *duzt* | *siezt* |
| sie / Sie | *duzen* | *siezen* |

*Im Büro duzen wir alle.* — In the office we all say *du*.
*Ich sieze meine Chefin.* — I say *Sie* to my boss.
*Duzt du deine Lehrerin?* — Do you say *du* to your teacher?

When people move from *Sie* to *du*, someone offers it, often with *Wir können gern du sagen*
or *Wollen wir uns duzen?* (Shall we say *du* to each other?). The offer is usually made by the
older person, the person in the higher position, or, between equals, simply by whoever thinks
of it first. Accepting is easy: *Gern! Ich bin Paul.* It's polite to accept; going back to
*Sie* afterwards would feel cold. The chart shows the usual pattern, which is a custom, not a
fixed rule:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How people switch from Sie to du
  accDescr: Two adults who meet usually start with Sie. If one is older or in a higher position, that person usually offers du; if they are equals, either one can offer it. The offer is something like Wir können gern du sagen. The other person accepts, for example Gern, ich bin Paul, and from then on they use du and first names.
  A["Two adults meet: Sie"] --> B{"Is one older or more senior?"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["That person usually offers du"]
  B -- "no" --> D["Either one can offer du"]
  C --> E["Wir können gern du sagen."]
  D --> E
  E --> F["Gern! Ich bin Paul."]
  F --> G["From now on: du and first names"]
```

Some patterns from everyday life, with the usual hedge that families, regions and companies
differ:

- Many workplaces, especially young companies, use *du* for everyone, sometimes including the
  boss. Banks, offices and older firms often keep *Sie*.
- Online, in sports clubs and among students, *du* is the norm.
- In shops, restaurants and offices, staff and customers say *Sie*, though some shops with a
  young image address customers with *du* on purpose.
- For a group, use *ihr* if you'd say *du* to each person (*Kommt ihr mit?*), and *Sie* if
  you'd say *Sie* to them. When a group is mixed, *Sie* is the safe choice in formal settings.
- Titles: a doctor may be addressed as *Frau Doktor* or *Herr Doktor*. In Austria, academic
  titles are used more often than in Germany, also in everyday address.

### Example 1: Choosing the form of address

For each situation, decide *du*, *ihr* or *Sie*, and say how you'd greet the person.

1. Your new neighbour, about 60, in Graz, in the morning. An adult you don't know: *Sie*.
   Austria, morning: *Grüß Gott!* or *Guten Morgen!*, then *Wie geht es Ihnen?*
2. Two children at a playground in Berlin. Children, two of them: *ihr*. *Hallo! Wie heißt
   ihr?*
3. A colleague in a Hamburg start-up who said *Ich bin Lea* on your first day. She has given
   you her first name in a *du* setting: *du*. *Moin, Lea!*
4. A shop assistant in Zurich. A stranger at work: *Sie*. *Grüezi!*

### Example 2: Forms of duzen and siezen

Fill in: *Wir ___ uns.* (duzen) — *Lisa ___ Frau Klein.* (siezen) — *___ du Frau Klein?*
(duzen)

1. *wir* takes the infinitive form: *Wir duzen uns.* (We say *du* to each other.)
2. *Lisa* is *sie* (she); the ending is *-t*. The stem *siez-* ends in *z*, but *-t* is added
   anyway: *Lisa siezt Frau Klein.*
3. *du*: the stem *duz-* ends in *-z*, so add only *-t*, not *-st*: *Duzt du Frau Klein?* It's
   a yes/no question, so the verb comes first.

## Reading: new in Vienna

Nadia, from Canada, writes to her German teacher in Toronto.

> Liebe Frau Becker,
>
> viele Grüße aus Wien! Ich wohne jetzt hier und arbeite in einem Büro. Das Deutsch hier ist ein
> bisschen anders. Am Morgen sagen die Leute nicht "Guten Morgen", sie sagen "Grüß Gott", und im
> Büro sagt mein Kollege Florian immer "Servus". Er sagt auch "Servus" am Abend, für "Tschüss"!
> Ich duze Florian, er ist sehr nett. Meine Chefin sieze ich. Sie heißt Frau Magistra Huber.
> Magistra ist ein Titel, und in Österreich sind Titel wichtig. Der Januar heißt hier "Jänner".
> Ich verstehe viel, aber nicht alles!
>
> Viele Grüße
> Nadia

Dear Mrs Becker, Many greetings from Vienna! I live here now and work in an office. The German
here is a bit different. In the morning people don't say *Guten Morgen*, they say *Grüß Gott*,
and in the office my colleague Florian always says *Servus*. He also says *Servus* in the
evening, for "bye"! I say *du* to Florian; he's very nice. I say *Sie* to my boss. She's called
Frau Magistra Huber. *Magistra* is a title, and in Austria titles are important. January is
called *Jänner* here. I understand a lot, but not everything! Best wishes, Nadia

(*ein bisschen* means a bit, *anders* different, *die Leute* people, *der Kollege* the
colleague, *die Chefin* the boss, *der Titel* the title and *alles* everything. *in einem Büro*
uses the dative from Lesson 18; read it as "in an office". Notice *Meine Chefin sieze ich*: the
object comes first and the verb stays in position 2.)

### Example 3: Reading between the lines

What can you work out from Nadia's message?

1. *Grüß Gott* in the morning: Nadia expected *Guten Morgen*, but in Austria *Grüß Gott* works
   at any time of day.
2. *Servus* in the evening, "for *Tschüss*": *Servus* means both hello and goodbye.
3. *Ich duze Florian* but *Meine Chefin sieze ich*: the office is mixed; colleagues use *du*,
   the boss keeps *Sie*.
4. *Frau Magistra Huber*: *Magistra* is the female form of the Austrian academic title
   *Magister*, and using it shows respect.

## Common mistakes

- *Grüß dich* to someone you say *Sie* to. *dich* is a *du* form; say *Grüß Gott* or *Guten Tag*.
- *du duzst*, *du siezst*. The stems end in *-z*: *du duzt*, *du siezt*.
- Thinking *Moin* is only for the morning. It works all day.
- Thinking *Hochdeutsch* means "posh German" or that dialect speakers speak "bad German".
  Dialects are full languages of everyday life; the standard is simply shared by everyone.
- Calling Austrian or Swiss forms mistakes. *Jänner* and *Strasse* are correct in their countries.
- Saying *du* to a group of adults you'd call *Sie* (*Wie heißt ihr?* to two business
  clients). Use *Sie*: *Wie heißen Sie?*
- Switching back to *Sie* after someone has offered *du*. Once you've agreed, stay with *du*.

## Key points

- German is official in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Belgium (east)
  and South Tyrol (Italy).
- Standard German (*Hochdeutsch*) is understood everywhere; dialects live alongside it, and in
  Switzerland everyday speech is Swiss German.
- German is pluricentric: Germany, Austria and Switzerland each have their own standard
  (*Jänner*, *Velo*, *Strasse*).
- Regional greetings: *Moin* (north), *Grüß Gott* and *Servus* (south, Austria), *Grüezi* (Switzerland).
- *duzen* / *siezen*: *du duzt*, *du siezt*. The older or more senior person usually offers *du*.
- Groups: *ihr* for people you'd say *du* to, *Sie* for people you'd say *Sie* to.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Numbers in everyday life: sums, grades and handwriting
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 3 taught you to say the numbers from 0 to 100 and to give your age, phone number and
address. Numbers do more than that in daily life: you add up a bill out loud, help a child with
homework, hear that someone "got a one" at school, hold up fingers to order two coffees, and
read a handwritten note. Each of these works a little differently in the German-speaking
countries. This honors lesson covers doing sums in German, numbers used as nouns, school grades
in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, counting on your fingers and writing digits by hand. Along
the way you'll meet a new pattern in the present tense, in verbs like *rechnen* (to calculate).

## Doing sums out loud

The four basic operations:

| Sign | German | Example | Said |
|---|---|---|---|
| + | *plus* | 3 + 4 = 7 | *drei plus vier ist sieben* |
| − | *minus* | 9 − 5 = 4 | *neun minus fünf ist vier* |
| · or × | *mal* | 6 · 7 = 42 | *sechs mal sieben ist zweiundvierzig* |
| : or ÷ | *geteilt durch* | 20 : 4 = 5 | *zwanzig geteilt durch vier ist fünf* |

For "equals", say *ist*, or more formally *ist gleich* or *gleich*: *zwei plus zwei ist gleich
vier*. In casual speech, *und* often replaces *plus* (*zwei und zwei ist vier*), and *durch*
on its own replaces *geteilt durch* (*zwanzig durch vier*). The usual verb is singular, *ist*,
because the whole sum is treated as one thing (you'll also hear *sind*).

German schools usually write multiplication with a raised dot (6 · 7) and division with a colon
(20 : 4). The × and ÷ signs that English-speaking schools use are understood, but you'll rarely
see ÷ on a German worksheet.

To ask for a result, use *Wie viel ist …?* (How much is …?), which you'll use for prices in
Lesson 10:

*Wie viel ist acht mal neun? — Acht mal neun ist zweiundsiebzig.*

### Example 1: Reading sums aloud

Read each line aloud, then check the result.

1. 15 + 27 = 42: *fünfzehn plus siebenundzwanzig ist zweiundvierzig*. Remember: units first in
   27 and 42.
2. 81 − 36 = 45: *einundachtzig minus sechsunddreißig ist fünfundvierzig*. *ein* (not *eins*)
   inside *einundachtzig*; *sechs* keeps its *s* in *sechsunddreißig*.
3. 7 · 8 = 56: *sieben mal acht ist sechsundfünfzig*.
4. 96 : 4 = 24: *sechsundneunzig geteilt durch vier ist vierundzwanzig*.

## A new present-tense pattern: rechnen, zeichnen, öffnen

In Lesson 4 you added an *e* before *-st* and *-t* when the stem ends in *-t* or *-d*
(*arbeitest*). The same thing happens when the stem ends in *m* or *n* after another
consonant, because *rechnst* or *rechnt* would be almost impossible to say:

| | rechnen (to calculate) | zeichnen (to draw) | lernen (to learn) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | *rechne* | *zeichne* | *lerne* |
| du | *rechnest* | *zeichnest* | *lernst* |
| er / sie / es | *rechnet* | *zeichnet* | *lernt* |
| wir | *rechnen* | *zeichnen* | *lernen* |
| ihr | *rechnet* | *zeichnet* | *lernt* |
| sie / Sie | *rechnen* | *zeichnen* | *lernen* |

Look at *lernen*: its stem *lern-* also ends in consonant + *n*, but no *e* is added. After *l*
or *r*, the *n* or *m* is easy to say, so the regular endings stay. The same is true when the
letter before *n* is a silent *h*: *wohnen*, *du wohnst*. Other verbs with the extra *e* that
you'll meet: *öffnen* (to open: *er öffnet*, Lesson 15) and *regnen* (to rain: *es regnet*,
Lesson 16).

*zählen* (to count) is completely regular: *ich zähle, du zählst, er zählt*.

### Example 2: Which form?

Fill in the present tense: *Du ___ sehr schnell.* (rechnen) — *Mia ___ ein Haus.* (zeichnen) —
*Du ___ Deutsch.* (lernen) — *Ihr ___ bis zehn.* (zählen)

1. *rechnen*: stem *rechn-*. Before the *n* comes *ch*, a real consonant sound (not a silent
   *h* as in *wohnen*), so add the *e*: *Du rechnest sehr schnell.* (You calculate very fast.)
2. *zeichnen*: stem *zeichn-*, again *ch* + *n*: *Mia zeichnet ein Haus.* (Mia is drawing a
   house.)
3. *lernen*: stem *lern-*, *r* + *n*, so no extra *e*: *Du lernst Deutsch.*
4. *zählen*: stem *zähl-*, no *m* or *n* at the end, so regular: *Ihr zählt bis zehn.* (You
   count to ten.)

## Numbers as nouns

A **[[cardinal number]]** is a counting number: *eins, zwei, drei*. When you talk about a number as
a thing (a digit, a grade, a bus line), it becomes a **[[number noun]]**: it gets a capital letter
and the article *die*, whatever the number is:

*die Eins, die Zwei, die Drei, … die Zehn, die Zwanzig*

*Die Sieben ist meine Zahl.* — Seven is my number.
*Ich nehme die Fünf.* — I'm taking the number 5 (bus or tram).
*Ich habe eine Eins in Mathe.* — I got a one (the top grade) in maths.

That last sentence leads straight to school grades.

## School grades

In Germany, school grades (*die Noten*) run from 1 to 6, and 1 is best. Austria uses 1 to 5,
also with 1 as best. Switzerland turns the scale upside down: 6 is best, 1 is worst, and 4 is
the pass mark. Each German and Austrian grade also has a name:

![Three columns of school grades, best at the top. Germany: 1 sehr gut, 2 gut, 3 befriedigend, 4 ausreichend, 5 mangelhaft, 6 ungenügend; 1 to 4 pass, 5 and 6 fail. Austria: 1 Sehr gut, 2 Gut, 3 Befriedigend, 4 Genügend, 5 Nicht genügend; 1 to 4 pass, 5 fails. Switzerland: 6 best down to 1 worst; 4 is the pass mark, so 4 to 6 pass and 1 to 3 fail. Swiss schools often give half grades such as 5.5.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*sehr gut* means very good, *gut* good, *befriedigend* satisfactory, *ausreichend* sufficient,
*mangelhaft* poor and *ungenügend* insufficient. In everyday talk, people just use the number
noun: *eine Eins*, *eine Zwei*, *eine Fünf*. (In the upper school years of a German *Gymnasium*, the
*Oberstufe*, grades are given as points from 0 to 15 instead, with 15 the best.)

The scales are a classic misunderstanding between the countries. A Swiss pupil who proudly says
*Ich habe eine Sechs!* has the top grade; a German pupil with *eine Sechs* has the worst.

### Example 3: Good or bad news?

1. Jonas, in Munich, says: *Ich habe eine Zwei in Englisch.* Germany, 2 = *gut*. Good news.
2. Anna, in Zurich, says: *Ich habe eine Fünf in Mathe.* Switzerland, 5 is above the pass mark
   of 4. Good news.
3. Lukas, in Hamburg, says: *Ich habe eine Fünf in Mathe.* Germany, 5 = *mangelhaft*, a fail.
   Bad news.
4. Sara, in Graz, has *eine Vier*. Austria, 4 = *Genügend*, the lowest pass. She passed, just.

Notice that a 4 is a pass in all three countries, while a 5 is a fail in Germany and Austria
but a good grade in Switzerland.

## Counting on your fingers

To show "one" with your hand, most Germans hold up the thumb (*der Daumen*), not the index
finger (*der Zeigefinger*, the "pointing finger"; *der Finger* is finger). Two is thumb and index
finger, three adds the middle finger, and so on. If you order *zwei Kaffee* by
holding up your index and middle finger, you'll almost always get two, but thumb and index
finger is the local way and can't be misread. When Germans count aloud on their fingers, they
also start with the thumb.

## Writing digits by hand

Handwritten digits differ too. In Germany, a 1 is usually written with a long upstroke, which
can look like an American 7. To keep them apart, the 7 gets a short line across the middle.

![Handwritten digits. On the left, as often written in Germany: a 1 with a long sloping upstroke and a 7 with a short bar across the middle. On the right, as often written in the US: a 1 as a single straight line and a 7 without a bar.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

If you read German handwriting, a "7" without a bar is probably a 1. If you write numbers for
Germans, cross your sevens.

## Number mix-ups

Because German says 73 as "three and seventy", it's easy to write the digits in the wrong
order, even for native speakers. This mistake has its own name, *der Zahlendreher* (a number
"turner"), and it happens with phone numbers, prices and bank details. A small association,
*Zwanzigeins e.V.*, even campaigns for counting the English way (*zwanzig-eins* for 21). It's
a proposal only; standard German keeps *einundzwanzig*, and that's what you should learn.

When a number matters, do what Germans do: say the digits one by one (*sieben, drei*) or repeat
the number back. For decimals, remember the **[[decimal comma]]** from Lesson 10: *2,5* is
*zwei Komma fünf*.

## Reading: homework at the kitchen table

> Es ist sieben Uhr. Ben ist neun Jahre alt, und er macht Hausaufgaben. Er rechnet: "Acht mal
