complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Families and names: Annas Bruder
lessons.body:
## Beyond Mutter and Vater

In lesson 6 you learned the core family words and the possessive articles: *meine Mutter, sein
Bruder, ihre Eltern*. Real families are often bigger and more varied than a textbook family
tree. Many children in German-speaking countries grow up with a stepfather, a half-sister or
two homes. And when you talk about families, you constantly say *whose* someone is: Anna's
brother, Jonas's dog.

This honors lesson gives you the words for modern families, explains how German first names and
surnames work, and teaches the quickest way to say "Anna's": *Annas*. It ends with a longer
text, written by a teenager about his family, that puts everything together.

## Mama, Papa and the wider family

Children call their parents *Mama* and *Papa* (stress on the first syllable: MA-ma, PA-pa),
and adults often keep using these words: *Meine Mama wohnt in Graz.* As nouns they are *die
Mama* and *der Papa*. Grandparents are *Oma* and *Opa*, as you know.

You will also hear the words for the wider family. Recognise them now; you practise them in a
later course:

| Masculine | Feminine | English |
|---|---|---|
| der Onkel | die Tante | uncle, aunt |
| der Cousin | die Cousine | cousin |
| der Neffe | die Nichte | nephew, niece |
| der Enkel | die Enkelin | grandson, granddaughter |

*die Großeltern* are the grandparents, and *die Verwandten* are your relatives. *Cousin* and
*Cousine* come from French and keep a French sound: koo-ZANG (with a nasal ending) and
koo-ZEE-ne.

## Patchwork families

When parents separate and find new partners, the result is often called *die Patchworkfamilie*
(patchwork family; the first part is the English word *patchwork*). Its members have their own words:

| Word | Meaning |
|---|---|
| der Stiefvater / die Stiefmutter | stepfather / stepmother: your parent's new husband or wife |
| der Halbbruder / die Halbschwester | half-brother / half-sister: you share one parent |
| der Zwilling (plural die Zwillinge) | twin |
| das Einzelkind | only child: a child with no brothers or sisters |
| getrennt | separated (a couple that no longer lives together) |
| geschieden | divorced (lesson 6) |

*der Zwilling* is masculine even for a girl, like *die Person* for a man. To say "twin sister",
German builds a compound: *der Zwilling* + *die Schwester* = *die Zwillingsschwester*. The last
part decides the gender, as you learned in lesson 5, so it's *die*. Notice the *s* in the
middle: many compounds put a **[[linking s]]** between the parts (*Zwilling-s-schwester*,
*Geburt-s-tag*, "birthday"). It has no meaning of its own; it just joins the words.

Here is Ben's family. Ben is *ich*:

![Ben's patchwork family. In the top row: Anja (die Stiefmutter) is married to Markus (der Vater); Markus and Julia (die Mutter) are divorced, shown by a dashed line labeled geschieden; Julia is married to Tom (der Stiefvater). Markus and Julia's children are Ben (ich) and Lisa (die Zwillingsschwester). Julia and Tom's child is Emma (die Halbschwester).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Names

Every German has at least one *Vorname* (first name) and a *Nachname* (last name). *Nachname* is
the everyday word; *Familienname* (lesson 1) is the word on forms. Many people also have a
*Spitzname* (nickname): *Alexander* becomes *Alex*, *Katharina* becomes *Kathi*.

Many of the most common German surnames are old job titles. *Müller* (miller) is the most
common surname in Germany, and *Schmidt* (smith) comes second. Others you will meet everywhere:
*Schneider* (tailor), *Fischer* (fisher), *Weber* (weaver), *Becker* (baker), *Wagner* (cart
maker) and *Meyer* (originally a farm manager). So when you meet a *Frau Müller*, she is not
a miller: the name is hundreds of years old.

What happens to names when people marry? This is a question of law, and each country has its
own rules. In Germany, a married couple can choose one shared surname, the surname of one of
the two, or each can keep their own. Double names such as *Müller-Schmidt* have long been
possible for one partner; since a reform in May 2025, both partners can use one, and children
can be given a double name from both parents' surnames. Names with more than two parts, such
as *Müller-Schmidt-Weber*, are still not allowed. Austria and Switzerland have their
own rules.

Inside a family everyone uses *du*: children say *du* to their parents and grandparents, and
stepparents are usually *du* too.

## Whose? Annas Bruder

English adds *'s* to show whose something is: Anna's brother. German does almost the same with
names, but writes no apostrophe:

- *Annas Bruder* — Anna's brother
- *Peters Mutter* — Peter's mother
- *Lenas Familie* — Lena's family

This *-s* is a form of the **[[genitive]]**, the fourth German case (you know the nominative, and
you will learn the accusative and dative in lessons 9 and 18). At A1 you only need this one
use: *-s* after a name.

Three rules make it work:

1. The name with *-s* comes first, and the noun after it has no article: *Annas Bruder*, never
   ~~der Annas Bruder~~ or ~~Annas der Bruder~~.
2. If the name already ends in an *s* sound (*-s, -ss, -ß, -x, -z*), add only an apostrophe:
   *Jonas' Hund* (Jonas's dog), *Max' Schwester*, *Felix' Vater*.
3. In everyday speech, Germans often say *von* + name instead: *der Bruder von Anna*, *der Hund
   von Jonas*. This is especially common with names that end in *s*. Both are correct.

You will see shop signs like *Andrea's Café* with an apostrophe. The official rules allow this
only in a few cases, mainly to make the base form of a name clear, so in your own writing use
*Annas*, *Peters*, *Lenas*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Saying whose something is with a name
  accDescr: Check how the owner's name ends. If it does not end in an s sound, add -s with no apostrophe, as in Annas Bruder. If it ends in s, ss, ß, x or z, add only an apostrophe, as in Max' Schwester. Either way, in speech you can also say von plus the name, as in der Bruder von Anna.
  A{"Does the name end in s, ss, ß, x or z?"} -- no --> C["add -s, no apostrophe: Annas Bruder"]
  A -- yes --> D["add only an apostrophe: Max' Schwester"]
  C --> E["in speech, also fine: der Bruder von Anna"]
  D --> E
```

## Reading: Ben's family

Ben, fourteen, writes about his family for a school project.

> Hallo! Ich heiße Ben und ich bin vierzehn. Meine Familie ist eine Patchworkfamilie.
>
> Meine Eltern sind geschieden. Meine Mutter heißt Julia, mein Vater heißt Markus. Lisa ist meine Zwillingsschwester. Wir sind Zwillinge, aber wir sind sehr verschieden: Lisa ist groß und spricht sehr schnell. Ich bin klein und spreche langsam.
>
> Wir wohnen bei Mama und Tom. Tom ist mein Stiefvater. Er ist Koch und er kocht super! Mama und Tom haben eine Tochter, Emma. Sie ist zwei Jahre alt. Emma ist meine Halbschwester.
>
> Papa ist wieder verheiratet. Seine Frau heißt Anja. Sie ist meine Stiefmutter, aber ich sage einfach Anja. Anja hat keine Kinder.
>
> Ist das kompliziert? Ein bisschen. Aber ich bin kein Einzelkind! Und Emmas Lieblingsperson? Das bin ich!

Translation:

> Hello! My name is Ben and I'm fourteen. My family is a patchwork family.
>
> My parents are divorced. My mother is called Julia, my father is called Markus. Lisa is my twin sister. We're twins, but we're very different: Lisa is tall and speaks very fast. I'm short and speak slowly.
>
> We live with Mum and Tom. Tom is my stepfather. He's a cook and he cooks brilliantly! Mum and Tom have a daughter, Emma. She's two years old. Emma is my half-sister.
>
> Dad is married again. His wife is called Anja. She's my stepmother, but I just say Anja. Anja doesn't have any children.
>
> Is that complicated? A bit. But I'm not an only child! And Emma's favourite person? That's me!

(*verschieden* = different; *bei Mama und Tom* = at Mum and Tom's place, a set phrase with the
dative of lesson 18; *kochen* = to cook; *wieder* = again; *einfach* = simply, just;
*kompliziert* = complicated; *die Lieblingsperson* = favourite person.)

Look at how the possessives work in the text. Ben says *mein Stiefvater* and *meine
Halbschwester* (feminine, so *-e*). About his father he says *Seine Frau*: the owner is a man,
so *sein*; *Frau* is feminine, so *-e*. And *Emmas Lieblingsperson* uses the name *-s*.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: who is who?

Use the picture of Ben's family. Who is Emma to Lisa, and who is Anja to Emma?

1. Emma's parents are Julia and Tom. Lisa's parents are Julia and Markus. They share one parent,
   Julia, so Emma is Lisa's half-sister: *Emma ist Lisas Halbschwester.*
2. Anja is married to Markus. Markus is not Emma's father, so Anja is not Emma's stepmother;
   the two aren't related at all. A German speaker might say: *Anja ist die Frau von Bens
   Vater.* (Anja is the wife of Ben's father.)

### Example 2: three ways to say "Jonas's dog"

1. Is the owner a name? Yes: *Jonas*.
2. Does it end in an *s* sound? Yes, so add only an apostrophe: *Jonas' Hund*.
3. In speech the *von* form is very natural here: *der Hund von Jonas*.

Wrong: ~~Jonass Hund~~, ~~Jonas's Hund~~, ~~der Jonas' Hund~~.

### Example 3: choosing the possessive

Complete from Ben's family: *Tom ist ___ Stiefvater* (Lisa speaking); *Markus und ___ Frau
Anja*; *Julia und ___ Töchter*.

1. Lisa speaks about herself, so "my": *Tom ist mein Stiefvater* (*Stiefvater* is masculine,
   no ending).
2. The owner is Markus, a man, so *sein*; *Frau* is feminine, so *-e*: *Markus und seine Frau
   Anja*.
3. The owner is Julia, a woman, so *ihr*; *Töchter* is plural, so *-e*: *Julia und ihre
   Töchter*.

## Common mistakes

- Adding an English apostrophe: ~~Anna's Bruder~~ → *Annas Bruder*.
- Keeping an article: ~~die Annas Mutter~~ → *Annas Mutter*.
- Adding *-s* to a name in *s*: ~~Jonass Hund~~ → *Jonas' Hund* or *der Hund von Jonas*.
- Treating *Zwilling* as feminine for a girl: *Lisa ist ein Zwilling* (masculine *der
  Zwilling*), or *Lisa ist meine Zwillingsschwester*.
- Mixing up *Stief-* and *Halb-*: a stepfather is your parent's partner, a half-sister shares one
  of your parents.
- Confusing *getrennt* and *geschieden*: separated couples are not necessarily divorced.
- Reading *Müller* as a job: as a surname it's just a name, like English *Smith*.

## Key points

- Modern families: *der Stiefvater, die Stiefmutter, der Halbbruder, die Halbschwester, der
  Zwilling, das Einzelkind, die Patchworkfamilie*; couples can be *getrennt* or *geschieden*.
- Recognise *Onkel, Tante, Cousin, Cousine, Neffe, Nichte, Enkel, Enkelin*.
- *Vorname*, *Nachname* (= *Familienname*), *Spitzname*. Many surnames are old jobs: *Müller,
  Schmidt, Schneider*.
- Whose: name + *-s*, no apostrophe, no article: *Annas Bruder*. Names in *s, ss, ß, x, z* take
  only an apostrophe: *Max' Schwester*. In speech: *der Bruder von Anna*.
- Compounds often have a linking *s*: *die Zwillingsschwester*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Food, drink and the accusative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far your sentences have mostly described people and things: *Das ist ein Tisch.* *Meine Schwester ist Lehrerin.* *Der Computer ist kaputt.* In this lesson people start doing things to things: eating bread, drinking coffee, ordering a cake. To talk like that, German needs a new form of the article, the **[[accusative]]**. The good news is that the change is small: only masculine words change.

You will also learn the verbs you need at the table (*essen*, *trinken*, *nehmen*, *möchten*), how *essen* and *nehmen* change their vowel, and how to order politely in a café. By the end you can say what you like to eat and order breakfast in German.

## Food and drink

Learn every food word with its article, as always. Many drinks are masculine, which matters in a moment.

| der (masculine) | die (feminine) | das (neuter) |
|---|---|---|
| der Kaffee — coffee | die Milch — milk | das Wasser — water |
| der Tee — tea | die Butter — butter | das Bier — beer |
| der Saft — juice | die Wurst — sausage | das Brot — bread |
| der Wein — wine | die Kartoffel — potato | das Brötchen — bread roll |
| der Käse — cheese | die Nudeln — pasta (plural) | das Ei — egg |
| der Fisch — fish | | das Fleisch — meat |
| der Apfel — apple | | das Gemüse — vegetables |
| der Reis — rice | | das Obst — fruit |
| der Salat — salad | | das Essen — food, meal |
| der Kuchen — cake | | |

Here are six of these words on a breakfast table:

![A breakfast table seen from the front with six things on it, each labeled with its article: a jug of milk (die Milch), a cup of coffee on a saucer (der Kaffee), a bread roll on a plate (das Brötchen), a boiled egg in an egg cup (das Ei), a wedge of cheese (der Käse) and an apple (der Apfel).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The three meals are all neuter: *das Frühstück* (breakfast), *das Mittagessen* (lunch) and *das Abendessen* (dinner). *Mittag* means midday and *Abend* means evening, so the words explain themselves.

Two words name whole groups, and German treats them as one uncountable thing, like English *fruit*: *das Obst* (fruit) and *das Gemüse* (vegetables). So *Gemüse ist gesund* — "vegetables are healthy" — uses a singular verb. (*gesund* means healthy.)

German also builds long food words by sticking nouns together. The last part decides the gender: *der Apfel + der Saft = der Apfelsaft* (apple juice), *der Käse + das Brot = das Käsebrot* (cheese sandwich), *der Apfel + der Kuchen = der Apfelkuchen* (apple cake).

## Subject and object: what the accusative is

In "The woman drinks the coffee", the woman does the drinking: she is the subject. The coffee is what gets drunk: it is the **[[direct object]]**, the thing the action is done to. English shows this by word order alone. German also marks it on the article, and the form it uses for a direct object is the accusative.

In lesson 6 you met the nominative, the case of the subject (and of anything after *sein*). The accusative is the second of German's four cases; from lesson 18 you'll add a third, the dative.

### Only the masculine changes

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| nominative (subject) | der / ein / kein | die / eine / keine | das / ein / kein | die / – / keine |
| accusative (object) | den / einen / keinen | die / eine / keine | das / ein / kein | die / – / keine |

Feminine, neuter and plural forms are exactly the same in both cases. Only the masculine gets an -n: *der* becomes *den*, *ein* becomes *einen*, *kein* becomes *keinen*. A memory hook: the masculine is the only one that changes, and it always picks up an *n*: *den, einen, keinen*.

- *Der Kaffee ist heiß.* — The coffee is hot. (subject: nominative)
- *Ich trinke den Kaffee.* — I'm drinking the coffee. (object: accusative)
- *Ein Apfel kostet nicht viel.* — An apple doesn't cost much. (subject)
- *Er isst einen Apfel.* — He's eating an apple. (object)
- *Ich habe keinen Saft.* — I don't have any juice. (object, negative)
- *Sie trinkt eine Cola.* — She's drinking a cola. (feminine: no change)
- *Wir essen das Brot.* — We're eating the bread. (neuter: no change)
- *Ich kaufe die Eier.* — I'm buying the eggs. (plural: no change; *kaufen* = to buy)

Possessives follow *ein*: *mein* becomes *meinen* for a masculine object. *Ich trinke meinen Tee.* — I'm drinking my tea.

### Which verbs take the accusative?

Most verbs that act on something take a direct object in the accusative: *essen*, *trinken*, *nehmen*, *möchten*, *haben*, *machen*, *hören*, *lernen*, *fragen* and many more. One verb never does: *sein*. After *sein* you keep the nominative, because nothing is being done to anything: *Das ist ein Kuchen* but *Ich esse einen Kuchen*.

The questions you ask yourself for each noun fit in a small chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which article form? Nominative or accusative
  accDescr: Start with a noun in the sentence. If the verb is sein, use the nominative: der, ein, kein. If the verb is not sein, ask whether the noun is the direct object. If it is not, use the nominative. If it is the direct object and masculine, use den, einen or keinen. If it is the direct object and feminine, neuter or plural, nothing changes: die, das, eine, ein, keine, kein.
  A["A noun in your sentence"] --> B{"Is the verb sein?"}
  B -- yes --> N["Nominative: der, ein, kein"]
  B -- no --> C{"Is the noun the direct object?"}
  C -- no --> N
  C -- yes --> D{"Is it masculine?"}
  D -- yes --> M["Add n: den, einen, keinen"]
  D -- no --> F["No change: die, das, eine, ein, keine"]
```

## The verbs: essen, trinken, nehmen

*trinken* (to drink) is regular. *essen* (to eat) and *nehmen* (to take; when ordering, to have) change their vowel in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: e becomes i.

| | trinken | essen | nehmen |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | trinke | esse | nehme |
| du | trinkst | isst | nimmst |
| er / sie / es | trinkt | isst | nimmt |
| wir | trinken | essen | nehmen |
| ihr | trinkt | esst | nehmt |
| sie / Sie | trinken | essen | nehmen |

Notice three details. *du isst* has no extra *s* ending, because the stem already ends in *ss*. *er isst* sounds exactly like *er ist* (he is); only the spelling is different. *nehmen* loses its *h* and doubles the *m*: *du nimmst, er nimmt*.

- *Was isst du gern?* — What do you like to eat?
- *Paul nimmt einen Tee.* — Paul is having a tea.
- *Ihr esst viel Obst.* — You (all) eat a lot of fruit.

## möchten: the polite "would like"

*möchten* means "would like". It is the most useful word in any café or shop, and much more polite than "I want".

| | möchten |
|---|---|
| ich | möchte |
| du | möchtest |
| er / sie / es | möchte |
| wir | möchten |
| ihr | möchtet |
| sie / Sie | möchten |

Watch out: *ich möchte* and *er möchte* are identical — there is no *-t* on the *er* form. The object after *möchten* is accusative, like after any other verb:

- *Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.* — I'd like a coffee, please.
- *Möchten Sie ein Wasser?* — Would you like a water?
- *Sie möchte keinen Fisch.* — She doesn't want any fish.

You can also put a verb at the end: *Ich möchte Kuchen essen* (I'd like to eat cake). Lesson 14 explains this pattern; for now, use *möchten* with a noun.

## Saying what you like: gern

To say you like doing something, add *gern* after the verb. *Ich trinke Tee* is "I drink tea"; *Ich trinke gern Tee* is "I like drinking tea". For dislikes, use *nicht gern*.

- *Ich esse gern Nudeln.* — I like eating pasta.
- *Mein Bruder isst nicht gern Gemüse.* — My brother doesn't like eating vegetables.
- *Trinkst du gern Wein?* — Do you like wine?

When you talk about food in general, you usually leave out the article: *Ich esse gern Fisch* (fish in general), but *Ich esse den Fisch* (that particular fish).

## Hunger and thirst

German says "I have hunger": *Ich habe Hunger* (I'm hungry) and *Ich habe Durst* (I'm thirsty). There is no article. Ask *Hast du Hunger?* — Are you hungry? If food tastes good, it is *lecker*: *Der Kuchen ist lecker!*

## Ordering in a café

| Situation | German | English |
|---|---|---|
| The waiter asks | *Was möchten Sie?* / *Was nehmen Sie?* | What would you like? |
| You order | *Ich nehme einen Tee.* / *Ich möchte ein Brötchen, bitte.* | I'll have a tea. / I'd like a roll, please. |
| Asking about something | *Haben Sie Apfelkuchen?* | Do you have apple cake? |
| With / without | *mit Milch* / *ohne Milch* | with milk / without milk |

*mit* (with) and *ohne* (without) are useful here as set phrases; *Kaffee mit Milch*, *Tee ohne Zucker* (*der Zucker* = sugar).

## Dialogue: In the café

*Kellnerin* is a female waiter.

> Kellnerin: Guten Morgen! Was möchten Sie?
>
> Herr Weber: Ich nehme einen Kaffee mit Milch, bitte.
>
> Kellnerin: Und Sie?
>
> Frau Weber: Ich habe Durst. Ich möchte einen Orangensaft und ein Wasser.
>
> Kellnerin: Möchten Sie auch etwas essen? Das Frühstück ist heute sehr gut.
>
> Frau Weber: Ja, gern. Ein Brötchen mit Butter und Käse, bitte. Haben Sie auch Eier?
>
> Kellnerin: Ja, natürlich. Und Sie, Herr Weber? Nehmen Sie auch ein Brötchen?
>
> Herr Weber: Nein, ich habe keinen Hunger. Aber der Apfelkuchen dort sieht toll aus …
>
> Frau Weber: Paul! Du isst jeden Morgen Kuchen!
>
> Herr Weber: Ja, Kuchen ist lecker. Einen Apfelkuchen, bitte.

In English:

> Waitress: Good morning! What would you like?
>
> Mr Weber: I'll have a coffee with milk, please.
>
> Waitress: And you?
>
> Mrs Weber: I'm thirsty. I'd like an orange juice and a water.
>
> Waitress: Would you like something to eat too? The breakfast is very good today.
>
> Mrs Weber: Yes, please. A roll with butter and cheese, please. Do you have eggs too?
>
> Waitress: Yes, of course. And you, Mr Weber? Are you having a roll too?
>
> Mr Weber: No, I'm not hungry. But the apple cake there looks great …
>
> Mrs Weber: Paul! You eat cake every morning!
>
> Mr Weber: Yes, cake is delicious. An apple cake, please.

Look at the objects: *einen Kaffee*, *einen Orangensaft* and *einen Apfelkuchen* are masculine, so they take *einen*; *ein Wasser* and *ein Brötchen* are neuter and stay *ein*. *Ich habe keinen Hunger* uses *keinen* because *Hunger* is masculine. (*etwas* = something, *natürlich* = of course, *jeden Morgen* = every morning, *sieht … aus* = looks.) In a café, *einen Apfelkuchen, bitte* means a slice, not the whole cake; you can also say *ein Stück Apfelkuchen* (lesson 10).

## Pronunciation

- *Brötchen*: the *ö* is made by saying "ay" with rounded lips; *-chen* has the soft *ch* of *ich*.
- *Käse*: long *ä*, like the vowel in English "air" without the r: KÄ-se.
- *Ei* rhymes with English "eye"; *Eier* (eggs) is "EYE-er".
- *Gemüse* is stressed on the middle: ge-MÜ-se. *Kartoffel* too: kar-TOF-fel.
- *Frühstück*: stress on the first part, FRÜH-stück; the *h* is silent and makes the *ü* long.
- *isst* and *ist* sound the same; *nimmt* has a short *i*.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich möchte ein Kaffee.* — Wrong. *Kaffee* is masculine and the object, so: *Ich möchte einen Kaffee.*
- *Ich nehme einen Wasser.* — Wrong in the other direction. Only masculine words get *-en*; *Wasser* is neuter: *ein Wasser*.
- *Er esst Brot.* / *Du nehmst …* — Use the stem change: *er isst*, *du nimmst*.
- *Er möchtet …* — No *-t*: *er möchte*.
- *Ich bin Hunger.* / *Ich habe ein Hunger.* — Say *Ich habe Hunger*, with no article.
- *Ich gern esse Fisch.* — The verb comes second: *Ich esse gern Fisch.*
- *Das ist einen Apfel.* — After *sein*, no accusative: *Das ist ein Apfel.*

## Key points

- The accusative marks the direct object. Only masculine articles change: *den, einen, keinen* (and *meinen*, *deinen* …).
- Feminine, neuter and plural look the same as the nominative.
- *sein* is never followed by the accusative.
- *essen* and *nehmen* change e→i in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: *isst, nimmt*.
- *möchte* has no *-t* in the *er/sie/es* form. Use it to order politely.
- *gern* after the verb says you like doing something; *Ich habe Hunger / Durst* has no article.

lessons.title: Shopping and prices
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 9 you learned to order food and drink with the accusative: *Ich nehme einen Kaffee.* Now you go shopping. You will learn the big numbers (from 100 up to a million), how Germans write and say prices, how to ask what something costs, how to ask for a kilo, a litre or a bottle of something, and how to point at things with *dieser* (this) and ask about them with *welcher* (which). You will also meet *es gibt* (there is, there are), one of the most useful phrases in the language.

## Numbers from 100 up

You already know 0 to 100 (lesson 3). Bigger numbers follow the same logic and are written as one word, however long.

| Number | German |
|---|---|
| 100 | hundert / einhundert |
| 101 | hunderteins |
| 110 | hundertzehn |
| 125 | hundertfünfundzwanzig |
| 200 | zweihundert |
| 350 | dreihundertfünfzig |
| 999 | neunhundertneunundneunzig |
| 1.000 | tausend / eintausend |
| 1.500 | tausendfünfhundert / eintausendfünfhundert |
| 2.480 | zweitausendvierhundertachtzig |
| 10.000 | zehntausend |
| 100.000 | hunderttausend |
| 1.000.000 | eine Million |
| 3.000.000 | drei Millionen |

The pattern is: hundreds, then the rest exactly as you learned it. So 347 is *dreihundert* + *siebenundvierzig* = *dreihundertsiebenundvierzig*. Inside the last two digits the order is still "units and tens": 47 = *sieben-und-vierzig*.

Only *Million* is a separate word, and it is a feminine noun with a plural: *eine Million, zwei Millionen*.

### Writing numbers

German swaps the English comma and point:

- A point (or a small space) separates thousands: *1.000* or *1 000* = one thousand.
- A comma marks decimals: *2,5* = two point five, read *zwei Komma fünf*.

So *1.250* is one thousand two hundred and fifty, not one and a quarter. This matters a lot when you read prices.

Here is a price tag with every part of the German style in one price:

![A yellow price tag headed ANGEBOT (special offer) for a blue bicycle, Fahrrad, blau, showing the price 1.299,95 €. Labels point out that the point separates thousands, the comma separates euros from cents, 95 are the cents, and the euro sign comes after the number. Below: said tausendzweihundertneunundneunzig Euro fünfundneunzig.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Prices: Euro and Cent

Germany, Austria and most EU countries pay in *Euro* (*der Euro*) and *Cent* (*der Cent*). Prices are written with a comma, and the euro sign usually comes after the number: *3,50 €*.

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| 1,00 € | ein Euro |
| 3,50 € | drei Euro fünfzig |
| 12,99 € | zwölf Euro neunundneunzig |
| 0,80 € | achtzig Cent |
| 249,00 € | zweihundertneunundvierzig Euro |

Two habits to copy. First, you don't say "and" or "Cent" in the middle: 3,50 € is just *drei Euro fünfzig*. Second, *Euro* doesn't take a plural ending after a number: *zehn Euro*, never *zehn Euros*. The same goes for *Cent*: *fünfzig Cent*.

### Asking what it costs

There are two equally common questions:

- *Was kostet das Brot?* / *Wie viel kostet das Brot?* — How much is the bread?
- *Was kosten die Äpfel?* / *Wie viel kosten die Äpfel?* — How much are the apples?

The verb agrees with the thing: one thing *kostet*, several things *kosten*. The answer: *Das Brot kostet 2,80 €.* *Die Äpfel kosten 3,20 € das Kilo* (3.20 a kilo). At the till you'll hear the total as *Das macht 8,40 €* — That's 8.40.

*wie viel* (how much, how many) is two words. You also use it for other quantities: *Wie viel Geld hast du?* — How much money do you have?

## Quantities: no "of"

To buy a kilo of apples, say *ein Kilo Äpfel*. German puts the amount straight in front of the food, with no word for "of".

| German | English |
|---|---|
| ein Kilo Äpfel | a kilo of apples |
| 200 Gramm Käse | 200 grams of cheese |
| ein Liter Milch | a litre of milk |
| eine Flasche Wein | a bottle of wine |
| eine Packung Nudeln | a packet of pasta |
| ein Stück Kuchen | a piece of cake |

Measures that are masculine or neuter (*das Kilo*, *das Gramm*, *der Liter*, *das Stück*) stay singular after a number: *zwei Kilo Kartoffeln, drei Liter Wasser, zwei Stück Kuchen*. Feminine containers take their plural: *zwei Flaschen Wasser, drei Packungen Reis*. An easy rule of thumb: if it ends in *-e* or *-ung* like *Flasche* or *Packung*, use the plural.

The amount and the food together are one object, so the article of the measure word changes as usual: *Ich kaufe einen Liter Milch* (der Liter → einen).

## dieser and welcher

*dieser* means "this" (or "that", when you point); a pointing word like this is called a **[[demonstrative]]**. *welcher* means "which". Both take the same endings as *der, die, das* — compare the last letters.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| article | der / den | die | das | die |
| nominative | dieser / welcher | diese / welche | dieses / welches | diese / welche |
| accusative | diesen / welchen | diese / welche | dieses / welches | diese / welche |

Once again only the masculine changes in the accusative, and it gets the same *-n* as *den*: *der → den*, *dieser → diesen*, *welcher → welchen*.

- *Welcher Käse ist gut?* — Which cheese is good? *Dieser Käse ist sehr gut.* — This cheese is very good.
- *Welchen Wein möchten Sie?* — Which wine would you like? *Ich nehme diesen Wein.* — I'll take this wine.
- *Welche Flasche kostet 4 Euro?* — Which bottle costs 4 euros? *Diese.* — This one.
- *Welches Brot ist frisch?* — Which bread is fresh? (*frisch* = fresh) *Dieses Brot hier.* — This bread here.

You can drop the noun when it's clear: *Ich nehme diesen.* — I'll take this one (a masculine thing).

## es gibt: there is, there are

*es gibt* means "there is" or "there are". It never changes for plural, and the thing that exists is in the accusative.

- *Hier gibt es einen Supermarkt.* — There's a supermarket here.
- *Gibt es hier eine Bäckerei?* — Is there a bakery here?
- *Heute gibt es Fisch.* — There's fish today.
- *Es gibt keinen Reis mehr.* — There's no rice left. (*mehr* = more, any more)
- *Es gibt viele Geschäfte.* — There are many shops. (*viele* = many)

Use *es gibt* for what exists or is available somewhere. Use *Das ist …* to identify a thing in front of you.

## Shopping verbs

All of these take an accusative object.

| German | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| kaufen | to buy | *Ich kaufe einen Apfel.* — I'm buying an apple. |
| brauchen | to need | *Wir brauchen Brot und Milch.* — We need bread and milk. |
| suchen | to look for | *Ich suche den Markt.* — I'm looking for the market. |
| bezahlen | to pay (for) | *Er bezahlt den Kaffee.* — He's paying for the coffee. |
| kosten | to cost | *Das kostet 5 Euro.* — That costs 5 euros. |

Note that *suchen* and *bezahlen* need no preposition: "look *for*" and "pay *for*" are just *suchen* and *bezahlen* plus the object.

Some useful little words: *viel* (a lot, much), *wenig* (little, not much), *alles* (everything), *zusammen* (together). *Das kostet viel.* — That costs a lot. *Ich habe wenig Geld.* — I have little money. *Ist das alles?* — Is that everything? In a café the waiter asks *Zusammen oder getrennt?* — Together or separately? (*getrennt* = separately.)

Most short shopping conversations follow the same steps, and the dialogue below does too:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The steps of a shopping conversation
  accDescr: A shopping conversation at a market stall goes in seven steps. One, greet: Guten Tag. Two, ask about the price or whether there is something: Was kostet der Käse? or Gibt es Eier? Three, choose with welcher and dieser: Welchen Käse? Diesen, bitte. Four, say the amount with no word for of: 200 Gramm Käse, ein Kilo Äpfel. Five, finish: Das ist alles. Six, the seller gives the total: Das macht acht Euro. Seven, pay and get your change: Und zwei Euro zurück.
  A["1 Greet: Guten Tag!"] --> B["2 Ask: Was kostet …? Gibt es …?"]
  B --> C["3 Choose: Welchen Käse? Diesen, bitte."]
  C --> D["4 Amount: 200 Gramm Käse, ein Kilo Äpfel"]
  D --> E["5 Finish: Das ist alles."]
  E --> F["6 Seller: Das macht 8 Euro."]
  F --> G["7 Pay: Hier sind 10 Euro. Und 2 Euro zurück."]
```

## Dialogue: At the market

> Verkäuferin: Guten Tag! Was brauchen Sie?
>
> Lena: Guten Tag! Was kosten die Äpfel?
>
> Verkäuferin: Welche? Diese hier kosten 2,40 € das Kilo, und diese dort 3,10 €.
>
> Lena: Dann nehme ich die hier. Ein Kilo, bitte. Und 200 Gramm Käse.
>
> Verkäuferin: Gern. Welchen Käse möchten Sie? Der Gouda ist heute im Angebot: 100 Gramm kosten nur 1,20 €.
>
> Lena: Super, dann 200 Gramm Gouda. Gibt es auch Eier?
>
> Verkäuferin: Ja, natürlich. Zehn Stück kosten 3,20 €.
>
> Lena: Gut, zehn Eier, bitte. Das ist alles. Was macht das zusammen?
>
> Verkäuferin: Das macht zusammen acht Euro.
>
> Lena: Hier sind zehn Euro.
>
> Verkäuferin: Und zwei Euro zurück. Vielen Dank und einen schönen Tag noch!

In English:

> Saleswoman: Hello! What do you need?
>
> Lena: Hello! How much are the apples?
>
> Saleswoman: Which ones? These here are 2.40 a kilo, and those there 3.10.
>
> Lena: Then I'll take these here. A kilo, please. And 200 grams of cheese.
>
> Saleswoman: Sure. Which cheese would you like? The Gouda is on special offer today: 100 grams cost only 1.20.
>
> Lena: Great, 200 grams of Gouda then. Are there eggs too?
>
> Saleswoman: Yes, of course. Ten cost 3.20.
>
> Lena: Good, ten eggs, please. That's everything. What does that come to altogether?
>
> Saleswoman: That's eight euros altogether.
>
> Lena: Here's ten euros.
>
> Saleswoman: And two euros back. Thank you and have a nice day!

Check the maths: 2,40 + 2,40 + 3,20 = 8,00 €. *Verkäuferin* is a female shop assistant (lesson 7 had *der Verkäufer*). *im Angebot* means "on special offer"; take it as a fixed phrase. *zurück* = back; *einen schönen Tag noch* = have a nice day.

## Places to shop

*das Geschäft* is the general word for a shop. *der Supermarkt* is a supermarket, *der Markt* an open-air market, *die Bäckerei* a bakery (from *der Bäcker*, the baker). In a supermarket you pay at *die Kasse*, the checkout, and you look for *das Angebot*, the special offer. *der Preis* is the price: *Der Preis ist gut.*

## Pronunciation

- *Euro* is "OY-ro": *eu* sounds like the *oy* in "boy".
- *Bäckerei* is stressed on the last syllable: bä-cke-REI. Most words ending in *-ei* do this.
- *Supermarkt*: stress on the first syllable, SU-per-markt, and say the *k* and the *t*.
- *Million* is mil-YOHN, stressed on the last syllable.
- *Gramm* and *Kilo*: short *a* in *Gramm*, long *i* in *Kilo*.

## Common mistakes

- *zehn Euros*, *zwei Kilos* — No plural after a number: *zehn Euro, zwei Kilo*.
- *ein Kilo von Äpfeln* — No *von* after a measure: *ein Kilo Äpfel*.
- *Wie viel kosten das?* — One thing, singular verb: *Wie viel kostet das?*
- Reading *1.500 €* as "one and a half euros". The point is the thousands separator: 1,500 euros.
- *Welche Käse möchten Sie?* — *Käse* is masculine and the object: *Welchen Käse …?*
- *Es gibt ein Supermarkt.* — *es gibt* takes the accusative: *einen Supermarkt*.
- *Ich suche für eine Bäckerei.* — No preposition: *Ich suche eine Bäckerei.*

## Key points

- Big numbers are one word: *dreihundertsiebenundvierzig*. Only *Million* is separate.
- A point separates thousands, a comma marks decimals and cents: *1.000*, *3,50 €*.
- Say prices as *drei Euro fünfzig*; no plural after numbers: *zehn Euro*.
- Amount + food with no "of": *ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Flasche Wasser*.
- *dieser* and *welcher* take the endings of *der/die/das*; masculine accusative is *diesen, welchen*.
- *es gibt* + accusative = there is / there are.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Days, times and the clock
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can count, order food and pay. Now you need to say when things happen: what time it is, when the shop opens, on which day you work, and how often you do something. This lesson teaches the clock (the official 24-hour way and the everyday way), the days of the week and the parts of the day, the little prepositions *um*, *am*, *von … bis* that go with them, and a few words for how often. The numbers you need are 0 to 59, which you know from lesson 3.

## What time is it?

There are two ways to ask, and both are everyday German:

- *Wie spät ist es?* — What time is it? (literally "How late is it?")
- *Wie viel Uhr ist es?* — What time is it? (literally "How much clock is it?")

The answer always starts with *Es ist …*: *Es ist acht Uhr.* — It's eight o'clock.

*die Uhr* is the clock or watch from lesson 5. In times it means "o'clock", and it never takes a plural: *Es ist zehn Uhr*, not *zehn Uhren*.

## The official time

Timetables, radio, shops, appointments and anything written use the 24-hour clock. You say the hour, then *Uhr*, then the minutes:

| Written | Said | English |
|---|---|---|
| 7:00 | sieben Uhr | 7 a.m. |
| 8:15 | acht Uhr fünfzehn | 8:15 a.m. |
| 12:30 | zwölf Uhr dreißig | 12:30 p.m. |
| 14:05 | vierzehn Uhr fünf | 2:05 p.m. |
| 19:45 | neunzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig | 7:45 p.m. |
| 0:20 | null Uhr zwanzig | 12:20 a.m. |

*Uhr* sits between the hours and the minutes, where English writes the colon. Germans often write *14.05 Uhr* with a point, or *14:05 Uhr*.

## The everyday time

When people talk, they normally use the 12-hour clock and count minutes *nach* (after, past) and *vor* (before, to) the hour.

| Time | Said |
|---|---|
| 3:00 | drei (Uhr) |
| 3:05 | fünf nach drei |
| 3:10 | zehn nach drei |
| 3:15 | Viertel nach drei |
| 3:20 | zwanzig nach drei |
| 3:30 | halb vier |
| 3:40 | zwanzig vor vier |
| 3:45 | Viertel vor vier |
| 3:50 | zehn vor vier |
| 3:55 | fünf vor vier |

*das Viertel* is a quarter. *Viertel nach drei* is a quarter past three and *Viertel vor vier* a quarter to four, just like English.

### The famous trap: halb

*halb vier* does not mean half past four. It means "half (of the way) to four", so 3:30. Think of the hour you are moving towards: at 3:30 you are halfway to four. *halb eins* is 12:30, *halb acht* is 7:30.

The clock below shows the whole system for the hour between three and four. The right half counts *nach drei*, the left half counts *vor vier*, and the bottom is *halb vier*:

![A clock face showing the hour between 3:00 and 4:00, with the hands at half past three. A green band on the right, from 12 to 4, is labeled nach drei (5, 10, 20 past). A purple band on the left, from 8 to 12, is labeled vor vier (20, 10, 5 to). The 3 is labeled 3:15 Viertel nach drei and the 9 is labeled 3:45 Viertel vor vier. A yellow band at the bottom is labeled 3:30 halb vier (halfway to four), with 3:25 fünf vor halb vier and 3:35 fünf nach halb vier.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

People also count from *halb*: *fünf vor halb vier* is 3:25 and *fünf nach halb vier* is 3:35. You don't have to say these yourself, but you will hear them.

In parts of southern and eastern Germany and in Austria you may also hear *viertel vier* for 3:15 and *drei viertel vier* (also written *dreiviertel vier*) for 3:45, counting quarters towards the next hour like *halb*. Everyone understands *Viertel nach* and *Viertel vor*, so use those.

### One o'clock

With *Uhr*, one is *ein*: *Es ist ein Uhr.* Without *Uhr*, it is *eins*: *Es ist eins.* Never say *eins Uhr*.

### Uhr or Stunde?

*Uhr* tells you the time on the clock. *die Stunde* is an hour as a length of time, and *die Minute* a minute.

- *Es ist zwei Uhr.* — It's two o'clock.
- *Der Film ist zwei Stunden lang.* — The film is two hours long.
- *Ich warte zehn Minuten.* — I'm waiting ten minutes. (*warten* = to wait)

To ask how long, say *Wie lange?*: *Wie lange arbeitest du heute?* — *Acht Stunden.*

## Days, parts of the day and the week

All days are masculine and capitalized, because they are nouns.

| Day | Short | Memory hook |
|---|---|---|
| der Montag | Mo | moon day, like Monday |
| der Dienstag | Di | |
| der Mittwoch | Mi | *Mitte* = middle: mid-week |
| der Donnerstag | Do | *Donner* = thunder: Thor's day, like Thursday |
| der Freitag | Fr | like Friday |
| der Samstag | Sa | in northern Germany also *der Sonnabend* |
| der Sonntag | So | *Sonne* = sun: Sunday |

*die Woche* is the week and *das Wochenende* the weekend (*Ende* = end). *der Tag* is the day.

The parts of the day are masculine too, except the night:

| German | Roughly | English |
|---|---|---|
| der Morgen | 5 to 9 | the morning |
| der Vormittag | 9 to 12 | the late morning, before noon |
| der Mittag | 12 to 14 | noon, midday |
| der Nachmittag | 14 to 18 | the afternoon |
| der Abend | 18 to 23 | the evening |
| die Nacht | 23 to 5 | the night |

*vor* means before and *nach* means after, so *Vormittag* is "before midday" and *Nachmittag* "after midday".

On a 24-hour line the parts of the day look like this:

![A bar from 0 to 24 hours divided into the parts of the day: die Nacht from 0 to 5, der Morgen from 5 to 9, der Vormittag from 9 to 12, der Mittag from 12 to 14, der Nachmittag from 14 to 18, der Abend from 18 to 23 and the night again from 23 to 24. The title says the edges are rough, not fixed.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Today, tomorrow, yesterday

*heute* (today, lesson 4), *morgen* (tomorrow) and *gestern* (yesterday) combine with the parts of the day: *heute Abend* (this evening), *gestern Abend* (last night, yesterday evening), *morgen Nachmittag* (tomorrow afternoon). Careful: *morgen* in small letters is tomorrow, *der Morgen* with a capital is the morning. Tomorrow morning is *morgen früh*, not *morgen Morgen* (*früh* = early).

## When? um, am, von … bis

| Preposition | Used with | Example |
|---|---|---|
| um | clock times | *um acht Uhr* — at eight o'clock |
| am | days, parts of the day, the weekend | *am Montag, am Abend, am Wochenende* — on Monday, in the evening, at the weekend |
| in der | the night | *in der Nacht* — at night |
| von … bis | from … until | *von neun bis fünf* — from nine to five |

*am* is short for *an dem*, but you can learn it as one word. Notice that the night is the exception: not *am Nacht* but *in der Nacht*.

To pick the right word, ask what kind of time you mean:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: um, am, in der or von … bis?
  accDescr: To choose the little word before a time, ask what kind of time it is. A clock time takes um, as in um acht Uhr. A day or the weekend takes am, as in am Montag and am Wochenende. A part of the day also takes am, as in am Abend, except the night, which is in der Nacht. A stretch of time from one point to another takes von … bis, as in von neun bis fünf.
  Q{"What kind of time is it?"}
  Q -- "a clock time" --> U["um acht Uhr"]
  Q -- "a day or the weekend" --> A["am Montag, am Wochenende"]
  Q -- "a part of the day" --> P{"Is it the night?"}
  P -- no --> A2["am Morgen, am Abend"]
  P -- yes --> N["in der Nacht"]
  Q -- "from … until …" --> V["von neun bis fünf"]
```

- *Der Kurs beginnt um halb neun.* — The course starts at half past eight. (*beginnen* = to begin)
- *Am Freitag arbeite ich nicht.* — I don't work on Friday.
- *Am Nachmittag lerne ich Deutsch.* — In the afternoon I study German.
- *Die Bäckerei ist von sieben bis achtzehn Uhr offen.* — The bakery is open from 7 a.m. to 6 p.m. (*offen* = open)
- *Ich arbeite bis fünf.* — I work until five.
- *Wann kommst du? — Um sieben.* — When are you coming? — At seven.

When a time phrase comes first, the verb stays in second place and the subject moves after it: *Am Freitag arbeite ich nicht.* You met verb-second word order in lesson 4; lesson 12 practises it in detail.

## How often?

A **[[frequency adverb]]** says how often something happens. You know *immer* (always) and *oft* (often) from lesson 4; add *manchmal* (sometimes) and *nie* (never).

| immer | oft | manchmal | nie |
|---|---|---|---|
| always | often | sometimes | never |

They usually come straight after the verb, or after the subject when the subject follows the verb:

- *Am Morgen trinke ich immer Kaffee.* — In the morning I always drink coffee.
- *Wir essen oft Nudeln.* — We often eat pasta.
- *Am Sonntag schlafe ich manchmal bis zehn.* — On Sundays I sometimes sleep until ten. (*schlafen* = to sleep)
- *Er kommt nie zu spät.* — He's never late. (*zu spät* = too late)

*nie* is already negative, so never add *nicht* to it. *früh* (early) and *spät* (late) are the opposites you need here: *Es ist schon spät.* — It's already late.

For "every day" German uses the accusative from lesson 9: *jeden Tag* (der Tag → jeden), *jede Woche*, *jedes Wochenende*.

## Dialogue: Do you have time on Saturday?

> Anna: Hallo Tom! Hast du am Samstag Zeit?
>
> Tom: Am Samstag? Am Vormittag arbeite ich. Aber am Nachmittag habe ich Zeit.
>
> Anna: Super! Möchtest du einen Kaffee trinken?
>
> Tom: Gern! Wann denn? Um zwei?
>
> Anna: Um zwei habe ich noch Deutschkurs. Der Kurs ist von zehn bis halb drei.
>
> Tom: Dann um drei?
>
> Anna: Ja, um drei. Und ich habe Zeit bis sechs. Am Abend kommt meine Schwester.
>
> Tom: Gut. Dann bis Samstag um drei!
>
> Anna: Bis Samstag! Tschüss!

In English:

> Anna: Hi Tom! Do you have time on Saturday?
>
> Tom: On Saturday? In the morning I work. But in the afternoon I have time.
>
> Anna: Great! Would you like to have a coffee?
>
> Tom: I'd love to! When? At two?
>
> Anna: At two I still have my German course. The course is from ten until half past two.
>
> Tom: At three, then?
>
> Anna: Yes, at three. And I have time until six. In the evening my sister is coming.
>
> Tom: Good. See you on Saturday at three, then!
>
> Anna: See you Saturday! Bye!

*die Zeit* means time in general: *Hast du Zeit?* — Do you have time? *denn* in *Wann denn?* just makes the question sound friendlier. *Bis Samstag!* (until Saturday) is how you say "see you on Saturday".

## Pronunciation

- *Viertel*: the *v* is an *f* and the *ie* is short here: FIR-tel.
- *Uhr* sounds like "oor" with a long *u*.
- *Abend* and *Tag* end in a *t* and a *k* sound: AH-bent, tahk. That's the final devoicing from lesson 1.
- *Mittwoch* is stressed on the first syllable: MIT-voch, with the *ch* of *Bach*. *Nacht* has the same *ch*.
- *Dienstag*: long *ie*, DEENS-tahk. Don't confuse it with *Donnerstag*, DON-ners-tahk.
- *gestern*: GES-tern, with a hard *g*.

## Common mistakes

- *halb drei* is 2:30, not 3:30. Count towards the next hour.
- *am acht Uhr* — Clock times take *um*: *um acht Uhr*.
- *in Montag*, *an Montag* — Days take *am*: *am Montag*.
- *am Nacht* — The exception: *in der Nacht*.
- *Ich lerne zwei Uhr.* — For a length of time use *Stunden*: *Ich lerne zwei Stunden.*
- *Es ist eins Uhr.* — Say *ein Uhr* or just *eins*.
- *morgen Morgen* — Say *morgen früh*.
- *Ich nicht nie esse Fisch.* — *nie* is enough, and the verb is second: *Ich esse nie Fisch.*

## Key points

- Ask *Wie spät ist es?* or *Wie viel Uhr ist es?* and answer *Es ist …*.
- Official time: hours + *Uhr* + minutes (*vierzehn Uhr zehn*). Everyday time: *nach*, *vor*, *Viertel*, *halb*.
- *halb* points to the next hour: *halb vier* = 3:30.
- *um* + clock time, *am* + day or part of the day, *in der Nacht*, *von … bis*.
- *Uhr* = o'clock, *Stunde* = an hour of time.
- Days and parts of the day are masculine nouns (except *die Nacht*); *morgen* = tomorrow, *der Morgen* = morning.
- Frequency: *immer, oft, manchmal, nie*, usually after the verb.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: A day in my life: separable verbs and word order
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

With the clock and the days from lesson 11 you can say when things happen. Now you'll describe a whole day: getting up, showering, going to work, shopping, watching TV. Many of these everyday actions are expressed in German by a special kind of verb that splits in two, the **[[separable verb]]**. You'll also practise putting a time word first (*Um sieben stehe ich auf*) and linking actions with *zuerst*, *dann* and *danach*.

## Separable verbs: the verb that splits

Look at the verb *aufstehen* (to get up). In the dictionary it is one word. In a sentence it breaks apart:

- *Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.* — I get up at seven o'clock.

The main part, *stehen*, is conjugated and sits in its usual place, second. The small front part, *auf*, jumps to the very end of the sentence. That front part is called the **[[separable prefix]]**. English does something similar with phrasal verbs: "I get *up*", "I pick you *up*", "Call me *back*". German simply pushes the little word all the way to the end.

| | aufstehen | anfangen | fernsehen |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | stehe … auf | fange … an | sehe … fern |
| du | stehst … auf | fängst … an | siehst … fern |
| er / sie / es | steht … auf | fängt … an | sieht … fern |
| wir | stehen … auf | fangen … an | sehen … fern |
| ihr | steht … auf | fangt … an | seht … fern |
| sie / Sie | stehen … auf | fangen … an | sehen … fern |

The verb part keeps all its habits. *fangen* changes a→ä (*du fängst, er fängt*) and *sehen* changes e→ie (*du siehst, er sieht*), so *anfangen* and *fernsehen* do too.

### The separable verbs in this lesson

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| aufstehen | to get up | *Wir stehen früh auf.* — We get up early. |
| anfangen | to begin, to start | *Der Film fängt um acht an.* — The film starts at eight. |
| einkaufen | to go shopping | *Am Samstag kaufe ich ein.* — On Saturday I go shopping. |
| anrufen | to phone | *Ich rufe meine Mutter an.* — I'm phoning my mother. |
| fernsehen | to watch TV | *Siehst du oft fern?* — Do you often watch TV? |
| aufräumen | to tidy up | *Er räumt die Küche auf.* — He's tidying the kitchen. |
| mitkommen | to come along | *Kommst du mit?* — Are you coming along? |
| abholen | to pick up | *Ich hole das Kind um vier ab.* — I pick up the child at four. |
| ankommen | to arrive | *Der Zug kommt um neun an.* — The train arrives at nine. |

(*die Küche* = kitchen, *der Zug* = train.)

The prefixes often carry a hint of their meaning: *auf* = up, *an* = on or at, *ein* = in, *mit* = with or along, *ab* = off or away, *fern* = far (*fernsehen* is literally "far-see", like "tele-vision").

### Where everything goes

The rule is the same in statements and in questions: the conjugated verb in its usual place, the prefix at the very end, everything else in between.

- *Ich rufe heute Abend meine Schwester an.* — I'm calling my sister this evening.
- *Wann stehst du am Sonntag auf?* — When do you get up on Sundays?
- *Räumst du dein Zimmer auf?* — Are you tidying your room? (*das Zimmer* = room)
- *Wir kaufen nicht ein.* — We're not going shopping. (*nicht* comes before the prefix.)

When the verb is in the infinitive, for example after *möchte*, it stays in one piece at the end: *Ich möchte heute einkaufen.* — I'd like to go shopping today.

Here is one sentence taken apart, slot by slot:

![Five boxes in a row: Morgen früh, labeled Position 1; rufe, labeled Position 2 (verb); ich, labeled Subject; meine Mutter, labeled Object; and an., labeled Prefix (end). A bracket joins rufe and an, with the note rufe … an = anrufen (to phone): the verb splits. Below: Tomorrow morning I'm phoning my mother.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

And here is the whole decision as a chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Building a sentence with a separable verb
  accDescr: Start with a separable verb such as anrufen. If the sentence already has möchte, the separable verb stays in one piece at the end: Ich möchte meine Mutter anrufen. If not, split it. Conjugate the verb part and put it in position 2 (rufe), then put the prefix at the very end (an): Ich rufe meine Mutter an.
  A["A separable verb: anrufen"] --> B{"Is there a möchte in the sentence?"}
  B -- yes --> W["Keep it whole at the end: Ich möchte meine Mutter anrufen."]
  B -- no --> C["Conjugate the verb part, position 2: rufe"]
  C --> D["Prefix to the very end: an"]
  D --> E["Ich rufe meine Mutter an."]
```

### Not every verb splits

Only these little prefixes split off. Ordinary verbs stay whole, even when they look long:

- *frühstücken* (to have breakfast) is not separable: *Ich frühstücke um acht.* Never *Ich stücke früh*.
- *duschen* (to shower), *kochen* (to cook), *putzen* (to clean) are regular: *Ich dusche, du duschst; ich koche; du putzt.*
- *schlafen* (to sleep) and *waschen* (to wash) change a→ä: *du schläfst, er schläft; du wäschst, er wäscht.*

## Word order: time first, verb second

You learned the verb-second rule in lesson 4: in a statement the verb is the second element, and the first place does not have to be the subject. When a time phrase comes first, the subject moves behind the verb. This swap is called **[[inversion]]**, and it is how Germans tell a day in order:

| Position 1 | Position 2 (verb) | Subject | Rest | End |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | stehe | | um sieben | auf. |
| Um sieben | stehe | ich | | auf. |
| Am Montag | arbeite | ich | bis fünf. | |
| Normalerweise | frühstücke | ich | um acht. | |
| Dann | rufe | ich | meine Mutter | an. |

German speakers start sentences with a time phrase all the time; it sounds natural and lets you tell a day in order. The subject still comes right after the verb, and the prefix still goes to the end.

### Telling things in order

These words put actions in a sequence, and each one fills position 1 on its own:

- *zuerst* — first (of all)
- *dann* — then
- *danach* — after that, afterwards
- *später* — later

*Zuerst dusche ich, dann frühstücke ich. Danach räume ich auf, und später kaufe ich ein.* — First I shower, then I have breakfast. After that I tidy up, and later I go shopping.

Note the last part: *und* doesn't count as a position, so after *und später* the verb comes next: *und später kaufe ich ein*.

*normalerweise* (normally, usually) works the same way: *Normalerweise sehe ich am Abend fern.*

## Reading: Jonas's day

> Ich heiße Jonas und ich bin Koch. Normalerweise stehe ich um neun Uhr auf. Zuerst dusche ich, dann frühstücke ich: ein Kaffee und ein Brötchen. Danach räume ich die Wohnung auf, und um elf kaufe ich ein. Meine Arbeit fängt um zwölf Uhr an. Ich koche bis drei, dann habe ich zwei Stunden Pause. Am Abend ist das Restaurant immer voll. Um elf Uhr habe ich Feierabend. Dann bin ich sehr müde. Ich sehe noch eine Stunde fern und gehe um eins ins Bett. Am Montag arbeite ich nicht. Dann rufe ich meine Eltern an, oder ich hole meine Freundin ab und wir kochen zusammen.

In English:

> My name is Jonas and I'm a cook. Normally I get up at nine o'clock. First I shower, then I have breakfast: a coffee and a roll. After that I tidy the flat, and at eleven I go shopping. My work starts at twelve. I cook until three, then I have a two-hour break. In the evening the restaurant is always full. At eleven I finish work. Then I'm very tired. I watch TV for another hour and go to bed at one. On Mondays I don't work. Then I phone my parents, or I pick up my girlfriend and we cook together.

(*die Wohnung* = flat, apartment; *die Pause* = break; *voll* = full; *noch eine Stunde* = for another hour; *ins Bett* = to bed.)

*der Feierabend* is the time after work, and *Ich habe Feierabend* means "I've finished work for the day". It's a very German word and a very popular one. *der Alltag* is everyday life, the normal routine: *Mein Alltag ist ziemlich ruhig* (*ruhig* = quiet).

## Dialogue: Are you coming along?

> Lukas: Wann stehst du morgen auf?
>
> Sara: Um halb sechs. Mein Zug kommt um acht in Köln an.
>
> Lukas: So früh! Ich habe morgen frei. Zuerst schlafe ich lange, dann räume ich die Küche auf.
>
> Sara: Und danach?
>
> Lukas: Danach kaufe ich ein. Und am Abend gehen Tim und ich ins Kino. Kommst du mit?
>
> Sara: Wann fängt der Film an?
>
> Lukas: Um acht.
>
> Sara: Nein danke, morgen Abend bin ich sicher müde. Ich gehe früh ins Bett.
>
> Lukas: Schade! Vielleicht am Samstag?
>
> Sara: Ja, am Samstag komme ich gern mit!

In English:

> Lukas: When are you getting up tomorrow?
>
> Sara: At half past five. My train arrives in Cologne at eight.
>
> Lukas: So early! I've got the day off tomorrow. First I'll sleep in, then I'll tidy the kitchen.
>
> Sara: And after that?
>
> Lukas: After that I'll do the shopping. And in the evening Tim and I are going to the cinema. Are you coming along?
>
> Sara: When does the film start?
>
> Lukas: At eight.
>
> Sara: No thanks, tomorrow evening I'll surely be tired. I'm going to bed early.
>
> Lukas: Pity! Maybe on Saturday?
>
> Sara: Yes, on Saturday I'd love to come along!

German often uses the present tense for the future when a time word makes it clear: *Morgen kaufe ich ein* — Tomorrow I'll go shopping. (*frei haben* = to have the day off, *ins Kino* = to the cinema, *sicher* = surely, *schade* = pity, *vielleicht* = maybe.)

*fertig* means finished or ready: *Ich bin fertig!* — I'm done! / I'm ready! In casual speech it can also mean exhausted.

## Pronunciation

- Separable verbs are stressed on the prefix: AUF-stehen, AN-rufen, FERN-sehen, EIN-kaufen, MIT-kommen, AB-holen. *frühstücken* is also stressed at the front (FRÜH-stücken) but never splits, because *früh* is not a separable prefix. Stress alone doesn't tell you, so learn which verbs split.
- In a sentence the prefix at the end keeps a strong stress: *Ich stehe um sieben AUF.*
- *duschen*: the *sch* is like English "sh"; the *u* is short in some regions and long in others (DU-shen or DOO-shen), and both are fine.
- *müde*: long *ü*; round your lips as for "oo" and say "ee".
- *Feierabend*: FEI-er-ah-bent; *ei* as in "eye".

## Common mistakes

- *Ich aufstehe um sieben.* — Split it: *Ich stehe um sieben auf.*
- *Ich stehe auf um sieben.* — The prefix goes to the very end: *Ich stehe um sieben auf.*
- *Um sieben ich stehe auf.* — After a time phrase the verb comes next: *Um sieben stehe ich auf.*
- *Ich rufe an meine Mutter.* — The person goes in the middle: *Ich rufe meine Mutter an.*
- *Er fangt um acht an.* — Keep the stem change: *er fängt an*.
- *Ich stücke früh.* — *frühstücken* doesn't split: *Ich frühstücke.*
- *Dann ich dusche.* — *dann* takes position 1, so: *Dann dusche ich.*

## Key points

- A separable verb splits in a statement or question: the verb part is second (or first in a yes/no question), the prefix goes to the end.
- The prefix is stressed: AUF-stehen.
- The verb part keeps its stem change: *er fängt an, du siehst fern*.
- In the infinitive (after *möchte*) the verb stays together: *Ich möchte einkaufen.*
- A time phrase or *zuerst, dann, danach, später, normalerweise* can fill position 1; then the verb comes second and the subject follows it.
- *und* doesn't count as a position: *und dann frühstücke ich*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Brötchen, Kaffee und Kuchen — eating the German way
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 9 you ordered in a café with *möchten* and the accusative, and in lesson 10 you shopped at the market and paid. This honors lesson looks at the culture around those words: when Germans eat what, why the bread roll has five names, and how people pay and tip. You'll also learn the politest way to order, *Ich hätte gern …*, and how to ask for another one with *noch ein*.

Everything here builds on grammar you already know. Descriptions of "how Germans eat" are generalizations: habits differ between families, regions and generations.

## A day of meals

The picture shows a traditional day of meals. It is simplified, but you'll meet all four ideas in German life and texts.

![A timeline from 6 to 21 Uhr with four meals. At about 7 Uhr, das Frühstück (morning): a cup of coffee and a roll. At about 12:30, das Mittagessen (often the warm meal): a steaming plate of food. At about 15:30, Kaffee und Kuchen (afternoon, often Sunday): a slice of cake and a cup of coffee. At about 18:30, das Abendbrot (cold, with bread): slices of bread and cheese on a board. The title says the picture is simplified.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

- *das Frühstück* — breakfast. On weekdays it is often quick. On weekends many families sit down to fresh *Brötchen* with butter, jam (*die Marmelade*), honey (*der Honig*), cheese, cold meat and a boiled egg.
- *das Mittagessen* — lunch. Traditionally the main warm meal of the day, and many people still eat warm at midday, for example in a work canteen (*die Kantine*). At work, colleagues often greet each other at lunchtime with *Mahlzeit!* — literally "mealtime!" — which works as both "hello" and "enjoy your lunch".
- *Kaffee und Kuchen* — coffee and cake, around three or four in the afternoon, especially on Sundays and birthdays.
- *das Abendbrot* — "evening bread": a cold supper of bread, butter, cheese, cold meat and maybe a salad. The word is used mostly in northern and eastern Germany; everyone also says *das Abendessen*. Many working families now eat their warm meal in the evening instead.

Before a meal, people say *Guten Appetit!* (enjoy your meal), and the answer is *Danke, gleichfalls!* (thanks, you too). When you've had enough, say *Ich bin satt* — I'm full. Don't translate "I'm full" word for word: *Ich bin voll* can sound like "I'm drunk" in casual speech.

## The bakery and the bread roll

Germany is a bread country. Even small towns usually have a bakery, and in 2014 "German bread culture" (*die deutsche Brotkultur*) was added to Germany's national list of intangible cultural heritage. A typical bakery sells dark rye breads, wholegrain breads with seeds, white rolls, pretzels (*die Brezel*) and cakes. You buy bread by the loaf or ask for it sliced; a slice is *eine Scheibe*, and it works like the quantities in lesson 10: *eine Scheibe Brot*, *zwei Scheiben Käse* (no "of", and feminine *Scheibe* takes the plural).

The plain bread roll is the star, and its name changes as you travel. This is a **[[regional variant]]**: a word that is normal in one region but not everywhere. The map in people's heads looks roughly like this (simplified: the borders are fuzzy, and *Brötchen* is understood everywhere):

| Word | Where you'll hear it |
|---|---|
| das Brötchen | most of northern and central Germany; the standard word |
| die Semmel | Bavaria and Austria, and also parts of eastern Germany such as Saxony |
| die Schrippe | Berlin and around it |
| der Weck, das Weckle | the southwest (for example Baden-Württemberg) |
| das Rundstück | Hamburg and the far north |

In Bavaria the pretzel is also called *die Breze* or *die Brezn*. Recognize these words on a bakery sign; you don't need to use them.

### Same food, different words

German is the language of Germany, Austria, much of Switzerland and some other places, and each has its own food words. **[[Standard German]]** (*Hochdeutsch*), the form taught in this course, is understood everywhere, but in Austria you'll see these on menus and in shops:

| Germany | Austria | English |
|---|---|---|
| die Kartoffel | der Erdapfel (die Erdäpfel) | potato |
| die Tomate | der Paradeiser | tomato |
| die Sahne | das Schlagobers, das Obers | cream, whipped cream |
| der Quark | der Topfen | quark (a soft fresh cheese) |
| das Brötchen | die Semmel | bread roll |

*Erdapfel* means "earth apple", like French *pomme de terre*. Learn the standard word actively; recognize the others.

## Polite orders: Ich hätte gern …

*Ich möchte einen Kaffee* is perfectly polite. Many Germans, especially at a bakery counter or in a shop, say *Ich hätte gern …* instead: "I would have, gladly …" — in English, "I'd like …". *hätte* is a form of *haben* called the **[[subjunctive]]** (in German grammar, *Konjunktiv II*): the "would" form that makes a request softer. *möchte* is actually the same kind of form, from *mögen*, which is why both sound polite.

You only need four forms, and they follow the pattern of *möchte*:

| | hätte gern |
|---|---|
| ich | hätte gern |
| du | hättest gern |
| er / sie / es | hätte gern |
| wir / sie / Sie | hätten gern |

What you'd like is the object of *hätte*, so it is in the accusative, exactly as after *haben*: *Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee* (der → einen), *eine Brezel*, *ein Brötchen*, *zwei Semmeln*.

### Example 1: making an order polite

You want a coffee and a pretzel at a bakery counter. Build the sentence step by step.

1. Start with the polite frame: *Ich hätte gern …*
2. *Kaffee* is masculine (*der Kaffee*) and it is the object, so the article becomes *einen*: *einen Kaffee*.
3. *Brezel* is feminine (*die Brezel*); feminine doesn't change: *eine Brezel*.
4. Join them with *und* and add *bitte*: *Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee und eine Brezel, bitte.*

With *möchte* the accusative is the same: *Ich möchte einen Kaffee und eine Brezel, bitte.*

### Another one: noch ein

To ask for one more, put *noch* in front of the article: *noch ein*, "another one". The article still follows the accusative rule.

- *Noch einen Kaffee, bitte!* — Another coffee, please! (der Kaffee)
- *Ich hätte gern noch ein Brötchen.* — I'd like another roll. (das Brötchen)
- *Möchtest du noch eine Brezel?* — Would you like another pretzel? (die Brezel)

The opposite is *kein … mehr*, "no more": *Ich möchte keinen Kaffee mehr, danke.* — I don't want any more coffee, thanks. You met *mehr* in *Es gibt keinen Reis mehr* in lesson 10.

### Example 2: another one, or no more?

Your host asks *Möchtest du noch ein Stück Kuchen?* (Would you like another piece of cake?)

- To say yes: *Ja, gern!* or *Ja, noch ein Stück, bitte.* *das Stück* is neuter, so *ein* stays *ein*.
- To say no: *Nein danke, ich bin satt.* Or with *kein … mehr*: *Nein danke, ich möchte keinen Kuchen mehr.* *der Kuchen* is masculine and the object, so *kein* becomes *keinen*.

## Paying and tipping

In a café or restaurant you pay at the table. You call *Zahlen, bitte!* (or *Die Rechnung, bitte!*, "the bill, please"), and the server often asks *Zusammen oder getrennt?* — together or separately? Splitting the bill, with each person paying for what they had, is completely normal.

A tip (*das Trinkgeld*, "drink money") isn't added to the bill. In cafés and restaurants people usually round up or add about 5 to 10 percent, and they don't leave it on the table: they tell the server the total they want to pay. There are two ways:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Paying in a German café
  accDescr: Paying in a café in five steps. You call the server: Zahlen, bitte! The server asks: Zusammen oder getrennt? You answer, for example: Getrennt, bitte. The server says your total: Das macht 3,40 Euro. Then there are two ways to add a tip. Either you hand over a 10-euro note and say the total you want to pay, Vier Euro, bitte, and get 6 euros back; or you hand over exactly 4 euros and say Stimmt so, which means keep the change.
  A["You: Zahlen, bitte!"] --> B["Server: Zusammen oder getrennt?"]
  B --> C["You: Getrennt, bitte."]
  C --> D["Server: Das macht 3,40 Euro."]
  D --> E{"How do you add the tip?"}
  E -- "say a total" --> F["Give 10 Euro: Vier Euro, bitte. You get 6 Euro back."]
  E -- "keep the change" --> G["Give exactly 4 Euro: Stimmt so!"]
```

*Stimmt so* literally means "it's right like that": the money you handed over is the right amount, so keep the change.

Cash (*das Bargeld*) is still more common in Germany than in many other countries. Cards are now widely accepted, but some small bakeries, market stands and cafés take only cash: look for *Nur Barzahlung* or *Nur bar* (cash only).

### Example 3: working out what to say

Your coffee and cake cost 7,60 €. You want to give a tip of about 10 percent, and you have a 10-euro note.

1. Ten percent of 7,60 € is 0,76 €, so about 8,36 €. Round to a friendly number: 8,40 €.
2. Hand over the note and say the total: *Acht Euro vierzig, bitte.*
3. The server keeps 8,40 € and gives you back 10,00 − 8,40 = 1,60 €: *Und eins sechzig zurück.* (In quick speech people often drop *Euro*: *eins sechzig* = 1,60 €.)

## Reading: Sonntag bei Oma

> Am Sonntag sind mein Bruder Jonas und ich oft bei Oma in Lübeck. Wir kommen um halb drei an. Oma hat immer zwei Kuchen: einen Apfelkuchen und eine Torte mit Sahne. Um drei Uhr gibt es Kaffee und Kuchen. Jonas trinkt keinen Kaffee, er nimmt einen Kakao. Oma fragt: „Möchtest du noch ein Stück Kuchen?" Ich sage: „Nein danke, Oma, ich bin satt!" Aber Jonas isst noch ein Stück, und dann noch eins.
>
> Um sieben Uhr gibt es Abendbrot: Brot, Butter, Käse, Wurst und ein bisschen Salat. Oma kauft das Brot immer in der Bäckerei am Markt, nie im Supermarkt. Am Abend essen wir nicht warm, das ist bei Oma normal. Wir sagen „Guten Appetit!" und essen zusammen. Um neun fahren wir nach Hause. Jonas ist müde und satt, und ich bin auch satt.

In English:

> On Sundays my brother Jonas and I are often at Grandma's in Lübeck. We arrive at half past two. Grandma always has two cakes: an apple cake and a gateau with cream. At three o'clock there's coffee and cake. Jonas doesn't drink coffee; he has a hot chocolate. Grandma asks: "Would you like another piece of cake?" I say: "No thanks, Grandma, I'm full!" But Jonas eats another piece, and then another one.
>
> At seven o'clock there's Abendbrot: bread, butter, cheese, sausage and a little salad. Grandma always buys the bread at the bakery by the market, never at the supermarket. In the evening we don't eat a warm meal; that's normal at Grandma's. We say "Enjoy your meal!" and eat together. At nine we drive home. Jonas is tired and full, and I'm full too.

(*bei Oma* = at Grandma's; *die Torte* = gateau; *der Kakao* = hot chocolate; *noch eins* = another one, without a noun; *in der Bäckerei am Markt* = at the bakery by the market; *nach Hause* = home. Lübeck is in northern Germany, where *Abendbrot* is the natural word.)

## Dialogue: An der Bäckerei in München

> Verkäuferin: Grüß Gott! Was hätten Sie gern?
>
> Kunde: Grüß Gott! Ich hätte gern vier Semmeln und eine Breze, bitte.
>
> Verkäuferin: Gern. Sonst noch etwas?
>
> Kunde: Ja, noch zwei Stück Apfelkuchen.
>
> Verkäuferin: Das macht zusammen 7,10 €.
>
> Kunde: Nehmen Sie auch Karte?
>
> Verkäuferin: Leider nein, nur bar.
>
> Kunde: Kein Problem. Hier sind zehn Euro.
>
> Verkäuferin: Und 2,90 € zurück. Schönen Sonntag noch!

In English:

> Shop assistant: Hello! What would you like?
>
> Customer: Hello! I'd like four rolls and a pretzel, please.
>
> Shop assistant: Sure. Anything else?
>
> Customer: Yes, two more pieces of apple cake.
>
> Shop assistant: That's 7.10 altogether.
>
> Customer: Do you take cards too?
>
> Shop assistant: No, I'm afraid not, cash only.
>
> Customer: No problem. Here's ten euros.
>
> Shop assistant: And 2.90 back. Have a nice Sunday!

*Grüß Gott* is the everyday greeting in Bavaria and Austria, and in Munich the customer naturally says *Semmeln* and *Breze*. *Sonst noch etwas?* means "anything else?". Many bakeries open for a few hours on Sunday mornings, when most other shops are closed.

## Pronunciation

- *Semmel*: ZEM-mel; *s* before a vowel sounds like English *z*. *Brezel*: BRAY-tsel.
- *Mahlzeit*: MAAL-tsite (*ei* like "eye"); the *h* only makes the *a* long.
- *Appetit*: stressed at the end, a-pe-TEET.
- *hätte*: short *ä* like the *e* in "bet": HET-te. *Stimmt so*: SHTIMMT zo.

## Common mistakes

- *Ich hätte gern ein Kaffee.* — The object of *hätte* is accusative: *einen Kaffee*.
- *Noch ein Kaffee, bitte!* — After *noch*, the accusative rule still applies: *Noch einen Kaffee, bitte!*
- *Ich bin voll.* — Say *Ich bin satt* for "I'm full".
- Leaving coins on the table as a tip. Tell the server the total, or say *Stimmt so*.
- *zwei Scheibe Brot* — *Scheibe* is feminine and takes the plural after a number: *zwei Scheiben Brot*.
- Thinking *Semmel* or *Schrippe* is wrong German. They are regional variants, correct where they're used.

## Key points

- Traditional meals: *Frühstück*, a warm *Mittagessen*, *Kaffee und Kuchen* in the afternoon (especially on Sundays) and a cold *Abendbrot* — a simplified picture that many families vary.
- *Guten Appetit!* before eating; *Ich bin satt* when you've had enough; *Mahlzeit!* as a lunchtime greeting at work.
- The bread roll has regional names: *Brötchen*, *Semmel*, *Schrippe*, *Weck*, *Rundstück*. Austria has its own food words (*Erdapfel*, *Paradeiser*, *Topfen*).
- *Ich hätte gern* + accusative is the most polite way to order: *Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.*
- *noch ein(en)* = another one; *kein(en) … mehr* = no more.
- Pay at the table, say the total including the tip or say *Stimmt so*; some small shops take only cash.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: Planning the week — opening hours, habits and time without a preposition
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 11 you learned the clock and the little words *um*, *am* and *von … bis*, and in lesson 12 you described a day with separable verbs and a time phrase in position 1. This honors lesson takes you from one day to a whole week. You'll read real-style opening hours, say what you do regularly (*montags*, *abends*), and use a neat piece of grammar: time phrases with no preposition at all, in the accusative (*jeden Tag*, *nächsten Montag*, *eine Stunde*). You'll also learn to say "around eight" and "shortly after eight", and how to put two time phrases in one sentence.

## Reading opening hours

Every shop, bakery, doctor's practice and café has a sign with its *Öffnungszeiten* (opening hours). They use short forms for the days: *Mo, Di, Mi, Do, Fr, Sa, So*, and a dash means *bis*.

![Two door signs. Left: Bäckerei Krume, Öffnungszeiten: Mo–Fr 6:30–18:00, Sa 7:00–13:00, So 8:00–11:00, feiertags geschlossen. Right: Café am Markt, Öffnungszeiten: Di–Fr 8–18 Uhr, Sa–So 9–18 Uhr, Montag Ruhetag.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To read a line aloud, join the days with *bis* (or *von … bis*) and say the times with *von … bis*:

- *Mo–Fr 6:30–18:00* → *Montag bis Freitag von sechs Uhr dreißig bis achtzehn Uhr* (in conversation also *von halb sieben bis sechs*).
- *Sa 7:00–13:00* → *Samstag von sieben bis dreizehn Uhr*.

Three more words you'll see on signs:

- *geöffnet* — open; *geschlossen* — closed. *Heute geschlossen!* — Closed today!
- *der Ruhetag* — the "rest day": a restaurant's or café's fixed day off each week. *Montag Ruhetag* means it is closed every Monday.
- *feiertags* — on public holidays (*der Feiertag*, public holiday). *feiertags geschlossen* = closed on public holidays.

A cultural note, simplified: in Germany most shops are closed on Sundays and public holidays. The exact rules are set by each federal state, and there are exceptions: bakeries may open for a few hours on Sunday morning, and shops at petrol stations, big train stations and airports stay open. So the bakery on the sign opening *So 8:00–11:00* is completely normal.

### Example 1: Questions about the signs

Use the two signs above.

1. *Kann ich am Sonntag um halb elf Brötchen kaufen?* — Can I buy rolls on Sunday at 10:30? The bakery is open on Sunday from 8:00 to 11:00, and 10:30 is inside that time: yes.
2. *Ist das Café am Montag geöffnet?* — No: *Montag Ruhetag*. It's closed every Monday.
3. *Wie lange ist die Bäckerei am Samstag geöffnet?* — From 7:00 to 13:00: *sechs Stunden*.
4. How many hours a week is the bakery open? Monday to Friday 6:30–18:00 is 11½ hours a day, so 5 × 11,5 = 57,5 hours; plus 6 on Saturday and 3 on Sunday: 66,5 hours (*sechsundsechzigeinhalb Stunden*).

## Habits: montags, abends

In lesson 11 you said *am Montag* (on Monday) and *am Abend* (in the evening). For something you do regularly, German has a short **[[adverb of time]]** made from the noun plus *-s*, written with a small letter:

| am … (one time, or from context) | regularly: every … |
|---|---|
| am Montag | *montags* — on Mondays |
| am Sonntag | *sonntags* — on Sundays |
| am Morgen | *morgens* — in the mornings |
| am Nachmittag | *nachmittags* — in the afternoons |
| am Abend | *abends* — in the evenings |
| in der Nacht | *nachts* — at night |

Every day works the same way: *dienstags, mittwochs, donnerstags, freitags, samstags*, and also *vormittags* and *mittags*.

- *Montags arbeite ich bis sieben.* — On Mondays I work until seven.
- *Abends sehe ich oft fern.* — In the evenings I often watch TV.
- *Die Bäckerei ist sonntags geöffnet.* — The bakery is open on Sundays.

*am Montag* can also describe a habit when the context makes it clear (*Am Montag arbeite ich nicht* in lesson 12), but *montags* always means "every Monday". Remember the capital letter only at the start of a sentence: *Montags …*, but *Ich arbeite montags.*

## Time without a preposition: the accusative

Some time phrases have no preposition at all. With *jeder* (every), *nächster* (next), *dieser* (this) and *ganz* (whole), German puts the time word in the accusative. This is the **[[accusative of time]]**. You already know the endings: they are the endings of *der/den, die, das*, and as always only the masculine changes.

| | masculine | feminine | neuter |
|---|---|---|---|
| every | jeden Tag, jeden Morgen | jede Woche | jedes Jahr, jedes Wochenende |
| next | nächsten Montag, nächsten Monat | *nächste Woche* | nächstes Jahr |
| this | diesen Freitag, diesen Sommer | diese Woche | dieses Wochenende |
| the whole | den ganzen Tag | die ganze Woche | das ganze Wochenende |

(*das Jahr* = year from lesson 3; *der Monat* = month and *der Sommer* = summer, words you'll meet in lesson 16.)

- *Nächsten Montag habe ich frei.* — Next Monday I've got the day off.
- *Ich jogge jeden Morgen.* — I go jogging every morning. (*joggen* = to jog)
- *Am Samstag schlafe ich den ganzen Vormittag.* — On Saturday I sleep the whole morning.

You can also say *am nächsten Montag*, with *am*, but the short accusative form is more common.

### How long: dauern and the accusative

The same accusative says how long something lasts. The verb for "to last, to take (time)" is *dauern*: *Wie lange dauert der Film?* — How long is the film?

- *Der Film dauert zwei Stunden.* — The film lasts two hours. (plural: no change)
- *Der Kurs dauert einen Tag.* — The course takes one day. (*der Tag* → *einen Tag*)
- *Ich bleibe eine Woche in Wien.* — I'm staying in Vienna for a week. (*bleiben* = to stay)

English often adds "for"; German usually needs no word at all. (*Ich bleibe für eine Woche* is also heard, but after *dauern* the accusative always stands alone.)

### Example 2: building the phrase

Say "I go shopping every Saturday" and "The appointment takes an hour".

1. "every Saturday": *der Samstag* is masculine, *jeder* takes the masculine accusative ending *-en*: *jeden Samstag*. The verb is *einkaufen*, separable: *Ich kaufe jeden Samstag ein.* (Or with the time first: *Jeden Samstag kaufe ich ein.*)
2. "an hour": *die Stunde* is feminine, so it stays *eine Stunde*. *Der Termin* (appointment) *dauert* … : *Der Termin dauert eine Stunde.*

## Around eight, shortly after eight

| German | English |
|---|---|
| um acht | at eight |
| *gegen* acht | around eight, at about eight |
| kurz nach acht | shortly after eight |
| kurz vor acht | shortly before eight |
| Punkt acht | at eight on the dot |

*gegen* replaces *um*: *Ich komme gegen sieben* — I'll come at around seven. Never *um gegen*.

## How often: a longer scale

Lesson 11 gave you *immer, oft, manchmal, nie*. Add *meistens* (mostly, usually) and *selten* (rarely):

immer → meistens → oft → manchmal → selten → nie

To count, use *einmal* (once), *zweimal* (twice), *dreimal* … with *pro* (per) or with the accusative: *einmal pro Woche* or *einmal die Woche* — once a week; *dreimal am Tag* — three times a day.

- *Ich gehe zweimal pro Woche schwimmen.* — I go swimming twice a week.
- *Wir essen selten im Restaurant.* — We rarely eat in a restaurant.

## Two time phrases in one sentence

When a sentence has two time phrases, the general one comes before the specific one: day before clock time.

- *Ich komme morgen um acht.* — I'm coming tomorrow at eight.
- *Am Freitag gegen sieben gehen wir ins Kino.* — On Friday at around seven we're going to the cinema.
- *Der Kurs ist dienstags von sechs bis acht.* — The course is on Tuesdays from six to eight.

A time phrase usually comes before a place: *Ich bin um acht im Büro* (*im Büro* = at the office). Both time phrases can stand together in position 1, since they count as one element: *Morgen um acht rufe ich dich an* (*dich* = you).

### Example 3: putting the pieces in order

Words: *ich*, *spiele*, *Fußball*, *samstags*, *um zehn*.

1. The verb goes second: *spiele*.
