2. Two time phrases: general (*samstags*) before specific (*um zehn*).
3. Start with the subject: *Ich spiele samstags um zehn Fußball.* Or start with the time: *Samstags um zehn spiele ich Fußball.*

The whole choice of time words fits in one chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a time expression
  accDescr: First ask whether you mean a clock time. If yes and it is exact, use um, as in um acht. If it is only roughly that time, use gegen, as in gegen acht. If it is not a clock time, ask whether you are saying how long something lasts. If yes, use the accusative with no preposition: eine Stunde, einen Tag. If not, ask whether the time word has jeder, nächster or dieser. If yes, use the accusative with no preposition: jeden Tag, nächsten Montag, diese Woche. If not, ask whether it is a regular habit. If yes, use the adverb with s: montags, abends. If not, use am: am Montag, am Abend.
  A{"A clock time?"} -- yes --> B{"Exactly?"}
  B -- yes --> U["um acht"]
  B -- "roughly" --> G["gegen acht"]
  A -- no --> C{"How long it lasts?"}
  C -- yes --> D["eine Stunde, einen Tag"]
  C -- no --> E{"With jeder, nächster or dieser?"}
  E -- yes --> J["jeden Tag, nächsten Montag, diese Woche"]
  E -- no --> H{"A regular habit?"}
  H -- yes --> S["montags, abends"]
  H -- no --> M["am Montag, am Abend"]
```

## Reading: Unsere Woche

> Wir sind Familie Yilmaz: Mama, Papa, Ela und ich, Can. Unsere Woche ist voll. Papa arbeitet morgens in der Bäckerei, er steht jeden Tag um vier auf. Mama arbeitet nachmittags im Büro, meistens bis halb sieben. Ela hat dienstags und donnerstags Fußball, das dauert anderthalb Stunden. Ich spiele montags Gitarre. Nächste Woche haben wir viele Termine: Am Mittwoch gegen drei kommt Oma, und am Freitag kurz nach fünf holen wir Tante Ayşe am Bahnhof ab. Samstags kaufen wir zusammen ein, aber sonntags sind die Geschäfte geschlossen. Dann schlafen wir lange, nur Papa nicht: Die Bäckerei ist sonntags bis elf geöffnet. Abends essen wir alle zusammen. Das ist selten in der Woche, und deshalb ist der Sonntag mein Lieblingstag.

In English:

> We're the Yilmaz family: Mum, Dad, Ela and me, Can. Our week is full. Dad works mornings at the bakery; he gets up at four every day. Mum works afternoons at the office, usually until half past six. Ela has football on Tuesdays and Thursdays, which takes an hour and a half. I play guitar on Mondays. Next week we have lots of appointments: on Wednesday at around three Grandma is coming, and on Friday shortly after five we're picking up Aunt Ayşe from the station. On Saturdays we go shopping together, but on Sundays the shops are closed. Then we sleep in, except Dad: the bakery is open until eleven on Sundays. In the evening we all eat together. That's rare during the week, and that's why Sunday is my favourite day.

(*anderthalb* = one and a half; *nur Papa nicht* = except Dad; *die Gitarre* = guitar; *die Tante* = aunt; *am Bahnhof* = at the station; *deshalb* = that's why; *der Lieblingstag* = favourite day.)

## Pronunciation

- *montags*, *abends*: the final *-gs* and *-ds* sound like *ks* and *ts* (final devoicing): MOHN-tahks, AH-bents.
- *nachts*: the *ch* of *Bach*, then *ts*: nahkhts.
- *geöffnet*: three syllables, ge-ÖFF-net, with a tiny break before the *ö*.
- *gegen*: GAY-gen, both *g*s hard.

## Common mistakes

- *Montags* in the middle of a sentence. The adverb is small: *Ich arbeite montags.*
- *am nächste Woche*, *in nächste Woche* — Use the plain accusative: *nächste Woche*.
- *nächste Montag*, *jede Tag* — Masculine needs *-en*: *nächsten Montag, jeden Tag*.
- *für zwei Stunden* — In "it takes two hours" use the accusative alone: *Es dauert zwei Stunden.*
- *um gegen acht* — *gegen* replaces *um*: *gegen acht*.
- *um acht morgen* — General before specific: *morgen um acht*.
- *Das Café ist am Montag Ruhetag geöffnet.* — *Ruhetag* means it's closed: *Montag ist Ruhetag* / *Montags ist das Café geschlossen.*

## Key points

- Opening hours: *Mo–Fr 8–18 Uhr* is read *Montag bis Freitag von acht bis achtzehn Uhr*; *geöffnet* = open, *geschlossen* = closed, *Ruhetag* = weekly closing day. Most German shops are closed on Sundays (rules vary by state).
- *montags, abends, nachts* (small letter, *-s*) mean every Monday, every evening, every night.
- With *jeder, nächster, dieser, ganz* the time phrase is in the accusative with no preposition: *jeden Tag, nächsten Montag, diese Woche, den ganzen Tag*.
- How long: *dauern* + accusative: *Es dauert eine Stunde / einen Tag.*
- *gegen acht* = around eight; *kurz nach / kurz vor acht*; *Punkt acht*.
- Frequency: *immer, meistens, oft, manchmal, selten, nie*; *einmal pro Woche*.
- Two time phrases: general before specific (*morgen um acht*), time before place.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Hobbies and stem-changing verbs
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 is about free time and plans. In this first lesson you learn to talk about your
hobbies: what you do in your free time, what you like, what you like more, and what you like
most of all.

On the way you meet an important group of verbs. In lesson 4 you learned the regular present
tense endings (-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en), and you have already seen a few verbs that change
their vowel, such as *sprechen* (du sprichst) in lesson 7 and *essen* and *nehmen* in lesson 9.
Here that pattern gets a name and a full explanation, because many of the most common German
verbs, including several hobby verbs, behave this way.

## Talking about hobbies

The easiest way to ask about free time is with *gern*, which you know from lesson 4. *Gern*
goes right after the verb (after a short pronoun like *das* if there is one: *Ich mache das
gern*) and before the rest: *Ich spiele gern Gitarre.* It means that you like doing it.

- *Was machst du gern?* — What do you like doing?
- *Was machen Sie in der Freizeit?* — What do you do in your free time?
- *Hast du ein Hobby?* — Do you have a hobby?
- *Mein Hobby ist Musik.* — My hobby is music.
- *Ich lese gern.* — I like reading.
- *Ich tanze nicht gern.* — I don't like dancing.

*In der Freizeit* means "in (your) free time". Learn it as a fixed chunk for now; the
grammar behind *der* after *in* comes in lesson 18.

Many hobbies are just verbs: *lesen* (to read), *schwimmen* (to swim), *tanzen* (to dance),
*singen* (to sing), *reisen* (to travel), *wandern* (to hike), *joggen* (to jog), *malen* (to
paint), *fotografieren* (to take photos). Others use *spielen* or *fahren* with a noun:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *Fußball spielen* | to play football (soccer) |
| *Gitarre spielen* | to play the guitar |
| *Fahrrad fahren* | to ride a bike, to cycle |
| *Musik hören* | to listen to music |
| *Filme sehen* | to watch films |
| *Freunde treffen* | to meet friends |
| *spazieren gehen* | to go for a walk |
| *ins Kino gehen* | to go to the cinema |

Here are six of these hobbies as pictures. Say each one aloud as a sentence: *Ich lese gern.
Ich fahre gern Fahrrad.*

![Six picture tiles with captions: an open book (lesen), a bicycle (Fahrrad fahren), a guitar (Gitarre spielen), a football (Fußball spielen), a camera (fotografieren) and mountains with a dotted path and a signpost (wandern).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Two small notes. German drops the article with sports and instruments here: *Ich spiele
Fußball* (no *den*), *Ich spiele Gitarre*. And *ins Kino*, *ins Theater* and *ins Konzert* are
fixed chunks for going somewhere; you will see why in later lessons.

## Stem-changing verbs

The **[[stem]]** of a verb is the infinitive without *-en*: *mach-en*, *lern-en*, *fahr-en*. In
regular verbs the stem never changes. A **[[stem-changing verb]]** changes the vowel of its stem,
but only in the du form and the er/sie/es form. Every other form is regular. There are
three patterns at A1.

### Pattern 1: a → ä

| | fahren (to go by vehicle) | schlafen (to sleep) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | fahre | schlafe |
| du | *fährst* | *schläfst* |
| er/sie/es | *fährt* | *schläft* |
| wir | fahren | schlafen |
| ihr | fahrt | schlaft |
| sie/Sie | fahren | schlafen |

*Waschen* (du wäschst, er wäscht) follows the same pattern.

### Pattern 2: e → i

| | sprechen | geben (to give) | helfen (to help) | treffen (to meet) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | spreche | gebe | helfe | treffe |
| du | *sprichst* | *gibst* | *hilfst* | *triffst* |
| er/sie/es | *spricht* | *gibt* | *hilft* | *trifft* |
| wir | sprechen | geben | helfen | treffen |
| ihr | sprecht | gebt | helft | trefft |
| sie/Sie | sprechen | geben | helfen | treffen |

*Essen* (du isst, er isst) and *nehmen* (du nimmst, er nimmt) belong here too. *Nehmen* also
changes its consonants (*du nimmst, er nimmt*), so learn those two forms by heart; *treffen*
keeps its double *f* (*du triffst, er trifft*).

### Pattern 3: e → ie

| | lesen (to read) | sehen (to see) |
|---|---|---|
| ich | lese | sehe |
| du | *liest* | *siehst* |
| er/sie/es | *liest* | *sieht* |
| wir | lesen | sehen |
| ihr | lest | seht |
| sie/Sie | lesen | sehen |

*Lesen* has one more twist: its stem ends in -s, so du gets only -t (*du liest*, not
"du liesst"), just like *heißen* (du heißt) in lesson 4.

### A memory hook

Think of the change as a "spotlight" on the two singular persons you talk to or about: *du*
and *er/sie/es*. The plural forms, and *ich*, stay in the dark and keep the plain vowel. If you
know the er form, you know the du form: *er fährt → du fährst*, *er liest → du liest*.

You can't see from the infinitive whether a verb changes, so the vocabulary list notes every
stem change. Many common verbs with *e* or *a* do not change: *gehen*, *lernen*, *machen*,
*spielen*, *wandern*, *malen*, *tanzen*.

This chart sums up the decision you make each time you conjugate a verb in the present tense:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Does the stem vowel change?
  accDescr: A decision chart for the present tense. First ask who the subject is. With ich, wir, ihr, sie (they) or Sie, use the plain stem with no vowel change, as in ich fahre and ihr fahrt. With du or er, sie, es, check the word list for a stem change. If there is none, use the plain stem, as in du spielst and er spielt. If there is one, it is a to ä as in du fährst and er fährt, e to i as in du gibst and er gibt, or e to ie as in du liest and er liest.
  A{"Who is the subject?"} --> B["ich, wir, ihr, sie (they), Sie"]
  A --> C["du or er/sie/es"]
  B --> D["Plain stem: ich fahre, ihr fahrt"]
  C --> E{"Stem change in the word list?"}
  E -- no --> F["Plain stem: du spielst, er spielt"]
  E -- yes --> G["a to ä: du fährst, er fährt"]
  E -- yes --> H["e to i: du gibst, er gibt"]
  E -- yes --> I["e to ie: du liest, er liest"]
```

Examples:

- *Mein Vater fährt am Wochenende Fahrrad.* — My father cycles at the weekend.
- *Liest du gern?* — Do you like reading?
- *Anna sieht jeden Abend einen Film.* — Anna watches a film every evening.
- *Wann triffst du deine Freunde?* — When are you meeting your friends?
- *Er hilft oft im Garten.* — He often helps in the garden.
- *Was gibt es heute im Kino?* — What's on at the cinema today? (*es gibt*, lesson 10)
- *Wir fahren zusammen, und ihr fahrt allein.* — We're going together, and you're going alone.

## gern, lieber, am liebsten

*Gern* has two more forms for comparing. *Lieber* is its **[[comparative]]** ("rather, prefer")
and *am liebsten* its **[[superlative]]** ("most of all, like best").

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| *gern* | like doing | *Ich schwimme gern.* — I like swimming. |
| *lieber* | prefer, would rather | *Ich jogge lieber.* — I prefer jogging. |
| *am liebsten* | like most of all | *Am liebsten tanze ich.* — Most of all I like dancing. |

Picture them as three steps, each one higher than the last:

![Three steps rising from left to right. The lowest is gern, like doing, with the example Ich schwimme gern. The middle one is lieber, prefer, with Ich jogge lieber. The highest is am liebsten, like most of all, with Am liebsten tanze ich. An arrow underneath is labeled how much you like it.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

They all sit where *gern* sits, after the verb:

- *Ich sehe gern Filme, aber ich lese lieber.* — I like watching films, but I prefer reading.
- *Trinkst du lieber Kaffee oder Tee?* — Do you prefer coffee or tea?
- *Ich höre am liebsten Musik.* — Most of all I like listening to music.

When *am liebsten* comes first in the sentence, remember the rule from lesson 4: the verb stays
in position 2 and the subject moves behind it. *Am liebsten wandere ich* (not "Am liebsten ich
wandere").

*Lieber* also works for choosing between things: *Ich sehe gern Filme, aber ich gehe lieber
ins Konzert.* — I like watching films, but I'd rather go to a concert. (For liking a thing
itself, German uses *mögen*, which you meet properly in the next lesson.)

## Dialogue: Was machst du gern?

Jonas and Mia are new in a German course and chat in the break.

> Jonas: Was machst du gern in der Freizeit, Mia?
>
> Mia: Ich lese viel, und ich male gern. Und du?
>
> Jonas: Ich spiele gern Fußball, aber am liebsten fahre ich Fahrrad.
>
> Mia: Fährst du allein?
>
> Jonas: Nein, mein Bruder fährt auch gern. Wir fahren am Sonntag immer zusammen.
>
> Mia: Ich fahre nicht so gern Fahrrad. Ich wandere lieber.
>
> Jonas: Siehst du auch gern Filme?
>
> Mia: Ja! Ich treffe am Freitag Freunde, und wir gehen ins Kino. Kommst du mit?
>
> Jonas: Gern! Wann fängt der Film an?
>
> Mia: Um acht. Und danach singen wir Karaoke!

Translation:

> Jonas: What do you like doing in your free time, Mia?
>
> Mia: I read a lot, and I like painting. And you?
>
> Jonas: I like playing football, but most of all I like cycling.
>
> Mia: Do you ride alone?
>
> Jonas: No, my brother likes cycling too. We always ride together on Sundays.
>
> Mia: I don't like cycling so much. I prefer hiking.
>
> Jonas: Do you like watching films too?
>
> Mia: Yes! I'm meeting friends on Friday and we're going to the cinema. Are you coming?
>
> Jonas: I'd love to! When does the film start?
>
> Mia: At eight. And afterwards we're singing karaoke!

Notice *Fährst du …?* and *mein Bruder fährt* with ä, but *wir fahren* without it.

## Pronunciation

- *fährt, schläft*: ä is pronounced like the e in English "bed" (long here: "fairt").
- *liest, sieht*: ie is a long "ee". The h in *sieht* is silent; it only shows that the vowel
  is long.
- *Theater*: the th is a plain t, and the stress is on the second syllable: the-A-ter.
- *fotografieren*: verbs ending in -ieren are stressed on *-ie-*: fo-to-gra-FIE-ren.
- *Konzert*: the z sounds like "ts"; stress on the second syllable: kon-ZERT.
- *joggen* is an English loanword, but the j is said like English "dj" by most speakers and the
  -en is German.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the change in the wrong person. *Ich fähre* and *wir sprichen* are wrong: only
  du and er/sie/es change. *Ich fahre, wir sprechen.*
- Adding the umlaut to ihr. *Ihr fahrt* (no ä), *ihr lest*, *ihr seht*.
- Using the English word order with gern. Not "Ich gern lese" but *Ich lese gern*.
- Saying "mehr gern" for "more". The comparative of *gern* is *lieber*: *Ich schwimme
  lieber* (not "Ich schwimme mehr gern").
- "I play the guitar" with an article. In German: *Ich spiele Gitarre*.
- Using *gehen* for travel by vehicle. *Gehen* is on foot. For bikes, cars, trains and so
  on use *fahren*: *Ich fahre nach Berlin.* — I'm going to Berlin.

## Key points

- A stem-changing verb changes its vowel only in the du and er/sie/es forms: a → ä (*fahren,
  schlafen*), e → i (*sprechen, essen, geben, helfen, treffen, nehmen*), e → ie (*lesen,
  sehen*).
- Learn the er form with each verb: *er fährt, er gibt, er liest*.
- *gern* = like doing, *lieber* = prefer, *am liebsten* = like most of all; all go after the
  verb.
- With sports and instruments there's no article: *Ich spiele Fußball / Gitarre.*
- Ask *Was machst du gern?* or *Hast du ein Hobby?*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Modal verbs: können, wollen, möchten
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson you talked about what you like doing. Now you learn to say what you can
do, what you want to do and what you would like to do: *Ich kann schwimmen*, *Ich will
Gitarre lernen*, *Ich möchte eine Party feiern*. These sentences need a new kind of verb and a
new word order, and both are central to German. Once you have them, you can also make plans
and invitations.

## What a modal verb does

A **[[modal verb]]** adds an attitude to another verb: ability (can), wish (want, would like),
obligation (must) or permission (may). In English: "I *can* swim", "I *want to* travel". In
German it works the same way, with one big difference in word order:

- *Ich kann schwimmen.* — I can swim.
- *Ich will reisen.* — I want to travel.
- *Ich möchte tanzen.* — I'd like to dance.

The modal verb is conjugated and sits in position 2. The second verb stays in the infinitive
(the form ending in -en, as in the dictionary) and goes to the very end of the sentence. There
is no "zu" (no "to") in front of it.

This lesson covers *können*, *wollen*, *mögen* and *möchten*. Lesson 15 adds *müssen*,
*dürfen* and *sollen*.

## The forms

Modal verbs are irregular in the singular. Three things are true of all of them:

1. The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending: *ich kann, er kann*.
   (*möchten* is the one exception: *ich möchte, er möchte* are the same but end in *-e*.)
2. Most of them change their vowel in the singular: *können → ich kann*.
3. The plural is regular, built from the infinitive: *wir können, ihr könnt, sie können*.

| | können (can) | wollen (want) | mögen (like) | möchten (would like) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | kann | will | mag | möchte |
| du | kannst | willst | magst | möchtest |
| er/sie/es | kann | will | mag | möchte |
| wir | können | wollen | mögen | möchten |
| ihr | könnt | wollt | mögt | möchtet |
| sie/Sie | können | wollen | mögen | möchten |

You know *möchte* from ordering food in lesson 9 (*Ich möchte einen Kaffee*). It is really a
polite form of *mögen*, but at A1 treat it as its own verb. Note that its er form is *er möchte*,
with no -t.

Memory hook: *ich* and *er* are twins with modal verbs. If you remember *ich kann*, you
already know *er kann*.

## The sentence bracket

German puts the two parts of the verb at two fixed points and fills the middle with
everything else. This is called the **[[sentence bracket]]**: the modal verb opens it in
position 2, the infinitive closes it at the end.

| Position 1 | Position 2 (modal) | middle | end (infinitive) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | kann | gut | kochen. |
| Mein Bruder | will | am Samstag eine Party | feiern. |
| Am Sonntag | möchten | wir | wandern. |
| Was | kannst | du | spielen? |

In English the two verbs stay together ("I can cook well"). In German they separate: *Ich
kann gut kochen*, never "Ich kann kochen gut".

The picture shows the bracket as a clamp: the modal verb and the infinitive hold everything in
between. In a W-question the question word takes position 1, and the bracket works the same way.

![Two sentences split into four boxes each. Top: Ich (position 1), kann (modal verb), am Samstag gut (middle), kochen. (infinitive at the end). Bottom: Wann (position 1), willst (modal verb), du (middle), mitkommen? (infinitive at the end). In both, a red bracket joins the modal verb box to the infinitive box over the middle.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Yes/no questions start with the modal; the infinitive is still at the end:

- *Kannst du Ski fahren?* — Can you ski?
- *Willst du am Wochenende Freunde treffen?* — Do you want to meet friends at the weekend?
- *Möchten Sie etwas trinken?* — Would you like something to drink?

*Nicht* usually goes just before the infinitive: *Ich kann heute nicht kommen.* — I can't come
today.

You already know a bracket from lesson 12: *Ich stehe um sieben auf.* With a modal verb, a
separable verb comes back together as one word at the end: *Ich will um sieben aufstehen.*
*Kommst du mit?* becomes *Willst du mitkommen?* And *einladen* (to invite): *Ich möchte
meine Freunde einladen.*

## können: ability and possibility

*Können* says that you are able to do something, or that something is possible:

- *Ich kann ein bisschen Gitarre spielen.* — I can play the guitar a bit.
- *Kannst du gut kochen?* — Can you cook well? / Are you a good cook?
- *Meine Schwester kann Klavier spielen, aber sie kann nicht singen.* — My sister can play the
  piano, but she can't sing.
- *Kannst du am Freitag?* — Can you (make it) on Friday?
- *Wir können zusammen Auto fahren.* — We can drive together.

For languages, German often leaves out the second verb: *Ich kann Deutsch* — I can speak
German. *Kannst du Englisch?* — Do you speak English?

To say how well, use *gut, sehr gut, ein bisschen, nicht so gut, nicht*, and put it before the
infinitive (or before the noun that goes with it): *Ich kann sehr gut schwimmen.*

## wollen and möchten: wishes and plans

Both express a wish, but they feel different:

- *möchte* is polite and soft: "would like". Use it with strangers, in shops, and whenever you
  ask for something.
- *will* is direct and firm: "want". Fine for plans and for talking about yourself with
  friends, but *Ich will einen Kaffee* to a waiter sounds pushy, like a child saying "I want…".

Examples:

- *Ich will im Sommer nach Spanien reisen.* — I want to travel to Spain in the summer.
- *Was willst du heute machen?* — What do you want to do today?
- *Ich möchte bitte zwei Brötchen.* — I'd like two rolls, please.

False friend warning: *Ich will* does not mean "I will". It means "I want". The English future
"I will" is a different verb that you meet after A1.

## mögen: liking things and people

*Mögen* mostly takes a noun, not an infinitive: *Ich mag Pizza.* — I like pizza. *Magst du
Jazz?* — Do you like jazz? *Ich mag meine Kollegen.* — I like my colleagues. For liking
activities, keep using *gern* from lesson 13: *Ich tanze gern* (I like dancing).

This chart helps you pick the right verb:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing können, wollen, möchten, mögen or gern
  accDescr: Start with what you want to say. For an ability or a possibility, use können, as in Ich kann schwimmen. For a wish or a plan, ask whether you are asking for something politely: if yes, use möchten, as in Ich möchte einen Kaffee; if it is a firm plan, use wollen, as in Ich will reisen. For liking a thing or a person, use mögen, as in Ich mag Jazz. For liking an activity, use the verb with gern, as in Ich tanze gern.
  A{"What do you want to say?"} --> B["Ability or possibility"]
  A --> C["A wish or a plan"]
  A --> D["Liking a thing or person"]
  A --> E["Liking an activity"]
  B --> B1["können: Ich kann schwimmen."]
  C --> C1{"Asking politely for something?"}
  C1 -- yes --> C2["möchten: Ich möchte einen Kaffee."]
  C1 -- "no, a firm plan" --> C3["wollen: Ich will reisen."]
  D --> D1["mögen: Ich mag Jazz."]
  E --> E1["verb + gern: Ich tanze gern."]
```

## Useful little words for plans

| German | English | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *natürlich* | of course | *Natürlich kann ich helfen.* — Of course I can help. |
| *vielleicht* | maybe | *Vielleicht komme ich später.* — Maybe I'll come later. |
| *leider* | unfortunately | *Ich kann leider nicht.* — Unfortunately I can't. |
| *schon* | already | *Kannst du schon Auto fahren?* — Can you drive already? |
| *noch* | still | *Ich lerne noch.* — I'm still learning. |
| *noch nicht* | not yet | *Ich kann noch nicht Ski fahren.* — I can't ski yet. |
| *gleich* | right away, in a moment | *Ich komme gleich!* — I'm coming right away! |
| *wirklich* | really | *Das ist wirklich toll.* — That's really great. |
| *sicher* | sure, certainly | *Sie kommt sicher.* — She's sure to come. |

Two useful nouns: *die Lust* (desire, being in the mood) and *der Spaß* (fun).

- *Hast du Lust auf eine Party?* — Do you feel like a party? (*auf* is part of the chunk.)
- *Ich habe keine Lust.* — I don't feel like it.
- *Tanzen macht Spaß.* — Dancing is fun.

## Dialogue: Eine Idee

Lea calls her friend Max.

> Lea: Du, Max, ich habe eine Idee. Ich will am Samstag eine Party machen.
>
> Max: Super! Was möchtest du feiern?
>
> Lea: Das Wochenende! Ich möchte alle Freunde aus dem Kurs einladen. Kannst du kommen?
>
> Max: Natürlich! Kann ich helfen? Ich kann ein bisschen kochen.
>
> Lea: Ja, gern. Und du spielst Gitarre, oder? Kannst du etwas spielen?
>
> Max: Hm, ich lerne noch. Ich kann noch nicht wirklich gut spielen.
>
> Lea: Egal! Wir wollen ja nur singen und tanzen.
>
> Max: Okay, dann bringe ich die Gitarre mit. Kommt Jana auch?
>
> Lea: Vielleicht. Ich frage sie gleich.
>
> Max: Toll, ich habe wirklich Lust auf eine Party!

Translation:

> Lea: Hey, Max, I've got an idea. I want to have a party on Saturday.
>
> Max: Great! What would you like to celebrate?
>
> Lea: The weekend! I'd like to invite all my friends from the course. Can you come?
>
> Max: Of course! Can I help? I can cook a bit.
>
> Lea: Yes, please. And you play the guitar, don't you? Can you play something?
>
> Max: Hm, I'm still learning. I can't really play well yet.
>
> Lea: Doesn't matter! We only want to sing and dance anyway.
>
> Max: Okay, then I'll bring the guitar. Is Jana coming too?
>
> Lea: Maybe. I'll ask her right away.
>
> Max: Great, I'm really in the mood for a party!

New in passing: *egal* (it doesn't matter), *oder?* at the end of a sentence ("…, don't
you?"), *mitbringen* (to bring along, separable like *mitkommen*).

## Pronunciation

- *können, möchten, mögen*: ö is made by saying "e" with rounded lips. Don't flatten it to
  "o": *können* with ö (we can) and *kann* with a (I can) sound clearly different.
- *will* has a short i, like English "will"; the w is a German w, which sounds like English v:
  "vill".
- *Klavier*: the v sounds like English v here (it's a foreign word), and the stress is at the
  end: kla-VIER. *Gitarre* is stressed on the second syllable: gi-TAR-re. *Instrument*: in-stru-MENT.
- *Lust*: the u is short, as in English "put", and the st is said "st", not "sht".

## Common mistakes

- Keeping the two verbs together, as in English: "Ich kann spielen Gitarre". Correct: *Ich
  kann Gitarre spielen.*
- Adding "zu": "Ich will zu reisen". Modal verbs never take *zu*: *Ich will reisen.*
- Adding endings to ich and er: "ich kanne", "er kannt", "er möchtet". Correct: *ich kann, er
  kann, er möchte.*
- Conjugating both verbs: "Ich kann schwimme". Only the modal changes; the other verb stays in
  the infinitive.
- Reading *Ich will* as "I will". It means "I want".
- Using *will* when ordering. Say *Ich möchte …* to be polite.
- Using *mögen* for activities: "Ich mag schwimmen" is understood but sounds odd at this level;
  say *Ich schwimme gern*.

## Key points

- Modal verbs: *können* (can), *wollen* (want), *mögen* (like), *möchten* (would like).
- ich and er/sie/es forms are identical: *ich kann, er kann; ich will, er will; ich möchte, er
  möchte* (no ending, except the *-e* of *möchte*).
- Sentence bracket: modal in position 2, infinitive at the end, everything else in between.
- Questions: *Kannst du …?* with the infinitive at the end. *Nicht* goes before the infinitive.
- Separable verbs join up again at the end: *Willst du mitkommen?*
- *möchte* is polite, *will* is direct; *will* never means "will".
- *Hast du Lust?* and *Das macht Spaß* are everyday phrases for plans.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Modal verbs: müssen, dürfen, sollen — rules and obligations
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 14 you met the modal verbs *können, wollen, mögen* and *möchten* and the sentence
bracket (modal in position 2, infinitive at the end). This lesson adds the other three modal
verbs: *müssen* (must, have to), *dürfen* (may, be allowed to) and *sollen* (should, be supposed
to). With them you can talk about rules, signs, appointments and paperwork, which is exactly
what you meet when you live in a German-speaking country, and you can ask politely for
permission.

## The forms

The pattern is the one you already know: ich and er/sie/es are the same with no ending, the
singular has its own vowel, and the plural is regular.

| | müssen (must) | dürfen (may) | sollen (should) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | muss | darf | soll |
| du | musst | darfst | sollst |
| er/sie/es | muss | darf | soll |
| wir | müssen | dürfen | sollen |
| ihr | müsst | dürft | sollt |
| sie/Sie | müssen | dürfen | sollen |

Watch the spelling: *muss* and *musst* have ss (short u), and the umlaut disappears in the
singular: *müssen → ich muss*, *dürfen → ich darf*. *Sollen* doesn't change its vowel at all.

The word order is the same as in lesson 14:

| Position 1 | Position 2 (modal) | middle | end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | muss | morgen früh | arbeiten. |
| Hier | darf | man nicht | parken. |
| Sie | müssen | das Formular | ausfüllen. |
| | Soll | ich das Fenster | öffnen? |

*Ausfüllen* (to fill in) is separable, so it stays together at the end, as you saw with
*mitkommen* in lesson 14. *Unterschreiben* (to sign) is not separable: *Sie unterschreibt
hier* and *Sie muss hier unterschreiben.*

## müssen: necessity

*Müssen* says that something is necessary, because of a rule, a situation or your own
feeling:

- *Ich muss um sieben aufstehen.* — I have to get up at seven.
- *Du musst pünktlich sein. Der Termin ist um neun.* — You have to be on time. The
  appointment is at nine.
- *Wir müssen leider warten.* — Unfortunately we have to wait.
- *Musst du heute noch die Hausaufgabe machen?* — Do you still have to do the homework today?

## dürfen: permission

*Dürfen* says that something is allowed:

- *Darf ich hier rauchen?* — May I smoke here?
- *Kinder dürfen hier spielen.* — Children are allowed to play here.
- *Im Kurs dürfen wir Englisch sprechen.* — In the course we're allowed to speak English.

## nicht müssen vs nicht dürfen

This is the most important trap of the lesson. In English, "must not" means "it's forbidden".
In German, *nicht müssen* only means "not necessary". For "forbidden" you need *nicht dürfen*.

| German | Meaning | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Du musst nicht kommen.* | not necessary, you choose | You don't have to come. |
| *Du darfst nicht kommen.* | forbidden | You mustn't come. / You're not allowed to come. |
| *Man muss hier nicht warten.* | no need to wait | You don't need to wait here. |
| *Man darf hier nicht parken.* | parking is forbidden | You mustn't park here. |

Memory hook: *müssen* is about need. Take the need away (*nicht müssen*) and you are free.
*Dürfen* is about permission. Take the permission away (*nicht dürfen*) and it is forbidden.

When you want to say "not", ask one question first:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: nicht dürfen or nicht müssen?
  accDescr: Ask whether the action is forbidden. If yes, use nicht dürfen, for example Du darfst hier nicht parken, which means you mustn't park here. If it is allowed but simply not necessary, use nicht müssen, for example Du musst nicht kommen, which means you don't have to come. English must not matches nicht dürfen; English don't have to matches nicht müssen.
  A{"Is it forbidden?"} -- yes --> B["nicht dürfen"]
  A -- "no, just not necessary" --> C["nicht müssen"]
  B --> B1["Du darfst hier nicht parken. = You mustn't park here."]
  C --> C1["Du musst nicht kommen. = You don't have to come."]
```

## sollen: what someone else wants

*Sollen* passes on an instruction, advice or expectation that comes from another person:

- *Der Arzt sagt, ich soll viel Wasser trinken.* — The doctor says I should drink a lot of
  water.
- *Wir sollen das Formular bis Freitag ausfüllen.* — We're supposed to fill in the form by
  Friday.

In questions with *ich* or *wir*, *sollen* is a friendly offer or a request for instructions:

- *Soll ich das Fenster öffnen?* — Shall I open the window?
- *Wo soll ich unterschreiben?* — Where should I sign?
- *Sollen wir zusammen warten?* — Shall we wait together?

## man: rules for everyone

*Man* is an **[[indefinite pronoun]]**: it means people in general, like English "one", "you" or
"they" in "they say…". It always takes the er/sie/es form of the verb, and it goes very well
with modal verbs when you talk about rules:

- *Hier darf man nicht rauchen.* — You can't smoke here. / Smoking isn't allowed here.
- *Im Kino muss man leise sein.* — In the cinema you have to be quiet.
- *Was muss man hier machen?* — What does one have to do here?
- *Wie schreibt man das?* — How do you spell that? (lesson 1)

Don't confuse *man* (one, people) with *der Mann* (the man): one n, small m.

## Signs and rules

Signs (*das Schild*, plural *die Schilder*) are often very short. Many use *verboten*
(forbidden) or *erlaubt* (allowed) with a verb used as a noun:

| Sign | Meaning | With man + modal |
|---|---|---|
| *Rauchen verboten* | No smoking | *Hier darf man nicht rauchen.* |
| *Parken erlaubt* | Parking allowed | *Hier darf man parken.* |
| *Bitte leise sein!* | Please be quiet! | *Hier muss man leise sein.* |
| *Bitte Ausweis zeigen* | Please show ID | *Man muss den Ausweis zeigen.* |
| *Heute geschlossen* | Closed today | *Man kann heute nicht einkaufen.* |

Many signs use only a picture. A red ring with a red bar across means "not allowed":

![Four signs with captions. A cigarette inside a red ring with a red bar across it: Rauchen verboten. A white P on a blue square: Parken erlaubt. A mobile phone inside a red ring with a red bar: Telefonieren verboten. A face with a finger on its lips: Bitte leise sein!](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Geschlossen* (closed) comes from *schließen* (to close); its opposite on a door is *geöffnet*
(open), from *öffnen*.

## Polite requests

Modal verbs are the normal way to ask for something politely:

- *Kann ich hier warten?* — Can I wait here?
- *Darf ich das Fenster öffnen?* — May I open the window? (a little more polite)
- *Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?* — Could you repeat that, please?
- *Können Sie mir helfen?* — Can you help me? (*mir* = me, lesson 20)

Possible answers: *Ja, natürlich.* — Yes, of course. *Ja, gern.* — Yes, sure. *Nein, leider
nicht.* — No, I'm afraid not.

## Dialogue: Im Bürgeramt

Ana Silva is new in Leipzig and must register her address at the *Bürgeramt* (citizens'
office).

> Herr Krüger: Guten Tag. Haben Sie einen Termin?
>
> Ana: Ja, um zehn Uhr. Ich bin ein bisschen früh. Darf ich hier warten?
>
> Herr Krüger: Natürlich. Aber Sie müssen zuerst dieses Formular ausfüllen.
>
> Ana: Okay. Muss ich alles ausfüllen?
>
> Herr Krüger: Nein, Sie müssen nicht alles ausfüllen. Name, Adresse und Geburtsdatum sind
> wichtig. Und Sie müssen hier unten unterschreiben.
>
> Ana: Gut. Brauchen Sie auch meinen Ausweis?
>
> Herr Krüger: Ja, bitte. Ach, und Sie dürfen hier leider nicht telefonieren. Das ist eine Regel.
>
> Ana: Kein Problem. Soll ich die Tür schließen? Es ist ziemlich laut.
>
> Herr Krüger: Ja, gern. Vielen Dank!

Translation:

> Herr Krüger: Hello. Do you have an appointment?
>
> Ana: Yes, at ten o'clock. I'm a bit early. May I wait here?
>
> Herr Krüger: Of course. But you have to fill in this form first.
>
> Ana: Okay. Do I have to fill in everything?
>
> Herr Krüger: No, you don't have to fill in everything. Name, address and date of birth are
> important. And you have to sign down here.
>
> Ana: Fine. Do you need my ID too?
>
> Herr Krüger: Yes, please. Oh, and I'm afraid you're not allowed to make phone calls here.
> That's a rule.
>
> Ana: No problem. Shall I close the door? It's quite loud.
>
> Herr Krüger: Yes, please. Thanks a lot!

Notice *Sie müssen nicht alles ausfüllen* (no need) next to *Sie dürfen nicht telefonieren*
(not allowed). *Geburtsdatum* (date of birth) and *Problem* come up again in lesson 23.

## Pronunciation

- *müssen, dürfen*: ü is "ee" with rounded lips. Without the umlaut, *muss* has a short u as in
  "put".
- *muss*: the double s after a vowel tells you the vowel is short.
- *schließen*: ie is a long "ee" and ß is a sharp s: "shlee-sen".
- *Ausweis*: both syllables have a diphthong: au as in "how", ei as in "eye": "OWS-vice".
- *unterschreiben*: the stress is on *schrei*: un-ter-SCHREI-ben, because *unter-* here is not
  a separable prefix. Compare *AUS-füllen*, stressed on the separable prefix.
- *Information*: -tion is said "tsyohn" and carries the stress: in-for-ma-TSYOHN.

## Common mistakes

- Using *nicht müssen* for "must not". *Du musst nicht rauchen* means "you don't have to
  smoke". For a ban: *Du darfst nicht rauchen.*
- Adding endings to ich and er: "ich musse", "er darft". Correct: *ich muss, er darf.*
- Keeping the umlaut in the singular: "ich müss", "ich dürf". Correct: *ich muss, ich darf.*
- Using *man* with a plural verb: "man müssen". *Man* takes the er form: *man muss.*
- Spelling the pronoun with two n's. *Der Mann* is a man; *man* is "one, people".
- Splitting *unterschreiben*: "Ich schreibe unter". It is not separable: *Ich unterschreibe.*

## Key points

- *müssen* = must, have to; *dürfen* = may, be allowed to; *sollen* = should, be supposed to.
- ich and er/sie/es forms: *muss, darf, soll*; no umlaut in the singular.
- *nicht müssen* = don't have to; *nicht dürfen* = mustn't, not allowed.
- *man* + modal for rules: *Hier darf man nicht parken.* *Man* takes the er form.
- Polite requests: *Kann ich …? Darf ich …? Können Sie …?* Offers: *Soll ich …?*
- Signs: *verboten* (forbidden), *erlaubt* (allowed), *geschlossen* (closed).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Dates, seasons, weather and invitations
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 14 and 15 you learned to make plans and talk about what you can, want and have to
do. To make real plans you also need dates (*am dritten Oktober*), months and seasons
(*im Sommer*), and a way to talk about the weather, which in German conversation is almost as
popular as in English. You will also learn four short prepositions that always take the
accusative, and how to accept or turn down an invitation politely.

## Months and seasons

All months are masculine (*der Januar*) and, like all nouns, written with a capital letter.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Januar* | *Februar* | *März* | *April* |
| *Mai* | *Juni* | *Juli* | *August* |
| *September* | *Oktober* | *November* | *Dezember* |

The seasons (*die Jahreszeiten*) are masculine too: *der Frühling* (spring), *der Sommer*
(summer), *der Herbst* (autumn, fall), *der Winter* (winter).

The year wheel shows which months belong to which season. It uses whole months, the way weather
services count; by the calendar, spring starts around 20 March, summer around 21 June, autumn
around 22 or 23 September and winter around 21 December.

![A ring of the twelve months, starting with Januar at the top and running clockwise. Dezember, Januar and Februar are shaded blue and marked der Winter; März, April and Mai green, der Frühling; Juni, Juli and August yellow, der Sommer; September, Oktober and November pink, der Herbst.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To say "in" a month or season, use *im*: *im Mai* (in May), *im Winter* (in winter). *Im* is
short for *in dem*; for now just learn *im* + month or season as a chunk.

- *Im Sommer fahre ich gern Fahrrad.* — In summer I like cycling.
- *Mein Bruder hat im Januar Geburtstag.* — My brother's birthday is in January.
- *Ein Jahr hat zwölf Monate.* — A year has twelve months.

In Austria January is *Jänner*. On the phone or over a loudspeaker, some people say *Juno*
for *Juni* and *Julei* for *Juli*, so the two aren't confused.

## Ordinal numbers and dates

An **[[ordinal number]]** says the position in a row: first, second, third. German makes them from
the normal numbers you learned in lesson 3:

| Number | Rule | Ordinal |
|---|---|---|
| 1–19 | number + -te | *zweite, vierte, fünfte, zehnte, zwölfte, neunzehnte* |
| 20 and up | number + -ste | *zwanzigste, einundzwanzigste, dreißigste* |
| irregular | learn these | *erste* (1st), *dritte* (3rd), *siebte* (7th), *achte* (8th) |

*Achte* has just one t, because *acht* already ends in t.

In writing, an ordinal is a number with a full stop: *der 3. Oktober* is read *der dritte
Oktober*. Dates are written day first, then month: *3.10.* or *03.10.2026* is the 3rd of
October, never March 10th.

There are two patterns to learn, and the ending tells them apart:

| Use | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| What's the date? | *der* + ordinal with -e | *Heute ist der erste Mai.* — Today is the first of May. |
| On which day? | *am* + ordinal with -en | *Am ersten Mai habe ich frei.* — On the first of May I'm off. |

To ask: *Welches Datum ist heute?* or, more colloquially, *Der Wievielte ist heute?* — What's
the date today? To ask "when": *Wann …?* and answer with *am*:

- *Wann hast du Geburtstag?* — When is your birthday?
- *Ich habe am zwölften März Geburtstag.* — My birthday is on the twelfth of March.
- *Der Kurs fängt am einundzwanzigsten September an.* — The course starts on the twenty-first of
  September.

German says "I have birthday": *Ich habe Geburtstag* (no article). And on the day itself, you
say *Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!* — Happy birthday!

Years up to 1999 are read in hundreds: 1995 is *neunzehnhundertfünfundneunzig*. From 2000 on
they are read as thousands: 2026 is *zweitausendsechsundzwanzig*. Don't put *in* before a
year: say just *2026* or *im Jahr 2026*.

## The weather

*Das Wetter* is talked about with *es*. With weather verbs, *es* doesn't stand for anything;
it is just a placeholder subject, like "it" in "it's raining". These verbs are called
**[[impersonal verbs]]**, and they are used only with *es*.

- *Es regnet.* — It's raining. (*regnen*)
- *Es schneit.* — It's snowing. (*schneien*)
- *Die Sonne scheint.* — The sun is shining. (*scheinen*)
- *Es ist warm / kalt / heiß / kühl.* — It's warm / cold / hot / cool.
- *Es ist windig.* — It's windy. (from *der Wind*)
- *Es sind 25 Grad.* — It's 25 degrees (Celsius).

To ask: *Wie ist das Wetter heute?* — What's the weather like today?

![Four weather pictures with captions: a bright sun (Die Sonne scheint.), a cloud with rain (Es regnet.), a cloud with snowflakes (Es schneit.), and gusts of wind bending a small tree (Es ist windig.).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Nouns for the weather: *die Sonne* (sun), *der Regen* (rain), *der Schnee* (snow), *der Wind*
(wind). *Im Winter gibt es oft Schnee.* — In winter there's often snow.

Remember inversion when you start with a time phrase: *Im Herbst regnet es oft* (not "Im
Herbst es regnet").

## Four accusative prepositions: für, ohne, durch, um

A preposition is a little word like "for" or "through" that links a noun to the rest of the
sentence. In German each preposition decides the case of the noun after it. An
**[[accusative preposition]]** is always followed by the accusative, which you know from lesson 9: only the
masculine changes (*der → den*, *ein → einen*, *mein → meinen*).

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *für* | for | *Das Geschenk ist für meinen Bruder.* — The present is for my brother. |
| *ohne* | without | *Ich gehe nie ohne einen Schirm.* — I never go without an umbrella. |
| *durch* | through | *Wir gehen durch den Park.* — We walk through the park. |
| *um* | at (a time), around | *Die Party fängt um acht an.* — The party starts at eight. |

With feminine, neuter and plural nouns nothing changes: *für die Party, ohne das Auto, für
meine Eltern*. *Ohne* is often used with no article at all: *ohne Jacke* (without a jacket).
You also know a fixed phrase with *für*: *Danke für die Einladung!*

## Invitations

An invitation is *die Einladung* (from *einladen*, lesson 14). Here are ways to answer.

Saying yes:

- *Ja, gern! Ich komme gern.* — Yes, I'd love to. I'd be glad to come.
- *Super, danke für die Einladung!* — Great, thanks for the invitation!

Saying no politely, with a reason:

- *Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.* — Unfortunately I can't. I have to work.
- *Schade, da habe ich keine Zeit.* — What a pity, I don't have time then.

The whole conversation follows one of two paths:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Answering an invitation
  accDescr: An invitation arrives, for example Kommst du am Samstag? If you can come, say Ja, gern! Ich komme gern, and thank the person: Danke für die Einladung! If you can't come, say Leider kann ich nicht, give a reason such as Ich muss arbeiten, and end kindly with Schade! Viel Spaß!
  A["Einladung: Kommst du am Samstag?"] --> B{"Can you come?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Ja, gern! Ich komme gern."]
  C --> D["Danke für die Einladung!"]
  B -- no --> E["Leider kann ich nicht."]
  E --> F["Reason: Ich muss arbeiten."]
  F --> G["Schade! Viel Spaß!"]
```

## A message and two answers

> Hallo Sophie, hallo Tom,
>
> ich habe am 14. Juni Geburtstag. Das ist ein Samstag! Ich möchte im Garten feiern und lade
> euch ein. Die Party fängt um 18 Uhr an. Hoffentlich regnet es nicht! Kommt ihr?
>
> Paula

> Hallo Paula,
>
> danke für die Einladung! Ich komme sehr gern. Ich habe auch schon ein Geschenk für dich.
> Bis Samstag!
>
> Sophie

> Hallo Paula,
>
> leider kann ich nicht kommen. Ich muss am 14. Juni zu meiner Oma fahren. Schade! Aber
> herzlichen Glückwunsch schon jetzt und viel Spaß!
>
> Tom

Translation:

> Hi Sophie, hi Tom, my birthday is on the 14th of June. It's a Saturday! I'd like to
> celebrate in the garden and I'm inviting you. The party starts at 6 p.m. Hopefully it won't
> rain! Are you coming? Paula

> Hi Paula, thanks for the invitation! I'd love to come. I've already got a present for you
> too. See you on Saturday! Sophie

> Hi Paula, unfortunately I can't come. On the 14th of June I have to go to my grandma's. What a
> pity! But happy birthday in advance and have fun! Tom

New in passing: *euch* (you, plural object), *dich* (you, object) — both in lesson 20;
*hoffentlich* (hopefully); *zu meiner Oma* (to my grandma's, lesson 18); *schade* (what a
pity); *bis* (until) from lesson 11.

## Pronunciation

- *Juni* and *Juli*: the J is like English y: "YOO-nee", "YOO-lee".
- *März*: ä as in "bed", and z is "ts": "mehrts".
- *Herbst*: say every consonant: "hairpst" (the b sounds like p at the end of a syllable).
- *August* as a month is stressed on the second syllable: au-GUST.
- *Geburtstag*: stress on *-burts-*: ge-BURTS-tag.
- *regnet*: g before n stays a hard g: "RAYG-net".
- *Schnee* is a long "ay": "shnay"; *schneit* has ei as in "eye": "shnite".

## Common mistakes

- Using *in* with months: "in Mai". Correct: *im Mai*.
- Forgetting the ending after *am*: "am drei Oktober" or "am dritte Oktober". Correct: *am
  dritten Oktober*.
- Saying "erste" for 3rd or "dreite". The irregular ones are *erste, dritte, siebte, achte*.
- Reading 3.10. as March 10th. Germans write day.month.
- Dropping *es*: "Regnet." Weather verbs need *es*: *Es regnet.*
- Using the nominative after *für*: "für der Bruder". *Für* takes the accusative: *für den
  Bruder*.
- "Mein Geburtstag ist im 5. Mai." Use *am* with a date: *Mein Geburtstag ist am 5. Mai.*

## Key points

- Months and seasons are masculine; use *im* with them: *im Juli, im Herbst*.
- Ordinals: 1–19 + -te, 20+ + -ste; irregular *erste, dritte, siebte, achte*.
- Date: *Heute ist der dritte Mai.* On a date: *am dritten Mai*. Written *3. Mai* or *3.5.*
- *Wann hast du Geburtstag? — Am …* and *Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag!*
- Weather with *es*: *es regnet, es schneit, es ist kalt*; *die Sonne scheint*.
- *für, ohne, durch, um* always take the accusative: *für den Vater, durch den Park*.
- Accept with *Ich komme gern*, decline with *Leider kann ich nicht …* and a reason.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Clubs, quiet hours and favourite things
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 13 to 15 you learned to say what you like doing (*Ich spiele gern Fußball*), what
you can and want to do (*Ich kann schwimmen, ich will reisen*) and what the rules are (*Hier
darf man nicht rauchen*). This honors lesson puts that to work in three texts you could meet
in Germany: a sports club notice, the house rules of a block of flats and an e-mail from a
friend. You also learn two things that make your German sound more natural: the *Lieblings-* words (*mein
Lieblingsfilm*, my favourite film) and comparisons with *lieber … als …* (*Ich spiele lieber
Tennis als Fußball*).

## Vereine: free time in a club

A *Verein* is a club or association. Germans organize a great deal of their free time in
clubs: football and tennis, choirs and brass bands, chess, gardening, hiking, carnival and
much more. A club that is entered in the official register adds the letters *e. V.* to its
name, short for *eingetragener Verein* (registered club): *TC Rotbuche e. V.* (TC is short
for *Tennisclub*).

In March 2026 Germany had about 629,000 registered clubs (count by the research group ZiviZ),
and the German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) counted about 86,000 sports clubs with about
29.3 million memberships in 2025 (memberships, not people: one person can join several clubs).
In a small town the *Sportverein* (sports club) is often the centre of social life. Members
usually pay a yearly fee, and many clubs are run by volunteers. To say that you are in
a club, use the chunk *im Verein*:

- *Ich spiele im Verein Fußball.* — I play football in a club.
- *Meine Tochter singt im Chor.* — My daughter sings in a choir.

Here is a notice (*der Aushang*) of the kind you find on the board at a sports hall:

> **TC Rotbuche e. V. — Tennis für alle!**
>
> Möchtest du Tennis spielen? Dann komm zu uns!
>
> Training für Kinder (ab 8 Jahren): Montag und Mittwoch, 16 bis 17:30 Uhr.
>
> Training für Erwachsene: Dienstag und Donnerstag, 19 bis 21 Uhr.
>
> Du musst nicht Mitglied sein: Das erste Training ist kostenlos.
>
> Du hast keinen Schläger? Kein Problem, wir haben Schläger für dich.
>
> Wichtig: In der Halle darf man nur mit Hallenschuhen spielen.
>
> Information und Anmeldung: Frau Becker (nach dem Training in der Halle)

Translation:

> TC Rotbuche (registered tennis club). Tennis for everyone! Would you like to play tennis?
> Then come to us! Training for children (from age 8): Monday and Wednesday, 4 to 5:30 p.m.
> Training for adults: Tuesday and Thursday, 7 to 9 p.m. You don't have to be a member: the
> first training session is free. You haven't got a racket? No problem, we have rackets for
> you. Important: in the hall you may only play in indoor shoes. Information and registration:
> Ms Becker (after training, in the hall).

New words: *das Mitglied* (member), *kostenlos* (free of charge), *der Schläger* (racket),
*die Halle* (hall, sports hall), *die Hallenschuhe* (indoor sports shoes: shoes that don't
leave marks on the floor), *die Anmeldung* (registration), *Erwachsene* (adults), *ab* (from, with an age or a time).

### Example 1: Reading the notice

Question: *Muss ich Mitglied sein?*

1. Find the sentence with *Mitglied*: *Du musst nicht Mitglied sein.*
2. Look at the modal verb: *musst nicht*. From lesson 15, *nicht müssen* means "not necessary",
   not "forbidden".
3. Answer: *Nein, ich muss nicht Mitglied sein.* — No, I don't have to be a member.

Question: *Was darf man in der Halle nicht machen?*

1. Find *Halle*: *In der Halle darf man nur mit Hallenschuhen spielen.*
2. *Nur* means "only", so other shoes (such as *Straßenschuhe*, outdoor shoes) are not allowed.
3. Answer: *Man darf nicht mit Straßenschuhen spielen.* — You mustn't play in outdoor shoes.

## Ruhezeiten: quiet times

Many newcomers are surprised by how quiet a German Sunday is. Sundays and public holidays are
protected as days of rest (*die Sonntagsruhe*, Sunday rest) by the constitution (Article 140 of the Basic Law, which takes over
Article 139 of the Weimar Constitution of 1919), so most shops are closed on Sundays. Bakeries
may open for a few hours, and shops at large stations, airports and petrol stations stay open;
the exact rules are made by each of the 16 states.

There are also quiet times (*Ruhezeiten*) for noise:

- *Die Nachtruhe* (night quiet) usually runs from 22:00 to 6:00. It comes from state noise laws
  and local rules.
- *Die Mittagsruhe* (midday quiet), often 13:00 to 15:00, is not a general law. Whether it
  applies depends on the town and, above all, on the house rules of your building.
- On Sundays and public holidays, noisy work such as mowing the lawn with a motor mower is not
  allowed in residential areas at all, under a federal noise regulation.

![Two 24-hour bars. Montag bis Samstag: Nachtruhe shaded from 0 to 6 and from 22 to 24, and a dashed box from 13 to 15 marked Mittagsruhe (oft, Hausordnung). Sonntag und Feiertage: the whole bar is shaded and labeled Ruhetag: den ganzen Tag keine laute Arbeit. A note says the exact rules depend on the state, the town and the house rules.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The picture is a simplified guide, not the law itself. Most blocks of flats have a *Hausordnung* (house rules), usually hanging in the entrance. Here
is a short original example:

> **Hausordnung — Lindenstraße 12**
>
> Von 22 bis 6 Uhr ist Nachtruhe. Dann darf man keine laute Musik hören.
>
> Von 13 bis 15 Uhr ist Mittagsruhe. Bitte leise sein!
>
> Am Sonntag soll man nicht laut arbeiten.
>
> Fahrräder darf man nicht im Treppenhaus parken.
>
> Kinder dürfen im Hof spielen.
>
> Den Müll muss man trennen: Papier, Glas und Restmüll.

Translation:

> House rules, Lindenstraße 12. From 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. is night quiet time. Then you mustn't
> listen to loud music. From 1 to 3 p.m. is midday quiet time. Please be quiet! On Sundays you
> shouldn't do noisy work. You mustn't park bicycles in the stairwell. Children may play in the
> courtyard. You have to sort your rubbish: paper, glass and general waste.

New in passing: *das Treppenhaus* (stairwell, from *die Treppe*), *der Hof* (courtyard),
*der Müll* (rubbish), *trennen* (to separate, sort). The rules use *man* with the er form of a
modal (*darf, soll, muss*), except *Kinder dürfen* (plural subject). In *Fahrräder darf man
nicht … parken* and *Den Müll muss man trennen* the object comes first for emphasis; the modal
stays in position 2 and *man* moves behind it, as after a time phrase.

### Example 2: Turning a rule into your own sentence

A neighbour asks: *Kann ich um 23 Uhr Klavier spielen?* Build the answer step by step.

1. Check the time: 23:00 is between 22:00 and 6:00, so it is *Nachtruhe*.
2. Decide the meaning: it is not allowed, so you need *nicht dürfen* (not *nicht müssen*, which
   would mean "you don't have to").
3. Use *man* for a general rule and give it the er form: *man darf*.
4. Build the bracket: *darf* in position 2, *spielen* at the end, *nicht* just before
   *Klavier spielen*.
5. Answer: *Nein, leider nicht. Um 23 Uhr ist Nachtruhe. Da darf man nicht Klavier spielen.*

## Favourites: the Lieblings- words

German has no separate word for "favourite". Instead it puts *Lieblings-* in front of a noun
and writes the two as one word. *Lieblings-* works as a **[[prefix]]**: a piece added to the front
of a word to change its meaning. The result is a **[[compound noun]]**, and as you know from
lesson 5, a compound takes its gender from the last noun:

| Noun | Favourite … |
|---|---|
| *der Film* | *der Lieblingsfilm* — favourite film |
| *das Essen* | *das Lieblingsessen* — favourite food |
| *die Farbe* | *die Lieblingsfarbe* — favourite colour |
| *das Buch* | *das Lieblingsbuch* — favourite book |
| *der Sport* | *der Lieblingssport* — favourite sport |
| *die Musik* | *die Lieblingsmusik* — favourite music |

With a possessive (lesson 6), the ending follows the gender as usual:

- *Mein Lieblingsfilm ist „Lola rennt“.* — My favourite film is "Run Lola Run".
- *Meine Lieblingsfarbe ist Grün.* — My favourite colour is green.
- *Was ist dein Lieblingsessen?* — What's your favourite food?

*Lieblings-* (from *der Liebling*, darling) always keeps its *-s*: *der Lieblingssport* has a
double s.

## Comparing two things: lieber … als …

In lesson 13 you used *lieber* to say what you prefer. To name the thing you are comparing
with, add *als* (than) and put it after the preferred thing:

- *Ich spiele lieber Tennis als Fußball.* — I prefer playing tennis to football.
- *Ich trinke lieber Tee als Kaffee.* — I prefer tea to coffee.

The verb is in position 2 as always, *lieber* stays right after it (or after a short
pronoun), and the *als* part goes at the end. If a sentence has a sentence bracket, the *als*
part usually comes after the infinitive: *Ich möchte lieber Tennis spielen als Fußball.*

You can now say how much you like something on a whole scale:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *Ich tanze gar nicht gern.* | I don't like dancing at all. |
| *Ich tanze nicht so gern.* | I don't really like dancing. |
| *Ich tanze gern.* | I like dancing. |
| *Ich tanze sehr gern.* | I really like dancing. |
| *Ich tanze lieber.* | I prefer dancing. |
| *Am liebsten tanze ich.* | Most of all I like dancing. |

### Example 3: Building a comparison

Say in German: "My brother prefers chess to football."

1. Chess is a game, so use *spielen*; *mein Bruder* is er: *Mein Bruder spielt*.
2. *lieber* goes right after the verb, then the preferred thing, *Schach* (chess, no article,
   like *Fußball*): *Mein Bruder spielt lieber Schach …*
3. The comparison goes last with *als*: *Mein Bruder spielt lieber Schach als Fußball.*

This chart sums up every way of saying what you like:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to say what you like
  accDescr: If you like a thing or a person, use mögen, as in Ich mag Jazz, or a Lieblings- word for your top choice, as in Mein Lieblingsfilm ist Lola rennt. If you like an activity, use the verb with gern, as in Ich tanze gern. To compare two activities or things, use lieber with als, as in Ich spiele lieber Tennis als Fußball. For your top choice of all, use am liebsten, as in Am liebsten tanze ich.
  A{"What do you like?"} --> B["A thing or a person"]
  A --> C["An activity"]
  B --> B1["mögen: Ich mag Jazz."]
  B --> B2["Top choice: Mein Lieblingsfilm ist ..."]
  C --> C1["gern: Ich tanze gern."]
  C --> C2["Comparing: Ich spiele lieber Tennis als Fußball."]
  C --> C3["Top choice: Am liebsten tanze ich."]
```

## An e-mail: Mein Wochenende

> Liebe Mia,
>
> wie geht's? Ich bin jetzt seit zwei Monaten in Freiburg, und ich bin schon in zwei Vereinen!
> Am Dienstag spiele ich Tennis, und am Donnerstag singe ich im Chor. Am liebsten singe ich,
> aber Tennis macht auch Spaß. Ich spiele lieber Tennis als Fußball!
>
> Am Wochenende ist es hier sehr ruhig. Am Sonntag sind die Geschäfte geschlossen, und man darf
> nicht laut sein. Am Anfang war das komisch, aber jetzt finde ich es schön. Am Sonntag wandere
> ich oft im Schwarzwald. Das ist mein Lieblingshobby!
>
> Kommst du mal nach Freiburg? Dann können wir zusammen wandern.
>
> Viele Grüße
>
> Jana

Translation:

> Dear Mia, how are you? I've been in Freiburg for two months now, and I'm already in two
> clubs! On Tuesdays I play tennis, and on Thursdays I sing in a choir. Most of all I like
> singing, but tennis is fun too. I prefer tennis to football! At the weekend it's very quiet here. On Sundays the
> shops are closed and you mustn't be loud. At first that was strange, but now I think it's
> nice. On Sundays I often go hiking in the Black Forest. That's my favourite hobby! Will you
> come to Freiburg some time? Then we can go hiking together. Best wishes, Jana

Two forms here are beyond A1 and are only for reading: *seit zwei Monaten* (for two months;
*seit* + dative comes in lesson 18) and *war* (was; lesson 22). Also new: *am Anfang* (at
first), *komisch* (strange, funny), *mal* (some time) and *der Schwarzwald* (the Black Forest,
the hills around Freiburg).

## Pronunciation

- *Verein*: the v sounds like f and the stress is on the second syllable: fer-EIN.
- *Chor*: the ch sounds like k here: "kohr" (as in English "chorus").
- *Lieblings-*: the b is said like p because it ends a syllable: "LEEP-lings".
- *Ruhe, Ruhezeit*: the h is silent and only shows that the u is long: "ROO-e".

## Common mistakes

- Writing *Lieblings-* as a separate word: "mein Lieblings Film". It is one word with a
  capital L: *mein Lieblingsfilm*.
- Taking the gender from *Liebling*: "der Lieblingsfarbe". The last noun decides: *die Farbe →
  die Lieblingsfarbe*, so *meine Lieblingsfarbe*.
- Using *wie* or *dann* for "than": "lieber Tee wie Kaffee". In standard German it is *als*:
  *lieber Tee als Kaffee*. (You may hear *wie* in some regions; it is informal.)
- Treating the *Mittagsruhe* as a national law. It is common in house rules, but the night
  quiet and the Sunday rest are the firm rules.

## Key points

- A *Verein* is a club; *e. V.* means a registered club. *Ich spiele im Verein Fußball.*
- Sundays and public holidays are protected days of rest; most shops are closed.
- *Nachtruhe* usually runs from 22 to 6 Uhr; *Mittagsruhe* depends on the town and the house
  rules.
- Rules in a *Hausordnung* use *man* + modal: *Hier darf man nicht …, man muss …, man soll …*
- *Lieblings-* + noun = favourite: *der Lieblingsfilm, die Lieblingsfarbe*. Gender from the
  last noun.
- *lieber … als …* compares: *Ich trinke lieber Tee als Kaffee.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The German year: holidays, customs and date ranges
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Lesson 16 taught you months, seasons, ordinal numbers (*der dritte Oktober, am dritten
Oktober*) and how to answer an invitation. This honors lesson takes you through the German
year: which days are public holidays, what people do on the big days from New Year's Eve to
Christmas, and how birthdays are celebrated. You also learn to read and say date ranges (*vom
24. bis zum 26. Dezember*) and the date at the top of a letter (*Berlin, den 3. Oktober*),
which means learning one small grammar idea: ordinal numbers take endings just like
adjectives.

## Public holidays: who decides?

A public holiday is *ein Feiertag* (from *feiern*, to celebrate, and *der Tag*). On a public
holiday most people don't work, schools are closed and shops are shut, just as on a Sunday.

In Germany, most holidays are set by the 16 states, not by the national government. Nine of
them are holidays in every state:

| Date | Holiday | English |
|---|---|---|
| 1 January | *Neujahr* | New Year's Day |
| moves (March or April) | *Karfreitag* | Good Friday |
| moves (March or April) | *Ostermontag* | Easter Monday |
| 1 May | *Tag der Arbeit* | Labour Day (May Day) |
| moves (Thursday, May or June) | *Christi Himmelfahrt* | Ascension Day |
| moves (May or June) | *Pfingstmontag* | Whit Monday |
| 3 October | *Tag der Deutschen Einheit* | Day of German Unity |
| 25 December | *1. Weihnachtsfeiertag* | Christmas Day |
| 26 December | *2. Weihnachtsfeiertag* | Boxing Day, St Stephen's Day |

The Day of German Unity remembers the reunification of East and West Germany on 3 October 1990.
It is the only public holiday fixed by national law (the Unification Treaty of 1990). Other
holidays exist only in some states, for example 6 January (Epiphany) in Bavaria,
Baden-Württemberg and Saxony-Anhalt, or 31 October (Reformation Day) in several northern and
eastern states. Bavaria has the most: 12 to 14, depending on the town. Austria's national day
is 26 October and Switzerland's is 1 August.

Easter moves every year. It falls on a Sunday between 22 March and 25 April, and several
holidays are counted from it: Good Friday is two days before, Ascension Day is always a
Thursday, 39 days after Easter Sunday, and Whit Monday is 50 days after it. In 2027, Easter
Sunday is on 28 March.

Some of the best-known days are not public holidays at all: *Heiligabend* (Christmas Eve,
24 December), *Silvester* (New Year's Eve, 31 December), *Rosenmontag* (the Monday of carnival),
*Sankt Martin* (11 November) and the *Nikolaustag* (6 December). On 24 and 31 December, shops
usually close in the early afternoon.

![Six calendar pages, each with a date and a picture: 1. Mai with a flower (Tag der Arbeit), 3. Oktober with the black, red and gold German flag (Tag der Deutschen Einheit), 11. November with a paper lantern on a stick (Sankt Martin), 6. Dezember with a boot full of sweets (Nikolaustag), 24. Dezember with a decorated Christmas tree (Heiligabend), and 31. Dezember with fireworks (Silvester).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Customs through the year

Here is the German year in short A1 sentences. Read the German first, then check the English.

- **Silvester and Neujahr.** *Am 31. Dezember feiert man mit Freunden. Um Mitternacht gibt es
  Feuerwerk. Man sagt: „Frohes neues Jahr!"* — On 31 December people celebrate with friends.
  At midnight there are fireworks. People say "Happy New Year!" (Before midnight people wish
  each other *Guten Rutsch!*, "a good slide" into the new year.)
- **Karneval or Fasching.** *Im Februar oder März tragen viele Leute Kostüme, vor allem im
  Rheinland (Köln, Düsseldorf, Mainz).* — In February or March many people wear costumes,
  especially in the Rhineland. The carnival season officially opens on 11 November at 11:11, and
  its high point is the week before Ash Wednesday, with big parades on *Rosenmontag*. Its date
  depends on Easter, so it is usually in February and in some years in early March. *Karneval*
  is the usual word in Cologne and Düsseldorf; Bavaria and Austria say *Fasching*, and Mainz and
  the south-west say *Fastnacht*.
- **Ostern.** *Zu Ostern suchen Kinder Ostereier im Garten.* — At Easter children look for
  Easter eggs in the garden.
- **Sankt Martin.** *Am 11. November gehen Kinder mit Laternen durch die Straßen und singen.* —
  On 11 November children walk through the streets with lanterns and sing.
- **Advent.** *Im Dezember gibt es Weihnachtsmärkte. Auf dem Adventskranz brennen vier Kerzen:
  jeden Sonntag eine mehr.* — In December there are Christmas markets. On the Advent wreath four
  candles burn: one more every Sunday. Many families bake *Plätzchen* (Christmas biscuits).
- **Nikolaus.** *Am Abend vor dem 6. Dezember stellen Kinder Schuhe vor die Tür. Am Morgen sind
  Süßigkeiten drin.* — On the evening before 6 December children put their shoes outside the
  door. In the morning there are sweets in them.
- **Weihnachten.** *Am 24. Dezember, am Abend, gibt es die Geschenke.* — On 24 December, in the
  evening, there are the presents. In Germany most families open their presents on Christmas
  Eve (this is called *die Bescherung*), not on the morning of the 25th.

New in passing: *die Leute* (people), *tragen* (to wear; er trägt), *vor allem* (above all),
*brennen* (to burn), *stellen* (to put, stand something up), *Süßigkeiten* (sweets), *drin*
(inside it). Christmas greetings: *Frohe Weihnachten!* or *Fröhliche Weihnachten!*; at Easter,
*Frohe Ostern!*

## Birthdays

Birthdays are important in German-speaking countries, and a few customs differ from the
English-speaking world:

- Say *Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!* (all the best for your birthday) or *Herzlichen Glückwunsch
  zum Geburtstag!* (lesson 16).
- Many people think it brings bad luck to congratulate someone before the birthday. This is a
  superstition, and not everyone follows it, but to be safe, wait for the day itself. (Tom in
  lesson 16 congratulates Paula early; many Germans would wait.)
- At work or in a course, the person who has a birthday often brings a cake for everyone, and
  may invite friends to a party themselves.
- Big birthdays such as 30, 40 or 50 (*runde Geburtstage*, "round" birthdays) are often
  celebrated with a large party.

## Ordinal numbers take adjective endings

In lesson 16 you learned two patterns: *der erste Mai* and *am ersten Mai*. The reason the
ending changes is that an ordinal number behaves like an adjective. An **[[adjective ending]]** is
the short ending (*-e, -en, …*) that an adjective takes in front of a noun; it depends on the
word before it and the case. You will learn the whole system at A2. For dates you need only
two endings:

| Word before the ordinal | Ending | Example | Read as |
|---|---|---|---|
| *der* | -e | *Heute ist der 3. Oktober.* | *der dritte Oktober* |
| *am* (= an dem) | -en | *am 3. Oktober* | *am dritten Oktober* |
| *vom* (= von dem) | -en | *vom 24. Dezember* | *vom vierundzwanzigsten Dezember* |
| *zum* (= zu dem) | -en | *bis zum 26. Dezember* | *bis zum sechsundzwanzigsten Dezember* |
| *den* | -en | *Berlin, den 3. Oktober* | *den dritten Oktober* |

The rule of thumb: only *der* gives -e; every other word in the table gives -en. *Am, vom* and
*zum* are short forms of a preposition plus *dem*; you learn them properly in lesson 18 (the
dative), so for now treat them as chunks.

### Date ranges

To say "from … to …" with dates, use *vom … bis zum …*:

- *Der Weihnachtsmarkt ist vom 27. November bis zum 23. Dezember geöffnet.* — The Christmas
  market is open from 27 November to 23 December.
- *Die Ferien dauern vom 1. bis zum 14. August.* — The holidays last from 1 to 14 August.
  (*dauern* = to last, take time)

In writing you will often see the shorter *vom 1. bis 14. August* or *1.–14.8.*; read them
aloud with *vom … bis zum …*. With days of the week there are no articles: *von Montag bis
Freitag* (lesson 11).

### The date in a letter

At the top of a letter or card, the place comes first, then *den* and the date: *Hamburg, den
6. Dezember 2026* (read *den sechsten Dezember zweitausendsechsundzwanzig*). The *den* is
accusative, which is why the ordinal ends in -en. The same pattern appears after a weekday:
*Freitag, den 6. November*. Many modern letters leave out *den* and write just *Hamburg,
6. Dezember 2026* or *Hamburg, 06.12.2026*; both styles are correct.

This chart helps you choose the pattern:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which date pattern do I need?
  accDescr: If you are saying what today's date is, use der with the ending -e, as in Heute ist der dritte Mai. If you are saying when something happens on one day, use am with -en, as in am dritten Mai. If you are giving a range of dates, use vom with -en and bis zum with -en, as in vom ersten bis zum dritten Mai. If you are writing the date at the top of a letter, use den with -en, as in Berlin, den dritten Mai.
  A{"What are you saying?"} --> B["Today's date"]
  A --> C["When, on one day"]
  A --> D["From one date to another"]
  A --> E["Date at the top of a letter"]
  B --> B1["der + -e: Heute ist der dritte Mai."]
  C --> C1["am + -en: am dritten Mai"]
  D --> D1["vom + -en, bis zum + -en: vom ersten bis zum dritten Mai"]
  E --> E1["den + -en: Berlin, den dritten Mai"]
```

### Example 1: Reading a notice aloud

A sign says: *Weihnachtsmarkt: 27.11. bis 23.12., täglich 11–21 Uhr.* (*täglich* = daily.)
Read it as a full sentence.

1. Turn the numbers into months: 27.11. is the 27th of the 11th month, November; 23.12. is the
   23rd of December. Remember: day first, then month.
2. A range needs *vom … bis zum …*, and both words want -en.
3. 27th: 27 is above 19, so add -ste: *siebenundzwanzigste*, with -n: *siebenundzwanzigsten*.
   23rd: *dreiundzwanzigste*, so *dreiundzwanzigsten*.
4. Times: *von elf bis einundzwanzig Uhr* (official clock, lesson 11).
5. Result: *Der Weihnachtsmarkt ist vom siebenundzwanzigsten November bis zum
   dreiundzwanzigsten Dezember geöffnet, jeden Tag von elf bis einundzwanzig Uhr.*

### Example 2: Working out Easter Monday

*Ostern 2027 ist am 28. März. Wann ist Ostermontag? Und wann ist Karfreitag?*

1. Easter Monday is the day after Easter Sunday: 28 + 1 = 29, so the 29th of March.
2. Ordinal: 29 is above 19, so *neunundzwanzigste*; after *am* add -n: *am neunundzwanzigsten
   März*.
3. Good Friday is two days before Easter Sunday: 28 − 2 = 26, *am sechsundzwanzigsten März*.
4. Answer: *Ostermontag ist am neunundzwanzigsten März, und Karfreitag ist am
   sechsundzwanzigsten März.*

### Example 3: Writing a greeting card

You want to write to your German friend Lukas on 20 December 2026: you wish him a merry
Christmas and a happy new year, and you'll visit from the 2nd to the 5th of January.

1. Place and date at the top: *Toronto, den 20. Dezember 2026* (read *den zwanzigsten*).
2. Greeting: *Lieber Lukas,* (lesson 23: *lieber* for a man, *liebe* for a woman).
3. Wishes: *Frohe Weihnachten und einen guten Rutsch!* It's before New Year, so *Guten Rutsch*
   fits, not *Frohes neues Jahr*. *Einen* is accusative because the phrase is short for "I wish
   you a good slide".
4. The visit: *Ich komme vom 2. bis zum 5. Januar.* (read *vom zweiten bis zum fünften*).
5. Closing: *Viele Grüße* and your name.

## Text: A card from Oma

> Kassel, den 18. Dezember 2026
>
> Liebe Emma, lieber Paul,
>
> bald ist Weihnachten! Kommt ihr vom 22. bis zum 27. Dezember zu uns? Am 24. Dezember gibt es
> am Abend die Bescherung, und am 25. Dezember essen wir zusammen. Der Weihnachtsmarkt in Kassel
> ist toll: Wir können am 23. noch hingehen, er ist bis zum 23. geöffnet. Opa backt schon
> Plätzchen!
>
> Frohe Weihnachten und bis bald!
>
> Eure Oma

Translation:

> Kassel, 18 December 2026. Dear Emma, dear Paul, it will soon be Christmas! Are you coming to
> stay with us from 22 to 27 December? On 24 December, in the evening, we'll open the presents,
> and on 25 December we'll eat together. The Christmas market in Kassel is great: we can still go
> on the 23rd, it's open until the 23rd. Grandpa is already baking Christmas biscuits! Merry
> Christmas and see you soon! Love, Grandma

New in passing: *bald* (soon), *zu uns* (to our place), *hingehen* (to go there), *backen* (to
bake), *eure* (your, plural: a possessive from lesson 6). Notice *am 23.* and *bis zum 23.*:
the ordinal is read *am dreiundzwanzigsten* and *bis zum dreiundzwanzigsten*.

## Pronunciation

- *Weihnachten*: ei as in "eye", ch as in Scottish "loch": "VYE-nakh-ten".
- *Silvester*: here the v sounds like English v and the s like z: "zil-VES-ter".
- *Feiertag*: "FYE-er-tahk"; the final g sounds like k.
- *vierundzwanzigsten*: stress the first number: VIER-und-zwan-zig-sten; the g before s is a
  soft "ch" in standard pronunciation (as in *ich*), though many speakers say k.
- *Fasching*: "FASH-ing", with a short a; *Karneval*: "KAR-ne-val", with a v sound.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the -en after *vom* and *bis zum*: "vom vierundzwanzigste". Correct: *vom
  vierundzwanzigsten bis zum sechsundzwanzigsten*.
- Using *der* in the letter date: "Berlin, der 3. Oktober". The traditional form is *den*: *Berlin,
  den 3. Oktober* (or no article at all).
- Thinking Christmas Eve or New Year's Eve are public holidays. They aren't, but shops close
  early.
- Expecting presents on the morning of 25 December. In Germany they usually come on the evening
  of the 24th.
- Saying *Frohes neues Jahr* on 30 December. Before New Year, say *Guten Rutsch!*
- Wishing someone happy birthday the day before. Many Germans consider it bad luck; wait for the
  day.

## Key points

- Nine public holidays apply in all of Germany; the states set the rest. 3 October is the
  only one fixed by national law.
- Heiligabend, Silvester, Rosenmontag, Sankt Martin and Nikolaus are not public holidays.
- Presents come on the evening of 24 December (*die Bescherung*).
- Ordinals take adjective endings: *der* + -e; *am, vom, zum, den* + -en.
- Date ranges: *vom 1. bis zum 14. August* = *vom ersten bis zum vierzehnten August*.
- Letter date: *Hamburg, den 6. Dezember 2026*.
- *Frohe Weihnachten! Guten Rutsch! Frohes neues Jahr! Frohe Ostern! Alles Gute zum
  Geburtstag!*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: In the city: places, directions and the imperative
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 4 was about free time, plans and rules. Module 5 takes you out of the door: into town, onto
trains, into a flat and, finally, to the doctor. This first lesson gives you the places you find in
any German town, the words for giving and following directions, and a new verb form, the
**[[imperative]]**, which you use to tell or ask someone to do something: *Gehen Sie geradeaus!* — Go
straight ahead! *Nimm die zweite Straße links!* — Take the second street on the left!

You already know most of the pieces. The imperative is built from the present-tense forms you
learned in lesson 4, and the stem changes from lesson 13 (*nehmen → du nimmst*) come back here.
Separable verbs from lesson 12 behave exactly as they do in statements: the prefix goes to the end.

## Places in town

Learn every place with its article; you'll need the gender in the next lesson.

| German | English | German | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| *die Straße* | street, road | *die Kirche* | church |
| *der Platz* | square, place | *der Park* | park |
| *die Bank* | bank | *die Brücke* | bridge |
| *die Post* | post office | *das Zentrum* | centre, town centre |
| *die Apotheke* | pharmacy | *die Haltestelle* | stop (bus, tram) |
| *das Krankenhaus* | hospital | *die Ecke* | corner |
| *das Hotel* | hotel | *die Ampel* | traffic lights |
| *das Restaurant* | restaurant | *der Stadtplan* | city map |
| *das Café* | café | *der Weg* | way, path |
| *das Museum* | museum | | |

Here are eight of these places in a small town centre. The label colours show the gender: blue for
*der* words and pink for *die* words (in the next pictures, green is for *das* words).

![A small town centre. A main street crosses a side street. Top left: die Kirche (church) with a tower. Top right: die Post (post office) with an envelope sign. Bottom left: der Park (park) with trees, and die Haltestelle (bus stop) with a round H sign on the pavement. At the corner of the crossing: die Ampel (traffic lights). Bottom right: die Bank (bank) with a euro sign and die Apotheke (pharmacy) with a large A. On the right, the main street crosses a river on die Brücke (bridge). Feminine labels are pink and the masculine label is blue.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To ask whether something exists nearby, use *es gibt* (lesson 10) with the accusative:

- *Gibt es hier in der Nähe eine Apotheke?* — Is there a pharmacy nearby?
- *Gibt es hier einen Park?* — Is there a park here?
- *Im Zentrum gibt es viele Cafés.* — There are lots of cafés in the town centre.

To ask where a particular place is, use *Wo ist …?*:

- *Entschuldigung, wo ist die Post?* — Excuse me, where is the post office?
- *Wo ist hier ein Hotel?* — Where is there a hotel around here?

*In der Nähe* (nearby) is a fixed chunk; learn it as a whole. *Im Zentrum* means "in the centre";
you'll see why *in dem* becomes *im* in lesson 19.

## Directions: links, rechts, geradeaus

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *links* | (on the) left |
| *rechts* | (on the) right |
| *geradeaus* | straight ahead, straight on |
| *die erste / zweite / dritte Straße* | the first / second / third street |
| *an der Ampel* | at the traffic lights |
| *an der Ecke* | on the corner |
| *bis zur Ampel* | as far as the traffic lights |
| *weit* | far |
| *nah* | near, close |
| *zu Fuß* | on foot |
| *gegenüber* | opposite, across the street |

Some examples:

- *Die Bank ist links.* — The bank is on the left.
- *Das Hotel ist nicht weit. Sie können zu Fuß gehen.* — The hotel isn't far. You can walk.
- *Der Park ist ganz nah.* — The park is very close.
