| gestern Abend | last night, yesterday evening |
| letzte Woche | last week |
| letzten Montag | last Monday |
| letztes Wochenende | last weekend |
| vor zwei Tagen | two days ago |
| damals | back then, at that time |
| gerade | just (a moment ago) |
| schon | already, ever |

Here are the most important ones on a strip of days. Imagine today is Thursday:

![A strip of days. The first seven, Monday to Sunday, are bracketed as "letzte Woche". The next five, Monday to Friday, are "diese Woche". Today, Thursday, is shaded. Tuesday is labeled vorgestern, Wednesday gestern, Thursday heute and Friday morgen.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

*Letzte* ("last") takes the ending of the noun's gender: *letzte Woche* (die Woche),
*letzten Monat* (der Monat), *letztes Wochenende* (das Wochenende). Learn them as chunks.
*Vor* + a time means "ago" and the time comes after it, not before: *vor drei Jahren*
(three years ago). The *-n* on *Jahren* and *Tagen* is the dative plural; just copy it.

- *Ich habe gerade gegessen.* — I've just eaten.
- *Hast du schon die Hausaufgabe gemacht?* — Have you done the homework yet?
- *Vorgestern habe ich einen Brief geschrieben.* — The day before yesterday I wrote a letter.
- *Damals habe ich in Wien gewohnt.* — Back then I lived in Vienna.

## Dialogue: Monday morning

Lena and Tom work in the same office.

> Lena: Hallo Tom! Na, wie war dein Wochenende?
>
> Tom: Super! Am Samstag habe ich meine Eltern besucht.
>
> Lena: Schön. Was habt ihr gemacht?
>
> Tom: Wir haben einen Ausflug gemacht und im Park ein Picknick gemacht. Mein Vater hat
> viele Geschichten von damals erzählt. Wir haben viel gelacht.
>
> Lena: Und am Sonntag?
>
> Tom: Da habe ich lange geschlafen und dann eingekauft. Aber ich habe mein Handy im
> Supermarkt vergessen!
>
> Lena: Oh nein! Hast du es verloren?
>
> Tom: Nein, eine Verkäuferin hat es gefunden und mich angerufen.
>
> Lena: Da hast du aber Glück gehabt!

Translation:

> Lena: Hi Tom! So, how was your weekend?
>
> Tom: Great! On Saturday I visited my parents.
>
> Lena: Nice. What did you do?
>
> Tom: We went on an outing and had a picnic in the park. My dad told lots of stories from
> the old days. We laughed a lot.
>
> Lena: And on Sunday?
>
> Tom: I slept in and then went shopping. But I left my phone in the supermarket!
>
> Lena: Oh no! Have you lost it?
>
> Tom: No, a shop assistant found it and called me.
>
> Lena: You were lucky there!

Notes: *wie war …?* means "how was …?"; *war* comes in lesson 22. *Glück haben* means "to be
lucky", and its perfect is *Glück gehabt*. German says *ein Handy vergessen* for leaving
something behind by accident.

## Pronunciation

- The prefix *ge-* is never stressed and its *e* is a weak, short sound, like the "a" in
  "about": *ge-MACHT*, *ge-SE-hen*. Stress the stem.
- In *-ieren* verbs the stress is on *-ie-*: *stu-DIERT*, *fo-to-gra-FIERT*.
- *Gewusst* has a short *u* and a sharp *ss*: [gəˈvʊst]. Compare *weiß* with a long
  diphthong and *ß*.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the participle in the middle. *Ich habe gegessen Pizza* is English word order.
  The participle goes last: *Ich habe Pizza gegessen.*
- Adding ge- to inseparable verbs. Not *gebesucht* or *geverkauft*, but *besucht*,
  *verkauft*. Not *gestudiert* either, but *studiert*.
- ge- in the wrong place. Not *geeinkauft* or *eingekaufen*, but *eingekauft*.
- Weak endings on strong verbs. Not *gesehet* or *getrinkt*, but *gesehen*, *getrunken*.
- Using "did" for questions. German has no "do/did" helper. "Did you see it?" is
  *Hast du es gesehen?*
- Mixing up kennen and wissen. *Ich weiß Anna* is wrong; you *know* a person with
  *kennen*: *Ich kenne Anna.*

## Key points

- The perfect = *haben* (position 2, with the normal present endings) + past participle
  (last). It translates both "I did" and "I have done".
- Weak verbs: *ge- … -t* (*gemacht*, *gearbeitet*). Strong verbs: *ge- … -en*, often with a
  new vowel (*gesehen*, *getrunken*). Mixed: *gebracht, gedacht, gekannt, gewusst*.
- Separable verbs put *-ge-* after the prefix: *eingekauft*, *angerufen*.
- No *ge-* for *-ieren* verbs and verbs with *be-*, *ver-*, *er-*: *studiert*, *besucht*,
  *verloren*, *erzählt*.
- *Kennen* is for people and places, *wissen* for facts.
- Past time words: *gestern, vorgestern, letzte Woche, vor zwei Tagen, damals, gerade,
  schon*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The perfect tense reference sheet lists all the participles you need at
A1.

lessons.title: The perfect with sein, and war/hatte
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 21 you built the perfect with *haben*: *Ich habe eingekauft*, *Wir haben viel
gelacht*. A smaller but very common group of verbs uses *sein* as the auxiliary instead:
*Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren* (I went to Berlin). These are mostly verbs of going somewhere,
which is exactly what you need for holiday stories.

You also learn *war* and *hatte*, the short past forms of *sein* and *haben*. Germans use
them all the time instead of the perfect of these two verbs. After this lesson you can say
where you were, what you had, where you went and what happened.

## When to use sein

Use *sein* + participle for two kinds of verbs.

Verbs of movement from one place to another:

- *Ich bin nach Hause gegangen.* — I went home.
- *Wir sind nach Spanien geflogen.* — We flew to Spain.
- *Bist du mit dem Zug gefahren?* — Did you go by train?
- *Anna ist schnell zum Bus gelaufen.* — Anna ran quickly to the bus.

Verbs of a change of state, where someone or something becomes different:

- *Ich bin um sechs aufgestanden.* — I got up at six.
- *Er ist Lehrer geworden.* — He became a teacher.

Plus three verbs you just have to learn, because they use *sein* although nothing moves or
changes:

- *sein*: *Ich bin schon in Wien gewesen.* — I've already been to Vienna.
- *bleiben*: *Wir sind zu Hause geblieben.* — We stayed at home.
- *passieren*: *Was ist passiert?* — What happened?

A memory hook: if you can ask "from where to where?", it's *sein*. And verbs that take a
direct object (an accusative: *einen Film sehen*, *ein Buch kaufen*) use *haben*. Almost all
the *sein* verbs at A1 have no object at all.

This chart puts the questions in order. It is a rule of thumb that works for the verbs at A1:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: haben or sein in the perfect?
  accDescr: A rule of thumb in order. First, does the verb have an accusative object? If yes, use haben, as in Ich habe das Auto gefahren. If no, is it a verb of movement, such as gehen, fahren, fliegen, laufen or schwimmen? If yes, use sein, as in Ich bin nach Köln gefahren. If no, does someone or something change state? If yes, use sein, as in Ich bin aufgestanden. If no, is the verb sein, bleiben or passieren? If yes, use sein, as in Ich bin zu Hause geblieben. Otherwise use haben, as in Ich habe lange geschlafen.
  A["Accusative object?"] -- yes --> H1["haben: Ich habe das Auto gefahren."]
  A -- no --> B["Verb of movement (gehen, fahren, fliegen, laufen, schwimmen)?"]
  B -- yes --> S1["sein: Ich bin nach Köln gefahren."]
  B -- no --> C["Change of state?"]
  C -- yes --> S2["sein: Ich bin aufgestanden."]
  C -- no --> D["sein, bleiben or passieren?"]
  D -- yes --> S3["sein: Ich bin zu Hause geblieben."]
  D -- no --> H2["haben: Ich habe lange geschlafen."]
```

The word order is the same as with *haben*: the form of *sein* in position 2, the
participle last.

| | sein (position 2) | … | participle (end) |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | bin | nach Hamburg | gefahren. |
| du | bist | gestern | gekommen. |
| er/sie/es | ist | ans Meer | geflogen. |
| wir | sind | in die Berge | gewandert. |
| ihr | seid | spät nach Hause | gegangen. |
| sie/Sie | sind | im Hotel | geblieben. |

*Ans Meer* (to the seaside) and *in die Berge* (into the mountains) are chunks for movement
to a place; the grammar behind them comes at A2.

## The sein verbs you need

Most of these are strong verbs, so their participles end in *-en*. Learn them as a group.

| infinitive | perfect | | infinitive | perfect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| gehen | ist gegangen | | bleiben | ist geblieben |
| kommen | ist gekommen | | sein | ist gewesen |
| fahren | ist gefahren | | werden | ist geworden |
| fliegen | ist geflogen | | laufen | ist gelaufen |
| schwimmen | ist geschwommen | | passieren | ist passiert |
| reisen | ist gereist | | wandern | ist gewandert |

*Reisen*, *wandern* and *passieren* are weak or *-ieren* verbs; they only need to be
remembered for the *sein*.

Separable verbs of movement and change also use *sein*, with *-ge-* in the middle as in
lesson 21:

| infinitive | perfect | |
|---|---|---|
| aufstehen | ist aufgestanden | got up |
| ankommen | ist angekommen | arrived |
| abfahren | ist abgefahren | departed |
| einsteigen | ist eingestiegen | got on/in |
| aussteigen | ist ausgestiegen | got off/out |
| umsteigen | ist umgestiegen | changed (trains, buses) |
| mitkommen | ist mitgekommen | came along |
| zurückkommen | ist zurückgekommen | came back |
| umziehen | ist umgezogen | moved (house) |

- *Der Zug ist pünktlich abgefahren.* — The train left on time.
- *Wann seid ihr zurückgekommen?* — When did you come back?
- *Meine Schwester ist nach München umgezogen.* — My sister has moved to Munich.

One small exception you may notice: *fahren* takes *haben* when there is an object, because
then you are driving something: *Ich habe das Auto gefahren* (I drove the car). Without an
object, it's *sein*: *Ich bin nach Köln gefahren.*

*Schwimmen* can also take *haben* when you mean the activity and not going anywhere (*Ich
habe eine Stunde geschwommen*), but *ist geschwommen* is always correct.

In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland people also say *ich bin gesessen, gestanden,
gelegen* (sat, stood, lain). In the north and in most textbooks these take *haben*.

## war and hatte

*Sein* and *haben* have their own short past forms, called the **[[simple past]]**
(*Präteritum*). With these two verbs Germans much prefer the simple past to the perfect:
*Ich war in Rom* sounds more natural than *Ich bin in Rom gewesen*, and *Ich hatte keine
Zeit* is more common than *Ich habe keine Zeit gehabt*. Both are correct.

| | sein | haben |
|---|---|---|
| ich | war | hatte |
| du | warst | hattest |
| er/sie/es | war | hatte |
| wir | waren | hatten |
| ihr | wart | hattet |
| sie/Sie | waren | hatten |

The pattern is easy: ich and er/sie/es have the same form (*war*, *hatte*), and the other
endings are the ones you know from the present (-st, -en, -t, -en).

- *Wo warst du gestern?* — Where were you yesterday?
- *Ich war krank.* — I was ill.
- *Wie war der Urlaub?* — How was the holiday?
- *Das Wetter war schön, aber wir hatten nicht viel Zeit.* — The weather was nice, but we
  didn't have much time.
- *Hattest du Fieber?* — Did you have a temperature?
- *Wart ihr schon einmal in der Schweiz?* — Have you ever been to Switzerland?

## Holidays and places

Some words for travel stories:

- *die Ferien* (plural only) are the school or university holidays: *In den Sommerferien
  sind wir ans Meer gefahren.* — In the summer holidays we went to the seaside.
- *das Meer* is the sea, *der See* a lake. Same sound, different gender and meaning:
  *Wir sind im See geschwommen.* — We swam in the lake.
- *der Berg, das Dorf, die Insel, der Strand, der Fluss* — mountain, village, island,
  beach, river.
- *im Ausland* means "abroad": *Letztes Jahr war ich im Ausland.* — Last year I was abroad.
- *in der Natur* means "out in nature, outdoors".

![A landscape with labels: der Berg (a mountain with a snowy peak), der See (a lake in a green valley), das Dorf (a few houses and a church), der Strand (a strip of sand), das Meer (the sea, reaching to the horizon) and die Insel (a small island with a palm tree).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The lake is surrounded by land; the sea stretches to the horizon. That is the difference
between *der See* and *das Meer*.

Remember *wohin* (where to) from lesson 18 for asking about a destination. *Wo* asks about
a position:

- *Wohin seid ihr gefahren?* — Where did you go?
- *Wo wart ihr?* — Where were you?

And as in lessons 18 and 19, *nach Hause* means "(to) home", with movement; *zu Hause*
means "at home", without it:
*Ich bin nach Hause gegangen*, but *Ich bin zu Hause geblieben*.

## Telling a story

A story needs words that move it along. You know *zuerst, dann, danach* from lesson 12.
Add these:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| früher | in the past, formerly, used to |
| letztes Jahr | last year |
| plötzlich | suddenly |
| endlich | finally, at last |
| zurück | back |

- *Früher habe ich in einem Dorf gewohnt.* — I used to live in a village.
- *Plötzlich ist der Bus gekommen.* — Suddenly the bus came.
- *Endlich sind wir angekommen!* — At last we've arrived!

Remember: when one of these words starts the sentence, the verb (*bin, ist, habe…*) comes
next, in position 2.

## Dialogue: Wie waren die Ferien?

Sara meets her neighbour Herr Klein in the stairwell.

> Herr Klein: Hallo Sara! Sie sind ja wieder da! Wo waren Sie denn?
>
> Sara: Wir waren zwei Wochen in Italien. Wir sind am Samstag zurückgekommen.
>
> Herr Klein: Schön! Sind Sie geflogen?
>
> Sara: Nein, wir sind mit dem Auto gefahren. Zuerst waren wir in den Bergen, dann sind wir
> ans Meer gefahren.
>
> Herr Klein: Und wie war das Wetter?
>
> Sara: Super. Wir waren jeden Tag am Strand und sind viel geschwommen. Nur einmal hatten
> wir Regen.
>
> Herr Klein: Ist etwas passiert? Ihr Auto ist ja ganz schmutzig.
>
> Sara: Ja, plötzlich ist es kaputtgegangen, mitten in einem Dorf. Aber wir hatten Glück:
> Der Mechaniker war sehr nett.

Translation:

> Herr Klein: Hello Sara! You're back! Where were you, then?
>
> Sara: We were in Italy for two weeks. We came back on Saturday.
>
> Herr Klein: Lovely! Did you fly?
>
> Sara: No, we went by car. First we were in the mountains, then we drove to the seaside.
>
> Herr Klein: And how was the weather?
>
> Sara: Great. We were on the beach every day and swam a lot. We only had rain once.
>
> Herr Klein: Did something happen? Your car is really dirty.
>
> Sara: Yes, suddenly it broke down, right in the middle of a village. But we were
> lucky: the mechanic was very nice.

Notes: *wieder da sein* means "to be back"; *in den Bergen* is "in the mountains"; *jeden
Tag* is "every day"; *schmutzig* means "dirty"; *mitten in* is "right in the middle of"; *kaputtgehen* (to break down, to break) is *kaputt* + *gehen*, so it takes *sein*:
*ist kaputtgegangen*.

## Pronunciation

- *war* has a long *a*; *wart* (ihr) is short and ends in a clear *t*.
- *das Meer* sounds exactly like *mehr* (more): a long, closed *e*.
- *der See* is said [zeː], like English "zay" with a long vowel; the *s* is voiced, like
  English z.
- *die Ferien* is stressed on the first syllable, and the *i* glides into the ending:
  FAY-ryen, not "fe-REE-en".
- *plötzlich*: the *ö* is short, and *tz* sounds like "ts": PLÖTZ-lich.

## Common mistakes

- Using *haben* with movement verbs. Not *Ich habe nach Berlin gefahren*, but *Ich bin nach
  Berlin gefahren*. Not *Was hat passiert?*, but *Was ist passiert?*
- Forgetting to change *sein* for the person. *Wir sind gegangen, ihr seid gegangen* (not
  *wir ist*, not *ihr sind*).
- Adding an ending to ich/er in the simple past. Not *ich ware* or *er hatt*, but *ich war,
  er hatte*.
- Using *bekommen* for "become". *Bekommen* means "to get"; "to become" is *werden*: *Er
  ist Arzt geworden* (he became a doctor).
- Mixing up *wo* and *wohin*. *Wo* is the position, *wohin* the direction.
- Mixing up *das Meer* (sea) and *der See* (lake). The gender tells you which is which.

## Key points

- Verbs of movement (*gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen, laufen*) and change (*aufstehen,
  werden*), plus *sein, bleiben, passieren*, form the perfect with *sein*: *Ich bin
  gefahren.*
- Separable movement verbs too: *ist angekommen, ist zurückgekommen, ist umgezogen*.
- Verbs with an accusative object use *haben*.
- *Sein* and *haben* usually appear in the simple past: *ich war, du warst, wir waren; ich
  hatte, du hattest, wir hatten*.
- *Wohin?* asks where to, *wo?* where. *Nach Hause* is going home, *zu Hause* being at home.
- Story words: *früher, letztes Jahr, plötzlich, endlich, zurück*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. The perfect tense reference sheet has every *sein* verb in one table.

lessons.title: Linking sentences and writing short messages
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far most of your sentences have been short and single: *Ich bin müde. Ich gehe nach
Hause.* That is correct, but it sounds a bit like a robot. In this lesson you learn five
small words that join two sentences into one, and one word that links them in a different
way. Then you put everything to work in two practical skills: writing a short message or
e-mail (to a friend, or to someone you don't know), and filling in a form. Both are tasks
you meet in daily life in a German-speaking country, and both are part of the writing
section of the A1 exam (lesson 24).

## Joining sentences: und, oder, aber, denn, sondern

A **[[conjunction]]** is a word that links words or sentences. The five in this lesson are
easy for one important reason: they don't change the word order. They stand in front of
the second sentence in a slot outside the sentence, called **[[position zero]]**, and the
sentence after them stays exactly as it was, with the verb in position 2.

| conjunction | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| und | and | *Ich koche, und du räumst auf.* |
| oder | or | *Kommst du mit, oder bleibst du hier?* |
| aber | but | *Das Hotel ist alt, aber es ist schön.* |
| denn | because, as | *Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.* |
| sondern | but (rather), instead | *Er kommt nicht heute, sondern morgen.* |

Look at the second half of each example. *Du räumst auf*, *bleibst du hier*, *es ist schön*,
*ich bin krank*: these are complete normal sentences, as if the conjunction weren't there.

- *Ich habe Hunger, aber ich habe kein Geld.* — I'm hungry, but I have no money.
- *Wir können ins Kino gehen, oder wir sehen zu Hause einen Film.* — We can go to the
  cinema, or we can watch a film at home.
- *Ich lerne Deutsch, denn meine Freundin kommt aus Österreich.* — I'm learning German
  because my girlfriend is from Austria.
- *Sie hat die Prüfung bestanden, und jetzt feiert sie.* — She passed the exam, and now
  she's celebrating.

### Leaving words out

When both halves have the same subject, you can drop it after *und*, *oder* and *aber*:

- *Ich stehe auf und dusche.* — I get up and shower.
- *Ich lese am Abend oder höre Musik.* — In the evening I read or listen to music.

Don't do this with *denn*; it always needs a full sentence after it.

### denn: the A1 way to say "because"

*Denn* gives a reason. It always comes second, after the thing it explains: *Ich komme
nicht, denn ich muss arbeiten.* It can't stand alone as the answer to *Warum?* For that,
Germans use *weil*, which sends the verb to the end and comes at A2. For now, answer with
a full sentence: *Warum kommst du nicht? — Ich muss arbeiten.*

### sondern: not this, but that

*Sondern* corrects something negative. You need *nicht* or *kein* in the first half, and
then *sondern* gives the right information. If the first half is not negative, use *aber*.

- *Das ist kein Tee, sondern Kaffee.* — That's not tea, it's coffee.
- *Ich wohne nicht in Berlin, sondern in Hamburg.* — I don't live in Berlin but in Hamburg.
- *Das Zimmer ist klein, aber hell.* — The room is small but bright. (no negative, so
  *aber*)

### Commas

Put a comma before *aber*, *denn* and *sondern*. Before *und* and *oder* a comma is
optional when they join two complete sentences, and there is none when they join single
words: *Brot und Butter*, *Tee oder Kaffee*.

## deshalb: a preview

*Deshalb* (that's why, so, therefore) also links two ideas, but it works differently. It is
not a conjunction but an adverb, so it takes position 1 itself. The verb comes straight
after it, and the subject moves behind the verb, like after *heute* or *dann*.

- *Ich bin krank. Deshalb komme ich nicht.* — I'm ill. That's why I'm not coming.
- *Der Bus ist nicht gekommen, deshalb bin ich zu Fuß gegangen.* — The bus didn't come, so
  I walked.

Compare: *…, denn ich bin krank* (reason, normal order) but *Deshalb komme ich nicht*
(result, verb first). Using *deshalb* correctly in a message shows good control of word
order, but you can always say the same thing with *denn*.

The picture compares the two kinds of linking word. *Denn* and *aber* sit in front of the
sentence, in position 0, so the verb is still in position 2. *Deshalb* takes position 1
itself, so the verb comes right after it.

![Three sentences in slots. After "Ich komme heute nicht,": denn in position 0, ich in position 1, bin in position 2, then krank. After "Gestern war ich müde,": aber in position 0, heute in position 1, habe in position 2, then "ich Zeit". After "Ich bin krank.": position 0 is empty, Deshalb in position 1, komme in position 2, then "ich nicht".](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Writing a short message

Personal messages and e-mails in German follow a simple frame.

| | informal (du) | formal (Sie) |
|---|---|---|
| opening | *Liebe Anna,* / *Lieber Tom,* / *Hallo Anna,* | *Sehr geehrte Frau Weber,* / *Sehr geehrter Herr Klein,* |
| unknown person | — | *Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,* |
| closing | *Viele Grüße* / *Liebe Grüße* / *Bis bald!* | *Mit freundlichen Grüßen* |
| "your" | *dein, deine* | *Ihr, Ihre* |

Some rules that make your message look right:

- *Liebe* is for a woman, *Lieber* for a man. In the formal opening it's *Sehr geehrte*
  for a woman and *Sehr geehrter* for a man.
- After the opening put a comma, and start the next line with a small letter (unless the
  word is a noun or *Sie*): *Liebe Anna, vielen Dank für …*
- No comma after the closing; just put your name on the next line.
- Stay with one form: if you start with *Liebe Anna*, write *du* and *dein* throughout.
  To a stranger, an office or a landlord, use *Sie* and *Ihr*.

### What goes in the message

A good short message has a clear purpose and answers the points it must cover. A typical
pattern is: say why you are writing, give the information or reason, ask a question or
make a suggestion, and close. About 30 words is enough.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The building blocks of a short message
  accDescr: Six steps from top to bottom. The opening, such as Liebe Julia. The reason for writing, such as vielen Dank für die Einladung. The information or reason, such as Leider kann ich nicht kommen, denn meine Mutter hat Geburtstag. A question or suggestion, such as Hast du am Sonntag Zeit. The closing, such as Viele Grüße. Your name.
  A["Opening: Liebe Julia,"] --> B["Why you are writing: vielen Dank für die Einladung!"]
  B --> C["Information and reason: Leider kann ich nicht kommen, denn ..."]
  C --> D["Question or suggestion: Hast du am Sonntag Zeit?"]
  D --> E["Closing: Viele Grüße"]
  E --> F["Your name: Marco"]
```

Here is an informal message that says no to an invitation (an *Absage*):

> Liebe Julia,
>
> vielen Dank für die Einladung! Leider kann ich am Samstag nicht zur Party kommen, denn
> meine Mutter hat Geburtstag. Hast du am Sonntag Zeit? Wir können zusammen frühstücken.
>
> Viele Grüße
> Marco

Translation: Dear Julia, thanks a lot for the invitation! Unfortunately I can't come to the
party on Saturday, because it's my mother's birthday. Are you free on Sunday? We could have
breakfast together. Best wishes, Marco.

And a formal one that cancels an appointment (*einen Termin absagen*):

> Sehr geehrte Frau Berger,
>
> ich habe am Dienstag um 10 Uhr einen Termin bei Ihnen. Leider kann ich nicht kommen, denn
> ich bin krank. Haben Sie am Freitag Zeit? Bitte schicken Sie mir eine Nachricht.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
> Paul Novak

Translation: Dear Ms Berger, I have an appointment with you on Tuesday at 10 o'clock.
Unfortunately I can't come, because I'm ill. Do you have time on Friday? Please send me a
message. Yours sincerely, Paul Novak.

Notice how both use *denn* for the reason and a question to keep things moving. Useful
building blocks:

- *Vielen Dank für deine Nachricht.* — Thanks for your message.
- *Leider habe ich keine Zeit.* — Unfortunately I don't have time.
- *Ich habe ein Problem.* — I have a problem.
- *Kannst du mir bitte antworten?* — Can you answer me, please?
- *Ich freue mich auf deine Antwort.* — I look forward to your answer.
- *Bis bald!* — See you soon!

## Filling in a form

Forms (*Formulare*, lesson 15) ask for the same facts again and again. Learn the field
names and you can fill in almost any form, from a course registration to a hotel check-in.

| field | meaning | example answer |
|---|---|---|
| Vorname | first name | Elif |
| Familienname / Nachname | surname | Kaya |
| Geburtsdatum | date of birth | 14.03.1995 |
| Geburtsort | place of birth | Izmir |
| Staatsangehörigkeit | nationality | türkisch |
| Familienstand | marital status | ledig / verheiratet / geschieden |
| Geschlecht | sex, gender | männlich / weiblich / divers |
| Adresse (Straße, Hausnummer, PLZ, Ort) | address | Bergstraße 12, 50667 Köln |
| Telefonnummer, E-Mail | | |
| Datum, Unterschrift | date, signature | |

Points to watch:

- Dates are written day, month, year with full stops: *14.03.1995* is 14 March 1995.
- *Staatsangehörigkeit* is usually answered with an adjective: *deutsch*, *amerikanisch*,
  *türkisch*. *PLZ* is short for *Postleitzahl*.
- *Ledig* means single (never married), *verheiratet* married, *geschieden* divorced (lesson
  6). *Divers* is the third official option for gender.
- The *Unterschrift* is your signature, written by hand; *unterschreiben* is to sign.

Here is a filled-in form for a German course. Compare each field name with the answer next
to it:

![A course registration form for "Sprachschule am Markt: Deutschkurs A1", filled in by hand: Vorname Lukas, Familienname Berger, Geburtsdatum 02.11.2001, Geburtsort Graz, Staatsangehörigkeit österreichisch, Familienstand verheiratet, and a handwritten signature in the Unterschrift field.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Dialogue: help with a course registration

Elif wants to register for a German course and asks at the language school office.

> Elif: Guten Tag. Ich möchte mich für den Kurs am Abend anmelden.
>
> Frau Roth: Gern. Hier ist das Formular. Haben Sie eine Frage?
>
> Elif: Ja. Was heißt „Familienstand“?
>
> Frau Roth: Sind Sie verheiratet oder ledig?
>
> Elif: Ich bin nicht verheiratet, sondern ledig.
>
> Frau Roth: Gut, dann kreuzen Sie hier „ledig“ an. Und unten ist die Unterschrift.
>
> Elif: Wann ist die Prüfung? Ich muss sie unbedingt bestehen, denn ich brauche das Zertifikat.
>
> Frau Roth: Im Juni. Aber keine Sorge, Sie haben genug Zeit!

Translation:

> Elif: Hello. I'd like to sign up for the evening course.
>
> Frau Roth: Of course. Here's the form. Do you have a question?
>
> Elif: Yes. What does "Familienstand" mean?
>
> Frau Roth: Are you married or single?
>
> Elif: I'm not married, I'm single.
>
> Frau Roth: Good, then tick "ledig" here. And the signature goes at the bottom.
>
> Elif: When is the exam? I really have to pass it, because I need the certificate.
>
> Frau Roth: In June. But don't worry, you have enough time!

Notes: *sich anmelden* means "to register, to sign up"; *unbedingt* is "absolutely, really";
*keine Sorge* is "don't worry"; *ankreuzen* (to tick, to put a cross) comes in lesson 24.

## Pronunciation

- *Staatsangehörigkeit* is long but regular: STAATS-an-ge-hö-rig-keit. Stress the first
  part.
- *Unterschrift*: stress on the first syllable, UN-ter-schrift.
- *geehrte* has two separate e sounds: ge-EHR-te.
- *Grüße* has a long *ü* and *ß*: say "ee" with rounded lips.

## Common mistakes

- Putting the verb at the end after *denn*. Not *…, denn ich krank bin*, but *…, denn ich
  bin krank*.
- Normal order after *deshalb*. Not *Deshalb ich komme nicht*, but *Deshalb komme ich
  nicht*.
- Using *sondern* without a negative, or *aber* to correct a negative: *Ich trinke keinen
  Tee, sondern Kaffee.*
- Mixing *du* and *Sie* in one message, or writing *Lieber Anna*. Match the ending to the
  person: *Liebe Anna, Lieber Tom*.
- A capital letter after the opening: *Liebe Julia, Vielen Dank* is wrong; write *vielen
  Dank*.
- Writing dates the American way. 03.04. is the third of April, not March fourth.

## Key points

- *Und, oder, aber, denn, sondern* stand in position zero: the verb stays in position 2.
- *Denn* gives a reason; *sondern* corrects a negative (*nicht/kein … sondern*).
- *Deshalb* is in position 1, so the verb follows it directly.
- Informal messages: *Liebe/Lieber …,* → *Viele Grüße*. Formal: *Sehr geehrte/geehrter
  …,* → *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*.
- Forms: *Vorname, Familienname, Geburtsdatum, Geburtsort, Staatsangehörigkeit,
  Familienstand, Geschlecht, Unterschrift*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The Goethe A1 exam and review
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

This is the last lesson of the course. It does three things. First, it explains what
"A1" actually means and what you can now do. Second, it describes the best-known A1 exam,
the Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1, with strategies for each part. Third, it reviews
the grammar of the whole course and tells you where to look if something is still shaky.
The questions at the end of this lesson cover all 24 lessons, so treat them as a final
check.

You don't have to take an exam. But even if you never sit one, the free official practice
tests are a good way to see whether you have really reached A1.

## What A1 means

The levels A1 to C2 come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages
(CEFR), used across Europe and beyond. A1 is the first level. In plain words, a learner at
A1 can:

- understand and use very common phrases from everyday life, as long as they are about
  concrete, immediate needs: shopping, food, times, directions;
- introduce themselves and other people, and ask and answer simple questions about where
  someone lives, who they know and what they have;
- take part in a simple conversation, if the other person talks slowly and clearly and is
  willing to help.

That last point matters. At A1 nobody expects you to follow a fast conversation between two
native speakers. You are expected to manage with patience on both sides, and to ask for help
when you need it. That is a skill too, and this lesson gives you the words for it.

The six levels form a staircase. A1 and A2 are the "basic user" levels, B1 and B2
"independent user", and C1 and C2 "proficient user":

![The six CEFR levels drawn as a staircase rising from left to right: A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, C2. A1 and A2 are bracketed as basic user, B1 and B2 as independent user, C1 and C2 as proficient user. An arrow labeled "You are here" points to A1.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## The Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1

The exam has four parts. Hören, Lesen and Schreiben are written in one block of about 65
minutes; Sprechen is a separate oral exam.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The parts of the Goethe-Zertifikat A1
  accDescr: The written exam, about 65 minutes, has three parts in this order: Hören, about 20 minutes, then Lesen, about 25 minutes, then Schreiben, about 20 minutes. Sprechen is a separate oral exam of about 15 minutes in a small group. Together the parts give 100 points, and you pass with 60.
  W["Written exam, about 65 min"] --> H["Hören, about 20 min"]
  H --> L["Lesen, about 25 min"]
  L --> S["Schreiben, about 20 min"]
  O["Oral exam: Sprechen, about 15 min, small group"]
  S --> R["100 points in total, pass with 60"]
  O --> R
```

| part | time (about) | what it tests |
|---|---|---|
| Hören (listening) | 20 minutes | short everyday conversations, telephone messages, announcements |
| Lesen (reading) | 25 minutes | short notes and e-mails, signs and notices, small ads |
| Schreiben (writing) | 20 minutes | filling in a form; writing a short message of about 30 words |
| Sprechen (speaking) | 15 minutes | in a small group, with no time to prepare: introducing yourself, asking and answering questions on a topic with word cards, making requests and responding |

There are 100 points in total, and you pass with 60. The grades are:

| points | grade |
|---|---|
| 90–100 | sehr gut (very good) |
| 80–89 | gut (good) |
| 70–79 | befriedigend (satisfactory) |
| 60–69 | ausreichend (sufficient, a pass) |

The Goethe-Institut publishes the official description and free practice material,
including a full model test (*Modellsatz*) with audio and answers:

- [Exam overview: Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1](https://www.goethe.de/ins/si/de/spr/prf/gzsd1.html)
- [Free practice material (Modellsatz and Übungssätze)](https://www.goethe.de/de/spr/prf/ueb/pa1.html)
- [Official exam regulations (Durchführungsbestimmungen, PDF)](https://www.goethe.de/resources/files/pdf325/durchfuehrungsbestimmungen_a1_start_deutsch_1.pdf)

Details such as dates, fees and the exact format can change, so always check with the exam
centre where you register. Other A1 exams (for example telc or ÖSD) are similar in level.

## Strategies for each part

### Hören

- Read the questions before you listen. They tell you what to listen for: a time, a price,
  a place, a day.
- You don't need every word. Listen for the key facts: numbers, times and days (lessons 3,
  10, 11, 16) come up again and again.
- Watch out for changes: *Der Termin ist am Montag … nein, am Dienstag.* The second piece of
  information is usually the one that counts.

### Lesen

- Look at the type of text first: a sign, an ad, a short e-mail. Then read the question,
  then look for the part of the text that answers it.
- Signs and notices use the words of lesson 15: *geöffnet, geschlossen, verboten, nicht
  rauchen, bitte warten*.
- Don't panic about unknown words. Many tasks can be answered with the words you know.

### Schreiben

- In the form, copy the information exactly, with correct capital letters and umlauts.
  Dates go day.month.year (lesson 23).
- In the message, cover every point the task gives you. A point you forget costs more than
  a small grammar mistake.
- Use a correct frame: *Liebe …, / Lieber …,* or *Sehr geehrte …,* and a matching closing.
  Link your sentences with *und, aber, denn*.
- Check at the end: verb in position 2? Nouns with capitals? *du* or *Sie* all the way
  through?

### Sprechen

- Prepare your self-introduction at home until it is automatic: name, age, country, where you
  live, languages, job, hobbies. Use lessons 2, 3, 6, 7 and 13.
- When you get a word card, make a simple, correct question: *Was isst du gern zum
  Frühstück?* A short question you can say clearly is better than a long one you can't
  finish.
- For requests, use the polite forms from lessons 14, 15 and 17: *Können Sie bitte …? Gib
  mir bitte …, Darf ich …?* And answer other people's requests: *Ja, gern. / Hier, bitte. /
  Nein, tut mir leid.*
- If you don't understand, ask. That is a normal part of the conversation.

## Words for the classroom and the exam

These phrases help in any lesson, exam or real conversation:

- *Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?* — Could you repeat that, please?
- *Ich verstehe das nicht.* — I don't understand (that).
- *Was bedeutet das?* — What does that mean?
- *Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?* — How do you say that in German?
- *Können Sie das bitte erklären?* — Could you explain that, please?

And these are typical words in exam instructions and textbooks:

| German | English |
|---|---|
| die Aufgabe | task, exercise |
| der Teil | part |
| der Text | text |
| das Beispiel | example |
| die Lösung | answer, solution |
| die Seite | page |
| der Punkt | point |
| der Fehler | mistake |
| ankreuzen | to tick, to mark with a cross |
| ergänzen | to complete, to fill in (a gap) |
| üben | to practise |

- *Lesen Sie den Text und kreuzen Sie an.* — Read the text and tick (the right answer).
- *Ergänzen Sie die Wörter.* — Fill in the words.
- *Wie viele Punkte hast du?* — How many points have you got?
- *Ich habe drei Fehler gemacht.* — I made three mistakes.

### etwas, nichts, jemand, niemand, alle, beide, genug

These small words are everywhere, so they finish off your A1 vocabulary:

- *Hast du etwas gesagt? — Nein, ich habe nichts gesagt.* — Did you say something? — No, I
  didn't say anything.
- *Ist jemand da? — Nein, hier ist niemand.* — Is anybody there? — No, nobody's here.
- *Alle sind gekommen.* — Everybody came.
- *Wir haben beide bestanden.* — We both passed.
- *Hast du genug Zeit?* — Do you have enough time?

Note that German uses one negative word only: *Ich habe nichts gesagt* ("I have nothing
said"), never *nicht nichts*. *Nichts* and *etwas* never change their form.

## Review of the course

Use this table to go back to the lesson you need.

| topic | the core idea | lessons |
|---|---|---|
| sounds and spelling | ä ö ü ß, ei/ie, ch, nouns with capitals | 1 |
| du and Sie, sein | *Wie heißen Sie? Woher kommst du?* | 2 |
| numbers | *einundzwanzig*: ones before tens; prices | 3, 10 |
| present tense | endings -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en; verb in position 2 | 4 |
| questions | yes/no: verb first; W-question: W-word, then verb | 4 |
| nouns | der/die/das, plurals, learn each noun with its article | 5 |
| possessives | *mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr* | 6 |
| negation | *nicht* for verbs and adjectives, *kein* for nouns | 8 |
| accusative | only masculine changes: *den, einen, keinen* | 9 |
| time | *um acht Uhr, am Montag, halb drei* | 11 |
| separable verbs | *Ich stehe um sieben auf.* | 12 |
| stem changes | *fahren → fährt, sprechen → spricht, lesen → liest* | 13 |
| modal verbs | modal in position 2, infinitive at the end | 14, 15 |
| dates and weather | *am dritten Mai, es regnet*; für, ohne | 16 |
| imperative | *Gehen Sie! Geh! Geht!* | 17 |
| dative | *mit dem Bus, zum Bahnhof, bei der Arbeit* | 18 |
| location | *im Wohnzimmer, auf dem Tisch* | 19 |
| pronouns | *mich, dich, ihn; mir, dir* | 20 |
| perfect | *habe gemacht, bin gefahren; war, hatte* | 21, 22 |
| linking | *und, oder, aber, denn, sondern* | 23 |

If you had to remember only three things from this course, make them these: the verb is
always the second element in a statement; every noun has a gender, so learn it with *der*,
*die* or *das*; and the second verb (modal, perfect, separable prefix) goes to the end.

## Dialogue: practising for the speaking test

Ben and Yuki are practising together for the speaking part.

> Ben: Okay, du bist dran. Stell dich bitte vor.
>
> Yuki: Ich heiße Yuki. Ich bin 28 Jahre alt und komme aus Japan. Ich wohne seit einem
> Jahr in Leipzig. Ich spreche Japanisch, Englisch und ein bisschen Deutsch.
>
> Ben: Sehr gut! Jetzt die Karte. Das Thema ist „Freizeit“, das Wort ist „Sport“.
>
> Yuki: Machst du gern Sport?
>
> Ben: Ja, ich spiele Fußball in einem Verein.
>
> Yuki: Entschuldigung, was bedeutet „Verein“?
>
> Ben: Das ist eine Gruppe, zum Beispiel für Sport. Auf Englisch sagt man „club“.
>
> Yuki: Ah, danke!
>
> Ben: Gut, jetzt eine Bitte. Deine Karte zeigt ein Fenster.
>
> Yuki: Kannst du bitte das Fenster öffnen?
>
> Ben: Ja, natürlich. Siehst du? Die Prüfung ist kein Problem für uns!

Translation:

> Ben: OK, it's your turn. Introduce yourself, please.
>
> Yuki: My name is Yuki. I'm 28 and I'm from Japan. I've been living in Leipzig for a year.
> I speak Japanese, English and a little German.
>
> Ben: Very good! Now the card. The topic is "free time", the word is "sport".
>
> Yuki: Do you like doing sport?
>
> Ben: Yes, I play football in a club.
>
> Yuki: Sorry, what does "Verein" mean?
>
> Ben: It's a group, for example for sport. In English you say "club".
>
> Yuki: Ah, thanks!
>
> Ben: OK, now a request. Your card shows a window.
>
> Yuki: Can you open the window, please?
>
> Ben: Yes, of course. See? The exam is no problem for us!

Notes: *du bist dran* means "it's your turn"; *sich vorstellen* is "to introduce yourself";
*der Verein* is a club or association.

## Pronunciation

- *wiederholen* is stressed on *-ho-*: wie-der-HO-len. The *ie* is a long "ee".
- *jemand* and *niemand* are stressed on the first syllable: JE-mand, NIE-mand.
- *ergänzen*: stress on *-gän-*, and *z* is "ts": er-GÄN-tsen.
- *ankreuzen*: AN-kreu-zen, with *eu* like "oy".

## Common mistakes

- Answering a different question. In the speaking test, listen for the question word: *wo*
  (where), *wohin* (where to), *woher* (where from), *wann* (when), *wie lange* (how long).
- Leaving out a point in the message task. Tick off each point as you write.
- Translating word for word from English: *Ich bin 28 Jahre alt* (not *Ich habe 28 Jahre*),
  *Mir ist kalt* (not *Ich bin kalt*).
- Double negatives: *Ich habe nichts gesagt* (not *Ich habe nicht nichts gesagt*).
- Staying silent. If you didn't understand, say *Wie bitte?* or *Können Sie das bitte
  wiederholen?*

## What comes next

At A2 you will learn to talk about your past in more detail, compare things (*größer, am
größten*), use adjective endings (*ein großes Haus*), say why with *weil* and give opinions
with *dass*, and use more dative and two-way prepositions. Keep your vocabulary reviews
going: the words you learned here are the foundation for everything that follows. Reading
graded readers from the reading list and listening to slow German podcasts are the best
ways to keep growing on your own.

## Key points

- A1 means you can manage simple, everyday situations if people speak slowly and help.
- The Goethe A1 exam has four parts: Hören (about 20 min), Lesen (about 25 min), Schreiben
  (about 20 min), Sprechen (about 15 min, in a group). You need 60 of 100 points to pass.
- Practise with the free official model tests on goethe.de.
- Ask for help in German: *Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? Was bedeutet das?*
- *Etwas/nichts, jemand/niemand, alle, beide, genug* complete your A1 word list.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you
complete the lesson. Herzlichen Glückwunsch: you have finished German A1!

lessons.title: Honors: telling a story in the past (konnte, musste, wollte)
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 21 and 22 you learned the two tools of spoken German for the past: the **perfect
tense** for almost every verb (*Ich habe eingekauft*, *Ich bin gefahren*) and the short
forms *war* and *hatte* for *sein* and *haben*. With those you can say what happened. But a
real story also needs what you *could*, *had to* and *wanted to* do: "I wanted to get up
early, but I couldn't, and I had to wait for the bus." That is what this honors lesson adds.

You learn the **[[simple past]]** of the modal verbs (*konnte, musste, wollte, durfte, sollte*,
and *mochte*), a few more simple past forms that Germans like to use in conversation (*es
gab*, *ich wusste*, *ich dachte*), and how to put a whole story together. At the end you read
a longer story that uses everything from this module. This is a step beyond A1: the modal
past forms are usually taught at A2, but they follow exactly the pattern you already know
from *war* and *hatte*.

## The simple past of modal verbs

Why do you need a new form? Try to say "I had to work" with the perfect. You would need
*haben*, a participle and an infinitive: *Ich habe arbeiten müssen*. That is correct German,
but it is heavy, and it puts two infinitives at the end (*arbeiten müssen*), a pattern called
the **[[double infinitive]]**. Most speakers avoid it and use the simple past instead: *Ich
musste arbeiten.* For modal verbs, as for *sein* and *haben*, the simple past is the normal
choice in speech as well as in writing.

The forms are built in three steps:

1. Take the infinitive and drop the umlaut: *können* → *konn-*, *müssen* → *muss-*,
   *dürfen* → *durf-*. (*Wollen* and *sollen* have no umlaut to drop.)
2. Add *-te*: *konnte, musste, durfte, wollte, sollte*.
3. Add the person endings you know from *war* and *hatte*: nothing for *ich* and *er/sie/es*,
   *-st* for *du*, *-n* for *wir* and *sie/Sie*, *-t* for *ihr*.

![The verb können loses its umlaut to become konn-, then adds -te to give konnte. Below, its six forms: ich konnte, du konntest, er/sie/es konnte, wir konnten, ihr konntet, sie/Sie konnten, with the endings st, n, t and n highlighted and empty boxes for ich and er. On the right, the same pattern: müssen to musste, dürfen to durfte, wollen to wollte, sollen to sollte, and mögen to mochte, where g becomes ch.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| | können | müssen | wollen | dürfen | sollen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | konnte | musste | wollte | durfte | sollte |
| du | konntest | musstest | wolltest | durftest | solltest |
| er/sie/es | konnte | musste | wollte | durfte | sollte |
| wir | konnten | mussten | wollten | durften | sollten |
| ihr | konntet | musstet | wolltet | durftet | solltet |
| sie/Sie | konnten | mussten | wollten | durften | sollten |

*Mögen* (to like) follows the same idea but also changes *g* to *ch*: *ich mochte, du
mochtest, wir mochten*. *Ich mochte den Film* means "I liked the film".

And *möchte*? It has no past form of its own. To say what you would have liked or wanted in
the past, use *wollte*: *Ich möchte einen Kaffee* (now) → *Ich wollte einen Kaffee* (then).

### The word order doesn't change

The sentence bracket from lesson 14 stays exactly the same. Only the modal changes its form;
the infinitive still goes to the end.

- *Ich kann heute nicht kommen.* → *Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen.* — I couldn't come
  yesterday.
- *Wir müssen lange warten.* → *Wir mussten lange warten.* — We had to wait a long time.
- *Darfst du allein fahren?* → *Durftest du allein fahren?* — Were you allowed to go alone?
- *Er soll um acht da sein.* → *Er sollte um acht da sein.* — He was supposed to be there
  at eight.

### konnte or könnte?

Watch the dots. *Konnte* (no umlaut) is the past: "could, was able to". *Könnte* (with
umlaut) is a different form, the **[[subjunctive]]**, which means "could, would be able to" and
is used for polite requests and possibilities. You already know a subjunctive form:
*möchte* is the subjunctive of *mögen*.

- *Ich konnte nicht schlafen.* — I couldn't sleep. (past: it really happened)
- *Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?* — Could you help me, please? (polite request, now)

The same goes for *musste* (had to) and *müsste* (would have to), *durfte* (was allowed to)
and *dürfte*. For the past, never write the umlaut.

## A few more simple past forms you will hear

Apart from *war*, *hatte* and the modals, spoken German mostly uses the perfect. But a few
other simple past forms are so common that you will hear them all the time:

| simple past | infinitive | example |
|---|---|---|
| es gab | es gibt (lesson 10) | *Es gab keinen Kaffee.* — There was no coffee. |
| ich wusste | wissen | *Das wusste ich nicht.* — I didn't know that. |
| ich dachte | denken | *Ich dachte, du kommst.* — I thought you were coming. |

*Es gab* works like *es gibt*: it is followed by the accusative and is the same for one thing
or many: *Es gab einen Bus und zwei Taxis.* *Wusste* and *dachte* take the same endings as
the modals (*du wusstest, wir dachten*). Notice that after *ich dachte* the next part keeps
normal word order: *Ich dachte, du kommst.*

### Which past form? A rule of thumb

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which past form to use when speaking
  accDescr: A rule of thumb for spoken German. If the verb is sein or haben, use the simple past, war or hatte. If it is a modal verb, use the simple past, such as konnte, musste or wollte. A few other verbs, such as es gab, ich wusste and ich dachte, are also common in the simple past. For any other verb, use the perfect, such as habe gemacht or bin gefahren.
  A["Which verb?"] -- "sein or haben" --> B["Simple past: war, hatte"]
  A -- "modal verb" --> C["Simple past: konnte, musste, wollte"]
  A -- "es gibt, wissen, denken" --> D["Often simple past: es gab, wusste, dachte"]
  A -- "any other verb" --> E["Perfect: habe gemacht, bin gefahren"]
```

This is a simplification. In writing, especially in books and newspapers, the simple past is
used for many more verbs. And there are regional differences: in the south (southern
Germany, Austria and Switzerland) people use the simple past even less in everyday speech,
and you will often hear *ich bin gewesen* where a northerner says *ich war*. Both are
correct. For your own speaking and short messages, the chart above is a safe guide.

## Putting a story together

A good short story in the past has three parts:

1. The setting. When, where, who: *Letzten Montag …*, *Letztes Jahr im Sommer …* Here
   *war*, *hatte* and the modals do most of the work, because they describe the situation:
   *Ich hatte einen Termin. Ich wollte früh aufstehen.*
2. The events. What happened, one thing after another, mostly in the perfect, linked
   with *zuerst, dann, danach, plötzlich*: *Dann bin ich zur Haltestelle gelaufen.*
3. The end. How it finished and how you felt: *endlich*, *zum Schluss* (in the end):
   *Zum Schluss war alles gut.*

Remember the verb-second rule: when a time word or a linking adverb starts the sentence, the
verb (*bin, habe, war, musste*…) comes straight after it, and the subject follows.

### Example 1: from plan to past

You told a friend on Friday: *Am Samstag will ich wandern, aber ich muss noch arbeiten.* On
Monday you tell her what happened. Change the sentence step by step.

1. Find the verbs: *will* (wollen) and *muss* (müssen) are modals; *wandern* and *arbeiten*
   are infinitives at the end.
2. Modals go into the simple past: *will* → *wollte*, *muss* → *musste*. The subject is
   *ich*, so there is no ending.
3. The infinitives stay where they are, at the end.
4. Change the time word: the Saturday is now in the past, so *am Samstag* is still fine, or
   *letzten Samstag*.

Result: *Am Samstag wollte ich wandern, aber ich musste noch arbeiten.* — On Saturday I
wanted to go hiking, but I still had to work.

### Example 2: giving a reason

Your friend asks: *Warum warst du nicht auf der Party?* (Why weren't you at the party?) You
were ill, so you couldn't come, and you had to stay in bed all day; you slept a lot.

1. "I couldn't come" uses a modal: *Ich konnte nicht kommen.*
2. The reason with *denn* (lesson 23) and *hatte*: *…, denn ich hatte Fieber.*
3. "had to stay in bed" is a modal again, with *bleiben* at the end: *Ich musste im Bett
   bleiben.*
4. "I slept a lot" is an ordinary verb, so it takes the perfect: *Ich habe viel geschlafen.*

Answer: *Ich konnte leider nicht kommen, denn ich hatte Fieber. Ich musste im Bett bleiben
und habe viel geschlafen.* Notice how the forms mix naturally: simple past for the modals
and *hatte*, perfect for *schlafen*.

### Example 3: from notes to a story

Your notes say: *Samstag – Ausflug an den See – Regen! – Café – Kuchen – trotzdem schön.*
(*Trotzdem* means "all the same".) Build three parts.

- Setting: *Letzten Samstag wollten wir einen Ausflug an den See machen.*
- Events: *Zuerst war das Wetter schön, aber dann hat es plötzlich geregnet. Wir konnten
  nicht schwimmen. Deshalb sind wir in ein Café gegangen und haben Kuchen gegessen.*
- End: *Zum Schluss war der Tag doch schön.*

(*Doch* here means "after all"; you met it in lesson 8 as an answer word.) Count the past
forms: two modals (*wollten, konnten*), *war* twice, and three perfects (*hat geregnet*, *sind
gegangen*, *haben gegessen*). That mix is typical of spoken German.

## A story: Ein Montag zum Vergessen

Jonas tells his friend about a very bad Monday. Read it first without the translation.

> Letzten Montag hatte ich um neun Uhr einen Termin bei einer neuen Firma. Ich wollte früh
> aufstehen, aber mein Wecker hat nicht geklingelt. Ich bin erst um halb acht aufgewacht! Ich
> hatte keine Zeit für das Frühstück, und ich konnte nicht einmal duschen.
>
> Ich bin schnell zur Haltestelle gelaufen, aber der Bus war schon weg. Es gab kein Taxi, und
> ich musste zwanzig Minuten warten. Dann hat es auch noch geregnet. Um zehn nach neun war ich
> endlich bei der Firma, nass und müde.
>
> Die Chefin, Frau Wolf, hat gelacht: „Kein Problem, Herr Brandt. Unser Termin ist erst um
> halb zehn. Wir haben Ihnen am Freitag eine E-Mail geschickt.“ Oh nein: Am Wochenende habe
> ich keine E-Mails gelesen.
>
> Zum Schluss war der Tag doch noch gut. Ich habe den Job bekommen!

Translation:

> Last Monday I had an appointment at nine o'clock at a new company. I wanted to get up
> early, but my alarm clock didn't ring. I didn't wake up until half past seven! I had no
> time for breakfast, and I couldn't even shower.
>
> I ran quickly to the bus stop, but the bus had already gone. There was no taxi, and I had
> to wait twenty minutes. Then it rained as well. At ten past nine I was finally at the
> company, wet and tired.
>
> The boss, Ms Wolf, laughed: "No problem, Mr Brandt. Our appointment isn't until half past
> nine. We sent you an e-mail on Friday." Oh no: at the weekend I didn't read any e-mails.
>
> In the end the day turned out well after all. I got the job!

Notes: *ein Montag zum Vergessen* is "a Monday to forget"; *erst* + a time means "not until";
*nicht einmal* is "not even"; *weg* means "gone"; *auch noch* is "as well, on top of that";
*nass* means "wet"; *die Chefin* is a female boss; *der Job* is "the job". The story uses
every past form in this module: *hatte, war* (setting), *wollte, konnte, musste* (modals),
*es gab*, and perfects with *haben* (*hat geklingelt, hat gelacht*) and with *sein* (*bin
aufgewacht, bin gelaufen*).

## Pronunciation

- *konnte, musste, sollte, wollte* all have a short vowel followed by a double consonant:
  KON-te, MUS-te. The final *-e* is a weak "uh", like the *-e* in *habe*.
- *könnte* has the rounded *ö*: round your lips as for "o" and say "e". The difference from
  *konnte* is clear, so say it carefully.
- *Wecker*: short *e*, stress on the first syllable, WE-cker.

## Common mistakes

- Keeping the umlaut. *Ich könnte gestern nicht kommen* is wrong; the past is *Ich konnte
  gestern nicht kommen.* With an umlaut it means something else ("could, would be able to").
- Adding an ending to *ich* or *er*. Not *ich konnt* or *er musstet*, but *ich konnte, er
  musste*.
- Using a participle with a modal. *Ich habe nicht schlafen gekonnt* is wrong. Say *Ich
  konnte nicht schlafen* (or, rarely, *Ich habe nicht schlafen können*).
- Trying to put *möchte* in the past. There is no *möchtete*: use *wollte*.
- Moving the infinitive. The modal changes, the bracket doesn't: *Ich musste gestern lange
  arbeiten*, not *Ich musste arbeiten gestern lange*.
- Forgetting the verb-second rule in a story. *Dann ich bin gelaufen* is wrong; *Dann bin ich
  gelaufen.*

## Key points

- Modal verbs in the past: drop the umlaut, add *-te*: *konnte, musste, durfte, wollte,
  sollte*; *mögen* → *mochte*. Endings as for *war*: *ich/er konnte, du konntest, wir
  konnten, ihr konntet, sie konnten*.
- Germans prefer these forms to the perfect of a modal (*habe … müssen*, the double
  infinitive).
- The sentence bracket stays: modal in position 2, infinitive at the end.
- *Konnte* = could (past); *könnte* = could (would be able to; polite).
- Also common in the simple past: *es gab, ich wusste, ich dachte*.
- A story: setting (*war, hatte*, modals), events (perfect with *zuerst, dann, plötzlich*),
  end (*endlich, zum Schluss*).

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Honors: letters, e-mails and postcards the German way
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 23 you learned the frame of a short message: *Liebe Anna, … Viele Grüße* for a
friend, *Sehr geehrte Frau Weber, … Mit freundlichen Grüßen* for someone you address with
*Sie*. This honors lesson goes further. You learn how a formal German letter is laid out, how
to choose between the many openings and closings Germans really use (there are more than
two!), the spelling rules for *Sie* and *du* in writing, and how to write a message that
covers three points, the kind of task you meet in the writing part of the A1 and A2 exams.
Along the way you meet some customs: who offers *du*, how people greet each other in
different regions, and the holiday postcard.

## The parts of a formal letter

A formal letter to an office, a school or a company has a fixed layout. German offices
follow a standard for business letters (DIN 5008), but you only need the basic order:

![A formal German letter with its parts labeled: the sender's name and address at the top left (Absender), the recipient's address below it (Empfänger), the place and date on the right (Ort und Datum: Bremen, 12. Mai 2026), the subject line in bold (Betreff), which reads Kurs am Dienstag, the salutation (Anrede: Sehr geehrte Frau Berger,), the text, the closing (Grußformel: Mit freundlichen Grüßen) and the handwritten signature (Unterschrift) above the typed name.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

| part | German name | example |
|---|---|---|
| your name and address | der Absender (sender) | Paul Novak, Gartenweg 4, 28195 Bremen |
| their name and address | der Empfänger (recipient) | Sprachschule am Markt, Frau Berger, … |
| place and date | Ort und Datum | Bremen, 12. Mai 2026 |
| subject line | der Betreff | Kurs am Dienstag |
| opening | die Anrede (**[[salutation]]**) | Sehr geehrte Frau Berger, |
| text | der Text | ich habe am Dienstag … |
| closing | die Grußformel (**[[sign-off]]**) | Mit freundlichen Grüßen |
| signature and name | die Unterschrift | Paul Novak |

A few details that make a letter look German:

- The date is written with the day first and a full stop after the day number, because it
  is an ordinal number (lesson 16): *12. Mai 2026* or *12.05.2026*. You read it *zwölfter
  Mai*. An older style adds *den*: *Bremen, den 12. Mai 2026*, read *den zwölften Mai*.
- The subject line is short and printed in bold. In modern letters the word *Betreff* itself
  is usually left out. In an e-mail, the subject goes in the field called *Betreff*.
- The text starts with a small letter after the comma of the salutation (lesson 23).
- There is no comma after the closing, and nothing like "Yours" before your name.

An e-mail keeps only the last five parts: subject, salutation, text, closing, name.

## Register: from Sehr geehrte to Hallo

The **[[register]]** of a text is how formal it is. In lesson 23 you saw the two ends of the
scale. Real messages use the steps in between too:

| opening | form of address | when |
|---|---|---|
| *Sehr geehrte Frau Berger,* | Sie | formal letters, offices, first contact |
| *Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,* | Sie | you don't know the name |
| *Liebe Frau Berger,* | Sie | friendly but still formal: a teacher you know |
| *Hallo Frau Berger,* | Sie | very common in e-mails; neutral |
| *Hallo zusammen,* | ihr or Sie | to a group, such as your course |
| *Liebe Anna,* / *Hallo Anna,* | du | friends, family, classmates |

Look carefully at the third and fourth rows. *Liebe Frau Berger* and *Hallo Frau Berger* are
friendlier than *Sehr geehrte*, but with a surname (*Frau Berger*) you still write *Sie*.
The first name (*Anna*) goes with *du*.

The closings have steps too:

| closing | register |
|---|---|
| *Mit freundlichen Grüßen* | formal, the safe choice for letters |
| *Freundliche Grüße* | formal, a little lighter; common in e-mails |
| *Viele Grüße* | neutral: colleagues, a teacher, friends |
| *Liebe Grüße* | warm: friends and family |
| *LG*, *VG* | only in quick text messages to friends |

Many people find the abbreviation *MfG* (for *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*) rude, because it looks
as if you couldn't be bothered to write three words. Don't use it.

### Saying hello around the German-speaking countries

A quick recap from the module 1 honors lesson on the German-speaking world: *Moin* is the
northern hello at any time of day, *Grüß Gott* the polite greeting of southern Germany and
Austria, *Servus* the informal hello and goodbye of Bavaria and Austria, and *Grüezi* the polite
Swiss hello. Recognize them when you hear them; in writing, stick to the openings in the table.

## Sie and du in writing

Two spelling rules:

1. The polite *Sie* and all its forms always have a capital letter, even in the middle of a
   sentence: *Sie, Ihnen, Ihr, Ihre*. This is how a reader can tell "you" from "she" or
   "they": *Können Sie mir helfen?* (Can you help me?) but *Können sie mir helfen?* (Can they
   help me?). *Ihr Brief* is "your letter", *ihr Brief* "her letter".
2. *du* and *dein* are normally written with a small letter. In letters and messages you may
   write them with a capital as a sign of warmth (*Wie geht es Dir?*); both are correct
   since the 2006 spelling reform. The same goes for *ihr* and *euer* when you write to
   several friends. Choose one way and keep to it.

### Who says du first?

A recap from the same module 1 lesson: traditionally the older or more senior person offers
*du* (*Wollen wir uns duzen?*). It's a custom, not a rule, and many young people, clubs and
companies use *du* from the start. In a letter, if you are not sure, write *Sie*.

## A message with three points

Exam writing tasks and real life often give you three things to say. Plan before you write:
one or two sentences for each point, joined with *und, aber, denn* or *deshalb*.

### Example 1: an informal e-mail

Task: You are on holiday. Write to your friend Lisa. Say where you are, what you did
yesterday, and when you are coming back.

Plan:

1. Where: *Ich bin auf Rügen.* (Rügen is an island in the Baltic Sea.) Add the weather
   with *war* or *ist*.
2. Yesterday: perfect tense (lesson 21 and 22): *Gestern sind wir … gefahren / haben wir …
   gemacht.*
3. Coming back: present tense with a time: *Am Samstag komme ich zurück.*

Message:

> Liebe Lisa,
>
> viele Grüße von der Insel Rügen! Das Wetter ist super. Gestern sind wir mit dem Fahrrad
> zum Strand gefahren und sind im Meer geschwommen. Das Wasser war kalt, aber schön. Am
> Samstag komme ich zurück. Hast du am Sonntag Zeit?
>
> Liebe Grüße
> Mira

Check: all three points are there, the opening and closing match (*Liebe Lisa* … *Liebe
Grüße*), the *du* form is used throughout, and the verbs of the statements are in position 2. About 45 words.

### Example 2: from informal to formal

Paul wrote this to his classmate Tom:

> Lieber Tom,
>
> ich kann am Freitag leider nicht zum Kurs kommen, denn ich bin krank. Kannst du mir bitte
> die Hausaufgabe schicken?
>
> Viele Grüße
> Paul

Now he needs to write the same thing to his teacher, Frau Weber, whom he addresses with
*Sie*. Go through it part by part:

1. Salutation: *Lieber Tom* → *Sehr geehrte Frau Weber* (she is a woman, so *geehrte*). If
   he knows her well, *Liebe Frau Weber* is also fine.
2. The first sentence has no *du* in it, so it stays the same.
3. *Kannst du* → *Können Sie*, with a capital *S*. Remember that the verb form changes too:
   *Sie* takes the *-en* form.
4. Closing: *Viele Grüße* → *Mit freundlichen Grüßen*, or *Viele Grüße* if the salutation
   was *Liebe Frau Weber*.
5. Name: the full name, *Paul Novak*.

> Sehr geehrte Frau Weber,
>
> ich kann am Freitag leider nicht zum Kurs kommen, denn ich bin krank. Können Sie mir bitte
> die Hausaufgabe schicken?
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
> Paul Novak

## The holiday postcard

Even in the age of the smartphone, many Germans still send postcards from their holidays,
especially to grandparents and to colleagues at work. A postcard is short and uses exactly
the grammar of this module: *war* for the weather, the perfect for what you did. The
address goes on the right, the message on the left, and you need a stamp (*die Briefmarke*).

> Liebe Oma,
>
> viele Grüße aus Wien! Wir sind am Montag mit dem Zug angekommen. Das Hotel ist klein, aber
> sehr gemütlich. Gestern waren wir im Museum, und heute haben wir viel Kuchen gegessen!
> Am Sonntag fahren wir zurück.
>
> Dein Max

Translation: Dear Grandma, greetings from Vienna! We arrived on Monday by train. The hotel is
small but very cosy. Yesterday we were at the museum, and today we've eaten lots of cake! On
Sunday we're going back. Love, Max.

Notice the closing: on a postcard to family, *Dein Max* (your Max) or *Deine Mira* is
common. The form matches the writer: *Dein* for a man or boy, *Deine* for a woman or girl.

## Pronunciation

- *Absender* is stressed on the first syllable: AB-sen-der. *Empfänger* is stressed on the
  second, emp-FÄN-ger, because *emp-* is an inseparable prefix and is never stressed.
- *Briefmarke*: BRIEF-mar-ke, with a long "ee".
- *Grüezi* is Swiss German: GRÜE-tsi, two syllables. The *üe* is one gliding sound, an *ü* that
  slides into a short "uh", and *z* is "ts" as always.
- *Servus*: SER-vus. In standard German pronunciation the *s* at the start is voiced, like
  English z, but in Bavaria and Austria, where the word is used, people say it as a soft,
  unvoiced *s*.

## Common mistakes

- Writing *sie* for *Sie*. In a message to Frau Berger, *Können sie mir helfen?* asks
  whether *they* can help you.
- Writing *du* after *Liebe Frau Berger*. *Frau* or *Herr* + surname goes with *Sie*. (A few
  workplaces mix the two, but these are rare local habits; follow the rule.)
- Mixing levels: *Sehr geehrte Frau Berger … Liebe Grüße*. Match the closing to the opening.
- The American date: *Mai 12, 2026* is wrong. Write *12. Mai 2026*, with the full stop.
- Forgetting a point of the task. In the exam, a missing point costs more than a small
  grammar mistake. Tick each point off your plan.
- Writing *MfG*, or putting a comma after the closing.

## Key points

- A formal letter: Absender, Empfänger, Ort und Datum, Betreff (bold), Anrede, text,
  Grußformel, Unterschrift. Dates: *12. Mai 2026*.
- Openings from formal to informal: *Sehr geehrte/r … → Liebe/r Frau/Herr … → Hallo Frau/Herr
  … → Liebe/r or Hallo + first name*. As a rule, surname = *Sie*, first name = *du*.
- Closings: *Mit freundlichen Grüßen → Freundliche Grüße → Viele Grüße → Liebe Grüße*.
- *Sie, Ihnen, Ihr* always have a capital; *du, dein* may have one in letters.
- *duzen* and *siezen*: traditionally the older or more senior person offers *du*.
- For a three-point message, plan one or two sentences per point and link them.

complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Ankommen: registering, appointments and letters from the Amt
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 15 you met *der Termin*, *der Ausweis* and *das Formular*, and in lesson 23 you filled
in a form and wrote short messages, formal and informal. This honors lesson is about the first
weeks after you arrive in a German-speaking country to live: registering your address, booking an
appointment at the *Amt* (the public office), and reading the formal letters that start to arrive
in your post box.

Official German is famous for its long words and short forms. So the reading point here is
the abbreviations you'll see in letters and on notices (*z. B., ca., ggf.*), and the capital *Ihr*
that tells you a sentence is about you. Everything is about Germany unless it says otherwise; the rules are a
simplified guide, and the details depend on the town.

## Die Anmeldung: registering your address

Everyone who lives in Germany must register their address with the town. This is *die
Anmeldung*, and the verb is *sich anmelden* (to register): *Ich muss mich anmelden.* You have two
weeks after you move in. The office is called *das Bürgeramt*, *das Bürgerbüro* or *das
Einwohnermeldeamt*, depending on the town; in everyday speech people just say *das Amt*.

You usually need:

- your passport (*der Pass*, *der Reisepass*) or ID card (*der Personalausweis*, lesson 15's
  *Ausweis*);
- the *Wohnungsgeberbestätigung*: a short form from your landlord or landlady (*der Vermieter,
  die Vermieterin*) that confirms you've moved in;
- the registration form, *das Anmeldeformular*, filled in and signed.

In most cities you book an appointment online first. At the end you get a *Meldebescheinigung*
(a certificate of registration), which banks, employers and other offices may ask for. When you
leave Germany for good, you deregister: *sich abmelden*.

Austria and Switzerland have the same idea with other names and time limits. In Austria you
register within three days and the form is the *Meldezettel*; in Switzerland the rules depend on
the canton, and you usually have about two weeks.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Registering your address in Germany, step by step
  accDescr: First you find a flat. The landlord or landlady gives you the Wohnungsgeberbestätigung. You book an appointment at the Bürgeramt, usually online. You go to the appointment with your passport or ID card and the forms, within two weeks of moving in. You receive the Meldebescheinigung. A few weeks later your tax ID arrives by post.
  A["Eine Wohnung finden"] --> B["Der Vermieter gibt Ihnen die Wohnungsgeberbestätigung"]
  B --> C["Einen Termin im Bürgeramt buchen"]
  C --> D["Zum Termin gehen: Pass und Formulare mitbringen"]
  D --> E["Die Meldebescheinigung bekommen"]
  E --> F["Ein paar Wochen später: Steuer-ID per Post"]
```

## After the Anmeldung: the first letters

Once you're registered, letters start to come. Three you'll almost certainly get:

- The tax ID (*die Steuer-ID*, short for *steuerliche Identifikationsnummer*): an
  11-digit number that the federal tax office sends by post a few weeks after your first
  registration. Your employer needs it. Keep the letter.
- The broadcasting fee (*der Rundfunkbeitrag*): every household pays one fee for public
  radio and television, whether or not it has a TV. Flatmates share one fee.
- Health insurance (*die Krankenversicherung*) is required by law, and your insurer sends you
  a card for the doctor.

To open a bank account (*das Konto*) you go to a bank with your passport, and often the
Meldebescheinigung. And one tip that saves a lot of trouble: put your name on the post box
(*der Briefkasten*) and on the doorbell at once, or the post can't be delivered.

![The entrance of a block of flats: a front door with glass, the house number 8 above it, a doorbell panel with six buttons and name tags beside the door, and a row of six post boxes with name tags on the wall. Labels name the parts: die Haustür, die Hausnummer, die Klingel and der Briefkasten.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The names on the bells and the post boxes are how the post carrier, delivery drivers and your
visitors find you: *Bei wem soll ich klingeln?* — Whose bell should I ring? *Klingeln Sie bei
Brandt!* (*klingeln*: to ring the bell; *die Klingel*: the bell.)

## Reading a letter from the Amt

Formal letters follow a fixed layout (the module 6 honors lesson on letters shows it in full; lesson
23 gave you the greeting and closing): the sender at the top, your address, the place and date, a
one-line subject (*der Betreff*), the greeting *Sehr geehrter Herr …* and the closing *Mit
freundlichen Grüßen*. Once you know where each part is, you can find the
important information fast, even if you don't understand every word.

Here is a letter from a Bürgeramt, written for this course:

> Bürgeramt Mitte · Rathausplatz 1 · 12345 Neustadt
>
> Herrn Lukas Brandt, Gartenstraße 8, 12345 Neustadt
>
> Neustadt, 12. Oktober 2026
>
> Ihre Anmeldung: Termin am 20. Oktober
>
> Sehr geehrter Herr Brandt,
>
> vielen Dank für Ihre Online-Anfrage. Ihr Termin ist am Dienstag, 20. Oktober, um 9:30 Uhr im Bürgeramt Mitte, Zimmer 104.
>
> Bitte bringen Sie diese Unterlagen mit: Ihren Reisepass oder Personalausweis, die Wohnungsgeberbestätigung von Ihrem Vermieter und das Anmeldeformular. Bitte füllen Sie das Formular vorher aus und unterschreiben Sie es.
>
> Sie können nicht kommen? Dann sagen Sie den Termin bitte bis zum 19. Oktober ab.
>
> Mit freundlichen Grüßen
>
> Ihr Bürgeramt Mitte

*Bürgeramt Mitte, Town Hall Square 1. To Mr Lukas Brandt. 12 October 2026. Subject: Your
registration: appointment on 20 October. Dear Mr Brandt, thank you for your online request. Your
appointment is on Tuesday 20 October at 9:30 in the Bürgeramt Mitte, room 104. Please bring these
documents: your passport or ID card, the landlord's confirmation from your landlord and the
registration form. Please fill in the form beforehand and sign it. You can't come? Then please
cancel the appointment by 19 October. Yours sincerely, your Bürgeramt Mitte.*

New in passing: *die Anfrage* (request, enquiry), *die Unterlagen* (documents, papers; plural
only), *vorher* (beforehand), *bis zum 19. Oktober* (by 19 October). *Herrn* in the address is
*Herr* with an extra *-n*: addresses always use this form, so copy it.

Formal letters talk to you with *Sie* and the polite imperative (lesson 17): *Bitte bringen Sie
… mit*, *füllen Sie … aus*, *sagen Sie … ab*. All three verbs are separable, so the prefix waits at
the end of the sentence.

### Example 1: Finding the key facts

Before you read every word, scan the letter for four things: who, what, when, what to bring.

1. Who wrote it? The *Absender*: the Bürgeramt Mitte.
2. What is it about? The *Betreff*: *Ihre Anmeldung: Termin am 20. Oktober*. So it's your
   registration appointment.
3. When and where? Look for numbers: *am Dienstag, 20. Oktober, um 9:30 Uhr*, *Zimmer 104*.
4. What must you do? Look for *Bitte* and imperatives: bring the passport, the landlord's form
   and the registration form, filled in and signed. And if you can't come: cancel by the 19th.

That's the whole letter in four lines. The words you didn't know (*Anfrage*, *vorher*) didn't
stop you, because the layout told you where to look.

## Abbreviations in official German

Letters, forms and notices are full of short forms. An **[[abbreviation]]** (*die Abkürzung*) that
you read aloud as the full words is written with a full stop: *z. B.* is said *zum Beispiel*, never
"zet be". Only a few are said letter by letter, and these are written without full stops, like
*PLZ* (lesson 3) or *ICE* (the fast train).

| Abbreviation | Full form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *z. B.* | *zum Beispiel* | for example |
| *d. h.* | *das heißt* | that is, i.e. |
| *usw.* | *und so weiter* | and so on, etc. |
| *bzw.* | *beziehungsweise* | or; or rather; respectively |
| *ca.* | *circa* | about, approximately |
| *ggf.* | *gegebenenfalls* | if necessary, if applicable |
| *evtl.* | *eventuell* | possibly, perhaps |
| *u. a.* | *unter anderem* | among other things |
| *Nr.* | *Nummer* | number |
| *Str.* | *Straße* | street |

Watch out for *evtl.*: *eventuell* means "possibly", not "eventually". *Ich komme eventuell
später* means "I may come later", not "I'll come in the end".

The second thing to watch in formal letters is the capital *I*. *Ihr, Ihre, Ihren* with a
capital letter means "your" (formal, from *Sie*, lesson 6); *ihr* with a small letter means "her",
"their", or "you" (several friends). In a letter from an office, the capital forms are always
about you: *Ihre Anmeldung* (your registration), *Ihren Reisepass* (your passport; masculine
accusative, so *-en*).

### Example 2: Decoding a notice

On the door of the Bürgeramt you read:

> Bitte bringen Sie Ihre Unterlagen (z. B. Pass, Mietvertrag usw.) mit. Wartezeit ca. 20 Minuten. Ggf. müssen Sie einen neuen Termin buchen.

Read each short form as its full words, then translate:

1. *z. B.* = *zum Beispiel*; *usw.* = *und so weiter*: "Please bring your documents (for example
   passport, rental contract and so on)." *Der Mietvertrag* is a compound: *die Miete* (rent,
   lesson 19) + *der Vertrag* (contract), so it's masculine.
2. *ca.* = *circa*: "Waiting time about 20 minutes."
3. *Ggf.* = *gegebenenfalls*: "If necessary you'll have to book a new appointment." The modal
   *müssen* is in position 2 after *ggf.*, so *Sie* comes after it (inversion, lesson 12).
4. *Ihre* has a capital *I*: it's your documents, not "her" documents.

## Dialogue: Am Bürgeramt

Lukas is at his appointment.

> Beamtin: Guten Morgen. Herr Brandt?
>
> Lukas: Ja, guten Morgen. Ich möchte mich anmelden.
>
> Beamtin: Gern. Haben Sie Ihren Pass dabei?
>
> Lukas: Ja, hier, bitte.
>
> Beamtin: Danke. Und die Wohnungsgeberbestätigung?
>
> Lukas: Hier ist sie. Das Formular habe ich auch ausgefüllt.
>
> Beamtin: Sehr gut. Seit wann wohnen Sie in der Gartenstraße?
>
> Lukas: Seit dem 10. Oktober.
>
> Beamtin: Gut. Unterschreiben Sie bitte hier. … So, das ist Ihre Meldebescheinigung. Ihre Steuer-ID bekommen Sie in ein paar Wochen per Post.
>
> Lukas: Vielen Dank! Das ging ja schnell.
>
> Beamtin: Gern geschehen. Auf Wiedersehen!

*Official: Good morning. Mr Brandt? — Lukas: Yes, good morning. I'd like to register.
— Official: Of course. Do you have your passport with you? — Lukas: Yes, here you are. — Official:
Thanks. And the landlord's confirmation? — Lukas: Here it is. I've filled in the form too. —
Official: Very good. Since when have you lived in Gartenstraße? — Lukas: Since the 10th of
October. — Official: Good. Please sign here. … There, that's your certificate of registration.
You'll get your tax ID by post in a few weeks. — Lukas: Thanks a lot! That was quick. — Official:
You're welcome. Goodbye!*

*Die Beamtin* (*der Beamte*) is a civil servant. *Dabeihaben* means to have with you. *Das ging
ja schnell* (that was quick) uses *ging*, the simple past of *gehen*; you'll meet more of these
forms in this module's fairy-tale lesson. *Gern geschehen* is a polite "you're welcome". Notice *Seit wann …? — Seit
dem 10. Oktober*: *seit* takes the dative (lesson 18), so the date has *dem* and is read *seit
dem zehnten Oktober*.

## Pronunciation

- *Amt*: short *a*, and the *m* and *t* both sound: "amt".
- *Anmeldung*: AN-mel-dung; the stress is on the separable prefix, as in *anmelden*.
- *Bürgeramt*: BÜR-ger-amt, with a tiny catch in the throat before *amt*.
- *Wohnungsgeberbestätigung*: say it in parts; the main stress is on the first one:
  WOH-nungs-geber-bestätigung.
- *beziehungsweise*: be-TSEE-ungs-vai-ze; *gegebenenfalls*: ge-GAY-be-nen-fals.
- *Personalausweis*: per-so-NAAL-aus-vice.

## Common mistakes

- Missing the two-week deadline for the Anmeldung, or going without the landlord's confirmation.
- Reading *evtl.* as "eventually". *Eventuell* means "possibly".
- Saying abbreviations letter by letter: *z. B.* is read *zum Beispiel*, *usw.* is *und so weiter*.
- Reading *Ihre Anmeldung* as "her registration". With a capital *I*, *Ihr/Ihre* means "your".
- Writing *Herr* in an address on a letter: it's *Herrn Lukas Brandt*. (In the greeting it's *Sehr
  geehrter Herr Brandt*, without the *-n*.)
- Forgetting the name on the post box: the post won't arrive.
- Throwing away the Steuer-ID letter. You'll need the number for every job.

## Key points

- Register your address (*sich anmelden*) at the *Bürgeramt* within two weeks of moving in; bring
  your passport or ID card and the *Wohnungsgeberbestätigung*; book a *Termin* first.
- After the Anmeldung: the *Meldebescheinigung*, then the *Steuer-ID* by post; also the
  *Rundfunkbeitrag* and health insurance.
- Scan a formal letter for who (*Absender*), what (*Betreff*), when (numbers) and what to do
  (*Bitte …*, imperatives).
- Abbreviations are read as full words: *z. B.* (zum Beispiel), *d. h.*, *usw.*, *bzw.*, *ca.*,
  *ggf.*, *evtl.* (possibly!), *u. a.*
- Capital *Ihr/Ihre/Ihren* = your (formal); small *ihr* = her, their, you (plural).
- Put your name on the post box and the doorbell.
