lessons.title: Zusammen wohnen: neighbours, quiet hours and recycling
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 15 you learned to talk about rules with *man* and a modal verb (*Hier darf man nicht
rauchen*) and to read short signs like *Rauchen verboten*. In lesson 19 you moved into a flat and
learned to say where things are (*auf dem Tisch, im Bad*). This honors lesson puts the two
together: life in a German block of flats, with its house rules and its famous rubbish bins.

You'll learn to read a real-style *Hausordnung* (house rules), the infinitive used as a command
(*Bitte Tür schließen!*), and the second half of the two-way prepositions, which lesson 19 left
for later: *Wohin?* with the accusative (*Die Flasche kommt in den Glascontainer*).

The customs here are typical for Germany; the exact rules depend on the town and the building.

## Neighbours and the Hausordnung

Most people in German cities rent a flat in a building with several neighbours (*der Nachbar,
die Nachbarin*). They share the stairwell (*das Treppenhaus*), the cellar (*der Keller*), often a
courtyard, and the bins. To keep the peace (*die Ruhe*), almost every building has a *Hausordnung*
hanging in the stairwell. Here is a typical one, written for this course:

> HAUSORDNUNG
>
> 1. Ruhezeiten: Bitte von 22 bis 7 Uhr und von 13 bis 15 Uhr leise sein. Am Sonntag und an Feiertagen ist den ganzen Tag Ruhezeit.
>
> 2. Keine Fahrräder und Kinderwagen im Treppenhaus abstellen.
>
> 3. Im Treppenhaus und im Keller nicht rauchen.
>
> 4. Den Müll bitte richtig trennen.
>
> 5. Die Haustür ab 22 Uhr abschließen.
>
> 6. Auf dem Balkon nur mit einem Elektrogrill grillen.
>
> Vielen Dank! Ihre Hausverwaltung

*House rules. 1. Quiet hours: please be quiet from 10 p.m. to 7 a.m. and from 1 to 3 p.m. On
Sundays and public holidays it's quiet time all day. 2. Don't leave bicycles or prams in the
stairwell. 3. No smoking in the stairwell or the cellar. 4. Please sort your rubbish correctly.
5. Lock the front door from 10 p.m. 6. Barbecues on the balcony with an electric grill only. Many
thanks! Your property management.*

New in passing: *die Ruhezeit* (quiet time), *den ganzen Tag* (all day), *der Kinderwagen*
(pram, stroller), *abstellen* (to put down and leave), *die
Haustür* (front door of the building), *grillen* (to barbecue), *die Hausverwaltung* (the company
that manages the building).

Notice how the rules are written: no *Sie*, no *man*, and the infinitive at the very end.

## Infinitive commands on notices

Notices, instructions and announcements often give an order with just the infinitive, placed at
the end. This is an **[[infinitive command]]**. It's impersonal: it talks to nobody in particular, so
it needs no *du* or *Sie*.

| Imperative (lesson 17) | Infinitive command | With man (lesson 15) |
|---|---|---|
| *Schließen Sie bitte die Tür!* | *Bitte Tür schließen!* | *Man muss die Tür schließen.* |
| *Rauchen Sie hier nicht!* | *Hier nicht rauchen!* | *Hier darf man nicht rauchen.* |
| *Steigen Sie bitte ein!* | *Bitte einsteigen!* | *Man soll jetzt einsteigen.* |

How to build one:

1. Start with *bitte* if you like, then everything else in the sentence: the place, the object,
   *nicht*.
2. Put the infinitive last. A separable verb stays joined in one word: *Bitte Tür abschließen!*,
   *Bitte einsteigen!*
3. Leave out the article if you want it to sound like a sign: *Bitte Tür schließen* and *Bitte
   die Tür schließen* are both fine.

You hear them too: on the Berlin U-Bahn a voice says *Zurückbleiben bitte!* (stand back, please)
before the doors close. Recipes are full of them: *Die Kartoffeln waschen und kochen.* — Wash and
boil the potatoes. But don't use them face to face: *Tür schließen!* said to a friend sounds like
an army order. With people, use the imperative and *bitte* (lesson 17).

## Quiet hours and parties

The first rule is about *Ruhezeiten*, which the module 4 honors lesson on clubs and quiet hours
covers in detail: no drilling (*bohren*) or loud music at night or on Sundays. Planning a party?
Put a note in the stairwell first: *Liebe Nachbarn, am Samstag feiern wir eine Party. Es kann ein
bisschen laut werden. Wir bitten um Verständnis!* — Dear neighbours, we're having a party on
Saturday. It may get a bit loud. Thank you for your understanding! (*Wir bitten um Verständnis*,
"we ask for your understanding", is a set phrase on notices.)

## Rubbish: four bins and a bottle bank

Germans sort their rubbish (*den Müll trennen*). The colours below are common, but they vary from
town to town, so check the stickers on the bins.

| Bin | What goes in | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *die gelbe Tonne* or *der Gelbe Sack* (yellow) | packaging (*die Verpackung*) of plastic and metal | yoghurt pots, tins, plastic wrap, drink cartons |
| *die blaue Tonne*, *die Papiertonne* (blue) | paper and cardboard | newspapers, boxes, envelopes |
| *die Biotonne* (often brown) | food and garden waste | apple cores, vegetable peel, coffee grounds |
| *der Restmüll* (often grey or black) | everything else | old sponges, nappies, broken toys |

Glass doesn't go in any of these. It goes in big street containers, the *Glascontainer*, sorted by
colour: *Weißglas* (clear), *Grünglas* (green) and *Braunglas* (brown). Blue and other colours go
with the green glass. Because they're noisy, glass bins can usually only be used on working days
(*werktags*, which in Germany includes Saturday) during the day, typically 7 to 20 Uhr, and never on
Sundays or public holidays; a sign on the container gives the times.

![Four wheelie bins in a row, each with a picture of what goes in it: a yellow bin with a tin and a yoghurt pot, labeled die gelbe Tonne; a blue bin with a newspaper, labeled die Papiertonne; a brown bin with an apple core, labeled die Biotonne; and a grey bin with an old sponge, labeled der Restmüll.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Where does it go? Sorting rubbish in Germany
  accDescr: First ask whether the bottle or can has a deposit (Pfand). If yes, take it back to the shop's deposit machine. If not, ask whether it is glass. Glass goes in the glass container, sorted by colour. If it is not glass, ask whether it is paper or cardboard: that goes in the blue paper bin. Otherwise, packaging of plastic or metal goes in the yellow bin, food and garden waste goes in the brown Biotonne, and everything else goes in the grey Restmüll bin.
  A{"Pfand?"} -- ja --> B["Pfandautomat im Supermarkt"]
  A -- nein --> C{"Glas?"}
  C -- ja --> D["Glascontainer: weiß, grün, braun"]
  C -- nein --> E{"Papier?"}
  E -- ja --> F["Blaue Tonne"]
  E -- nein --> G{"Verpackung aus Plastik oder Metall?"}
  G -- ja --> H["Gelbe Tonne"]
  G -- nein --> I{"Essen oder Garten?"}
  I -- ja --> J["Biotonne"]
  I -- nein --> K["Restmüll"]
```

## Pfand: money back for bottles and cans

Many drinks are sold with a deposit, *das Pfand*: you pay a little extra and get it back when you
return the empty (*leer*) bottle or can. Single-use plastic bottles and drink cans carry a
deposit logo and 25 cents Pfand. Reusable glass and plastic bottles (*Mehrweg*) usually have 8 or
15 cents. In the supermarket you put the empties into a machine, the *Pfandautomat*, which prints a
receipt, the *Pfandbon*. You give it to the cashier at the *Kasse* and the money comes off your
shopping.

Empty bottles standing next to a street bin, not in it, are there on purpose: people who collect
bottles for the deposit can take them easily.

## Wohin? Two-way prepositions with the accusative

In lesson 19 you met nine **[[two-way prepositions]]** (*in, an, auf, unter, über, neben, zwischen,
hinter, vor*). With *Wo?* (where something is) they take the dative. With *Wohin?* (where
something goes: movement to a place) they take the accusative.

| | *Wo?* + dative (location) | *Wohin?* + accusative (movement) |
|---|---|---|
| der Sack | *Die Dose ist im (in dem) Gelben Sack.* | *Die Dose kommt in den Gelben Sack.* |
| die Tonne | *Die Zeitung ist in der Papiertonne.* | *Ich werfe die Zeitung in die Papiertonne.* |
| das Treppenhaus | *Das Fahrrad steht im Treppenhaus.* | *Bitte kein Fahrrad ins Treppenhaus stellen!* |
| der Keller | *Die Fahrräder sind im Keller.* | *Wir bringen die Fahrräder in den Keller.* |

Only the article changes: *den* for masculine (lesson 9), *die* and *das* unchanged. *In das* is usually shortened to *ins*, just as *in dem*
becomes *im*. (*Stellen* means to put something somewhere upright, like a bike or a bottle.)

Two verbs help you here: *werfen* (to throw; *du wirfst, er wirft*): *Er wirft die Dose in den
Gelben Sack*; and *kommen in* (to go in, belong in): *Das kommt in die Biotonne.* — That goes in the
organic bin.

The colour adjectives in *die gelbe Tonne*, *den Gelben Sack* have endings you'll study at A2;
learn them as chunks. *Gelber Sack* is often written with a capital G because it's the name of a
thing.

### Example 1: Sorting the kitchen rubbish

After breakfast you have: a yoghurt pot, a newspaper, an apple core, an empty wine bottle (green
glass) and an empty water bottle with a 25-cent Pfand logo. Where does each go?

1. The water bottle has a Pfand logo → back to the shop: *Ich bringe die Flasche in den
   Supermarkt.* That comes first, before you think about glass or plastic.
2. The wine bottle is glass, no Pfand → *Die Weinflasche kommt in den Glascontainer, ins
   Grünglas.*
3. The newspaper is paper → *Die Zeitung kommt in die blaue Tonne.*
4. The yoghurt pot is plastic packaging → *Der Joghurtbecher kommt in die gelbe Tonne.*
5. The apple core is food → *Der Apfelrest kommt in die Biotonne.* (*der Rest*: the rest, leftover)

Each sentence is *Wohin?*, so each bin is accusative: masculine *den Glascontainer, den
Supermarkt*.

### Example 2: Rewriting the house rules

Your neighbour asks what the Hausordnung says. Change each infinitive command into a sentence with
*man* and a modal verb.

1. *Bitte von 22 bis 7 Uhr leise sein.* → *Von 22 bis 7 Uhr muss man leise sein.* (*muss*, because
   it's an obligation)
2. *Im Keller nicht rauchen.* → *Im Keller darf man nicht rauchen.* (*nicht dürfen* = not allowed;
   *nicht müssen* would mean "you don't have to", lesson 15)
3. *Die Haustür ab 22 Uhr abschließen.* → *Ab 22 Uhr muss man die Haustür abschließen.* The
   separable verb is in one piece at the end, because it's an infinitive after a modal.

The time or place phrase comes first, so the modal is in position 2 and *man* follows it.

## Dialogue: Im Treppenhaus

Lukas has just moved in. On the stairs he meets his neighbour, Frau Schmitt.

> Lukas: Guten Tag! Ich bin Lukas Brandt. Ich wohne seit Montag im zweiten Stock.
>
> Frau Schmitt: Ah, der neue Nachbar! Herzlich willkommen. Ich bin Frau Schmitt, ich wohne unten.
>
> Lukas: Freut mich. Sagen Sie, wo sind denn die Mülltonnen?
>
> Frau Schmitt: Im Hof, hinter dem Haus. Papier kommt in die blaue Tonne, Verpackungen in die gelbe.
>
> Lukas: Und die Flaschen?
>
> Frau Schmitt: Die Pfandflaschen bringen Sie in den Supermarkt. Die anderen werfen Sie in den Glascontainer an der Ecke, aber bitte nicht am Sonntag!
>
> Lukas: Ach so. Darf ich am Sonntag bohren? Ich muss noch ein Regal an die Wand hängen.
>
> Frau Schmitt: Lieber nicht. Am Sonntag ist Ruhezeit. Am Samstag ist es kein Problem.
>
> Lukas: Gut, dann mache ich das am Samstag. Vielen Dank!

*Lukas: Hello! I'm Lukas Brandt. I've lived on the second floor since Monday. — Mrs Schmitt: Ah,
the new neighbour! Welcome. I'm Mrs Schmitt, I live downstairs. — Lukas: Nice to meet you. Tell me,
where are the bins? — Mrs Schmitt: In the courtyard, behind the building. Paper goes in the blue
bin, packaging in the yellow one. — Lukas: And bottles? — Mrs Schmitt: You take the deposit
bottles to the supermarket. The others you throw in the bottle bank on the corner, but please not
on Sunday! — Lukas: I see. Am I allowed to drill on Sunday? I still have to hang a shelf on the
wall. — Mrs Schmitt: Better not. Sunday is quiet time. On Saturday it's no problem. — Lukas: Fine,
then I'll do it on Saturday. Thanks a lot!*

*Wohin?* phrases: *in die blaue Tonne, in den Supermarkt, in den Glascontainer, an die Wand*.
*Wo?* phrases: *im zweiten Stock, im Hof, hinter dem Haus, an der Ecke*. New: *hängen* (to hang),
*unten* (downstairs), *der Hof* (courtyard), *lieber nicht* (better not).

## Pronunciation

- *Nachbar*: NACH-bar, with the throaty *ach* sound.
- *Müll*: a short *ü*: say *i* as in *bitte* with tightly rounded lips. Don't say *Mull*.
- *Pfand*: the *pf* is one quick sound; start with *p* and slide into *f*.
- *wirft*: short *i*, and every consonant is said: virft.

## Common mistakes

- Using the dative for movement: *Ich werfe die Dose in der Tonne* is wrong. Throwing goes
  somewhere, so it's *Wohin?*: *in die Tonne*.
- Splitting a separable verb in an infinitive command: *Bitte Tür schließen ab!* is wrong. The
  infinitive stays in one piece: *Bitte Tür abschließen!*
- Using infinitive commands to people: to a friend say *Schließ bitte die Tür!*, not *Tür
  schließen!*
- Putting glass in the yellow bin, or Pfand bottles in the glass container. Pfand bottles go back
  to the shop.
- Saying *Mull* instead of *Müll*: the umlaut matters.

## Key points

- A *Hausordnung* sets the building's rules: quiet hours (*Ruhezeiten*), usually 22 to 6 or 7 Uhr,
  often a midday rest, and quiet all day on Sundays and public holidays.
- Infinitive commands (*Bitte Tür schließen! Nicht rauchen!*) are for notices, announcements and
  recipes: the infinitive goes last, separable verbs stay joined.
- Common bins: *gelb* (packaging), *blau* (paper), *Bio* (food), *Restmüll* (the rest); glass goes
  to the *Glascontainer* by colour; Pfand bottles go back to the shop.
- *Wo?* + dative (*in der Tonne*); *Wohin?* + accusative (*in die Tonne, in den Sack, ins
  Treppenhaus*).

lessons.title: Es war einmal: reading a fairy tale
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lessons 21 and 22 you learned to talk about the past with the perfect (*Ich bin nach Bremen
gefahren*) and met *war* and *hatte*, the simple past of *sein* and *haben*. When Germans
*speak* about the past, that's almost all they need. But when they *write* a story, a novel or a
fairy tale, they mostly use the simple past (*Präteritum*) of every verb: *Der Esel lief weg. Er
kam an einen Wald.*

This honors lesson teaches you to recognise those forms, so you can read real stories. You'll
read a German fairy tale, the Brothers Grimm's *Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten* (The Town Musicians of
Bremen), retold in simple German for this course. You won't need to use most of these forms
yourself at A1; the goal is to understand them when you read.

## The Brothers Grimm and their fairy tales

Jacob Grimm (1785–1863) and Wilhelm Grimm (1786–1859) were brothers and scholars of the German
language, born in Hanau, near Frankfurt. In Kassel they collected stories that people told, and
from 1812 they published them as *Kinder- und Hausmärchen* (Children's and Household Tales).
*Hänsel und Gretel*, *Rotkäppchen* (Little Red Riding Hood), *Schneewittchen* (Snow White) and
*Aschenputtel* (Cinderella) all come from this collection. The Grimms kept changing the stories
from one edition to the next; *Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten* first appeared in the second edition,
in 1819.

Today a tourist route, the *Deutsche Märchenstraße* (German Fairy Tale Route), runs about 600
kilometres from Hanau north to Bremen. In Bremen, next to the town hall, stands a bronze statue of
the four animals by the sculptor Gerhard Marcks, set up in 1953. Visitors hold the donkey's front
legs for luck, so they shine like gold.

Many fairy tales follow the same pattern, and knowing it helps you guess what comes next:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The usual shape of a German fairy tale
  accDescr: A fairy tale starts with the formula Es war einmal, once upon a time. Then comes a problem, for example the hero is poor, old or in danger. The hero sets out on a journey and meets helpers on the way. There is a danger or a test, such as robbers, a witch or a wolf. The heroes win with a trick or with help, and the tale ends happily, often with the formula Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann leben sie noch heute.
  A["Es war einmal …"] --> B["A problem: poor, old or in danger"]
  B --> C["A journey: helpers on the way"]
  C --> D["A danger or a test: robbers, a witch, a wolf"]
  D --> E["A trick or help wins"]
  E --> F["A happy end: … dann leben sie noch heute."]
```

The opening *Es war einmal …* means "once upon a time" (literally "there was once"), and many
tales end with *Und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann leben sie noch heute* — "and if they
haven't died, they're still living today", the German "happily ever after".

## The simple past in stories

You know the **[[simple past]]** of *sein* and *haben* (*war, hatte*) from lesson 22. Every other verb
has one too. There are two main patterns, matching the weak and strong verbs of the perfect
(lesson 21).

**[[Weak verbs]]** add *-te* to the stem. Their past participle ends in *-t*.

| Infinitive | Simple past (er/sie/es) | Perfect |
|---|---|---|
| *sagen* | *sagte* | *hat gesagt* |
| *machen* | *machte* | *hat gemacht* |
| *fragen* | *fragte* | *hat gefragt* |
| *wohnen* | *wohnte* | *hat gewohnt* |
| *arbeiten* | *arbeitete* | *hat gearbeitet* |

Stems ending in *-t* or *-d* add an extra *-e-*, just as in the present (*er arbeitet*): *arbeitete*.

**[[Strong verbs]]** change their vowel and add no ending for *ich* and *er/sie/es*. Their past
participle usually ends in *-en*.

| Infinitive | Simple past (er/sie/es) | Perfect |
|---|---|---|
| *gehen* | *ging* | *ist gegangen* |
| *kommen* | *kam* | *ist gekommen* |
| *laufen* | *lief* | *ist gelaufen* |
| *sehen* | *sah* | *hat gesehen* |
| *finden* | *fand* | *hat gefunden* |
| *sitzen* | *saß* | *hat gesessen* |
| *liegen* | *lag* | *hat gelegen* |
| *rufen* | *rief* | *hat gerufen* |
| *schreien* | *schrie* | *hat geschrien* |
| *springen* | *sprang* | *ist gesprungen* |
| *essen* | *aß* | *hat gegessen* |
| *trinken* | *trank* | *hat getrunken* |

For strong verbs there's no rule that gives you the new vowel, so dictionaries and grammar
tables list three forms for each verb: the infinitive, the simple past and the past participle
(*gehen, ging, gegangen*). These are the verb's **[[principal parts]]**. Learn them together, like a
noun with its article.

Modal verbs take *-te* and lose their umlaut, as you saw in the module 6 honors lesson: *konnte,
musste, wollte*.

The endings for the other persons are the same as for *war* (lesson 22): *ich ging, du gingst,
er ging, wir gingen, ihr gingt, sie gingen*. In stories you mostly meet *er, sie, es* and *sie*
(plural), so focus on those: *sie gingen*, *sie sagten*.

### How to recognise a simple past form

When you meet an unknown verb form in a story, ask:

1. Does it end in *-te* or *-ten*? Then it's probably a weak verb: take off *-te* and add *-en*
   to find the infinitive (*fragte → fragen*).
2. Is it a short word with a different vowel, and no ending? Then it's probably a strong verb
   (*kam, sah, lief*). Try the vowels you know from the participle or the present: *gesprungen →
   springen → sprang*.
3. Still stuck? Many strong verbs are strong in English too: *drink / drank*, *come / came*,
   *find / found*.

### Example 1: From the simple past to the infinitive

Find the infinitive of each verb in this sentence: *Die Katze saß am Weg und sah die Tiere.*

1. *saß*: short, no ending, vowel *a*. Which verb has an *s* sound and fits "sitting by the
   path"? *sitzen*. The pattern *i → a* is like *trinken → trank*. So *saß* = sat.
2. *sah*: short, no ending. *gesehen*, *sehen*. The vowel *e → a*, as in *essen → aß*. So *sah*
   = saw.
3. Translation: *The cat was sitting by the path and saw the animals.*

## The story: Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten

New words for the story: *der Esel* (donkey), *der Hahn* (rooster), *der Räuber* (robber), *der
Wald* (forest), *das Licht* (light), *die Angst* (fear; *Angst haben*: to be afraid), *der Herr*
(here: master), *traurig* (sad), *weglaufen* (to run away), *bellen* (to bark), *das Gespenst*
(ghost), *die Hexe* (witch).

> Es war einmal ein Esel. Er war alt und konnte nicht mehr schwer arbeiten. Sein Herr wollte ihn nicht mehr haben. Da lief der Esel weg. „Ich gehe nach Bremen", sagte er. „Dort mache ich Musik."
>
> Auf dem Weg fand er einen Hund. Der Hund lag müde an der Straße. „Ich bin alt, und mein Herr will mich nicht mehr", sagte er. „Komm mit nach Bremen!", rief der Esel. „Wir machen zusammen Musik."
>
> Bald sahen sie eine Katze. Sie saß traurig am Weg. Auch sie war alt und konnte keine Mäuse mehr fangen. Die Katze kam mit.
>
> Dann kamen die drei zu einem Bauernhof. Ein Hahn stand auf dem Zaun und rief: „Kikeriki! Morgen kocht die Bäuerin eine Suppe aus mir!" „Komm mit uns!", sagten die Tiere. Und so waren sie zu viert.
>
> Bremen war weit. Am Abend kamen sie in einen Wald. Da sahen sie ein Licht. Es war ein Haus. Der Esel ging zum Fenster und sah hinein. Am Tisch saßen Räuber. Sie aßen und tranken. Die Tiere hatten großen Hunger, und sie machten einen Plan.
>
> Der Esel stand am Fenster. Der Hund sprang auf den Esel, die Katze sprang auf den Hund, und der Hahn flog auf die Katze. Dann machten sie Musik: Der Esel schrie, der Hund bellte, die Katze miaute und der Hahn krähte. Sie fielen durch das Fenster ins Zimmer.
>
> Die Räuber hatten große Angst. „Ein Gespenst!", riefen sie und liefen in den Wald. Die vier Freunde aßen und tranken, und dann gingen sie schlafen.
>
> In der Nacht kam ein Räuber zurück. Im Haus war es dunkel. Die Katze kratzte ihn, der Hund biss ihn ins Bein, der Esel trat ihn, und der Hahn rief: „Kikeriki!" Der Räuber lief zu den anderen zurück. „Im Haus wohnt eine Hexe!", sagte er. Die Räuber kamen nie wieder.
>
> Und die vier Musikanten? Sie fanden das Haus sehr schön und blieben dort. Nach Bremen kamen sie nie.

*Once upon a time there was a donkey. He was old and couldn't do heavy work any more. His master
didn't want him any longer. So the donkey ran away. "I'm going to Bremen," he said. "There I'll
make music." On the way he found a dog. The dog was lying tired by the road. "I'm old, and my
master doesn't want me any more," he said. "Come with me to Bremen!" called the donkey. "We'll
make music together." Soon they saw a cat. She was sitting sadly by the path. She was old too and
couldn't catch mice any more. The cat came along. Then the three came to a farm. A rooster was
standing on the fence and called: "Cock-a-doodle-doo! Tomorrow the farmer's wife is going to make
soup out of me!" "Come with us!" said the animals. And so there were four of them. Bremen was far away. In
the evening they came into a forest. There they saw a light. It was a house. The donkey went to
the window and looked in. Robbers were sitting at the table. They were eating and drinking. The
animals were very hungry, and they made a plan. The donkey stood at the window. The dog jumped
onto the donkey, the cat jumped onto the dog, and the rooster flew onto the cat. Then they made
music: the donkey brayed, the dog barked, the cat miaowed and the rooster crowed. They fell
through the window into the room. The robbers were terrified. "A ghost!" they shouted, and ran
into the forest. The four friends ate and drank, and then they went to sleep. In the night one
robber came back. It was dark in the house. The cat scratched him, the dog bit him in the leg,
the donkey kicked him, and the rooster called "Cock-a-doodle-doo!" The robber ran back to the
others. "A witch lives in the house!" he said. The robbers never came back. And the four
musicians? They liked the house very much and stayed there. They never got to Bremen.*

This retelling is much shorter than the Grimms' version, where the frightened robber describes
each animal as a different monster. Their text is long out of copyright and free to read, but its
German is well above A1, so save it for later.

![Four animals standing on each other's backs, in the famous pose of the Bremen Town Musicians: a donkey at the bottom, a dog on the donkey, a cat on the dog and a rooster at the top, with a lit window behind them. Labels name them: der Esel, der Hund, die Katze and der Hahn.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### Example 2: Following the verbs through a paragraph

Take the paragraph that begins *Der Esel stand am Fenster.* List its verbs and turn each into the
perfect, the way you'd tell the story aloud.

| Simple past | Infinitive | Perfect (spoken) |
|---|---|---|
| *stand* | *stehen* | *hat gestanden* |
| *sprang* | *springen* | *ist gesprungen* |
| *flog* | *fliegen* | *ist geflogen* |
| *machten* | *machen* | *haben gemacht* |
| *schrie* | *schreien* | *hat geschrien* |
| *bellte* | *bellen* | *hat gebellt* |
| *fielen* | *fallen* | *sind gefallen* |

So, told aloud: *Der Hund ist auf den Esel gesprungen, und der Hahn ist auf die Katze geflogen.
Dann haben sie Musik gemacht.* Movement verbs (*springen, fliegen, fallen*) take *sein* in the
perfect, as in lesson 22. *Bellte* and *machten* end in *-te(n)*: weak verbs, like the two animal sounds the table leaves out,
*miaute* (*miauen*) and *krähte* (*krähen*). All the others
change their vowel: strong verbs. (In southern Germany and Austria you'll also hear *ist
gestanden*, lesson 22.)

Notice also *auf den Esel* (accusative, *Wohin?*) but *am Fenster* (dative, *Wo?*), as in the
*Zusammen wohnen* lesson.

## Pronunciation

- *Märchen*: MÄR-chen, with the soft *ch* of *ich*. It's a diminutive (see the next lesson), so it's *das
  Märchen*.
- *Esel*: AY-zel; the *s* between vowels is a soft *z* sound.
- *Räuber*: *äu* sounds like *eu*, "oy": ROY-ber.
- *schrie*: *ie* is a long "ee": shree. *Ging, sang, sprang*: short vowels.
- *Kikeriki*: German roosters say kee-ke-ree-KEE.

## Common mistakes

- Using these forms everywhere when you speak. *Ich ging gestern ins Kino* is correct but sounds
  like a book in most of Germany; in conversation say *Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen*. Use the
  simple past freely only for *war, hatte* and the modals.
- Reading *lief* as "left" or *fand* as "fanned": use the principal parts (*laufen, lief,
  gelaufen*) to find the real verb.
- Adding *-te* to a strong verb: *er kommte* or *er gehte* don't exist; it's *kam* and *ging*.
- Expecting an ending on strong verbs with *er/sie/es*: *er kam*, *sie sah*, not *er kamt*.
- Confusing *der Hahn* (rooster) with *das Huhn* (hen, chicken).

## Key points

- Stories, novels and fairy tales are written in the simple past; conversation uses the perfect
  (except *war, hatte* and the modals).
- Weak verbs: stem + *-te* (*sagte, machte*; *arbeitete*). Strong verbs: new vowel, no ending for
  *ich* and *er/sie/es* (*kam, sah, ging, lief*). Modals: *konnte, musste, wollte*.
- Learn strong verbs by their principal parts: *gehen, ging, gegangen*.
- Fairy tales start with *Es war einmal* and often end *… dann leben sie noch heute*.
- *Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten*: donkey, dog, cat and rooster scare robbers out of a house and never
  reach Bremen. The Grimms' *Kinder- und Hausmärchen* appeared from 1812.

lessons.title: Gemütlich: Feierabend, the Kleingarten and little words
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 12 you met *der Feierabend*, the free time after work, and in lesson 19 the adjective
*gemütlich* (cosy, comfortable). This last honors lesson of the module is about what many people
in Germany do with that free time: an evening in the *Kneipe* (pub), or a weekend in a small rented
garden on the edge of town, the *Kleingarten*.

The grammar point is a family of little words. You already know *das Brötchen* (lesson 9) and *das
Mädchen*, and in the fairy-tale lesson you read *das Märchen*. All three end in *-chen*, and all
three are neuter. Here you'll learn why, and how to make such words yourself.

## Feierabend and Gemütlichkeit

At the end of the working day, colleagues say goodbye with a wish:

- *Schönen Feierabend!* — Have a nice evening! (literally "a nice end of work")
- *Schönes Wochenende!* — Have a nice weekend! (on Friday)
- The answer to both: *Danke, gleichfalls!* — Thanks, you too! (*gleichfalls*: likewise)

*Schönen* and *Schönes* have endings because the whole wish is in the accusative: it's short for
*Ich wünsche Ihnen einen schönen Feierabend* (I wish you a nice evening). Learn the wishes as
chunks.

What makes a Feierabend good? Many Germans would answer with one word: *gemütlich*. The noun is
*die Gemütlichkeit*. It's often called untranslatable, which is an exaggeration, but it does cover
more than "cosiness": warmth, good company, no hurry, and the feeling that you belong. A candle on
the table, a long breakfast on Sunday or friends talking for hours over coffee can all be
*gemütlich*. A useful chunk: *Wir machen es uns gemütlich* — We're making ourselves comfortable.

One classic gemütlich place is *die Kneipe*, a simple pub. Many Kneipen have a *Stammtisch*: a
table kept for a group of regulars who meet there every week, sometimes with a sign on the table
that says so. *Wir haben jeden Donnerstag Stammtisch* — We meet at our regular table every
Thursday. Today the word is also used for any regular meeting: language learners often go to a
*Sprachstammtisch* to practise.

## Der Kleingarten

Most people in German cities live in flats, without a garden (see *Zusammen wohnen*). The answer, for many,
is *der Kleingarten*: a small garden you rent in a *Kleingartenanlage*, a group of gardens
with paths, hedges and fences, often near a railway line or on the edge of town. There are about
900,000 of them in Germany. You don't rent one from a landlord but from a club, the
*Kleingartenverein*, so you also become a member, go to meetings and help with jobs everyone
shares. (Simplified: strictly, the club usually leases the land from the town and sub-leases the
plots to its members.)

Another name is *der Schrebergarten*, after Moritz Schreber (1808–1861), a doctor in Leipzig who
wanted city children to play outdoors. In 1864, three years after his death, a club named after
him was founded in Leipzig. It started with a playground; garden plots for families came soon
after, and the idea spread across the country. In Austria the word *Schrebergarten* is common
too; in Switzerland people often say *der Familiengarten*.

A federal law, the *Bundeskleingartengesetz*, sets the main rules. Simplified:

- A garden may be at most 400 square metres.
- It may have a simple hut, *die Laube*, of at most 24 square metres, including a covered seating
  area. You may not live in it.
- Part of the garden must be used to grow fruit and vegetables. Courts have taken this to mean
  roughly a third of the plot; the rest can be lawn, flowers and a place to sit.

Each club also has its own *Gartenordnung* (garden rules) about hedges, water and quiet hours.
In big cities the waiting lists for a garden are often long.

![A small rented garden: a wooden hut with a little roof and a window, a tree with apples, a vegetable bed with tomato plants, red flowers, a watering can on the grass, and a low wooden fence around the garden. Labels name the parts: die Laube, der Baum, das Beet, die Blume, die Gießkanne and der Zaun.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The jobs in the garden have simple verbs: *gießen* (to water: *Ich gieße die Blumen*), *ernten* (to
harvest, pick: *Im Juli ernten wir Erdbeeren*) and *grillen* (to barbecue, from *Zusammen wohnen*). The things
you grow: *die Tomate, die Erdbeere* (strawberry), *der Apfel* (lesson 9), *die Blume* (flower).

## The diminutive: -chen and -lein

German makes a "little" version of a noun with an ending: *-chen* or *-lein*. This form is called
the **[[diminutive]]**. *Das Haus* is a house; *das Häuschen* is a little house. *Der Baum* is a tree;
*das Bäumchen* is a little tree.

Building one takes three steps:

1. If the noun ends in *-e*, drop it: *die Blume → Blum-*.
2. Most nouns with *a, o, u* or *au* take an umlaut: *Blum- → Blüm-*, *Haus → Häus-*.
3. Add *-chen*: *das Blümchen*, *das Häuschen*.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: How to make a diminutive
  accDescr: Start with the noun, for example die Katze. If it ends in -e, drop the -e, giving Katz-. If its vowel is a, o, u or au, it usually takes an umlaut, giving Kätz-. Then add -chen, or -lein, giving Kätzchen. The new word is always neuter, das, and its plural looks the same: das Kätzchen, die Kätzchen.
  A["Start with the noun: die Katze"] --> B{"Ends in -e?"}
  B -- yes --> C["Drop the -e: Katz-"]
  B -- no --> D{"Vowel a, o, u or au?"}
  C --> D
  D -- yes --> E["Usually add an umlaut: Kätz-"]
  D -- no --> F["Add -chen or -lein: Kätzchen"]
  E --> F
  F --> G["Always das; plural the same: das Kätzchen, die Kätzchen"]
```

Two facts make diminutives easy to use:

- They are always neuter, whatever the gender of the noun they come from: *der Hund → das
  Hündchen*, *die Katze → das Kätzchen*. This is why *das Mädchen* is neuter even though it means
  a girl (lesson 5).
- The plural looks the same as the singular: *ein Brötchen, zwei Brötchen*. Only the article
  changes: *das Brötchen, die Brötchen*.

The ending *-lein* means the same thing. It sounds older or more poetic, and you find it in fairy
tales, songs and southern German: *das Büchlein* (little book), *das Vöglein* (little bird). After
*-ch*, *-lein* is the usual choice, because *Büchchen* is hard to say.

### What diminutives do

A diminutive can simply mean "small": *ein Häuschen im Garten*. But very often it adds a feeling:
something is sweet, dear or harmless. That's why diminutives belong to *Gemütlichkeit*:

- *Trinken wir noch ein Tässchen Kaffee?* — Shall we have another (little) cup of coffee? (*die
  Tasse*: cup)
- *Möchten Sie ein Gläschen Wein?* — Would you like a (little) glass of wine?
- *mein Schätzchen* — my darling (*der Schatz*: treasure)

The little cup isn't smaller than a normal one; the *-chen* makes the offer friendly and relaxed.
Used too much, though, diminutives sound childish or sugary, so use them in friendly offers and
with children and animals, not in a job interview.

### Words that are only diminutives

Some words have *-chen* but no "big" version in everyday German any more, or have moved away from
it in meaning (a *Brötchen* is a roll, not a small loaf of *Brot*). Learn them as normal words,
always with *das*:

| Word | Meaning | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| *das Mädchen* | girl | an old word *Magd* (young woman, maid) |
| *das Märchen* | fairy tale | an old word *Märe* (news, story) |
| *das Brötchen* | bread roll | *das Brot* (bread) |
| *das Kaninchen* | rabbit | *Kanin* survives only in old or regional use |
| *das Eichhörnchen* | squirrel | *das Eichhorn*, now rare |
| *ein bisschen* | a little | *der Bissen* (a bite) |

Fairy-tale names are full of them: *Rotkäppchen* (Little Red Riding Hood) is the girl with the red
*Käppchen* (little cap, from *die Kappe*), and *Hänsel* and *Gretel* use *-el*, a southern
cousin of *-lein*.

### Around the German-speaking countries

Regions have their own little endings, and you'll see them on menus and signs:

| Region | Ending | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Swabia (south-west Germany) | *-le* | *das Häusle* (little house) |
| Switzerland | *-li* | *das Müesli* (from *Mues*, mash: the origin of *das Müsli*) |
| Bavaria and Austria | *-erl*, *-l* | *das Sackerl* (Austrian for a bag), *das Kipferl* (a crescent-shaped pastry) |

They are all neuter, just like *-chen* and *-lein*. You don't need to make them yourself; just
recognise them.

### Example 1: Making diminutives

Make the diminutive of *der Baum, die Tasse, das Haus* and *der Hund*.

1. *der Baum*: no *-e* to drop; *au* takes an umlaut → *Bäum-*; add *-chen* → *das Bäumchen*.
2. *die Tasse*: drop the *-e* → *Tass-*; *a* → *ä* → *Täss-*; add *-chen* → *das Tässchen*.
3. *das Haus*: *au → äu* → *das Häuschen*. Say it *Häus-chen*: the *s* and the *ch* are separate
   sounds, not *sch*.
4. *der Hund*: *u → ü* → *das Hündchen*.

All four are *das*, though they started as *der, die, das, der*. And the plurals: *die Bäumchen, die
Tässchen, die Häuschen, die Hündchen*.

## Reading: Feierabend im Kleingarten

> Es ist Freitag, fünf Uhr. Endlich Feierabend! Ilse und Kemal fahren mit dem Fahrrad zu ihrem Kleingarten. Der Garten ist nicht groß, aber er hat eine Laube, einen Apfelbaum und drei Beete.
>
> Kemal gießt die Tomaten und die Blumen. Ilse erntet Erdbeeren. Im Garten nebenan sitzt Herr Wolff vor seinem Häuschen und liest die Zeitung. „Na, Frau Berger, möchten Sie ein Gläschen Saft?", fragt er. „Gern!", sagt Ilse.
>
> Am Abend kommen zwei Freunde. Sie grillen Würstchen und essen Kartoffelsalat. Auf dem Zaun sitzt ein Eichhörnchen und schaut zu. Um zehn Uhr sind alle leise, denn ab 22 Uhr ist Ruhezeit, auch im Kleingarten.
>
> „Das war ein schöner Abend. Wirklich gemütlich!", sagt Kemal. Dann fahren sie nach Hause.

*It's Friday, five o'clock. Finally the end of the working day! Ilse and Kemal cycle to their
allotment garden. The garden isn't big, but it has a hut, an apple tree and three beds. Kemal
waters the tomatoes and the flowers. Ilse picks strawberries. In the garden next door Mr Wolff is
sitting in front of his little house reading the newspaper. "Well, Mrs Berger, would you like a
glass of juice?" he asks. "Yes, please!" says Ilse. In the evening two friends come. They grill
sausages and eat potato salad. A squirrel sits on the fence and watches. At ten o'clock everyone
is quiet, because from 10 p.m. it's quiet time, in the allotments too. "That was a lovely evening.
Really cosy!" says Kemal. Then they cycle home.*

New in passing: *nebenan* (next door), *zuschauen* (to watch; separable: *schaut zu*), *das
Würstchen* (sausage), *der Kartoffelsalat* (potato salad).

### Example 2: Finding the diminutives in a text

Find the diminutives in the reading, and for each one give the base word and the article.

1. *Häuschen*: from *das Haus* (*au → äu*). Herr Wolff's *Häuschen* is his *Laube*: a small,
   friendly word for it.
2. *Gläschen*: from *das Glas* (*a → ä*). It's a friendly offer, not a tiny glass.
3. *Würstchen*: from *die Wurst*; usually just means a sausage (often a small one).
4. *Eichhörnchen*: a word that is only a diminutive; it means squirrel, not "small squirrel".

All four are *das*: *das Häuschen, das Gläschen, das Würstchen, das Eichhörnchen*. *Wurst* is
feminine, but *Würstchen* is neuter. Two more words look similar but are not diminutives:
*Kleingarten* (*klein* + *Garten*: a compound, lesson 5) is masculine like *der Garten*, and
*Apfelbaum* is a compound too.

## Pronunciation

- *-chen* always has the soft *ch* of *ich*, even after *a, o, u*: *Häuschen, Brötchen,
  Kaninchen*.
- *s + chen*: *Häus-chen, Gläs-chen, Täss-chen*. Never read *sch* here.
- *Gemütlichkeit*: ge-MÜT-lich-keit; long *ü*, stress on the second syllable.
- *Eichhörnchen*: EICH-hörn-chen, two soft *ch* sounds.
- *gießen*: long *ie*, sharp *ß*: GEE-sen.
- *Laube*: LOU-be, *au* as in "house".

## Common mistakes

- Keeping the old gender: *die Kätzchen* for one kitten, *der Bäumchen*. Every *-chen* and *-lein*
  word is *das*.
- Forgetting the umlaut: *Hundchen, Hauschen*. It's *Hündchen, Häuschen*.
- Adding a plural ending: *zwei Brötchens*. The plural has no ending: *zwei Brötchen*.
- Reading *Häuschen* as *Häu-schen* with *sch*. It's *Häus-chen*.
- Thinking *Kleingarten* is a diminutive: it's a compound, and it's *der*.
- Using diminutives everywhere: they're friendly, but in formal situations they sound childish.
- Calling a Laube a holiday house: you may not live in it.

## Key points

- *Schönen Feierabend! Schönes Wochenende! — Danke, gleichfalls!*
- *Gemütlichkeit*: comfort, warmth, good company and no hurry; *Wir machen es uns gemütlich*.
- A *Stammtisch* is a regulars' table in a *Kneipe*, or any regular meeting.
- A *Kleingarten* (*Schrebergarten*) is rented through a club: at most 400 m², a *Laube* of at most
  24 m², and part of it for fruit and vegetables.
- Diminutive: drop final *-e*, umlaut *a, o, u, au* (usually), add *-chen* or *-lein*.
- Every diminutive is *das*, and its plural looks the same: *das Brötchen, die Brötchen*.
- Diminutives often add a friendly feeling: *ein Tässchen Kaffee*.
- *Mädchen, Märchen, Kaninchen, Eichhörnchen* are words in their own right; regional endings are
  *-le, -li, -erl*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete

sections.name: The past and the A1 exam
Honors: Kultur und Alltag (culture and everyday life)

questions.stem: How is the "w" in "wohnen" (to live) pronounced?
questions.explanation: German w always sounds like English v: wohnen is "VOH-nen", wie is "vee". English speakers often read it as an English w, which Germans hear as a foreign accent at once.

questions.stem: Which of these words has the long "ee" sound?
questions.explanation: ie sounds like English "ee", so sie is "zee". The others are spelled ei, which sounds like English "eye". Hook: say the English name of the second letter (ie ends in e, ei ends in i).

questions.stem: The "ei" in "heißen" (to be called) is a diphthong. Which spelling is correct in Germany?
questions.explanation: After a long vowel or a diphthong like ei, a sharp s is written ß: heißen. A single s between vowels would sound like English z (heisen = "HY-zen"). Only in Switzerland is it written heissen.

questions.stem: Which of these words must always start with a capital letter?
questions.explanation: Name is a noun, and every German noun is capitalized: der Name. Langsam (slow), bitte (please) and schreiben (to write) are not nouns, so they are lowercase unless they start a sentence.

questions.stem: How does the final "d" in "und" (and) sound?
questions.explanation: At the end of a word or syllable, b, d and g lose their voice and sound like p, t and k. So und sounds like "oont" and Tag like "tahk". The letter is still written d.

questions.stem: Where is the stress in "Entschuldigung" (excuse me)?
questions.explanation: German words are usually stressed on the first syllable, but the prefix ent- is never stressed, so the stress moves to the next syllable: ent-SCHUL-di-gung. The same happens with be- and ver- (ver-STE-hen).

questions.stem: It's 8 p.m. and you arrive at a friend's house for dinner. How do you greet her parents?
questions.explanation: Guten Abend is the greeting from about 6 p.m. Gute Nacht looks like the right time of day, but it is only said when someone goes to bed, as a goodbye. Tschüss is also a goodbye.

questions.stem: Someone says "Danke!" to you. What is the usual reply?
questions.explanation: Bitte (or Bitte schön) is the answer to Danke: "You're welcome." Wie bitte? asks someone to repeat, and Entschuldigung is "excuse me" or "sorry".

questions.stem: You didn't catch what someone said. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Wie bitte? means "Pardon?" and asks the speaker to repeat. Wie schreibt man das? asks how a word is spelled, which only helps once you have heard it. Bitte schön means "you're welcome".

questions.stem: You spell the name "Jens" in German. How do you say the first letter?
questions.explanation: The German letter J is called "yot", and it sounds like English y: Jens is "Yens". "Jay" is the English name and isn't a German letter name at all; "ee" is the German I, and "gay" is the German G.

questions.stem: Read the message: "Hallo! Mein Vorname ist Katrin, mein Familienname ist Vogt. Vogt schreibt man V – O – G – T." Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Der Familienname is the surname, so her surname is Vogt; der Vorname (Katrin) is her first name. She spells the surname, not the first name.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake?
questions.explanation: Vorname (first name) is a noun, so it needs a capital letter: Mein Vorname ist Ali. The possessive mein is not a noun, so it is lowercase in the middle of a sentence.

questions.stem: In which word is "ch" the rough sound at the back of the throat, as in Scottish "loch"?
questions.explanation: After a, o, u and au, ch is the rough back sound: Nacht, noch, auch. After other letters (ich, nicht, Milch) it is the soft front sound, like the h in "huge".

questions.stem: You meet your new neighbour, an older woman, for the first time. How do you ask her name?
questions.explanation: With an adult you don't know, use Sie, and the verb form is the same as the infinitive: Wie heißen Sie? Wie heißt du? is correct German but too familiar here. Wer means "who", not "how".

questions.stem: Complete the question: "___ du Lena?"
questions.explanation: The du form of sein is bist: Bist du Lena? (Are you Lena?) Bin goes with ich, ist with er/sie, and sind with Sie.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wie ___ du?" (What's your name?)
questions.explanation:
The du ending is normally -st, but the stem of heißen already ends in ß, so du adds only
-t: du heißt. Heiße goes with ich and heißen with Sie.

questions.stem: Which question asks where someone is from?
questions.explanation: Woher means "where from", so Woher kommst du? asks about origin. Wo wohnst du? asks where someone lives now, which is a different question.

questions.stem: What does "Wer ist das?" mean?
questions.explanation: Wer means "who", even though it looks like English "where". "Where" is wo, "how" is wie and "what" is was.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich komme ___ Kanada."
questions.explanation: Origin is expressed with kommen aus: Ich komme aus Kanada. Von looks like English "from", but Germans don't use it for the country you come from.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich wohne ___ Hamburg."
questions.explanation: Where you live is wohnen in: Ich wohne in Hamburg. Aus goes with kommen, for origin.

questions.stem: Mr Braun asks you: "Wie geht es Ihnen?" What is the best reply?
questions.explanation: He uses the formal Ihnen, so you answer formally and ask back with Und Ihnen? Und dir? is the informal version. Ich bin gut means "I'm good (at something)" or "I'm a good person", not "I'm fine".

questions.stem: Someone introduces himself: "Hallo, ich bin Jonas." What do you say?
questions.explanation: Freut mich means "Nice to meet you", the natural reply when you meet someone, followed by your own name. Auch gut ("fine too") answers Wie geht's? Und dir?

questions.stem: Which question has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Wie heißen du? mixes the Sie form of the verb with du. It must be Wie heißt du? (informal) or Wie heißen Sie? (formal). The other questions match their pronoun.

questions.stem: Read: "Das ist Herr Petrović. Er kommt aus Kroatien, aber er wohnt jetzt in Österreich, in Linz." Where does Mr Petrović live now?
questions.explanation: Er wohnt jetzt in Österreich: he now lives in Austria, in Linz. Croatia (Kroatien) is where he comes from (kommt aus), not where he lives.

questions.stem: How do you greet Ms Wagner, a colleague you call Sie?
questions.explanation: With Sie, use Frau (or Herr) plus the surname: Guten Tag, Frau Wagner! The surname alone sounds rude, and Frau without a name is not a polite form of address.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
questions.explanation: In a W-question the verb comes straight after the question word, then the subject: Woher kommen Sie? Aus is not needed in the question, because woher already means "where from".

questions.stem: How do you say 25 in German?
questions.explanation: From 21 to 99 German says the unit first, then und, then the ten: fünf-und-zwanzig ("five and twenty"), written as one word. Zweiundfünfzig is 52, the reversed number.

questions.stem: You hear "siebenundvierzig". Which number is it?
questions.explanation: Sieben (7) und vierzig (40) = 47. German says the unit first and the ten second, so you hear 7, then 40. 74 would be vierundsiebzig.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 30 in Germany?
questions.explanation: 30 is the only ten that doesn't end in -zig: dreißig. Dreizehn is 13. (Switzerland writes dreissig, because it doesn't use ß.)

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of 16?
questions.explanation: Sechzehn drops the s of sechs. Sechszehn is the most common spelling mistake. Sechzig is 60, which also drops the s.

questions.stem: How do you ask a child how old they are?
questions.explanation: German uses sein for age, as English does, and you say du to a child: Wie alt bist du? Wie alt sind Sie? is correct for adults you don't know. Haben is wrong for age.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Age uses sein and the same order as English: Ich bin 30 Jahre alt (or just Ich bin 30). Ich habe 30 Jahre is a direct copy of Spanish or French and is wrong in German.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ du eine Handynummer?"
questions.explanation: The du form of haben is hast, without the b. Hat goes with er/sie, haben with Sie, and habst doesn't exist.

questions.stem: On the phone someone says "null eins sieben zwo". What does "zwo" mean?
questions.explanation: Zwo is another word for zwei (2), used on the phone and in announcements so that it can't be confused with drei (3).

questions.stem: Read the address: "Thomas Berger, Mozartstraße 9, 80336 München". What is the house number?
questions.explanation: In a German address the house number comes after the street name: Mozartstraße 9. The five-digit number before the town, 80336, is the postcode (die Postleitzahl).

questions.stem: What does "die Postleitzahl" mean?
questions.explanation: Die Postleitzahl (PLZ) is the postcode or ZIP code. The phone number is die Telefonnummer and the house number die Hausnummer.

questions.stem: Someone asks: "Wie ist Ihre Telefonnummer?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: Die Telefonnummer is the phone number, so the answer is a number. The other replies answer Wie alt sind Sie?, Wo wohnen Sie? and Woher kommen Sie?

questions.stem: Mia says: "Ich bin einundzwanzig." How old is she?
questions.explanation: Ein(s) und zwanzig = 21. Inside a number eins becomes ein. 12 is zwölf and 31 is einunddreißig.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Ich habe eine Adresse in Köln.
questions.explanation: Haben is slightly irregular: the du form is du hast (and er hat), without the b. Du habst is a regular-looking form that doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ in Berlin." (wohnen)
questions.explanation: The wir ending is -en, so the form is the same as the infinitive: wir wohnen. Wohnt is the er/ihr form, wohnst the du form, wohne the ich form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ihr ___ heute." (arbeiten)
questions.explanation: The ihr ending is -t, and because the stem arbeit- ends in t, an extra e is added: ihr arbeitet. Arbeitest is the du form.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ihr aus Köln?"
questions.explanation: The ihr form of sein is seid: Seid ihr aus Köln? (Are you from Cologne?) Seit sounds the same but means "since". Sind goes with wir and sie/Sie.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The verb must be the second element. When heute comes first, the subject ich moves to just after the verb: Heute lerne ich Deutsch. Heute ich lerne copies English word order.

questions.stem: Turn "Du spielst Gitarre." into a yes/no question.
questions.explanation: For a yes/no question, put the verb first and keep its form: Spielst du Gitarre? German has no helper verb like English "do", and the du form stays spielst.

questions.stem: In "sie spielt", who is playing?
questions.explanation: The ending -t shows one person: sie spielt = she plays. "They play" is sie spielen, and formal "you play" is Sie spielen with a capital S.

questions.stem: Choose the question word: "___ lernst du Deutsch? – Ich wohne jetzt in Deutschland."
questions.explanation: The answer gives a reason, so the question is Warum (why)? Wann asks about time and wo about place.

questions.stem: Choose the question word: "___ arbeitest du? – Heute und morgen." (morgen = tomorrow)
questions.explanation: The answer is a time, so the question is Wann (when)? Wo would need a place in the answer, and was a thing.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm learning German"?
questions.explanation: German has no -ing form. The simple present ich lerne covers "I learn", "I'm learning" and "I do learn". Ich bin lernen is a word-for-word copy of the English.

questions.stem: Tom is a student at the university in Munich. Which sentence says that?
questions.explanation: Studieren means studying at a university. Lernen is learning in general (a language, for a test). Arbeitet means he works there, which is not what we want to say.

questions.stem: Read: "Das ist Elif. Sie kommt aus der Türkei, aber sie lebt jetzt in Hamburg. Sie arbeitet in einem Café. Sie hört gern Musik und spielt oft Gitarre." Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Sie hört gern Musik: gern after the verb means she likes doing it. She comes from Turkey but lives in Hamburg now, works in a café, and plays the guitar often (oft).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: The ihr form of sein is seid: Ihr seid heute hier. Sind is for wir and sie/Sie.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "We like playing"?
questions.explanation: Gern goes after the conjugated verb: Wir spielen gern. In the other sentences the verb is not in second position, and spielt is the wrong ending for wir.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "Tisch" (table)?
questions.explanation: Tisch is masculine: der Tisch. "die" is for feminine nouns and plurals, "das" for neuter nouns. "den" is a different case form you will meet in lesson 9. Learn every noun together with its article.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "das Buch" (book)?
questions.explanation: Buch belongs to the umlaut + -er group: das Buch, die Bücher. German rarely adds -s like English, and every plural takes the article "die", never "das".

questions.stem: Which noun is feminine? Look at the ending.
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in -ung are always feminine: die Zeitung. -chen is always neuter (das Mädchen). -er is a weaker hint: der Computer is masculine but das Fenster is neuter.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: "Das ist ___ Lampe."
questions.explanation: Lampe is feminine (die Lampe), so "a" is eine: Das ist eine Lampe. "ein" is for masculine and neuter nouns. "der" would be "the", and only for masculine nouns.

questions.stem: Which article goes with the compound noun "Handynummer" (das Handy + die Nummer)?
questions.explanation: In a compound noun the last part decides the gender. Nummer is feminine, so it is die Handynummer, even though das Handy is neuter.

questions.stem: You point at three keys on the table. Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: For several things you say "Das sind …". Schlüssel belongs to the no-ending group (der Schlüssel, die Schlüssel), so Schlüssels is wrong, and "ein" has no plural.

questions.stem: What does "das Handy" mean?
questions.explanation: Das Handy is the everyday German word for a mobile (cell) phone. It looks like English "handy" but means something quite different.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Uhr is feminine (die Uhr), so it must be "Das ist eine Uhr." Heft is neuter and Stift is masculine, so "ein" is correct for them, and Tasche is feminine with "eine".

questions.stem: Read the note: "Lena, hier sind zwei Bücher und ein Heft. Die Bücher sind für Max, das Heft ist für Jana. Danke! Ben" (für = for). What is for Jana?
questions.explanation: The note says "das Heft ist für Jana": the (one) exercise book is for Jana. The two books (die Bücher) are for Max.

questions.stem: Which noun is neuter?
questions.explanation: It is das Fenster. The others are die Brille, der Stuhl and die Tür. Fenster ends in -er, which often suggests masculine, so it is a good example of why you learn every article.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "die Lampe"?
questions.explanation: Most feminine nouns add -n or -en in the plural: die Lampe, die Lampen. German does not form this plural with -s or an umlaut.

questions.stem: Your friend says "Wo ist die Brille?" What is she looking for?
questions.explanation: Die Brille is singular: one pair of glasses. English says "glasses", but German treats it as one thing, so it is "Wo ist die Brille?", not "Wo sind …". Several pairs would be die Brillen.

questions.stem: Complete: "Anna und ___ Vater wohnen in Bonn."
questions.explanation: Anna is the owner, so the word is ihr (her). Vater is masculine, so there is no ending: ihr Vater. "ihre" would be for a feminine or plural noun, and sein/seine means "his".

questions.stem: Complete: "Paul und ___ Schwester wohnen in Wien."
questions.explanation: Paul is the owner, so the word is sein (his). Schwester is feminine, so it takes -e: seine Schwester. "ihre" would mean "her" or "their".

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ___ zwei Kinder."
questions.explanation: Mein Bruder is the same as er, and the er/sie/es form of haben is hat. "habt" belongs to ihr, "hast" to du and "haben" to wir, sie and Sie.

questions.stem: You ask two friends: "___ ihr ein Tier?"
questions.explanation: With ihr (you, plural) the form of haben is habt: Habt ihr ein Tier? The verb comes first because it is a yes/no question.

questions.stem: You ask two children: "Ist das ___ Katze?"
questions.explanation: Talking to two children you use ihr, so "your" is euer. Katze is feminine, so euer takes -e and usually drops its second e: eure Katze. "ihre" would mean her or their cat, not yours, and "deine" is for one person only.

questions.stem: What does "die Geschwister" mean?
questions.explanation: Die Geschwister means brothers and sisters together: siblings. Parents are die Eltern, grandparents die Großeltern.

questions.stem: What does "Meine Eltern sind geschieden." mean?
choices: My parents are separated by distance.
questions.explanation: Geschieden means divorced. Married is verheiratet and single is ledig.

questions.stem: Read: "Das ist meine Familie. Mein Vater heißt Klaus, meine Mutter heißt Petra. Ich habe einen Bruder, Max. Max ist verheiratet. Seine Frau heißt Lina, und sie haben ein Baby." Who is Lina?
questions.explanation: "Seine Frau heißt Lina": his (Max’s) wife is called Lina. Die Frau means both "woman" and "wife"; after a possessive it usually means wife. The mother is Petra, and the baby’s name isn’t given.

questions.stem: Someone shows you a photo and asks "Wer ist das?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: Schwester is feminine, so "my" is meine. "Das ist" never changes for one person; "Das sind" is only for several people, and "er" means "he".

questions.stem: You speak formally to Frau Berg: "Frau Berg, ist das ___ Hund?"
questions.explanation: The formal "your" is Ihr with a capital I, matching the formal pronoun Sie. Lower-case ihr would mean "her" or "their", and dein is informal.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Eltern is plural, and possessives take -e in the plural: Meine Eltern wohnen in Köln. The other sentences are correct: meine Tochter (feminine), unser Sohn and dein Opa (masculine).

questions.stem: Lisa und Tom haben einen Hund. "___ Hund heißt Rex."
questions.explanation: The dog belongs to Lisa and Tom, so you need "their": ihr. Hund is masculine, so no ending: Ihr Hund (capital only because it starts the sentence). Sein would mean "his", euer "your".

questions.stem: "Was sind Sie von Beruf?" Which answer is correct for a woman who teaches?
questions.explanation: German uses no article with jobs after sein, and a woman uses the -in form: Ich bin Lehrerin. "Lehrerinnen" is plural, and the verb here is sein (bin), not haben.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Vater ___ Spanisch."
questions.explanation: sprechen changes its stem vowel from e to i in the du and er/sie/es forms: er spricht. "sprecht" is the ihr form, and "sprechen" is for wir, sie and Sie.

questions.stem: Complete the question: "___ du Englisch?"
questions.explanation: The du form also has the stem change: du sprichst. "Sprechst" keeps the e by mistake, and "Spricht" is the er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich ___ ein bisschen Deutsch."
questions.explanation: The stem only changes for du and er/sie/es. The ich form is regular: ich spreche. "spriche" is a common mistake.

questions.stem: What is the feminine form of "der Arzt" (doctor)?
questions.explanation: Feminine job titles add -in, and Arzt also takes an umlaut: die Ärztin. The double n only appears in the plural: die Ärztinnen.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Die Türkei is one of the few countries that always take an article. After aus it becomes der: aus der Türkei (a set phrase for now; the dative comes in lesson 18). Most countries, like Spanien, need no article.

questions.stem: Which language do people speak in Frankreich?
questions.explanation: The language of France is Französisch. Many language names end in -isch, but they aren’t always formed from the country name. Französin means a Frenchwoman.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo, ich heiße Elif. Ich komme aus der Türkei, aber ich wohne in Berlin. Ich bin Studentin. Ich spreche Türkisch, Deutsch und ein bisschen Englisch. Mein Bruder ist Koch." (aber = but) Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Elif says "Ich bin Studentin": she is a (university) student. Her brother is the cook, she lives in Berlin, and she speaks "ein bisschen Englisch", a little English.

questions.stem: What does "die Firma" mean?
questions.explanation: Die Firma means a company or firm: Meine Firma ist international. It has nothing to do with English "farm".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The er form is spricht, and the name of a language is capitalized: Deutsch. English names like German are not used in German sentences.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "die Lehrerin" (female teacher)?
questions.explanation: Feminine nouns ending in -in add -nen in the plural: die Lehrerin, die Lehrerinnen.

questions.stem: Daniel is a man who studies at a university. What does he say?
questions.explanation: A man at university is a Student (no article after sein). A Schüler goes to school, Studentin is the female form, and Studenten is plural.

questions.stem: Your new colleague asks: "Welche Sprachen sprichst du?" Which is a fitting answer?
questions.explanation: Welche Sprachen sprichst du? means "Which languages do you speak?", so you name languages. The other answers say where you are from, what your job is, or don’t answer the question.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist ___ Hund, das ist eine Katze!"
questions.explanation: To negate a noun with ein, use kein: ein Hund becomes kein Hund. Hund is masculine, so there is no ending; keine is for feminine and plural nouns. German never says "nicht ein".

questions.stem: Complete: "Tut mir leid, ich habe ___ Zeit." (Tut mir leid = Sorry)
questions.explanation: Zeit has no article here, so you negate it with kein. Zeit is feminine (die Zeit), so it is keine: Ich habe keine Zeit.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist ___ mein Handy."
questions.explanation: A noun with a possessive (mein, dein …) or with der/die/das is negated with nicht, not kein: Das ist nicht mein Handy. "nein" means no as an answer.

questions.stem: A friend asks "Ist das nicht dein Schlüssel?" It is your key. What do you say?
choices: Ja, das ist nicht mein Schlüssel.
questions.explanation: To contradict a negative question you answer doch. "Nein" would agree with the negative ("No, it isn’t"), and "Nicht" is not an answer word.

questions.stem: Complete: "Die Stühle sind ___." (new)
questions.explanation: After sein an adjective never takes an ending, whatever the gender or number: Die Stühle sind neu. Endings only appear when the adjective stands before a noun.

questions.stem: What does "Die Tasche ist zu teuer." mean?
questions.explanation: zu before an adjective means "too", more than you want: zu teuer = too expensive. "Very" is sehr, and "also, too" is auch.

questions.stem: What is the opposite of "langweilig"?
questions.explanation: Langweilig means boring; its opposite is interessant. Lang (long) and langsam (slow) only look similar.

questions.stem: Read the ad: "Verkaufe Fahrrad, rot, 2 Jahre alt, sehr schnell. Das Licht ist kaputt. Nur 90 Euro!" (Verkaufe = I'm selling, Fahrrad = bicycle, Licht = light, nur = only) Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: Das Licht ist kaputt: the light is broken. The bike is red (rot), very fast (sehr schnell) and costs only 90 euros.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: To negate a whole simple sentence, nicht usually goes at the end: Ich verstehe das nicht. German doesn’t put nicht before the verb and has no helper like English "don’t".

questions.stem: Which colour is "gelb"?
questions.explanation: Gelb is yellow. Green is grün and grey is grau.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: After sein, adjectives don’t take endings: Das Auto ist rot. The other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: How do you say "I’m bored" in German?
questions.explanation: Mir ist langweilig is the fixed phrase for "I’m bored". "Ich bin langweilig" means "I’m boring", a classic learner mistake.

questions.stem: What does "Die Tasche ist ziemlich schwer." mean?
questions.explanation: Ziemlich means quite or fairly, and schwer means heavy (or difficult). "Too heavy" would be zu schwer.

questions.stem: Complete the order: "Ich möchte ___ Kaffee, bitte." (der Kaffee)
questions.explanation: Kaffee is masculine (der Kaffee) and it is the direct object of möchte, so it takes the accusative: einen Kaffee. "ein Kaffee" is the nominative form, the most common mistake here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir essen ___ Brot." (das Brot)
questions.explanation: Brot is neuter, and neuter articles don't change in the accusative: das Brot stays das Brot. Only masculine der becomes den, so "den Brot" is wrong.

questions.stem: Complete: "Paul ___ einen Apfel."
questions.explanation: essen changes e to i in the du and er/sie/es forms: er isst. "esst" is the ihr form (ihr esst), and it is the mistake you make if you forget the stem change.

questions.stem: Complete: "Du ___ einen Tee, oder?" (nehmen)
questions.explanation: nehmen changes in the du and er forms: du nimmst, er nimmt. The h disappears and the m doubles. "nimmt" is the er/sie/es form, and "nehmst" forgets the stem change.

questions.stem: Complete: "Er ___ ein Wasser."
questions.explanation: The er/sie/es form of möchten has no -t: er möchte, exactly like ich möchte. "möchtet" is the ihr form, and "möchtest" is the du form.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm hungry" in German?
questions.explanation: German says "I have hunger" with no article: Ich habe Hunger. In the same way, Ich habe Durst means I'm thirsty. "Ich bin Hunger" would mean "I am hunger", and "ich hat" has the wrong verb form (ich habe).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Wasser is neuter (das Wasser), so its accusative is ein Wasser, not einen Wasser. The -en only goes on masculine words such as Saft and Fisch. "Das ist ein Apfel" is right because sein is followed by the nominative.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I like eating pasta"?
questions.explanation: The verb comes second and gern follows it: Ich esse gern Nudeln. "Ich gern esse" uses English word order, and "Ich essen" has the wrong verb ending.

questions.stem: Read the sign in a café: "Café Sonne. Unser Frühstück: ein Kaffee oder ein Tee, zwei Brötchen mit Butter und Käse, ein Ei. Saft kostet extra." What do you get with the breakfast?
questions.explanation: The breakfast has zwei Brötchen (two rolls) and ein Ei (an egg), plus coffee OR tea (oder = or). Juice (Saft) costs extra, and there is no sausage (Wurst).

questions.stem: The waiter asks: "Was möchten Sie trinken?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: The question is what you would like to drink (trinken), so name a drink: Ich möchte einen Tee, bitte. A cake (Kuchen) is food, and "Ja, ich trinke" doesn't answer a was-question.

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe keinen Durst" mean?
questions.explanation: Durst is thirst, and Durst haben means to be thirsty, so keinen Durst haben means not to be thirsty. Hunger is the word for hunger, and juice is Saft.

questions.stem: Why is it "den" in "Ich trinke den Saft"?
choices: Because the sentence is a question.
Because Saft is masculine and the direct object.
questions.explanation: der Saft is masculine, and here it is the thing being drunk, the direct object. Masculine der becomes den in the accusative. With a feminine or neuter drink the article would not change: Ich trinke die Milch, das Wasser.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wie viel ___ die Äpfel?"
questions.explanation: die Äpfel is plural, so the verb is plural: Wie viel kosten die Äpfel? With one thing you'd say kostet: Wie viel kostet der Apfel?

questions.stem: How do you say the price 3,50 €?
questions.explanation: Say the euros, then the cents, without "und" or "Cent": drei Euro fünfzig. Euro has no plural after a number, so "drei Euros" is wrong.

questions.stem: How is 470 written in words?
questions.explanation: Hundreds first, then the rest: vierhundert + siebzig. Seventy is siebzig, not siebenzig (sieben loses -en). siebzehn is 17.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte ein Kilo ___, bitte."
questions.explanation: German puts the amount straight in front of the food with no word for "of" and no article: ein Kilo Äpfel, eine Flasche Wasser, 200 Gramm Käse. "ein Kilo von Äpfel" copies English.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Wein nehmen Sie?" (der Wein)
questions.explanation: Wein is masculine and the object of nehmen, so it's accusative: welchen, with the same -n as den. "Welcher" is the nominative (Welcher Wein ist gut?).

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Brot ist frisch." (das Brot)
questions.explanation: dieser takes the endings of der, die, das. Brot is neuter (das), so it's dieses Brot: das ends in -s, and so does dieses.

questions.stem: Complete: "Hier gibt es ___ Supermarkt."
questions.explanation: es gibt is followed by the accusative, and Supermarkt is masculine (der Supermarkt), so: einen Supermarkt. "ein Supermarkt" is the nominative form.

questions.stem: A sign in a supermarket: "Angebot! 500 Gramm Kaffee: nur 4,99 €. Normaler Preis: 6,49 €." How much do you save?
questions.explanation: The normal price (Preis) is 6,49 € and the offer (Angebot) price is 4,99 €: 6.49 − 4.99 = 1.50 euros. German writes the decimal comma where English writes a point.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: After a number, Euro stays singular: zehn Euro. Kilo stays singular too (zwei Kilo), while feminine Flasche takes its plural (zwei Flaschen), so the other sentences are correct.

questions.stem: At the market the saleswoman asks: "Ist das alles?" What is a good answer?
choices: Ja, das ist alles. Was macht das?
questions.explanation: "Ist das alles?" means "Is that everything?" Answer yes, and ask for the total: Was macht das? (What does that come to?). The other answers don't make sense here.

questions.stem: A bike costs 1.500 €. How much is that?
questions.explanation: In German the point separates thousands and the comma marks decimals. 1.500 € is one thousand five hundred euros (tausendfünfhundert Euro). One and a half euros would be 1,50 €.

questions.stem: In a café the waiter asks: "Zusammen oder getrennt?" What does he want to know?
choices: Do you want to pay together or separately?
questions.explanation: zusammen means together and getrennt means separately: the waiter is asking whether one person pays for everyone or each person pays for their own order.

questions.stem: It's 2:30. How do you say this in everyday German?
questions.explanation: halb points to the next hour: halb drei is "half way to three", so 2:30. "halb zwei" is 1:30, the classic mistake for English speakers.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Kurs beginnt ___ neun Uhr."
questions.explanation: Clock times take um: um neun Uhr. am is for days and parts of the day (am Montag, am Abend).

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Montag arbeite ich nicht."
questions.explanation: Days of the week take am: am Montag. um is only for clock times, and "in Montag" copies English "on Monday" with the wrong word.

questions.stem: A train leaves at 19:45. How does the announcement say it?
questions.explanation: Official times are hours, then Uhr, then minutes: neunzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig. Viertel, nach and vor belong to the everyday 12-hour clock, not to the 24-hour clock.

questions.stem: Which everyday time means 8:45?
questions.explanation: 8:45 is a quarter to nine: Viertel vor neun. Viertel nach acht is 8:15, halb neun is 8:30, and Viertel vor acht is 7:45.

questions.stem: Which phrase means "at night"?
questions.explanation: The night is the exception among the parts of the day: in der Nacht. The others take am: am Morgen, am Nachmittag, am Abend.

questions.stem: How do you say "tomorrow morning"?
questions.explanation: German avoids "morgen Morgen" and says morgen früh. Compare heute Morgen (this morning) and morgen Abend (tomorrow evening).

questions.stem: A sign on a door: "Bäckerei Kraus. Montag bis Freitag 6:30 bis 18 Uhr, Samstag 7 bis 13 Uhr, Sonntag geschlossen." (geschlossen = closed) Can you buy bread on Saturday at 2 p.m.?
choices: No, on Saturday it closes at 1 p.m.
No, it's closed all day on Saturday.
questions.explanation: On Saturday (Samstag) the bakery is open from 7 to 13 Uhr, so it closes at 1 p.m. The 18 Uhr closing time is for Monday to Friday, and it is closed (geschlossen) on Sunday.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kaffee? Nein danke, ich trinke ___ Kaffee."
questions.explanation: "Nein danke" tells you the person doesn't drink coffee: ich trinke nie Kaffee, I never drink coffee. immer (always), oft (often) and manchmal (sometimes) don't fit a refusal.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Film ist zwei ___ lang."
questions.explanation: For a length of time use die Stunde, plural Stunden: zwei Stunden. Uhr only gives the time on the clock (Es ist zwei Uhr) and has no plural in times.

questions.stem: Someone asks you: "Wie spät ist es?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: "Wie spät ist es?" means "What time is it?", even though spät means late. Answer with Es ist and the time. "Am Montag" answers wann?, and "Zwei Stunden" answers wie lange?

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: With Uhr, one is ein: Es ist ein Uhr. Without Uhr it's eins: Es ist eins. "eins Uhr" mixes the two. halb eins (12:30) is correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
Ich stehe auf um sieben Uhr.
questions.explanation: aufstehen is separable: the verb part stehe goes in second place and the prefix auf goes to the very end. "Ich stehe auf um sieben Uhr" puts the prefix too early, as in English "I get up at seven".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: When a time phrase comes first, the verb is second and the subject follows it (inversion): Am Montag kaufe ich. The prefix ein still goes to the end. "Am Montag ich kaufe" keeps English word order.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Der Film fangt um acht an.
Der Film fängt um acht an.
Der Film fängst um acht an.
questions.explanation: anfangen splits (fängt … an) and keeps the stem change of fangen in the er/sie/es form: er fängt. "fangt" forgets the umlaut, and "fängst" is the du form.

questions.stem: Which verb is NOT separable?
questions.explanation: frühstücken stays in one piece: Ich frühstücke um acht. früh is not a separable prefix. The others split: ich stehe auf, ich kaufe ein, ich sehe fern.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "He watches TV every evening"?
questions.explanation: fernsehen splits, and sehen changes e to ie in the er form: er sieht … fern. The prefix fern goes to the end of the sentence, after jeden Abend.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I'm phoning my mother"?
questions.explanation: The verb part rufe is second, the person you call comes in the middle, and the prefix an goes to the end: Ich rufe meine Mutter an. "Ich rufe an meine Mutter" follows English "call up my mother".

questions.stem: Complete: "Zuerst dusche ich, dann ___."
questions.explanation: dann takes position 1, so the verb comes next and the subject after it: dann frühstücke ich. frühstücken is not separable, so "ich stücke früh" is wrong.

questions.stem: Read: "Normalerweise steht Maria um sechs Uhr auf. Zuerst duscht sie, dann frühstückt sie. Um sieben holt sie ihre Freundin Eva ab. Die Arbeit fängt um acht an. Um vier hat Maria Feierabend, und danach kauft sie ein." What does Maria do after work?
questions.explanation: Um vier hat Maria Feierabend means she finishes work at four, and danach kauft sie ein means after that she goes shopping. She picks up Eva at seven, before work.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Ich gehe ins Kino. Kommst du mit?" What does she ask?
choices: Are you coming from the cinema?
questions.explanation: mitkommen means to come along (mit = with). Kommst du mit? is an invitation: "Are you coming along?" To arrive is ankommen.

questions.stem: Complete: "Psst! Das Baby ___."
questions.explanation: schlafen changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms: das Baby (es) schläft. "schläfst" is the du form, and "schlaft" is the ihr form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich möchte heute ___."
questions.explanation: After möchte the second verb is an infinitive at the end, and a separable verb stays in one piece in the infinitive: einkaufen. It only splits when it is the conjugated verb (Ich kaufe heute ein).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Dann räume ich die Küche auf.
Um acht kommt der Zug an.
questions.explanation: normalerweise fills position 1, so the verb must come next: Normalerweise stehe ich früh auf. The other sentences all have the verb second and the prefix at the end.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ___ jeden Tag Fahrrad." (fahren)
questions.explanation: Fahren changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms: er fährt. "Fahrt" without the umlaut is the ihr form, "fahre" is the ich form, and "fähren" doesn't exist.

questions.stem: What is the du form of "lesen" (to read)?
questions.explanation: Lesen changes e to ie: du liest. Because the stem ends in -s, du only adds -t, so it is not "liesst". "Lest" is the ihr form, which keeps the plain e.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ihr ___ heute zwei Filme." (sehen)
questions.explanation: The stem change e → ie only happens with du and er/sie/es. The ihr form is regular: ihr seht. "Sieht" (er) and "siehst" (du) are the changed forms; "säht" is not a form of sehen.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The verb comes in position 2 and gern follows it: Ich spiele gern Fußball. English word order ("Ich gern spiele") puts gern before the verb, which is wrong. "Mehr gern" doesn't exist; the comparative is lieber.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich trinke gern Kaffee, aber ___ trinke ich Tee." (most of all)
questions.explanation: Most of all = am liebsten, the superlative of gern. Lieber means "rather, prefer" (comparative). "Am lieber" mixes the two and is wrong. Note the inversion: am liebsten trinke ich.

questions.stem: What does "Ich jogge lieber." mean?
questions.explanation: Lieber is the comparative of gern: "rather, prefer". "I like jogging" would be Ich jogge gern; "most of all" would be am liebsten.

questions.stem: Which verb form is wrong?
