questions.explanation: The stem change (e → i) only happens with du and er/sie/es. With wir the verb is regular: wir sprechen. Du hilfst, er gibt and du triffst are all correct changed forms.

questions.stem: Read: "Ich heiße Ben. In der Freizeit spiele ich gern Gitarre und singe in einer Band. Sport mache ich nicht gern, aber ich wandere manchmal. Am liebsten sehe ich Filme." What does Ben like doing most?
questions.explanation: Am liebsten sehe ich Filme = most of all I like watching films. He also likes playing the guitar and singing (gern), and he hikes only sometimes (manchmal).

questions.stem: Choose the right answer. "Was machst du gern in der Freizeit?"
choices: Ich lese gern und ich male.
questions.explanation: The question asks what you like doing in your free time, so you name activities: Ich lese gern und ich male. A W-question can't be answered with ja or nein, and "Am Wochenende, um acht" answers "when?".

questions.stem: Complete: "Er ___ seine Freunde am Samstag." (treffen)
questions.explanation: Treffen changes e to i in the du and er forms and keeps the double f: er trifft. "Trefft" is the ihr form; "triefft" uses ie, which is the pattern of lesen and sehen, not treffen.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Ihr fährt am Wochenende zusammen, und Lena schläft lange."
questions.explanation: With ihr there is no stem change: ihr fahrt. Lena is er/sie/es, so schläft with ä is correct. "Lange" (for a long time) is the right word here.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm meeting friends and we're going to the cinema"?
choices: Ich trifft Freunde und wir gehen ins Kino.
Ich treffe Freunde und wir fahren Kino.
Ich treffe Freunde und gehen wir ins Kino.
Ich treffe Freunde und wir gehen ins Kino.
questions.explanation: Ich treffe (ich has no stem change) and ins Kino gehen is the fixed chunk for going to the cinema. "Ich trifft" uses the er form; after und the word order doesn't change, so "und gehen wir" is wrong.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ du Klavier spielen?" (können)
questions.explanation: The du form of können is kannst: the vowel changes to a in the singular. "Kann" is the ich/er form, "könnst" keeps the plural vowel, and "kennst" comes from kennen (to know a person).

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: With a modal verb the infinitive goes to the end: Ich will Gitarre lernen. English order ("will lernen Gitarre") is wrong, modals never take zu, and the second verb stays in the infinitive (lernen, not lerne).

questions.stem: Complete: "Er ___ am Wochenende eine Party feiern." (möchten)
questions.explanation: Like all modal forms, the er form is the same as the ich form and has no -t: er möchte. "Möchtet" is ihr, "möchten" is wir/sie, "möchtest" is du.

questions.stem: What does "Ich will morgen kommen." mean?
choices: I would like to come tomorrow, please.
questions.explanation: Wollen means "to want": ich will = I want. It is a false friend: it never means the English future "I will". "I can" would be ich kann, and the polite "would like" is ich möchte.

questions.stem: You are in a café. What is the most polite way to order?
questions.explanation: Möchte is the polite "would like" and is normal for ordering. "Ich will" is direct and sounds demanding; "ich mag" means "I like (tea in general)", and "ich kann" means "I can".

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ leider nicht Ski fahren." (können)
questions.explanation: The plural of a modal is regular and built from the infinitive: wir können. "Kann" is singular, "könnt" is the ihr form, and "kannen" doesn't exist.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Tim, ich mache am Freitag eine Party. Kannst du kommen? Du kannst auch deine Gitarre mitbringen. Jana kommt leider nicht. Lisa" What does Lisa ask Tim?
choices: to help Jana with the party
to come to a party and maybe bring his guitar
questions.explanation: Kannst du kommen? asks if he can come, and Du kannst auch deine Gitarre mitbringen invites him to bring (mitbringen) his guitar. Jana is not coming (kommt leider nicht); there is nothing about football or cooking.

questions.stem: Choose the right answer. "Hast du Lust auf Kino?"
questions.explanation: Hast du Lust auf …? means "Do you feel like …?", so a natural answer is Ja, gern! (Yes, I'd love to.) The other answers don't make sense; doch is only used to contradict a negative question.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Meine Schwester kannt sehr gut kochen."
questions.explanation: The er/sie/es form of a modal has no ending: sie kann. Meine is right for a feminine noun, the infinitive kochen at the end is right, and sehr gut is the normal way to say "very well".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "I can't come today"?
choices: Ich kann nicht heute kommen nicht.
questions.explanation: The modal is in position 2, the infinitive at the end, and nicht goes just before the infinitive: Ich kann heute nicht kommen. Nicht can't follow the infinitive or stand before the modal.

questions.stem: Which question is correct?
questions.explanation: With a modal, a separable verb is joined again at the end in the infinitive: Willst du mitkommen? Without a modal you would say Kommst du mit?

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe keine Lust." mean?
questions.explanation: Lust haben means to feel like doing something, so keine Lust haben is "not to feel like it". No time = keine Zeit, no idea = keine Ahnung, no plan = keinen Plan.

questions.stem: Complete: "Du ___ morgen früh aufstehen." (müssen)
questions.explanation: Müssen loses its umlaut in the singular: du musst. "Müsst" is the ihr form, "muss" is ich/er, and "müssen" is wir/sie/Sie.

questions.stem: A sign says "Rauchen verboten". What does it mean?
questions.explanation: Verboten means forbidden, so Rauchen verboten = no smoking. "Allowed" would be erlaubt.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "You don't have to fill in the form"?
choices: Sie dürfen das Formular nicht ausfüllen.
Sie müssen das Formular nicht ausfüllen.
Sie können das Formular nicht ausfüllen.
questions.explanation: Nicht müssen means "not necessary": Sie müssen das Formular nicht ausfüllen. The tempting "dürfen nicht" means you are not allowed to fill it in, which is the English "must not".

questions.stem: Which sentence means "You mustn't park here"?
questions.explanation: English "must not" (forbidden) is German nicht dürfen: Hier darf man nicht parken. "Hier muss man nicht parken" only says you don't have to park here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Im Kino ___ man leise sein." (müssen)
questions.explanation: Man always takes the er/sie/es form: man muss. It may feel plural ("people"), but "man müssen" is wrong. "Musst" is du and "müsst" is ihr.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Sie müssen das Formular füllen aus.
questions.explanation: The infinitive goes to the end, and a separable verb is written as one word there: … das Formular ausfüllen. The prefix only separates when ausfüllen itself is the conjugated verb (Sie füllen das Formular aus).

questions.stem: You want to ask politely if you may open the window. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Darf ich …? asks for permission politely. "Ich muss …" says it is necessary for you, and "Du sollst …" tells someone else what to do.

questions.stem: Read the notice: "In der Bibliothek muss man leise sein. Essen und Trinken sind verboten, aber Wasser dürfen Sie trinken. Die Bibliothek schließt um 20 Uhr." (Bibliothek = library) What is allowed?
questions.explanation: Wasser dürfen Sie trinken = you may drink water. Eating is verboten, you must be quiet (leise), and the library closes (schließt) at 20 Uhr, which is 8 p.m.

questions.stem: Your doctor wants you to drink a lot of water. Complete: "Mein Arzt sagt, ich ___ viel Wasser trinken."
questions.explanation: Sollen passes on what another person (here the doctor) wants you to do: ich soll. Darf would mean you are allowed to, and will is your own wish, not the doctor's.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Man müssen hier pünktlich sein."
questions.explanation: Man takes the er/sie/es form: Man muss hier pünktlich sein. "Mann" with two n's is a man (a person), and adjectives after sein have no ending at A1.

questions.stem: Choose the right answer. "Darf ich hier warten?"
questions.explanation: The person asks for permission, so a natural answer gives it: Ja, natürlich. "Du musst nicht" (you don't have to) doesn't fit a request for permission, and the other answers don't answer the question.

questions.stem: What does "pünktlich" mean?
questions.explanation: Pünktlich means on time or punctual: Der Termin ist um neun. Wir müssen pünktlich sein. Quiet is leise or ruhig, important is wichtig, allowed is erlaubt.

questions.stem: How do you say "on the third of October"?
questions.explanation: On a date you use am + ordinal with -en: am dritten Oktober. Dates need the ordinal, not the plain number drei; im is for months alone (im Oktober); and the ordinal of 3 is irregular: dritte, not "dreite".

questions.stem: Complete: "Heute ist der ___ Mai." (1.)
questions.explanation: After der the ordinal ends in -e: der erste Mai. The -en ending (ersten) is used after am: am ersten Mai. The ordinal of 1 is irregular: erste.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe ___ Juli Geburtstag." (in July)
questions.explanation: With months and seasons you use im: im Juli. Am goes with a day or date (am 5. Juli), um with clock times, and "in Juli" without the m is a typical mistake.

questions.stem: What does "Es schneit und es ist sehr kalt." mean?
choices: It is snowing and very cold.
questions.explanation: Es schneit = it is snowing (schneien), kalt = cold. Raining would be es regnet, and the sun shining is die Sonne scheint.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Das Geschenk ist für mein Bruder.
Das Geschenk ist für meinem Bruder.
Das Geschenk ist für meinen Bruder.
Das Geschenk ist für meiner Bruder.
questions.explanation: Für always takes the accusative, and masculine words change: mein → meinen. "Mein Bruder" is the nominative; "meinem" is dative, which für never takes.

questions.stem: A German form shows the date 04.07. Which date is it?
questions.explanation: Germans write the day first, then the month: 04.07. is der vierte Juli, the 4th of July. Reading it the American way (April 7th) is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Which ordinal number is spelled correctly?
questions.explanation: Siebte (7th) is right. The ordinal of 3 is dritte, of 8 is achte with one t, and numbers below 20 add -te, not -ste: zweite.

questions.stem: Read: "Hallo Max, am Samstag habe ich Geburtstag und ich mache eine Party. Sie fängt um 19 Uhr an. Kannst du Musik mitbringen? Eva" When does the party start?
questions.explanation: Am Samstag = on Saturday, and um 19 Uhr is 7 p.m. in the 24-hour clock. Don't confuse 19 (neunzehn) with 9.

questions.stem: A friend invites you, but you have to work. What do you say?
choices: Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.
questions.explanation: To decline politely, say leider (unfortunately) and give a reason: Leider kann ich nicht. Ich muss arbeiten. "Ja, gern" accepts, and Herzlichen Glückwunsch is for congratulating.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: "Im Winter es schneit oft."
questions.explanation: When a time phrase like im Winter comes first, the verb stays in position 2 and the subject follows: Im Winter schneit es oft. Im is right with seasons, and nouns like Winter are capitalized.

questions.stem: What do you say to someone on their birthday?
questions.explanation: The standard phrase is Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag! "Guten Geburtstag" is a word-for-word copy of English and isn't used; Gute Besserung means "get well soon".

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir gehen ___ den Park." (through)
questions.explanation: Through = durch, and like für, ohne and um it takes the accusative: durch den Park. Für means for, ohne without, um at (a time) or around.

questions.stem: A woman gives you directions. Which verb form fits? "___ Sie bitte geradeaus!"
questions.explanation: The polite imperative is the Sie form of the verb, then Sie: Gehen Sie geradeaus! Geht is the ihr imperative and Geh the du imperative, and neither can be used with Sie. Gehst is a present- tense du form, not an imperative.

questions.stem: You tell a friend how to get to your flat. Complete: "___ den Bus Nummer 5!"
questions.explanation: For the du imperative, start from the du form (du nimmst) and drop the ending -st: Nimm! The e to i change stays. Nehm is a very common mistake: it ignores the stem change. Nimmst still has its ending, and Nehmen without Sie is not a polite imperative.

questions.stem: Which is the correct du imperative of "fahren"?
questions.explanation: Verbs with the a to ä change (du fährst) lose the umlaut in the imperative: Fahr langsam! Fähr keeps an umlaut that belongs only to the du and er forms, and Fährst or Fahrst keep the -st ending.

questions.stem: You ask two noisy children to be quiet. Which is correct?
questions.explanation: Two children means ihr, and the ihr imperative of sein is Seid! Sei is for one person (du), Seien goes with Sie, and seit (with t) is the preposition "since", not a form of sein.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Abbiegen Sie an der Ampel links!
Biegen Sie an der Ampel links ab!
Sie biegen ab an der Ampel links!
Biegen ab Sie an der Ampel links!
questions.explanation: Abbiegen is separable. In the imperative the verb part comes first, then Sie, and the prefix ab goes to the very end: Biegen Sie an der Ampel links ab! The other choices keep the prefix attached or put it in the middle.

questions.stem: What does "geradeaus" mean?
questions.explanation: Geradeaus means straight ahead, straight on: Gehen Sie geradeaus. It has nothing to do with time, so it does not mean "straight away". On the right is rechts.

questions.stem: Complete the question: "Entschuldigung, wie komme ich ___ Post?"
questions.explanation: Post is feminine (die Post), so you say zur Post. Zum is for masculine and neuter places (zum Bahnhof, zum Museum). Zu die is never correct: after zu the article changes, and zu der is shortened to zur.

questions.stem: Read the message: "Hallo Mia! Geh vom Bahnhof geradeaus bis zum Marktplatz. Nimm dort die zweite Straße rechts. Unser Café ist an der Ecke, gegenüber der Kirche." Where is the café?
choices: on the corner, opposite the church
on the second street on the left
questions.explanation: The last sentence says the café is an der Ecke (on the corner), gegenüber der Kirche (opposite the church). The market square is only where Mia turns, and she turns rechts (right), not left.

questions.stem: You ask: "Entschuldigung, ist das Museum weit?" Which answer fits?
choices: Ja, das Museum hat ein Café.
Nein, nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß.
questions.explanation: Weit means far, so a good answer is about distance: Nein, nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß (No, only five minutes on foot). The other answers say yes or no but talk about something else.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Nehmen changes e to i in the du form (du nimmst), and the du imperative keeps that change: Nimm den Stadtplan! Lies, Sprich and Warte are all correct du imperatives.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Die Bank ist rechts." What does she mean?
choices: The bank is on the right.
questions.explanation: Rechts is the direction right. Correct is richtig, a different word that English speakers often mix up with rechts. Straight ahead is geradeaus and far is weit.

questions.stem: You ask a stranger in the street for help. Which request is polite and correct?
choices: Zeigen Sie mir bitte den Weg.
questions.explanation: With a stranger you use Sie, and the Sie imperative needs Sie after the verb: Zeigen Sie mir bitte den Weg. Zeig (du) and Zeigt (ihr) are for friends, and Zeigen without Sie is incomplete.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich fahre mit ___ Bus zur Arbeit."
questions.explanation: Mit always takes the dative, and Bus is masculine (der Bus), so the dative article is dem: mit dem Bus. Den is the accusative, which English speakers often choose because English has no difference here.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir fahren mit ___ U-Bahn."
questions.explanation: U-Bahn is feminine (die U-Bahn). After mit you need the dative, and the feminine dative article is der: mit der U-Bahn. Die is the nominative and accusative, and dem is for masculine and neuter nouns.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich gehe heute ___ Arzt."
questions.explanation: Going to a person or place with an article uses zu, and zu dem is shortened to zum: zum Arzt. Zur and zu der are feminine, but Arzt is masculine. Nach is for cities and countries.

questions.stem: Complete: "Im Sommer fliegen wir ___ Spanien."
questions.explanation: Countries and cities without an article take nach: nach Spanien, nach Berlin. Zu is for people and places with an article, and bei means at someone's place.

questions.stem: How do you say "I've been living in Hamburg for two years"?
choices: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Hamburg.
Ich wohne für zwei Jahre in Hamburg.
Ich wohne seit zwei Jahre in Hamburg.
Ich wohne zwei Jahre seit in Hamburg.
questions.explanation: For something that started in the past and is still going on, German uses seit with the present tense. Seit takes the dative, so the plural noun adds -n: seit zwei Jahren. Für zwei Jahre is a word-for-word translation of the English.

questions.stem: Complete: "Am Wochenende bin ich bei meinen ___."
questions.explanation:
Bei takes the dative. In the dative plural the article is den (here meinen), and the noun adds
-n unless it already ends in -n or -s: die Freunde becomes meinen Freunden.

questions.stem: It's late. Which sentence means "I'm going home now"?
questions.explanation: Going home is nach Hause; being at home is zu Hause. Ich bin jetzt zu Hause means "I'm at home now". Zum Haus means "to the house", not home.

questions.stem: Read the announcement: "Achtung an Gleis 5: Der Zug nach München, Abfahrt 14:12 Uhr, hat heute circa 20 Minuten Verspätung." When will the train probably leave?
questions.explanation: The train normally leaves (Abfahrt) at 14:12, but it has about 20 minutes of Verspätung (delay), so it will leave at about 14:32.

questions.stem: "Woher kommst du jetzt?" — "Ich komme ___ der Arbeit."
questions.explanation: Von is for the place you have just left: von der Arbeit, vom Bahnhof. Aus is for where you come from originally (aus Kanada) or for coming out of something. Zu and nach mean "to".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Umsteigen is separable: the verb part steigen is in position 2 and um goes to the end: Wir steigen in Köln um. In Köln wir steigen um breaks the verb-second rule; after In Köln it must be steigen wir.

questions.stem: At the ticket counter the clerk asks: "Einfach oder hin und zurück?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: The question is "single or return?", so you answer with one of the two: Hin und zurück, bitte (a return, please). The other answers talk about transport, platforms or changing trains.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Mit takes the dative, and possessives take dative endings too. Auto is neuter, so it must be mit ihrem Auto. The other sentences correctly use meiner (feminine), dem (masculine) and zur (zu der).

questions.stem: Complete: "Das Buch ist auf ___ Tisch."
questions.explanation: The question is Wo? (where is it?), so auf takes the dative. Tisch is masculine, so the article is dem: auf dem Tisch. Den would be the accusative, used for movement onto the table.

questions.stem: Complete: "Die Milch ist ___ Kühlschrank."
questions.explanation: Kühlschrank is masculine; in + dem becomes im: im Kühlschrank. In alone is missing the article, am means at or on, and ins (in das) is for movement into a place.

questions.stem: The photo is on the wall. Complete: "Das Foto ist ___ der Wand."
questions.explanation: Things on a vertical surface like a wall are an: an der Wand. Auf is for horizontal surfaces such as a table or the floor; English "on" covers both.

questions.stem: "Wie findest du den Schrank?" — "Ich finde ___ schön."
questions.explanation: Schrank is masculine (der Schrank), and here it is the object of finden, so you need the accusative pronoun ihn. Er is the subject form, and es would be for a neuter noun. English "it" covers all three.

questions.stem: "Wo ist die Lampe?" — "___ ist im Wohnzimmer."
questions.explanation: Lampe is feminine (die Lampe), so the pronoun is sie, even though English says "it". Using es for every thing is a common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Kühlschrank ist in ___ Küche."
questions.explanation: Küche is feminine (die Küche). For location (Wo?) in takes the dative, and the feminine dative article is der: in der Küche. There is no contraction for feminine nouns.

questions.stem: Read the advert: "Schöne 2-Zimmer-Wohnung im 3. Stock, helle Küche, Bad mit Fenster, Balkon. Miete: 750 Euro warm. Kein Aufzug." Which statement is true?
choices: The rent does not include heating.
The flat is on the ground floor.
The flat has two rooms plus a kitchen and a bathroom.
questions.explanation: In German adverts the kitchen and bathroom are not counted, so a 2-Zimmer-Wohnung has two rooms plus kitchen and bathroom. Warm means heating is included, kein Aufzug means there is no lift, and the flat is on the third floor.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The chair is between the sofa and the window"?
choices: Der Stuhl ist zwischen das Sofa und das Fenster.
Der Stuhl ist neben dem Sofa und dem Fenster.
Der Stuhl ist zwischen dem Sofa und dem Fenster.
Der Stuhl ist zwischen der Sofa und der Fenster.
questions.explanation: Zwischen means between. For location it takes the dative, and Sofa and Fenster are both neuter, so both become dem. Das is the nominative or accusative, der is the wrong gender, and neben means next to.

questions.stem: "Wo ist die Katze?" Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: Wo? asks about location, so unter takes the dative. Bett is neuter (das Bett), so the dative is dem: unter dem Bett.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Dein Wohnzimmer ist sehr gemütlich!" What does she mean?
choices: Your living room is very dark.
Your living room is very modern.
Your living room is very expensive.
Your living room is very cosy.
questions.explanation: Gemütlich means cosy, comfortable and pleasant to be in. Dark is dunkel, modern is modern, and expensive is teuer.

questions.stem: Someone says: "Ich wohne im ersten Stock." Where does this person live?
choices: one floor above the ground floor
in the first house on the street
in the first room on the left
questions.explanation: German floors are counted from the ground floor (das Erdgeschoss), so im ersten Stock is one floor up: the first floor in British English, the second floor in American English.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Die Lampe ist über dem Tisch.
Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.
Das Regal ist neben der Schrank.
Die Tasche ist auf dem Boden.
questions.explanation: Schrank is masculine, so the dative after neben is dem: neben dem Schrank. Der Schrank is the nominative; der before a noun is only dative for feminine nouns.

questions.stem: How do you say "I have a headache"?
questions.explanation: German uses haben with the plural Schmerzen: Ich habe Kopfschmerzen. Or with wehtun: Mein Kopf tut weh (not hat weh).

questions.stem: Complete: "Meine Füße ___ weh."
questions.explanation: Wehtun is separable: tun is the verb in position 2 and weh goes to the end. Füße is plural, so the verb is tun. Tut is for one body part: Mein Fuß tut weh.

questions.stem: "Wie geht es dir?" — "___ geht es nicht gut."
questions.explanation: The answer copies the pattern of the question: es geht + dative. Dir becomes mir: Mir geht es nicht gut. Ich is the nominative and mich the accusative.

questions.stem: Complete: "Kannst du ___ helfen?"
questions.explanation: Helfen always takes the dative, so you need mir: Kannst du mir helfen? Mich is the accusative, a very common mistake because English uses "me" for both.

questions.stem: You say to a friend: "I'll call you tomorrow." Complete: "Ich rufe ___ morgen an."
questions.explanation: Anrufen takes a direct object, so the accusative pronoun is needed: dich. Dir is the dative (Wie geht es dir?), du is the subject form, and dein means your.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'm cold"?
questions.explanation: Feeling cold uses the dative: Mir ist kalt. Ich bin kalt describes your character (a cold person). Ich habe kalt is a word-for-word translation from French or Spanish.

questions.stem: Read the sign: "Praxis Dr. Sommer. Sprechzeiten: Mo, Di, Do 8–12 und 15–18 Uhr; Mi, Fr 8–12 Uhr." (Sprechzeiten = opening hours) Can you see the doctor on Wednesday afternoon?
choices: No, on Wednesday the practice is only open in the morning.
No, the practice is closed all day on Wednesday.
questions.explanation: Mi (Mittwoch) is listed with Fr: only 8 to 12. The afternoon hours, 15 to 18, are only on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday.

questions.stem: A colleague says: "Ich bin krank, ich habe Fieber." What do you say?
questions.explanation: Gute Besserung! means Get well soon! Herzlichen Glückwunsch is for birthdays, Guten Appetit before a meal and Gute Reise for someone setting off on a trip.

questions.stem: What is the plural of "die Hand"?
questions.explanation: Hand takes an umlaut and -e in the plural: zwei Hände. The same pattern: der Fuß, die Füße; der Zahn, die Zähne.

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder ist krank. Wie geht es ___?"
questions.explanation: Es geht + dative: Wie geht es dir / Ihnen / ihm? The dative of er is ihm. Ihn is the accusative, er the nominative, and sein means his.

questions.stem: Your friend is picking you and your sister up. Complete: "Holst du ___ am Bahnhof ab?"
questions.explanation: You need the object form of wir, which is uns (the same in the accusative and dative). Unser means our, and euch means you (plural).

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: Helfen takes the dative: Kannst du mir helfen? The other sentences are correct: Mir ist schlecht (I feel sick), Mein Bauch tut weh (my stomach hurts), Ich verstehe dich nicht (I don't understand you).

questions.stem: Leon says: "Mein Hals tut weh." Where is the pain?
questions.explanation: Der Hals is the neck and throat; Halsschmerzen is a sore throat. Ear is das Ohr, back is der Rücken, and stomach is der Bauch.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: "Ich ___ gestern einen Ausflug gemacht."
questions.explanation: "Machen" forms its perfect with haben, and the subject is "ich", so the form is "habe". "Bin" is the sein auxiliary, used for movement verbs, not for "machen". "Hat" is for er/sie/es and "haben" for wir/sie/Sie.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of "kaufen" (to buy)?
questions.explanation: "Kaufen" is a regular (weak) verb: ge- + stem + -t gives "gekauft". "Gekaufen" mixes in the -en ending of strong verbs, which "kaufen" doesn't have. "Kaufte" is a different past form you don't need at A1.

questions.stem: Complete: "Am Sonntag haben wir unsere Oma ___." (visited)
questions.explanation: "Besuchen" has the inseparable prefix be-, which blocks ge-. The participle is simply "besucht". "Gebesucht" is the most common learner mistake: it adds ge- as if the verb had no prefix.

questions.stem: What is the past participle of the separable verb "einkaufen" (to go shopping)?
questions.explanation: In separable verbs, ge- goes between the prefix and the stem: ein + ge + kauft = "eingekauft", written as one word. "Geeinkauft" puts ge- in front of the whole verb, and "einkauft" leaves it out.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: In the perfect, haben is in position 2 and the participle goes to the very end, with the object in between: "Ich habe eine Pizza gegessen." Putting "gegessen" right after "habe" copies English word order ("I have eaten a pizza").

questions.stem: Complete: "Mein Bruder hat in Berlin ___." (studied)
questions.explanation: Verbs ending in -ieren never take ge- in the participle: "studieren" becomes "studiert", like "fotografiert". "Gestudiert" is a very common mistake.

questions.stem: Complete: "Hast du Brot ___?" (brought)
questions.explanation: "Bringen" is a mixed verb: the vowel changes like a strong verb, but the ending is -t like a weak verb. The participle is "gebracht". "Gebringt" treats it as regular, and "gebrungen" copies the pattern of "trinken – getrunken".

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich ___ Frau Müller schon lange." (I've known Ms Müller for a long time.)
questions.explanation: You know a person with "kennen", and the ich form is "kenne". "Wissen" (ich weiß) is for facts and information, not people. "Kennen" without an ending is the infinitive or the wir/sie form.

questions.stem:
Read the postcard:
"Liebe Mia, wir sind in Hamburg! Gestern haben wir den Hafen (the harbour) besucht und Fisch gegessen. Heute habe ich Postkarten gekauft. Leider habe ich meine Brille verloren! Viele Grüße, Jan" What went wrong for Jan?
questions.explanation: "Leider habe ich meine Brille verloren" means "Unfortunately I've lost my glasses". "Verloren" is the participle of "verlieren" (to lose). He did buy postcards ("Postkarten gekauft"), and nothing negative is said about the fish or the harbour.

questions.stem: What does "Ich habe gerade gegessen." mean?
questions.explanation: "Gerade" with the perfect means "just (a moment ago)": I've just eaten. With the present tense ("Ich esse gerade") it would mean "I'm eating right now", but here the verb is in the perfect.

questions.stem: Your friend asks: "Was hast du am Wochenende gemacht?" What is the best answer?
questions.explanation: The question is in the perfect and asks what you did, so answer in the perfect: "Ich habe meine Eltern besucht" (I visited my parents). "Ich mache am Wochenende Sport" is present tense and talks about a habit. "Ja" doesn't answer a W-question.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: "Verkaufen" has the inseparable prefix ver-, so its participle has no ge-: "Wir haben das Auto verkauft." The other three are correct: "gesehen" and "geholfen" are strong participles, and "verstanden" also has no ge- because of ver-.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ nach Spanien geflogen."
questions.explanation: "Fliegen" is a verb of movement from one place to another, so it takes sein, and the wir form of sein is "sind". "Haben" is the tempting English-style choice ("we have flown"). "Seid" is for ihr and "ist" for er/sie/es.

questions.stem: Complete: "Was ___ passiert?"
questions.explanation: "Passieren" (to happen) always forms its perfect with sein: "Was ist passiert?" (What happened?). It is one of the verbs you simply have to learn with sein, together with "sein" and "bleiben".

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich habe um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.
Ich bin um sieben Uhr aufgestehen.
Ich habe um sieben Uhr aufgesteht.
Ich bin um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.
questions.explanation: "Aufstehen" is a change of state (from lying to standing), so it takes sein, and its participle is strong: auf + ge + standen = "aufgestanden". The first choice uses the wrong auxiliary; the other two have invented participles.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wo ___ du gestern?"
questions.explanation: The du form of "war" takes the usual -st ending: "du warst". "War" is the ich and er/sie/es form, and "wart" is for ihr.

questions.stem: Complete: "Wir ___ leider keine Zeit." (We unfortunately didn't have time.)
questions.explanation: The wir form of "hatte" ends in -en: "wir hatten", just like "wir haben" in the present. "Hatte" is ich/er, "hattest" is du and "hattet" is ihr.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs forms its perfect with haben?
questions.explanation: "Essen" takes an object (etwas essen) and involves no movement, so it uses haben: "Ich habe gegessen." "Kommen" and "fliegen" are movement verbs (ist gekommen, ist geflogen), and "bleiben" is one of the special verbs with sein (ist geblieben).

questions.stem: What does "Wir sind im See geschwommen." mean?
choices: We are swimming in the lake.
questions.explanation: "Der See" (masculine) is a lake; the sea is "das Meer". "Sind … geschwommen" is the perfect, so it describes the past: we swam. "We saw" would be "Wir haben … gesehen".

questions.stem: Complete the question: "___ seid ihr gefahren?" — "Nach Österreich."
questions.explanation: The answer gives a destination ("to Austria"), so the question asks "where to": "Wohin". "Wo" asks about a position (where something is), and "Woher" asks where someone comes from.

questions.stem:
Read the text:
"Letztes Jahr bin ich mit meiner Freundin nach Kroatien gefahren. Wir waren auf einer Insel. Am Strand war es sehr heiß. Nach drei Tagen ist meine Freundin plötzlich krank geworden, und wir sind nach Hause gefahren." Why did they go home?
questions.explanation: "Nach drei Tagen ist meine Freundin plötzlich krank geworden" means "After three days my girlfriend suddenly became ill". "Geworden" is the participle of "werden" (to become), which takes sein. The weather was hot ("sehr heiß"), not bad.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
questions.explanation: "Gehen" is a movement verb, so it needs sein: "Wir sind nach Hause gegangen." The other sentences are correct: "bleiben", "werden" and "umziehen" all take sein.

questions.stem: Your neighbour asks: "Wie war der Urlaub?" What is the best answer?
questions.explanation: "Wie war …?" asks how something was, so a past answer that describes it fits: "Super! Das Wetter war toll." The other answers talk about the present or future, and "Ja" doesn't answer a W-question.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Zug ist pünktlich ___." (departed)
questions.explanation: "Abfahren" is separable and "fahren" is strong, so the participle is ab + ge + fahren = "abgefahren", written as one word. "Abgefahrt" gives it a weak ending, and "gefahren ab" splits the participle like a present-tense verb.

questions.stem: Complete: "___ ihr schon einmal in Wien?" (Have you ever been to Vienna?)
questions.explanation: The ihr form of "war" is "wart" (ihr wart), with the -t ending of ihr. "Waren" is for wir and sie/Sie, and "warst" for du. "Wartet" is a form of "warten" (to wait).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich komme heute nicht, ___ ich bin krank."
questions.explanation: The second half gives the reason, so the linking word is "denn" (because). "Aber" would contrast two ideas, and "sondern" needs to correct a negative. After "denn" the word order stays normal: "ich bin krank".

questions.stem: Which sentence has the correct word order?
choices: Ich gehe nach Hause, denn bin ich müde.
Ich gehe nach Hause, denn ich müde bin.
Ich gehe nach Hause, denn müde ich bin.
Ich gehe nach Hause, denn ich bin müde.
questions.explanation: "Denn" stands in position zero and doesn't change the word order: the second half is a normal sentence with the verb in position 2, "ich bin müde". Putting the verb at the end is the rule for "weil", which comes at A2.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist nicht mein Handy, ___ das Handy von Tom."
questions.explanation: The first half is negative ("nicht mein Handy") and the second half corrects it, so you need "sondern" (but rather). "Aber" is the tempting choice because English uses "but" for both.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das Zimmer ist klein, ___ es ist sehr hell."
questions.explanation: There is a contrast (small, but bright) and no negative to correct, so the word is "aber". "Sondern" only follows "nicht" or "kein". "Denn" would give a reason, which doesn't make sense here.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ich bin krank, deshalb ich bleibe zu Hause.
Ich bin krank, deshalb zu Hause bleibe ich.
Ich bin krank, deshalb ich zu Hause bleibe.
Ich bin krank, deshalb bleibe ich zu Hause.
questions.explanation: "Deshalb" is not a conjunction but an adverb in position 1, so the verb comes straight after it and the subject follows: "deshalb bleibe ich". Keeping "ich bleibe" treats deshalb like "denn".

questions.stem: You are writing an e-mail to your friend Tom. How do you start?
questions.explanation: For a man the opening is "Lieber" + name; "Liebe" is for a woman (Liebe Anna). "Sehr geehrte" is formal and is used with Frau/Herr and a surname, never with a first name.

questions.stem: You are writing to an office where you don't know anyone. Which closing is right?
questions.explanation: "Mit freundlichen Grüßen" is the standard formal closing, used with "Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren". "Viele Grüße", "Liebe Grüße" and "Bis bald!" are for friends and people you know.

questions.stem: On a German form, what does the field "Staatsangehörigkeit" ask for?
questions.explanation: "Staatsangehörigkeit" is your nationality or citizenship, usually written as an adjective (deutsch, amerikanisch). Place of birth is "Geburtsort", marital status "Familienstand" and signature "Unterschrift".

questions.stem: A form says "Geburtsdatum: 04.07.1998". When was this person born?
questions.explanation: German dates go day, month, year: 04.07. is the 4th of the 7th month, which is July. Reading it as 7 April is the American month-first order.

questions.stem:
Read the message:
"Hallo Ben, danke für die Einladung! Ich komme gern am Freitag zum Grillen (to the barbecue), aber ich kann erst um acht Uhr kommen, denn ich muss bis sieben arbeiten. Soll ich etwas mitbringen (bring along)? Viele Grüße, Nina" Why is Nina coming late?
choices: She has to work until seven.
She has to buy food first.
questions.explanation: The reason comes after "denn": "ich muss bis sieben arbeiten" (I have to work until seven). Nina is happy to come ("Ich komme gern"), and she offers to bring something, but she doesn't say she has to buy food.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake?
choices: Ich trinke keinen Tee, sondern Kaffee.
Er ist müde, aber er arbeitet.
Wir bleiben hier, denn es regnet.
Ich wohne in Berlin, sondern in Hamburg.
questions.explanation: "Sondern" needs a negative before it. Correct would be "Ich wohne nicht in Berlin, sondern in Hamburg." The first sentence is fine because "keinen" is negative.

questions.stem: What does "Ich muss den Termin leider absagen." mean?
choices: Unfortunately I have to cancel the appointment.
Unfortunately I have to make an appointment.
I have to confirm the appointment.
I'll be late for the appointment.
questions.explanation: "Absagen" means to cancel (an appointment or event), and "leider" means unfortunately. The noun is "die Absage", a message saying you can't come.

questions.stem: Which answer fits the form field "Familienstand"?
questions.explanation: "Familienstand" is marital status: ledig (single), verheiratet (married) or geschieden (divorced). "Weiblich" answers "Geschlecht", "deutsch" answers "Staatsangehörigkeit" and "Köln" could be your "Geburtsort" or "Ort".

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe die Prüfung ___!" (I passed the exam!)
questions.explanation: "Bestehen" has the inseparable prefix be-, so there is no ge-, and it is strong (like "verstehen – verstanden"): "bestanden". "Gebestanden" adds a ge- that the prefix blocks.

questions.stem: How many points do you need to pass the Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1?
questions.explanation: The pass mark is 60 of 100 points. 60–69 is "ausreichend", 70–79 "befriedigend", 80–89 "gut" and 90–100 "sehr gut".

questions.stem: Which part of the Goethe A1 exam takes place in a small group, without preparation time?
questions.explanation: Sprechen (speaking) is a short oral exam in a small group: you introduce yourself, ask and answer questions with word cards, and make and respond to requests. Hören, Lesen and Schreiben are written together in one block.

questions.stem: The examiner says something and you don't catch it. What do you say?
choices: Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?
questions.explanation: "Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?" asks the person to say it again. "Was bedeutet das?" asks about the meaning of a word you heard, and "Wie sagt man das auf Deutsch?" asks for a German word.

questions.stem: Complete: "Hast du etwas gesagt?" — "Nein, ich habe ___ gesagt."
questions.explanation: The opposite of "etwas" (something) is "nichts" (nothing). "Nicht" negates a verb but can't replace an object, "kein" goes with a noun, and "niemand" means nobody.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich nehme ___ Kaffee." (der Kaffee)
questions.explanation: "Kaffee" is the direct object, so it is in the accusative, and masculine "ein" becomes "einen" (lesson 9). "Ein" is the nominative, and "einem" is the dative.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The verb is always the second element in a statement. When "Am Montag" comes first, the verb follows and the subject moves behind it: "Am Montag arbeite ich" (lessons 4 and 12). "Am Montag ich arbeite" is English word order.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich kann heute leider nicht ___."
questions.explanation: After a modal verb such as "können", the second verb goes to the end in the infinitive: "kommen" (lesson 14). "Gekommen" is the participle, used with haben or sein in the perfect.

questions.stem: Which question is correct? (anfangen = to start)
questions.explanation: "Anfangen" is separable: the verb "fängt" stays in position 2 and the prefix "an" goes to the end (lesson 12). It also has a stem change, a → ä, in the er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich fahre mit ___ Bus zur Arbeit." (der Bus)
questions.explanation: "Mit" is always followed by the dative, and masculine "der" becomes "dem" (lesson 18). "Den" is the accusative, which is a common mix-up.

questions.stem: Complete: "Gestern ___ wir ins Kino gegangen."
questions.explanation: "Gehen" is a verb of movement, so its perfect uses sein, and the wir form is "sind" (lesson 22). "Haben" is the auxiliary for most other verbs.

questions.stem:
Read the sign:
"Bäckerei Schmidt. Montag bis Freitag 6:30–18:00 Uhr, Samstag 7:00–12:00 Uhr, Sonntag geschlossen." It is Saturday, 2 p.m. Is the bakery open?
choices: No, it is closed all day on Saturday.
questions.explanation: On Saturday ("Samstag") the bakery is open from 7:00 to 12:00, so at 2 p.m. (14:00) it is already closed. The 18:00 closing time is for Monday to Friday, and "geschlossen" (closed) is for Sunday.

questions.stem: Complete: "Das ist ___ Schwester." (my)
questions.explanation: "Schwester" is feminine (die Schwester), so the possessive takes -e: "meine Schwester" (lesson 6). "Mein" is for masculine and neuter nouns in the nominative.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: In German the first word of a sentence and every noun start with a capital letter: "Hund" is a noun, so it is capitalized, but verbs and articles are not (lessons 1 and 5).

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich habe ___ Auto." (I don't have a car.)
questions.explanation: A noun with "ein" is negated with "kein", and "Auto" is neuter, so "kein Auto" (lesson 8). "Nicht" doesn't replace an article, and "keine" is for feminine and plural nouns.

questions.stem: You move into a flat in Germany. By when must you register your address (die Anmeldung)?
choices: Within two weeks of moving in
Within three days of moving in
Within three months of moving in
Only when you start a job
questions.explanation: In Germany you have two weeks after moving in. Three days is the rule in Austria (the Meldezettel), not Germany. You register whether or not you have a job.

questions.stem: Which form does your landlord or landlady give you for the Anmeldung?
questions.explanation: The "Wohnungsgeberbestätigung" (Wohnungsgeber = the person who provides the flat, Bestätigung = confirmation) confirms that you've moved in. The "Meldebescheinigung" is what the Bürgeramt gives you at the end; the Steuer-ID comes by post later; the Rundfunkbeitrag is the broadcasting fee.

questions.stem: Read: "Ihr Termin ist am Dienstag, 20. Oktober, um 9:30 Uhr im Bürgeramt Mitte, Zimmer 104. Sie können nicht kommen? Dann sagen Sie den Termin bitte bis zum 19. Oktober ab." What should Lukas do if he can't come?
choices: Go to room 104 on 19 October instead
Phone the Bürgeramt on 20 October at 9:30
questions.explanation: "Absagen" means to cancel, and "bis zum 19. Oktober" means by 19 October. The letter doesn't offer another day or ask him to phone on the day itself.

questions.stem: Abbreviations are read aloud as full words. Type what you say for "z. B.": ___
questions.explanation: "z. B." stands for "zum Beispiel" (for example) and is always read as the full words, never as the letters "zet be".

questions.stem: Match each abbreviation to its full form.
questions.explanation: usw. = und so weiter (and so on); ca. = circa (about); ggf. = gegebenenfalls (if necessary); d. h. = das heißt (that is); u. a. = unter anderem (among other things). "Zum Beispiel" is z. B. and "beziehungsweise" is bzw.

questions.stem: A colleague writes: "Ich komme evtl. später." What does she mean?
choices: I'll come later in the end.
questions.explanation: evtl. = eventuell, which means "possibly", not "eventually". It's a classic false friend. The verb "komme" is present tense, so "I came" is wrong too.

questions.stem: A letter from the Amt says: "Bitte bringen Sie Ihren Reisepass mit." What does "Ihren" mean here?
questions.explanation: With a capital I, "Ihr/Ihre/Ihren" is the formal "your" that goes with Sie. "ihr" with a small i would mean "her" or "their". The ending -en is there because "Reisepass" is masculine and accusative.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the entrance to a block of flats.

image.alt: The entrance of a block of flats: a house number above the front door, a doorbell panel with six buttons to the right of the door, six post boxes on the wall to the left, and the front door with a glass panel. Four parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the house number above the door (die Hausnummer), 2 the panel of doorbells (die Klingel), 3 the post boxes (der Briefkasten), and 4 the front door of the building (die Haustür). Put your name on the bell and the post box as soon as you move in, or the post can't be delivered.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say, politely and formally: "Please bring your passport."
questions.explanation: "Bitte bringen Sie Ihren Pass mit." The formal imperative starts with the verb (after "bitte"), Sie follows it, and the separable prefix "mit" goes to the very end.

questions.stem: Which of these do you usually bring to your Anmeldung appointment? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: You bring your passport or ID card, the landlord's confirmation and the registration form. The Steuer-ID isn't needed: after a first registration it is sent to you by post a few weeks later. The Meldebescheinigung is what you receive at the appointment, so you don't bring it.

questions.stem: Which is the right name line for the address on a letter to Lukas Brandt?
questions.explanation: In an address, "Herr" takes an extra -n: "Herrn Lukas Brandt". "Herr" without -n belongs in the greeting ("Sehr geehrter Herr Brandt,"), "Herren" is the plural (gentlemen), and "Sehr geehrter …" is a greeting, not an address.

questions.stem: You leave Germany for good. Type the missing part of the verb for "to deregister": sich ___
questions.explanation: "Sich abmelden" is the opposite of "sich anmelden" (to register). Like anmelden, it's separable: "Ich melde mich ab."

questions.stem: Who pays the Rundfunkbeitrag (the broadcasting fee)?
choices: Only households that own a TV
Every adult in the household separately
Every household, one fee per household
questions.explanation: The Rundfunkbeitrag is one fee per household, whether or not it has a TV or radio. Flatmates share one fee instead of each paying.

questions.stem: At the Bürgeramt the official asks: "Haben Sie Ihren Pass dabei?" Which answer fits best?
questions.explanation: "Ja, hier, bitte." (Yes, here you are.) "Ich habe dabei" is missing the object ("Ich habe ihn dabei" would be right). "Gern geschehen" answers a thank-you, and "ich bin Pass" makes no sense.

questions.stem: A Hausordnung says: "Am Sonntag und an Feiertagen ist den ganzen Tag Ruhezeit." What does it mean?
choices: On Sundays you may only be loud in the afternoon.
On Sundays and public holidays it's quiet time all day.
On Sundays and public holidays the building is locked.
Quiet time ends at 7 on public holidays.
questions.explanation: "Den ganzen Tag" means all day, and "Feiertage" are public holidays. So no drilling, loud music or bottle throwing all day on those days.

questions.stem: Build the notice "Please lock the front door!" as an infinitive command.
questions.explanation: "Bitte die Haustür abschließen!" In an infinitive command the infinitive comes last, and a separable verb stays in one piece: "abschließen", never "schließen … ab".

questions.stem: Which is the infinitive command for a sign that says "No smoking in the cellar"?
questions.explanation: The infinitive "rauchen" goes at the end, with "nicht" before it: "Im Keller nicht rauchen!" The other choices put the verb in the wrong place or use a conjugated form ("raucht"), which an infinitive command doesn't have.

questions.stem: Turn the rule "Im Keller nicht rauchen." into a sentence with "man" and a modal verb.
choices: Im Keller muss man nicht rauchen.
Im Keller man darf nicht rauchen.
Im Keller darf man nicht rauchen.
Im Keller darf man nicht raucht.
questions.explanation: A ban is "nicht dürfen": "Im Keller darf man nicht rauchen." "Nicht müssen" means "don't have to", which is not a ban. The modal must be in position 2, right after "Im Keller", so "man darf" is wrong, and the verb at the end stays an infinitive.

questions.stem: Name the numbered bins.

image.alt: Four wheelie bins in a row, each with a sticker showing what goes in it: a yellow bin with a tin and a yoghurt pot, a blue bin with a newspaper, a brown bin with an apple core and a grey bin with an old sponge. The bins are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the yellow bin for packaging such as tins and yoghurt pots; 2 the blue paper bin; 3 the (often brown) Biotonne for food waste; 4 the grey bin for general waste (Restmüll). Glass goes in a separate street container, and Pfand bottles go back to the shop's machine.

questions.stem: Where does each item go?
questions.explanation: Paper goes in the blue paper bin, plastic packaging in the yellow bin, food waste in the Biotonne, glass without a deposit in the bottle bank (sorted by colour), and a bottle with a Pfand logo back to the shop's deposit machine. None of these is general waste.

questions.stem: How much Pfand (deposit) do you pay on a single-use plastic bottle with the deposit logo?
questions.explanation: Single-use plastic bottles and drink cans carry 25 cents. The lower amounts, 8 or 15 cents, are typical for reusable (Mehrweg) bottles.

questions.stem: Wohin? Type the missing article: "Die Dose kommt in ___ Gelben Sack."
questions.explanation: The can goes into the bag: movement to a place, so "Wohin?" and the accusative. "Der Sack" is masculine, so the accusative article is "den". ("im Gelben Sack" would describe where it already is.)

questions.stem: Wo? Type the missing word (one word, a contraction): "Das Fahrrad steht ___ Keller."
questions.explanation: The bike is standing in the cellar: no movement, so "Wo?" and the dative: in dem Keller, shortened to "im Keller". (For movement it would be "in den Keller".)

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich werfe die Dose in die Tonne.
Die Zeitung ist in der Papiertonne.
Wir bringen die Fahrräder in den Keller.
Ich werfe die Flasche in dem Glascontainer.
questions.explanation: Throwing and bringing are movement (Wohin? + accusative): "in die Tonne", "in den Keller". "Ist in der Papiertonne" is location (Wo? + dative). "In dem Glascontainer" after "werfen" should be "in den Glascontainer", and "steht" is location, so it should be "im Treppenhaus", not "ins".

questions.stem: Choose the right form: "Er ___ die Flasche in den Glascontainer."
questions.explanation: "Werfen" changes e → i in the du and er/sie/es forms: du wirfst, er wirft. "Werft" is the ihr form, and "wirfst" is the du form.

questions.stem: Lukas asks his neighbour: "Darf ich am Sonntag bohren?" Which answer is polite and matches the house rules?
choices: Ja, natürlich, am Sonntag ist das kein Problem.
Lieber nicht. Am Sonntag ist Ruhezeit.
questions.explanation: Sunday is quiet time all day, so drilling is not OK at any time on Sunday: "Lieber nicht" (better not) is a polite way to say no, and Saturday is the day for it.

questions.stem: You have an empty water bottle with a Pfand logo. What do you do with it?
choices: Take it back to a shop's deposit machine
Put it in the yellow bin
Put it in the glass container
questions.explanation: A Pfand bottle goes back to a shop's Pfandautomat, which prints a receipt (Pfandbon) you can cash at the till. Check for the Pfand logo first, before you think about glass or plastic.

questions.stem: A note in the stairwell: "Liebe Nachbarn, am Samstag feiern wir eine Party. Es kann ein bisschen laut werden. Wir bitten um Verständnis!" What is the last sentence?
choices: A request for the neighbours to come to the party
A request for the neighbours' understanding
An apology for a past party
A warning that the police may come
questions.explanation: "Wir bitten um Verständnis" is a set phrase on notices: "we ask for your understanding" (thank you for your understanding). It doesn't invite anyone, and the party is still to come ("am Samstag feiern wir").

questions.stem: Which past tense do written stories, novels and fairy tales mostly use?
questions.explanation: Written stories use the simple past (Präteritum): "Der Esel ging nach Bremen." In conversation Germans mostly use the perfect instead, except for war, hatte and the modals.

questions.stem: Match each simple past form from the story to its infinitive.
questions.explanation: These are strong verbs: the vowel changes and there's no -te ending. gehen, ging, gegangen; kommen, kam, gekommen; sehen, sah, gesehen; laufen, lief, gelaufen; finden, fand, gefunden. ("Saß" would be sitzen; "fuhr" would be fahren.)

questions.stem: "Machen" is a weak verb. Type its simple past to complete: "Die Tiere ___ einen Plan." (The animals made a plan.)
questions.explanation: Weak verbs add -te to the stem, and the plural (sie, wir) adds -n: mach + te + n = "machten". "Machte" is the er/sie/es form.

questions.stem: Which is the correct simple past: "Am Abend ___ der Esel an ein Haus."
questions.explanation: "Kommen" is strong: the past is "kam", with no ending for er/sie/es. "Kommte" adds the weak -te to a strong verb, "kamt" is the ihr form, and "gekommen" is the participle, which needs "ist".

questions.stem: Which are the correct principal parts (infinitive, simple past, past participle) of "gehen"?
questions.explanation: gehen, ging, gegangen. Strong verbs don't take -te or -t, so "gehte, gegeht" is wrong; the vowels of the simple past and the participle are often different, so you learn all three forms together.

questions.stem: Put these events from the story "Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten" (as retold in the lesson) in order.
choices: Die Tiere sahen im Wald ein Licht.
Die Tiere fielen durch das Fenster.
Die Räuber liefen in den Wald.
In der Nacht kam ein Räuber zurück.
questions.explanation: The donkey runs away, finds the dog (and later the cat and the rooster), they see a light in the forest, crash through the window while making their "music", the robbers flee, and one robber comes back in the night and is chased off.

questions.stem: Read: "Ein Hahn stand auf dem Zaun und rief: Kikeriki! Morgen kocht die Bäuerin eine Suppe aus mir!" Why does the rooster want to leave?
choices: He wants to sing in Bremen.
He is too old to catch mice.
The farmer's wife is going to make soup out of him.
questions.explanation: "Morgen kocht die Bäuerin eine Suppe aus mir" means "Tomorrow the farmer's wife is going to cook a soup out of me". Catching mice is the cat's problem, not the rooster's.

questions.stem: Read: "Die Räuber hatten große Angst. Ein Gespenst!, riefen sie und liefen in den Wald." Why did the robbers run away?
choices: They thought a ghost had come.
questions.explanation: "Angst haben" means to be afraid, and "Ein Gespenst!" means "A ghost!". The animals' noise and crash through the window made the robbers think a ghost had come in.

questions.stem: Name the four Bremen Town Musicians.

image.alt: Four animals standing on each other in front of a lit window: a donkey at the bottom, a dog on the donkey, a cat on the dog and a rooster at the top. The animals are numbered from the top.

questions.explanation: From the top: der Hahn (rooster), die Katze (cat), der Hund (dog) and der Esel (donkey) at the bottom. "Das Huhn" is a hen, and "die Maus" is what the old cat couldn't catch any more.

questions.stem: Which of these simple past forms belong to strong verbs (new vowel, no -te)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: sprang (springen), flog (fliegen) and fiel (fallen) change their vowel and have no ending: strong verbs. bellte, machten and wohnte have -te: weak verbs (bellen, machen, wohnen).

questions.stem: You're telling the story aloud. How do you say "Der Hund sprang auf den Esel" in the spoken past (the perfect)?
choices: Der Hund hat auf den Esel gesprungen.
Der Hund ist auf den Esel gesprungen.
Der Hund ist auf den Esel gespringt.
Der Hund hat auf den Esel gesprangen.
questions.explanation: "Springen" is movement, so it takes sein, and it's strong: springen, sprang, gesprungen. So: "Der Hund ist auf den Esel gesprungen." "Hat" is the wrong auxiliary, and "gespringt" and "gesprangen" are not words.

questions.stem: When did the Brothers Grimm publish the first volume of their "Kinder- und Hausmärchen"?
questions.explanation: The first volume appeared in 1812. "Die Bremer Stadtmusikanten" was added in the second edition of 1819; Wilhelm Grimm died in 1859; the bronze statue in Bremen was set up in 1953.

questions.stem: Type the infinitive of the verb in "Auf dem Weg fand er einen Hund." ___
questions.explanation: "Fand" is the simple past of the strong verb "finden" (finden, fand, gefunden), like English find / found. It has nothing to do with English "fanned".

questions.stem: What does "Es war einmal ein Esel." mean?
choices: It was a donkey once more.
Once upon a time there was a donkey.
A donkey was here only one time.
questions.explanation: "Es war einmal …" is the fixed opening of fairy tales: "Once upon a time there was …". "Einmal" here means "once" in the sense of "at one time", not "one more time" (that would be "noch einmal").

questions.stem: At 5 p.m. a colleague says: "Schönen Feierabend!" What do you answer?
questions.explanation: "Danke, gleichfalls!" means "Thanks, you too!" and is the usual answer to a good wish. "Gute Besserung" is for someone who is ill, "Herzlich willkommen" greets a guest, and "Guten Appetit" is said before a meal.

questions.stem: Type the diminutive (the "little" form with -chen) of "das Haus": das ___
questions.explanation: "Haus" has no final -e to drop; "au" takes an umlaut ("äu"); then add -chen: "Häuschen". Say it Häus-chen, with s and the ch of "ich", not "sch".

questions.stem: Which article goes with "Kätzchen" (kitten), from "die Katze"?
questions.explanation: Every noun ending in -chen or -lein is neuter: "das Kätzchen", even though "die Katze" is feminine. "Die" would only be right for the plural: "die Kätzchen".

questions.stem: Which of these nouns are diminutives (with the ending -chen)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Brötchen (from Brot), Mädchen (from the old word Magd) and Eichhörnchen are diminutives, and all three are das. "Der Kuchen" just happens to end in -chen, and "die Küche" in -che; neither is a diminutive, which is why they aren't neuter. "Kleingarten" is a compound of klein + Garten.

questions.stem: Match each noun to its diminutive.
questions.explanation: Drop a final -e (Tasse → Täss-, Blume → Blüm-), add the umlaut (a → ä, u → ü, au → äu) and add -chen. After -ch, -lein is used: Büchlein. "Baumchen" and "Hundchen" forget the umlaut.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things in this Kleingarten.

image.alt: A small rented garden: a hut on the left, an apple tree on the right, a wooden fence at the back, a vegetable bed with tomato plants in front, flowers on the right and a watering can on the left. Six things are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the garden hut (die Laube), 2 the apple tree (der Baum), 3 the fence (der Zaun), 4 the vegetable bed (das Beet), 5 the flowers (die Blume) and 6 the watering can (die Gießkanne, from gießen, to water).

questions.stem: Which is true of the Laube in a German Kleingarten, under the federal rules?
choices: It may be at most 24 square metres, and you may not live in it.
You may live in it all year round.
It must be at least 400 square metres.
Only the city may use it.
questions.explanation: The Bundeskleingartengesetz allows a simple hut of at most 24 m², including a covered seating area, and it's not for living in. 400 m² is the maximum size of the whole garden, not a minimum for the hut.

questions.stem: At the bakery: "Ich hätte gern zwei ___, bitte."
questions.explanation: Diminutives have no plural ending: one Brötchen, two Brötchen. Only the article shows the plural: das Brötchen, die Brötchen.

questions.stem: From whom do you usually rent a Kleingarten in Germany?
choices: From a landlord, like a flat
From a garden club, the Kleingartenverein
questions.explanation: You rent the garden through the Kleingartenverein and become a member, with meetings and shared jobs. (The club usually leases the land from the town; the lesson simplifies this.)

questions.stem: Read: "Im Garten nebenan sitzt Herr Wolff vor seinem Häuschen und liest die Zeitung. Na, Frau Berger, möchten Sie ein Gläschen Saft?, fragt er." What does Herr Wolff offer Ilse?
questions.explanation: "Ein Gläschen Saft" is a (little) glass of juice. The -chen makes the offer friendly; it doesn't mean the glass is tiny. "Häuschen" is where he is sitting, and "Zeitung" is what he is reading.

questions.stem: A friend asks: "Trinken wir noch ein Tässchen Kaffee?" Why "Tässchen" and not "Tasse"?
choices: Because it sounds friendly and relaxed
Because the cup is especially small
Because it's the formal form for Sie
questions.explanation: The diminutive often adds a warm, relaxed feeling, part of Gemütlichkeit; the cup is a normal cup. "Ein Tässchen" is singular, and diminutives have nothing to do with Sie.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "We're making ourselves comfortable."
questions.explanation: "Wir machen es uns gemütlich." It's a fixed chunk: subject, verb in position 2, then "es uns" (es before uns), and "gemütlich" at the end.

questions.stem: How do you say "Häuschen" (little house)?
choices: Häus-chen: an s, then the ch of "ich"
questions.explanation: The word is Häus + chen, so the s and the ch are separate: Häus-chen, with the soft ch of "ich". Reading it as "sch" is a common mistake; the same goes for Gläschen and Röschen.

questions.stem: What is a "Stammtisch"?
choices: The family's dining table at home
The table where you sign forms at the Bürgeramt
A picnic table in the Kleingarten
A table in a pub kept for a group of regulars who meet there often
questions.explanation: A Stammtisch is a regulars' table in a Kneipe, kept for a group that meets there regularly (often weekly). Today the word is also used for any regular get-together, like a Sprachstammtisch for language learners.

questions.stem: Where is each sound made? Pick the sound for each numbered part of the mouth.

image.alt: A simplified side view of the mouth with four numbered parts: the lips at the front, the hard palate just behind the top teeth, the soft palate further back, and the small uvula hanging at the very back.

questions.explanation: The lips (1) round and push forward for ü and ö. The soft ch of ich (2) is made with the middle of the tongue close to the hard palate. The rough ch after a, o, u (3) is made further back, at the soft palate. The throat r (4) is made near the uvula, at the very back. German has no English w sound, and a silent h isn't made anywhere.

questions.stem: Fill in ß or ss, as written in Germany. Type only the missing letters: "Stra___e" (street, long a) and "Wa___er" (water, short a).
questions.explanation: After a long vowel or a diphthong, a sharp s is written ß: Straße. After a short vowel it is ss: Wasser. (In Switzerland both are written with ss: Strasse.)

questions.stem: Which of these words have the soft ch sound of "ich"? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: After a, o, u and au, ch is the rough sound at the back of the mouth: Nacht, auch, noch. After any other letter it is the soft hiss of ich: nicht (after i) and Milch (after l).

questions.stem: Match each German spelling to the sound it usually makes.
questions.explanation: German w is English v (wie = "vee"), v is usually f (vier = "feer"), z is ts (zehn = "tsayn"), j is y (ja = "yah") and ei sounds like "eye" (nein = "nine"). No German letter makes the English w sound.

questions.stem: Why is "heißen" written with ß, but "Wasser" with ss?
choices: ß follows the diphthong ei; ss follows a short vowel
ß is used in verbs and ss in nouns
ß is the old spelling and ss is the new one
ß comes before -en and ss before -er
questions.explanation: The choice depends on the sound before it: after a long vowel or a diphthong (ei, au, eu) write ß, after a short vowel write ss. The ei in heißen is a diphthong; the a in Wasser is short. Verbs and nouns can have either (die Straße, essen), and both letters are current spelling.

questions.stem: Which greeting fits each part of the day? Pick a greeting for each number.

image.alt: A timeline from 6:00 to 24:00 split into three unlabeled parts: 1 is the morning until about 10:30, 2 is the middle of the day until about 18:00, 3 is the evening. Number 4 is on a bed with a moon.

questions.explanation: Guten Morgen is for the morning until about 10 or 11 (1), Guten Tag for the middle of the day (2) and Guten Abend from about 6 p.m. (3). Gute Nacht (4) is only said when someone goes to bed. Auf Wiedersehen means goodbye at any time, and Wie bitte? means "pardon?".

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of heißen: "Wie ___ du?"
questions.explanation: The du form normally ends in -st, but the stem heiß- already ends in ß, so du adds only -t: du heißt. (In Switzerland: du heisst.)

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask "How are you?" formally.
questions.explanation: Wie geht es Ihnen? The question word comes first and the verb geht second; es (it) and Ihnen (to you) follow. The informal version is Wie geht's? or Wie geht es dir?

questions.stem: Which people would you normally address with Sie? Select all that apply.
choices: a bank clerk you don't know
your new boss at a bank
a classmate at your language course
an older neighbour you call Frau Huber
questions.explanation: Sie is for adults you don't know, staff in shops and offices, your boss and anyone you call Herr or Frau. Family members (your brother) and classmates are du.

questions.stem: Match each question word to its meaning.
questions.explanation: wer = who (not "where", despite the look), wie = how (Wie heißt du? is literally "How are you called?"), woher = where from (answer with aus), wo = where (answer with in). "When" is wann, from Lesson 4.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this German address.

image.alt: An envelope addressed to Lisa Krämer, Lindenstraße 14, 04107 Leipzig. Each line has a number before its first part and after its last part: 1 before Lisa, 2 after Krämer, 3 before Lindenstraße, 4 after 14, 5 before 04107 and 6 after Leipzig.

questions.explanation: Lisa is the first name (1) and Krämer the surname (2). In a German address the street (3) comes first and the house number (4) after it. On the last line the five-digit postcode (5) comes before the town or city (6). There's no phone number on the envelope.

questions.stem: Write 73 as a German word.
questions.explanation: Units first, then und, then the ten, all as one word: drei + und + siebzig = dreiundsiebzig. Note siebzig, not siebenzig.

questions.stem: You hear "achtundvierzig". Write the number in digits. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: acht (8) und vierzig (40): 48. The unit comes first in German, so the most common mistake is writing 84.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers are spelled correctly? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: sechzehn (16) drops the s of sechs, dreißig (30) ends in -ßig, and einundzwanzig (21) uses ein, not eins. siebenzehn should be siebzehn (17), and sechszig should be sechzig (60).

questions.stem: Put the parts of a German address in the order they are written on an envelope, from top left to bottom right.
questions.explanation: Lisa Krämer / Lindenstraße 14 / 04107 Leipzig: first name and surname, then the street with the house number after it, then the postcode before the town.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of arbeiten: "Er ___ heute in Köln."
questions.explanation: The stem arbeit- ends in -t, so an e is added before the ending -t: er arbeitet. "Er arbeitt" can't be said clearly.

questions.stem: Put the words in order, starting with "Heute": "Today I'm working in Cologne."
questions.explanation: Heute arbeite ich in Köln. The verb must be the second element, so when the sentence starts with Heute, the subject ich moves to just after the verb. "Heute ich arbeite" is English word order.

questions.stem: Match each pronoun to the right form of sein.
questions.explanation: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid (and sie/Sie sind). seit means "since" and only sounds like seid.

questions.stem: Which of these are correct yes/no questions? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question puts the conjugated verb first, with the right ending: Wohnst du, Arbeitet ihr, Spielt Lara. "Wohnen du" has the wrong ending (du takes -st), and German has no helper verb like English "do", so "Tust du hier wohnen?" is wrong.

questions.stem: Which form is correct? "Du ___ sehr gut." (antworten)
questions.explanation: The stem antwort- ends in -t, so an e goes before the du ending -st: du antwortest. antwortst is hard to say and wrong; antwortet is the er or ihr form; antworten is the wir, sie or Sie form.

questions.stem: In which word is the stressed vowel long because it ends its syllable?
questions.explanation: Name splits into Na-me, so the a ends an open syllable and is long. Bett and Hallo have a double consonant, so the vowel is short; Stadt has a short a too.

questions.stem: Which word has a short vowel even though only one consonant follows it?
questions.explanation: das is one of the short everyday words (with was, es, in, mit, an, um, bis, man, hat). Tag, gut and Weg are long, because longer forms such as Ta-ge, gu-te and We-ge have open syllables.

questions.stem: How does the ending -er in "Lehrer" (teacher) usually sound in standard German?
choices: like a short "uh", with no consonant r
questions.explanation: Final -er is a vocalic r: the r melts into a short open vowel close to the u in English "but". So Lehrer is roughly "LAY-ruh". A hard English r is the clearest sign of an English accent; the ending is never silent.

questions.stem: How are "verreisen" (to go away on a trip) and "vereisen" (to ice over) told apart in speech?
choices: verreisen is stressed on the first syllable.
vereisen has a glottal stop before -eisen and no r sound there.
questions.explanation: verreisen is ver- + reisen, with an r sound starting the second part. vereisen is ver- + eisen: the second part starts with a vowel, so it begins with a glottal stop, "fer | EYE-zen". Both are stressed on the second part.

questions.stem: How is "Spiegelei" (fried egg) pronounced?
choices: "SHPEE-gel | ei", with a small catch before ei
questions.explanation: Spiegelei is Spiegel (mirror) + Ei (egg). The second part starts with a vowel, so it gets a glottal stop: "SHPEE-gel | ei". The first part of a compound carries the main stress, and sp at the start is "shp".

questions.stem: Which sentence usually rises at the end?
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions usually rise: Wohnst du in Berlin? Statements fall, and W-questions such as Wo wohnst du? and Woher kommst du? usually fall too, because the question word already marks them as questions.

questions.stem: Which is the current spelling of "must" in "ich ___"?
questions.explanation: The u is short, so since the 1996 spelling reform it's written ss: ich muss. muß is the old spelling you may still see in older books; mus would suggest a long u, as in das Mus (purée), and mußs is not a word.

questions.stem: How may "Straße" be written in capital letters under the official rules today?
choices: only STRAßE, with a small ß
questions.explanation: Traditionally ß had no capital, so capitals used SS: STRASSE. Since 2017 the official rules also allow the capital ẞ: STRAẞE. SS is still the more usual choice. STRASE drops a letter and would change the sound.

questions.stem: An Austrian newsreader says "zwanzig" with a k sound at the end ("-tsik"). This is…
choices: a dialect word, not standard German
questions.explanation: The ending -ig is said like ich in most of Germany, but with a k in the south, in Austria and in Switzerland, where it counts as standard. The spelling reform changed spellings, not pronunciation.

questions.stem: In careful German, a word or word part that starts with a vowel (ein | Ei) begins with a small catch in the throat called a ___.
questions.explanation: It's a glottal stop (German Knacklaut): a brief closing of the throat, like the break in English "uh-oh". It keeps ein Ei from running together as "ei-nei".

questions.stem: Match each spelling to how it is pronounced.
choices: ng as in singer, with no g
questions.explanation: pf keeps both letters (Apfel, Kopf); chs is usually ks (sechs, Fuchs); ng never adds a g (Finger is "FING-uh"); -tion is "tsion" and takes the stress (In-for-ma-TSION); v in loanwords like Klavier is an English v. "sh" is the sound of sch.

questions.stem: Which of these are minimal pairs, words that differ in only one sound? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: bitte/bitter differ only in the final sound (schwa vs vocalic r), Wein/Wien only in the vowel ("eye" vs "ee"), and schon/schön only in o vs ö. Stadt/Straße and Tag/Woche differ in several sounds.

questions.stem: Put the parts in order to make the second half of the tongue twister, starting with "Frische Fische": "Fisher's Fritz fishes fresh fish."
questions.explanation: Frische Fische fischt Fischers Fritz. The sentence starts with the object, so the verb fischt must still be second, and the subject Fischers Fritz follows it.

questions.stem: In which words does v sound like English v (not f)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: In loanwords such as Klavier, Universität and November, v is an English v. In old German words such as Vater (father) and vier (four), v sounds like f.

questions.stem: Name the numbered countries and regions where German is an official language.

image.alt: A simplified map of central Europe with six numbered areas: 1 is the large country in the north, 2 the country to the south-east of it, 3 the country to the south-west, 4 a tiny dot between 3 and 2, 5 a small country on the western border of 1, and 6 a region south of 2.

questions.explanation: Germany (1) is the large country in the north, Austria (2) lies to its south-east and Switzerland (3) to its south-west. Tiny Liechtenstein (4) sits between Switzerland and Austria, Luxembourg (5) on Germany's western border, and South Tyrol (6) is the northern Italian province just south of Austria. Poland and France are neighbours where German is not an official language.

questions.stem: In which of these countries is German the only official language?
questions.explanation: Liechtenstein has German as its only official language. Switzerland has four national languages (German, French, Italian, Romansh), Luxembourg three (Luxembourgish, French, German) and Belgium three (Dutch, French, German).

questions.stem: What does "hoch" (high) in "Hochdeutsch" refer to?
choices: the language of the upper classes
a more correct form of German
the higher-lying middle and south of the German-speaking area
German as spoken in the Swiss mountains only
questions.explanation: "High" is geography: standard German grew mainly out of the dialects of the higher, hilly middle and south, as opposed to the flat north where Low German (Plattdeutsch) is spoken. It says nothing about class or correctness.

questions.stem: A shop assistant in Hamburg says "Moin!" to you at 7 p.m. What does she mean?
questions.explanation: Moin is the everyday hello of northern Germany and works at any time of day, including the evening. Its origin is debated, but it isn't simply short for Guten Morgen.

questions.stem: Who can you greet with "Grüß dich"?
choices: a friend you say du to
a shop assistant you don't know
your friend's grandmother, whom you call Frau Huber
questions.explanation: dich is a du form, so Grüß dich is only for one person you say du to. For the others, use Grüß Gott or Guten Tag.

questions.stem: Complete with duzen: "___ du deine Lehrerin?" (Do you say du to your teacher?)
questions.explanation: The stem duz- ends in -z, so the du form adds only -t: du duzt. In a yes/no question the verb comes first: Duzt du deine Lehrerin?

questions.stem: Complete with siezen: "Wir ___ Frau Klein." (We say Sie to Ms Klein.)
questions.explanation: The wir form is the same as the infinitive: wir siezen.

questions.stem: Match each greeting to how it is used.
choices: hello in northern Germany, any time of day
informal hi and bye in Bavaria and Austria
questions.explanation: Moin is the northern hello, Grüezi the polite Swiss hello (for people you say Sie to), Servus the informal hello and goodbye of Bavaria and Austria, and Hoi the informal Swiss hi. Goodbye at bedtime is Gute Nacht.

questions.stem: German is pluricentric. Match each word from Germany to the form used in the country named.
questions.explanation: Austria says Jänner for January; Switzerland says Velo for bicycle and writes ss instead of ß (Strasse). Servus is a greeting, not one of these words.

questions.stem: Which statements about Swiss German (Schweizerdeutsch) are true? Select all that apply.
choices: German-speaking Swiss of every background use it in everyday speech.
In writing and on the news, Swiss Standard German is used.
As a learner in Switzerland, you speak standard German.
It is the language of Swiss newspapers.
Only older people in the countryside speak it.
questions.explanation: Swiss German dialects are the everyday spoken language of German-speaking Switzerland, across all ages and backgrounds. Newspapers, schools and the news use Swiss Standard German, and learners speak standard German there too.

questions.stem: Two colleagues, aged 58 and 26, have said Sie to each other for a month. Who usually offers du?
choices: whoever has worked there for less time
questions.explanation: The older or more senior person usually offers du (Wir können gern du sagen). It's a custom, not a law, and many workplaces use du from the first day.

questions.stem: You are talking to two business clients you say Sie to. Which question fits?
