questions.explanation: Sie is used for one person or many, so two clients you'd address formally get Sie: Wie heißen Sie? ihr is for two or more people you'd each say du to. "Wie heißen ihr" mixes the ihr pronoun with the wrong ending.

questions.stem: Put the words in order, starting with "Im Büro": "In the office we all say du."
questions.explanation: Im Büro duzen wir alle. The place phrase is first, so the verb duzen is second and the subject wir follows; alle (all) comes after the subject.

questions.stem: A colleague in Vienna writes "Jänner" for January. This is…
questions.explanation: German has several standards. Jänner is the standard Austrian word for January, just as correct in Austria as Januar is in Germany.

questions.stem: "Sieben mal acht ist ___." Write the result in digits. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: mal means times: 7 · 8 = 56 (sechsundfünfzig).

questions.stem: How do you say the sign ":" in "20 : 4 = 5"? Write the two German words.
questions.explanation: 20 : 4 is zwanzig geteilt durch vier (in casual speech also just zwanzig durch vier). German schools write division with a colon.

questions.stem: How do you say 81 − 36 = 45?
questions.explanation: Each two-digit number is unit + und + ten: einundachtzig, sechsunddreißig, fünfundvierzig. Inside a number eins becomes ein. vierundfünfzig is 54, the reversed number.

questions.stem: Which form is correct? "Du ___ sehr schnell." (rechnen)
questions.explanation: The stem rechn- ends in n after another consonant, so an e goes before the ending: du rechnest. rechnet is the er or ihr form, rechnen the wir, sie or Sie form.

questions.stem: Which verb forms are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: zeichnen and öffnen have consonant + n stems, so they add e: er zeichnet, er öffnet; for the same reason it's du rechnest, not rechnst. After r (lernen) or a silent h (wohnen) no e is added: du lernst, du wohnst.

questions.stem: Match each German school grade to its name.
questions.explanation: The German scale: 1 sehr gut, 2 gut, 3 befriedigend, 4 ausreichend, 5 mangelhaft, 6 ungenügend. ausgezeichnet (excellent) isn't a grade name.

questions.stem: Anna, at school in Zurich, says: "Ich habe eine Fünf in Mathe." What does that mean?
choices: She got a good grade, above the pass mark.
questions.explanation: Swiss grades run from 6 (best) to 1 (worst) with 4 as the pass mark, so a 5 is good. In Germany or Austria, a 5 would be a fail.

questions.stem: Which grade is a pass in Germany, Austria and Switzerland?
questions.explanation: A 4 passes everywhere: ausreichend in Germany, Genügend in Austria, and the pass mark in Switzerland. A 5 fails in Germany and Austria, a 6 fails in Germany, and a 1 fails in Switzerland.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: A number used as a noun is capitalized and feminine: die Eins, so eine Eins. einen and ein would be masculine or neuter, and lowercase eins is the counting number, not the noun.

questions.stem: You order two coffees in a German café by holding up fingers. What is the usual German way to show "two"?
questions.explanation: Germans usually count from the thumb: one is the thumb, two is thumb and index finger. Index and middle finger will usually be understood, but thumb and index finger is the local way and can't be misread.

questions.stem: A handwritten German 1 often has a long upstroke. How do Germans keep their 7 from looking like a 1?
choices: They put a short bar across the 7.
They add a curl at the bottom of the 7.
questions.explanation: A German 1 with a long upstroke looks like an American 7, so the German 7 gets a short line across its middle. A 7 without a bar may be read as a 1.

questions.stem: Put the German school grades in order, from best to worst.
questions.explanation: 1 sehr gut, 2 gut, 3 befriedigend, 4 ausreichend (the lowest pass), 5 mangelhaft, 6 ungenügend.

questions.stem: Which of these say 2 + 2 = 4? Select all that apply.
choices: zwei plus zwei ist gleich vier
questions.explanation: plus (or casually und) is +, and "equals" can be ist or ist gleich. zwei mal zwei is 2 · 2, a multiplication, and zwei minus zwei is 2 − 2.

questions.stem: Writing 52 when you hear "fünfundzwanzig" is a common mix-up. Its German name is "der ___".
questions.explanation: der Zahlendreher, a "number turner": the digits end up in the wrong order because German says the unit first. Saying important numbers digit by digit avoids it.

questions.stem: Write the definite article ("the") for each noun: ___ Zeitung (newspaper), ___ Handy (mobile phone), ___ Stuhl (chair).
questions.explanation: die Zeitung: -ung nouns are always feminine. das Handy: neuter, like many English loanwords in -y. der Stuhl: masculine, a noun to learn with its article (plural die Stühle).

questions.stem: Match each noun to its plural.
questions.explanation: Tisch adds -e, Buch takes an umlaut and -er, Lampe (feminine in -e) adds -n, the loanword Handy adds -s, and Schlüssel (masculine in -el) adds nothing: only the article die shows it is plural. German rarely adds -s to ordinary nouns, so die Tischs and die Buchs are wrong.

questions.stem: Which nouns are feminine? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: die Zeitung (-ung is always feminine), die Tür and die Brille are feminine. das Fenster is neuter even though it ends in -er, and das Mädchen is neuter because -chen nouns are always neuter.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things in this office corner, with their articles.

image.alt: An office corner with a window, a wall clock, a door, a lamp on a table, a chair and a bag on the floor. Six of the things are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is the window (das Fenster), 2 the clock (die Uhr), 3 the door (die Tür), 4 the lamp (die Lampe), 5 the chair (der Stuhl) and 6 the bag (die Tasche). There is no exercise book (das Heft) or pair of glasses (die Brille) in the picture.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "Those are Anna's books." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: Das sind … is the pattern for several things, and "die Bücher von Anna" (the books of Anna) is a simple way to say Anna's books. The verb sind stands in second place.

questions.stem: This is Lena's family tree. Lena is "ich". Name each numbered person from Lena's point of view.

image.alt: A family tree with first names only. Top row: Klaus and Helga. Middle row: their son Peter and his wife Sabine. Bottom row: their children Jonas, Lena (ich) and Mia. Six people are numbered.

questions.explanation: Klaus and Helga are the parents of Lena's father, so they are her Opa and Oma. Peter and Sabine are her Vater and Mutter. Jonas and Mia are her Bruder and Schwester. From Peter's point of view Lena would be die Tochter, but the question asks from Lena's.

questions.stem: Complete with the possessive article: "Paul und ___ Schwester" (his) and "Anna und ___ Vater" (her).
questions.explanation: The owner chooses the word: Paul is a man, so sein; Anna is a woman, so ihr. The thing owned chooses the ending: Schwester is feminine, so seine; Vater is masculine, so ihr with no ending.

questions.stem: Match each pronoun to its possessive article (the basic form, as before a masculine noun).
questions.explanation: ich → mein, du → dein, wir → unser, ihr → euer, Sie → Ihr (with a capital I). sein belongs to er and es. eure is the form of euer with an ending, before a feminine or plural noun.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Wir haben", "Meine Eltern sind" (Eltern is plural) and "Habt ihr" are right. The er form of haben is hat, not habt, and Mutter is feminine, so euer needs the ending -e (and drops its second e): eure Mutter.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask "Does your sister have a dog?" The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the verb: Hat deine Schwester einen Hund? After haben, masculine ein becomes einen (lesson 9 explains why).

questions.stem: Write the correct form of sprechen: "Du ___ sehr gut Deutsch." "Mein Vater ___ Polnisch."
questions.explanation: sprechen changes its stem vowel from e to i in the du and er/sie/es forms only: du sprichst, er spricht. "Mein Vater" is an er form.

questions.stem: Match each country to the main language spoken there.
questions.explanation: Most language names end in -isch: Spanisch, Polnisch, Türkisch, Französisch. Austria is German-speaking, so the language there is Deutsch; there is no language called Österreichisch.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A job after sein or als needs no article, so the first two are right, and die Schweiz keeps its article: aus der Schweiz. The ich form of sprechen doesn't change its vowel (ich spreche), and die Türkei needs its article too: aus der Türkei.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask "Which languages do you speak?" The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: In a W-question the question phrase (Welche Sprachen) comes first and the verb second: Welche Sprachen sprichst du?

questions.stem: Write the female job titles: der Lehrer → die ___, der Arzt → die ___.
questions.explanation: Female job titles add -in: die Lehrerin. Some words also take an umlaut: der Arzt → die Ärztin.

questions.stem: Name the colour of each numbered square.

image.alt: Eight colour squares in two rows. Top row: red, blue, green, yellow. Bottom row: black, white, grey, brown. Six of them are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 rot (red), 2 blau (blue), 3 grün (green), 4 gelb (yellow), 5 schwarz (black), 6 braun (brown). The two squares without numbers are weiß (white) and grau (grey).

questions.stem: Complete with kein or nicht: "Das ist ___ Hund, das ist eine Katze." "Das Buch ist ___ interessant."
questions.explanation: "ein Hund" becomes "kein Hund": kein negates a noun with ein. An adjective is negated with nicht, placed right before it: nicht interessant.

questions.stem: Match each adjective to its opposite.
questions.explanation: groß/klein (big/small), teuer/billig (expensive/cheap), neu/alt (new/old), richtig/falsch (right/wrong), interessant/langweilig (interesting/boring). The opposite of schnell (fast) is langsam.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Adjectives after sein have no ending (ist rot), kein negates a noun with no article (keine Zeit), and zu means "too". "nicht ein" must be kein (Das ist kein Hund), and German doesn't put nicht before the verb: Ich verstehe nicht.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "That isn't my key." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: A noun with a possessive (mein Schlüssel) is negated with nicht, which goes right before the part it negates: Das ist nicht mein Schlüssel.

questions.stem: Your friend says: "Das ist nicht dein Handy." But it IS your phone. What do you answer? "___, das ist mein Handy!"
questions.explanation: To contradict a negative statement or question, German says doch: Doch, das ist mein Handy! Ja answers a positive question, nein would agree that it isn't your phone, and nicht is not an answer word.

questions.stem: Why is "Mädchen" (girl) a neuter noun?
choices: Because all words for young people are neuter.
Because it is a "little" form in -chen, and those are always neuter.
Because the article das means "that girl".
It isn't neuter: the singular is die Mädchen.
questions.explanation: Nouns made with the "little" ending -chen are always neuter, whatever they mean: das Mädchen, das Brötchen. (der Kuchen, where -chen is not that ending, is masculine.) Not all words for young people are neuter (der Junge, boy, is masculine), and die Mädchen is the plural.

questions.stem: Choose the textbook pronoun: "Das Mädchen heißt Lea. ___ ist zehn Jahre alt."
questions.explanation: The grammar rule says the pronoun follows the noun's gender: das Mädchen → es. In everyday speech many people say sie here, thinking of the girl, but er (masculine) is wrong, and ihr and ihm are not subject pronouns for one person.

questions.stem: Write the female forms: der Koch → die ___, der Kaufmann → die ___.
questions.explanation: Koch adds -in and takes an umlaut: die Köchin. Words in -mann change -mann to -frau: die Kauffrau (never Kaufmännin).

questions.stem: Write the plural: die Ärztin → die ___
questions.explanation: Every -in word adds -nen in the plural, so it has a double n: die Ärztinnen.

questions.stem: Match each masculine job title to its female form.
questions.explanation: Kollege drops its -e before -in; -mann becomes -frau; Arzt takes an umlaut and -in; Polizist simply adds -in. Kaufmännin and Kollegein are not words.

questions.stem: Which of these can name a mixed group of female and male teachers? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The paired form names both groups, die Lehrkräfte is a neutral word for teaching staff, and the gender star is meant to include everyone. die Lehrerinnen means female teachers only.

questions.stem: A job advert says "Verkäufer (m/w/d)". What does (m/w/d) tell you?
choices: The job is only for men, because it says Verkäufer.
The job is on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday.
The job is open to everyone: männlich, weiblich, divers.
questions.explanation: (m/w/d) stands for männlich, weiblich, divers: male, female, diverse. German law says job adverts must not shut anyone out because of their gender, so the letters show the job is open to all.

questions.stem: What did the Council for German Orthography (Rat für deutsche Rechtschreibung) decide in 2023 about signs like the gender star?
choices: It made them compulsory in official texts.
It did not make them part of official spelling.
It banned them in all German-speaking countries.
It replaced the paired form with them.
questions.explanation: In 2023 the Council decided not to add the star, colon and similar signs to official spelling. It didn't ban them: many universities, cities and companies still use them, while in 2024 Bavaria and Hesse told their schools (and, in Bavaria, state offices) not to.

questions.stem: You write a formal letter to a company and don't know who will read it. Which greeting is accepted everywhere?
questions.explanation: Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren ("Dear Sir or Madam") is a paired form and the standard opening of a formal letter. Liebe Leute and Hallo are informal, and Sehr geehrte Damen addresses women only.

questions.stem: Read the advert. Which statement is true?

image.alt: A job advert on a notice board: Bäckerei Sonnenschein, Leipzig. Wir suchen: Verkäuferin / Verkäufer (m/w/d), Bäckerin / Bäcker (m/w/d). Unser Team: 12 Kolleginnen und Kollegen. Fragen? Bitte im Laden bei Frau Nowak.

choices: The bakery is looking for shop staff and bakers of any gender.
The bakery is looking for 12 new colleagues.
Frau Nowak is looking for a job.
questions.explanation: "Wir suchen" means "we are looking for", and both jobs are given in the paired form with (m/w/d). The 12 Kolleginnen und Kollegen are the team the bakery already has, and Frau Nowak is the person to ask.

questions.stem: Read: "Frau Demir ist Lehrerin für Englisch. Herr Wolf ist Lehrer für Mathe. Er spricht auch Polnisch. Frau Kim ist unsere neue Schulärztin." Who speaks Polish?
questions.explanation: "Er spricht auch Polnisch" follows the sentence about Herr Wolf, and er (he) can only mean him. Frau Demir teaches English, and Frau Kim is the school doctor.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask "Is the girl from Poland?" The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the verb: Ist das Mädchen aus Polen? Mädchen takes das because it is neuter.

questions.stem: Complete the paired form at the start of a school letter: "Liebe Schülerinnen und ___!"
questions.explanation: The paired form names the female and the male group: Schülerinnen und Schüler. The masculine plural of der Schüler has no ending.

questions.stem: Which sentence contains a mistake?
questions.explanation: Mädchen is neuter: Das Mädchen ist neu. "Die Mädchen" is the plural and would need sind. The other sentences are right: no article before a job, and -innen with double n.

questions.stem: This is Ben's family. Ben is "ich", and Lisa is his twin. Name each numbered person from Ben's point of view.

image.alt: A family tree with first names only. Top row: Anja is married to Markus; Markus and Julia are divorced; Julia is married to Tom. Markus and Julia's children are Ben (ich) and Lisa. Julia and Tom's child is Emma. Six people are numbered.

questions.explanation: Markus and Julia are Ben's parents. Anja is his father's new wife (Stiefmutter), and Tom is his mother's new husband (Stiefvater). Lisa has the same parents and is his twin (Zwillingsschwester). Emma shares only one parent, Julia, so she is his Halbschwester.

questions.stem: Write "Anna's brother" in German: ___ Bruder
questions.explanation: After a name German adds -s with no apostrophe and no article: Annas Bruder. In speech you can also say der Bruder von Anna.

questions.stem: Write "Max's sister" in German: ___ Schwester
questions.explanation: Max ends in x, an s sound, so it takes only an apostrophe: Max' Schwester. In speech: die Schwester von Max.

questions.stem: Which are correct ways to say "Jonas's dog"? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A name ending in s takes only an apostrophe, and von + name is common in speech. You never add a second s (Jonass, Jonas's), and the noun after the name takes no article.

questions.stem: Match each word to its meaning.
choices: a sister who shares one parent with you
a child with no brothers or sisters
one of two children born together
a short or friendly name like Kathi
questions.explanation: Stief- is for a parent's new partner, Halb- for a sibling who shares one parent. Einzelkind is an only child, Zwilling a twin, Spitzname a nickname. Your mother's sister is your aunt, die Tante.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "My parents are separated." The capitalised word comes first.
questions.explanation: Eltern is plural, so the possessive is meine and the verb sind. Like any adjective after sein, getrennt has no ending.

questions.stem: Which is the everyday word for "last name"?
questions.explanation: der Nachname is the everyday word; der Familienname means the same and is used on forms. der Vorname is the first name, der Spitzname a nickname and die Unterschrift a signature.

questions.stem: Many German surnames are old job titles. What did "Schneider" originally mean?
questions.explanation: Schneider means tailor (schneiden = to cut). Müller is a miller, Schmidt a smith and Becker a baker.

questions.stem: Lisa is a girl and a twin. Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: der Zwilling is masculine for girls too, so "a twin" is ein Zwilling. Lisa is also meine Zwillingsschwester, a compound whose last part decides the gender.

questions.stem: Why is it "die Zwillingsschwester"?
choices: Because the linking s makes a word feminine.
Because the first part, der Zwilling, decides the gender.
Because all words for family members are feminine.
Because the last part, die Schwester, decides the gender.
questions.explanation: In a compound noun the last part decides the gender: die Schwester → die Zwillingsschwester. The linking s only joins the parts; it carries no meaning or gender.

questions.stem: Read: "Meine Eltern sind geschieden. Wir wohnen bei Mama und Tom. Tom ist mein Stiefvater. Papa ist wieder verheiratet." Who is Tom?
questions.explanation: Tom is the Stiefvater: the mother's new husband. The father is Papa, who has a new wife, and the text says nothing about a half-brother or an uncle.

questions.stem: Which sentence is written correctly?
questions.explanation: Name + s comes first, with no apostrophe and no article: Lenas Familie. The English-style apostrophe is a common mistake, and the noun after the name never takes der, die or das.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT allowed for a married couple's surnames in Germany?
choices: a three-part name such as Müller-Schmidt-Weber
both use a double name such as Müller-Schmidt (since 2025)
questions.explanation: A couple can share one surname, keep their own, or, since the 2025 reform, both use a double name. Names with more than two parts are still not allowed.

questions.stem: Ben talks about his father: "Papa ist wieder verheiratet. ___ Frau heißt Anja."
questions.explanation: The owner is Papa, a man, so the word is sein. Frau is feminine, so it takes -e: Seine Frau. Ihre would mean "her" or "their".

questions.stem: Name the numbered things on this breakfast table.

image.alt: A breakfast table with six things on it, numbered from left to right: a jug of milk, a cup of coffee, a bread roll on a plate, a boiled egg in an egg cup, a wedge of cheese and an apple.

questions.explanation: 1 is a jug of milk (die Milch), 2 a cup of coffee (der Kaffee), 3 a bread roll (das Brötchen), 4 a boiled egg (das Ei), 5 cheese (der Käse) and 6 an apple (der Apfel). There is no sausage (die Wurst) or juice (der Saft) on the table.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of essen and the right article: "Mein Bruder ___ ___ Apfel." (My brother is eating an apple. der Apfel)
questions.explanation: essen changes e to i in the er/sie/es form: er isst. Apfel is masculine and the direct object, so "an apple" becomes einen Apfel. "esst" is the ihr form, and "ein Apfel" is the nominative. (For "the apple" you would say den Apfel.)

questions.stem: Complete "Ich möchte ___ …" for each food. Match each noun to the article it needs.
questions.explanation: After möchte the food is the direct object, so it is in the accusative. Only the masculine changes: der Tee → einen Tee. Feminine stays eine Cola, neuter stays ein Ei, and ein has no plural, so you say just Ich möchte Nudeln. einem and einer are dative forms you'll meet later.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Ich nehme einen Kaffee" is right: Kaffee is masculine and the object. "Er isst ein Brötchen" is right: Brötchen is neuter, so ein doesn't change. "Das ist einen Apfel" is wrong because sein never takes the accusative (Das ist ein Apfel). "einen Wasser" is wrong because Wasser is neuter: ein Wasser.

questions.stem: Put this café conversation in order.
choices: Kellner: Guten Tag! Was möchten Sie?
Gast: Ich nehme einen Tee, bitte.
Kellner: Mit Milch oder ohne Milch?
Gast: Ohne Milch, bitte. Haben Sie auch Apfelkuchen?
Kellner: Ja, natürlich. Ein Stück Apfelkuchen?
questions.explanation: The waiter opens with the question, the guest orders a tea, the waiter asks about milk, the guest answers and asks about cake, the waiter offers a piece, and the guest accepts. Each line answers the one before it.

questions.stem: Write the number 347 in German as one word.
questions.explanation: Hundreds first, then the last two digits as you learned them, units before tens: dreihundert + siebenundvierzig = dreihundertsiebenundvierzig. Big numbers are written as one word.

questions.stem: Match each written number or price to how it is said.
questions.explanation: In German a point separates thousands and a comma separates euros from cents. So 1.500 is one thousand five hundred (tausendfünfhundert), 1,50 € is ein Euro fünfzig, 15,00 € is fünfzehn Euro and 0,15 € is fünfzehn Cent. Prices are never read with "Komma".

questions.stem: Which are correct ways to ask for an amount? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: German puts the amount straight before the food with no word for "of", so "ein Kilo von Äpfeln" is wrong. Kilo and Stück stay singular after a number (zwei Kilo, drei Stück), so "zwei Kilos" is wrong, while the feminine Flasche takes its plural: zwei Flaschen Wasser.

questions.stem: Put this conversation at a market stall in order.
choices: Verkäufer: Guten Tag! Was brauchen Sie?
Kundin: Dann nehme ich zwei Kilo, bitte. Das ist alles.
questions.explanation: Greeting, asking the price, the answer, choosing the amount and finishing, the total (2 × 2,50 € = 5 €), then paying. This is the same sequence as the shopping chart in the lesson.

questions.stem: This price tag says 1.299,95 €. What does each numbered part show?

image.alt: A price tag headed ANGEBOT for a blue bicycle with the price 1.299,95 €. Four lines point to the point, the comma, the 95 and the euro sign, numbered 1 to 4.

questions.explanation: German swaps the English marks: the point (1) separates thousands and the comma (2) separates euros from cents. 95 (3) are the cents, and the euro sign (4) comes after the number. The price is said tausendzweihundertneunundneunzig Euro fünfundneunzig.

questions.stem: It is between three and four o'clock. When the minute hand points to each numbered spot, how do you say the time in everyday German?

image.alt: A clock face with no hands. Five spots on the rim are numbered: 1 at the 3, 2 at the 4, 3 at the 6, 4 at the 8 and 5 at the 9.

questions.explanation: The minute hand at the 3 means 3:15 (Viertel nach drei), at the 4 means 3:20 (zwanzig nach drei), at the 6 means 3:30 (halb vier: halfway to four), at the 8 means 3:40 (zwanzig vor vier) and at the 9 means 3:45 (Viertel vor vier). "halb drei" would be 2:30.

questions.stem: It is 7:30. Say it the everyday way: "Es ist ___ ___."
questions.explanation: halb points to the next hour: 7:30 is "half (of the way) to eight", halb acht. "halb sieben" would be 6:30.

questions.stem: Which little word goes before each time? Match them.
questions.explanation: Clock times take um (um acht Uhr). Days and parts of the day take am (am Montag, am Abend). The night is the exception: in der Nacht.

questions.stem: It is 15:45. Which are correct ways to say the time? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The official time is fünfzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig, and in everyday speech 3:45 is Viertel vor vier, a quarter to four. Viertel nach drei is 3:15, and halb vier is 3:30.

questions.stem: Put these parts of the day in order, from earliest to latest.
questions.explanation: der Morgen (early morning), der Vormittag (before midday), der Mittag (midday), der Nachmittag (after midday), der Abend (evening). vor = before and nach = after, so Vormittag comes before Mittag and Nachmittag after it.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to say "At seven I get up." Start with the time phrase.
questions.explanation: The time phrase fills position 1, so the verb part comes next (stehe), then the subject (ich), and the prefix auf goes to the very end: Um sieben stehe ich auf.

questions.stem: Complete with anrufen: "Ich ___ heute meine Mutter ___."
questions.explanation: anrufen is separable. The conjugated part rufe goes in position 2 and the prefix an goes to the very end: Ich rufe heute meine Mutter an.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs are separable? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: aufstehen, einkaufen and fernsehen have separable prefixes (auf, ein, fern): Ich stehe auf, ich kaufe ein, ich sehe fern. frühstücken and duschen never split: Ich frühstücke, ich dusche.

questions.stem: Match each separable verb to its meaning.
questions.explanation: aufräumen = to tidy up, abholen = to pick up, mitkommen = to come along, ankommen = to arrive. "to get up" is aufstehen and "to phone" is anrufen.

questions.stem: This sentence means "Tomorrow morning I'm phoning my mother." What job does each numbered box do?

image.alt: Five boxes in a row, numbered 1 to 5: Morgen früh, rufe, ich, meine Mutter, an.

questions.explanation: Morgen früh fills position 1, the conjugated verb part rufe is in position 2, the subject ich follows the verb (inversion), meine Mutter is the object, and an, the prefix of anrufen, goes to the very end.

questions.stem: Which is the most polite correct way to order a pretzel (die Brezel)?
questions.explanation: Ich hätte gern + accusative is the politest order, and Brezel is feminine, so eine stays eine. "Ich will" sounds blunt, "Ich habe gern eine Brezel" means "I like having a pretzel", and "einen Brezel" uses the masculine form for a feminine noun.

questions.stem: Complete the order: "Ich hätte gern ___ Kaffee, bitte." (der Kaffee)
questions.explanation: What you'd like is the object of hätte, so it is accusative, and masculine ein becomes einen: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.

questions.stem: You want another coffee. Complete: "Noch ___ Kaffee, bitte!"
questions.explanation: noch ein means "another one", and the article still follows the accusative rule: der Kaffee → noch einen Kaffee. "ein" forgets the masculine -en.

questions.stem: Your host asks: "Möchtest du noch ein Stück Kuchen?" You have had enough. What do you say?
questions.explanation: Ich bin satt means "I'm full". "Ich bin voll" is a word-for-word translation and can sound like "I'm drunk" in casual speech. Guten Appetit is said before a meal.

questions.stem: Match each regional or Austrian word to the standard German word.
questions.explanation: Semmel is the Bavarian and Austrian bread roll (Brötchen), Erdapfel the Austrian potato (Kartoffel), Topfen the Austrian and Bavarian quark, and Paradeiser the Austrian tomato. Cream (Sahne) is Schlagobers in Austria.

questions.stem: This timeline shows a traditional German day of meals (simplified). Name each numbered meal.

image.alt: A timeline from 6 to 21 Uhr with four meals numbered 1 to 4: at about 7 Uhr coffee and a roll, at about 12:30 a steaming plate of food, at about 15:30 a slice of cake and a cup of coffee, and at about 18:30 slices of bread and cheese on a board.

questions.explanation: Breakfast (das Frühstück) in the morning, the warm lunch (das Mittagessen) at midday, coffee and cake (Kaffee und Kuchen) in the afternoon, and the cold bread supper (das Abendbrot) in the evening. Feierabend is the end of the working day, not a meal.

questions.stem: At 12:30 a colleague passes you in the corridor and says "Mahlzeit!". What does it mean here?
choices: A lunchtime greeting, like "hello, enjoy your lunch"
A complaint that lunch is late
A request to go back to work
questions.explanation: Mahlzeit literally means "mealtime". Between colleagues around midday it works as a greeting and a wish to enjoy lunch; you simply answer "Mahlzeit!" too.

questions.stem: Your bill is 4,60 €. You want to tip about 10 percent, and you hand over a 10-euro note. What do you say?
questions.explanation: 10 percent of 4,60 € is 0,46 €, so about 5 €. You tell the server the total: Fünf Euro, bitte, and get 5 € back. "Stimmt so" with a 10-euro note would leave a 5,40 € tip, "Vier Euro sechzig" leaves no tip, and "Zehn Euro" means you want no change.

questions.stem: Which are true about tipping in a German café? Select all that apply.
choices: You usually tell the server the total you want to pay.
The tip is always added to the bill for you.
You usually leave the tip on the table when you go.
questions.explanation: The tip isn't on the bill. People round up or add about 5 to 10 percent by telling the server the total, or by handing over money and saying "Stimmt so" (keep the change). Leaving coins on the table is not the usual way.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich esse zwei ___ Brot." (die Scheibe, slice)
questions.explanation: Amounts go straight before the food with no "of", and a feminine measure word like Scheibe takes its plural after a number: zwei Scheiben Brot.

questions.stem: In the reading "Sonntag bei Oma", why does the narrator say "Nein danke, Oma"?
choices: The narrator doesn't like apple cake.
The narrator has to go home.
questions.explanation: Oma offers another piece of cake, and the narrator answers "Nein danke, Oma, ich bin satt!": the narrator is full. It is Jonas who doesn't drink coffee, and they go home only at nine.

questions.stem: In the reading, what do they eat at seven o'clock?
choices: A cold meal: bread, butter, cheese, sausage and a little salad
A warm meal with potatoes and meat
Apple cake and a gateau with cream
Rolls and pretzels from the supermarket
questions.explanation: At seven there's Abendbrot: "Brot, Butter, Käse, Wurst und ein bisschen Salat", and the text says they don't eat a warm meal in the evening. The cakes are at three, and Oma never buys bread at the supermarket.

questions.stem: Put these lines in order: paying for your coffee in a café.
questions.explanation: You ask to pay, the server asks whether you're paying together or separately, you answer, the server tells you your total, and you say the amount you want to pay including the tip (here 0,60 €).

questions.stem: Why do both "Ich möchte …" and "Ich hätte gern …" sound polite?
choices: They are both in the perfect tense.
questions.explanation: hätte is the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II) of haben, and möchte is the subjunctive of mögen. The "would" form softens the request, like English "I would like".

questions.stem: Which are regional words for a plain bread roll (das Brötchen)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Semmel (Bavaria, Austria, parts of eastern Germany), Schrippe (Berlin) and Weck (the southwest) all name the plain roll. A Brezel is a pretzel and a Torte is a layered cream cake.

questions.stem: Look at the signs. Can you buy rolls at Bäckerei Krume on Sunday at 10:30?

image.alt: Two door signs. Bäckerei Krume, Öffnungszeiten: Mo–Fr 6:30–18:00, Sa 7:00–13:00, So 8:00–11:00, feiertags geschlossen. Café am Markt, Öffnungszeiten: Di–Fr 8–18 Uhr, Sa–So 9–18 Uhr, Montag Ruhetag.

choices: No, bakeries are always closed on Sundays.
Yes, it is open on Sunday from 8:00 to 11:00.
No, it opens at 11:00 on Sunday.
Yes, but only if it is a public holiday.
questions.explanation: The bakery's sign says So 8:00–11:00, and 10:30 falls inside that time. Many German bakeries open for a few hours on Sunday mornings. On public holidays (feiertags) this bakery is closed.

questions.stem: Look at the signs. You want a coffee at Café am Markt on Monday at 10:00. What happens?

image.alt: Two door signs. Bäckerei Krume, Öffnungszeiten: Mo–Fr 6:30–18:00, Sa 7:00–13:00, So 8:00–11:00, feiertags geschlossen. Café am Markt, Öffnungszeiten: Di–Fr 8–18 Uhr, Sa–So 9–18 Uhr, Montag Ruhetag.

choices: It is open: it opens at 8:00.
It is open: it opens at 9:00.
It is closed: Monday is its closing day.
questions.explanation: "Montag Ruhetag" means the café closes every Monday. Its hours start on Tuesday (Di–Fr 8–18 Uhr).

questions.stem: Bäckerei Krume is open Sa 7:00–13:00. How many hours is it open on Saturday? Give only the number.
questions.explanation: From 7:00 to 13:00 is 13 − 7 = 6 hours: sechs Stunden.

questions.stem: How do you say "I work on Mondays (every Monday)"?
questions.explanation: montags is an adverb meaning "every Monday" and is written with a small letter, without am. A capital M is only right at the start of a sentence (Montags arbeite ich).

questions.stem: Complete: "___ Montag habe ich frei." (Next Monday I have the day off.)
questions.explanation: With nächster the time phrase is in the accusative with no preposition. Montag is masculine, so it takes -en: nächsten Montag. "nächste Montag" forgets the masculine ending.

questions.stem: Match each English time phrase to its German form.
questions.explanation: These are accusatives of time with no preposition. Tag is masculine (jeden, den ganzen), Woche feminine (nächste) and Wochenende neuter (dieses). "jede Tag" has the wrong ending, and "am nächste Woche" adds a preposition that isn't needed.

questions.stem: Complete: "Der Termin dauert ___ Stunde."
questions.explanation: After dauern, the length of time is in the accusative alone. Stunde is feminine, so eine doesn't change. "einen" is the masculine form, and dauern takes no preposition.

questions.stem: How do you say "I'll come at around seven"?
questions.explanation: gegen replaces um: gegen sieben (or gegen sieben Uhr). Uhr never takes a plural in times.

questions.stem: Put these frequency words in order, from most often to least often.
questions.explanation: immer (always), meistens (mostly, usually), oft (often), manchmal (sometimes), selten (rarely), nie (never).

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: With two time phrases, the general one comes first: morgen um acht, not um acht morgen. Morgen (the morning) is masculine, so it's jeden Morgen, not jede Morgen. Nächste Woche is a correct accusative of time with a feminine noun.

questions.stem: In the reading "Unsere Woche", how often does Ela have football?
questions.explanation: "Ela hat dienstags und donnerstags Fußball": on Tuesdays and Thursdays, twice a week. Can plays guitar on Mondays.

questions.stem: In the reading, who gets up at four every day?
questions.explanation: "Papa arbeitet morgens in der Bäckerei, er steht jeden Tag um vier auf." Mama works in the afternoons at an office.

questions.stem: Complete with the right form of dauern: "Wie lange ___ der Kurs? – Zwei Stunden."
questions.explanation: der Kurs is er, so the regular ending -t: der Kurs dauert. Wie lange dauert …? asks how long something takes.

questions.stem: Which sentence means "The café is closed on Mondays"?
choices: Am Montags ist das Café zu spät.
questions.explanation: geschlossen means closed, and montags means every Monday. geöffnet and offen both mean open.

questions.stem: Someone asks: "Wie oft gehst du schwimmen?" Which answer fits?
questions.explanation: Wie oft? asks how often, so the answer is a frequency: zweimal pro Woche, twice a week. "Zwei Stunden" answers Wie lange?, and "Um zwei" or "Gegen zwei" answer Wann?

questions.stem: Type the right form of "fahren": "Am Wochenende ___ meine Schwester Fahrrad."
questions.explanation: Fahren changes a to ä in the du and er/sie/es forms. Meine Schwester is sie (she), so: sie fährt. "Fahrt" without the umlaut is the ihr form.

questions.stem: Type the du form of "treffen": "Wann ___ du deine Freunde?"
questions.explanation: Treffen changes e to i in the du and er/sie/es forms and keeps its double f: du triffst, er trifft.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Most of all, my brother likes playing football." Start with "Am liebsten".
questions.explanation: When am liebsten comes first, the verb stays in position 2 and the subject moves behind it: Am liebsten spielt mein Bruder Fußball. (Not "Am liebsten mein Bruder spielt".)

questions.stem: Match each infinitive to its er/sie/es form.
questions.explanation: a → ä: fährt; e → ie: liest, sieht; e → i: hilft, gibt. "Lest" and "gebt" are ihr forms, which never change their vowel.

questions.stem: Which of these verbs change their stem vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Schlafen (du schläfst), geben (du gibst) and sehen (du siehst) are stem-changing verbs. Wandern (du wanderst) and spielen (du spielst) are regular, even though they contain a and e.

questions.stem: Which hobby does each numbered picture show?

image.alt: Six numbered picture tiles: an open book, a bicycle, a guitar, a football, a camera, and mountains with a dotted path and a signpost.

questions.explanation: The book is lesen (to read), the bicycle Fahrrad fahren, the guitar Gitarre spielen, the ball Fußball spielen, the camera fotografieren and the mountain path wandern (to hike). Nothing shows swimming or dancing.

questions.stem: Type the right form of "können": "Mein Bruder ___ sehr gut kochen."
questions.explanation: With modal verbs the ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending: ich kann, er kann. Not "kannt".

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "I would like to go to the cinema this evening." Start with "Ich".
questions.explanation: The modal möchte is in position 2 and the infinitive gehen closes the bracket at the end. Inside the bracket the time (heute Abend) comes before the place you go to (ins Kino), which stands right before the infinitive.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Können = ability or possibility, wollen = a firm wish, möchten = a polite wish, mögen = liking a thing or person (Ich mag Jazz). "Must" is müssen, from lesson 15.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Er kann has no ending (not "kannt"), and modal verbs never take zu: Ich will reisen. Willst du mitkommen? is right: the separable verb comes back together at the end. Sie möchte einen Tee is right: möchte can take a noun.

questions.stem: The sentence "Ich kann am Samstag gut kochen." is split into four boxes. Name the part of the sentence each numbered box is.

image.alt: Two sentences in boxes with a red bracket joining the second and fourth box. Top row, numbered 1 to 4: Ich, kann, am Samstag gut, kochen. Bottom row: Wann, willst, du, mitkommen?

questions.explanation: Ich fills position 1, the modal verb kann is in position 2 and opens the bracket, am Samstag gut is the middle, and the infinitive kochen closes the bracket at the end. The bottom row works the same way with the question word Wann in position 1.

questions.stem: Type the right form of "dürfen": "Hier ___ man nicht rauchen."
questions.explanation: Man takes the er/sie/es form, and dürfen has no umlaut and no ending there: man darf.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Nicht müssen = not necessary; nicht dürfen = forbidden; sollen passes on what another person wants; können = able or possible. "You want to come" would be Du willst kommen.

questions.stem: Which say that something is forbidden? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Nicht dürfen and verboten mean forbidden. Man muss hier nicht warten only says waiting is not necessary, and erlaubt means allowed.

questions.stem: What does each numbered sign mean?

image.alt: Four numbered signs: a cigarette in a red ring with a red bar across it, a white P on a blue square, a mobile phone in a red ring with a red bar across it, and a face with a finger on its lips.

questions.explanation: A red ring with a bar means forbidden: no smoking (1) and no phone calls (3). The blue P sign allows parking (2). The finger on the lips asks for quiet (4). "Hier muss man nicht parken" (you don't have to park here) is not what a sign says.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask politely: "May I open the window?"
questions.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the modal verb (Darf), then the subject (ich), the middle (das Fenster) and the infinitive at the end (öffnen).

questions.stem: "Heute ist der 3. Oktober" is read "Heute ist der ___ Oktober." Type the ordinal as a word.
questions.explanation: Third is irregular: dritte (not "dreite"). After der the ordinal ends in -e: der dritte Oktober.

questions.stem: "Ich habe am 1. Mai Geburtstag" is read "Ich habe am ___ Mai Geburtstag." Type the ordinal as a word.
questions.explanation: First is erste, and after am the ordinal ends in -en: am ersten Mai.

questions.stem: Put these dates in order, from earliest to latest in the year.
questions.explanation: März (3rd month), Mai (5th), Juli (7th), Oktober (10th), Dezember (12th). The day numbers are dritten (3rd), ersten (1st), siebten (7th), achten (8th) and zwölften (12th).

questions.stem: Describe the weather in each numbered picture.

image.alt: Four numbered weather pictures: a bright sun, a cloud with rain, a cloud with snowflakes, and gusts of wind bending a small tree.

questions.explanation: Sun: Die Sonne scheint. Rain: Es regnet (regnen). Snow: Es schneit (schneien). Wind: Es ist windig. The weather verbs need the placeholder es.

questions.stem: Which phrases are correct? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Für, ohne and durch always take the accusative, and only the masculine changes: für meinen Bruder, durch den Park, ohne den Schirm, für den Vater. Feminine stays the same: für die Party.

questions.stem: Match each written date to the way it is read.
questions.explanation: German dates are written day first, then month: 3.10. is the 3rd of October and 10.3. is the 10th of March. Seventh is siebte and first is erste.

questions.stem: What do the letters "e. V." after a club's name mean?
questions.explanation: E. V. is short for eingetragener Verein, a club entered in the official register, such as TC Rotbuche e. V.

questions.stem: A club notice says: "Du musst nicht Mitglied sein." What does it mean?
choices: You don't have to be a member.
questions.explanation: Nicht müssen means "not necessary": you can try the training without joining. "You mustn't" would be nicht dürfen.

questions.stem: The notice says: "In der Halle darf man nur mit Hallenschuhen spielen." Which statement is true?
choices: You may play in any shoes you like.
You mustn't play in outdoor shoes in the hall.
You have to buy shoes from the club.
questions.explanation: Nur means "only": indoor shoes are the only shoes allowed, so outdoor shoes (Straßenschuhe) are not. The notice says nothing about children or buying shoes.

questions.stem: Type the German word for "favourite colour": "Meine ___ ist Blau."
questions.explanation: Lieblings- + Farbe, written as one word: die Lieblingsfarbe. It is feminine like die Farbe, so meine.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "Lieblingsbuch"?
questions.explanation: A compound noun takes its gender from the last noun: das Buch, so das Lieblingsbuch. Liebling (der) doesn't decide.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich trinke lieber Tee als Kaffee.
Ich trinke mehr gern Tee als Kaffee.
questions.explanation: The comparative of gern is lieber, never "mehr gern", and the comparison word is als. Lieblings- words are written as one word: Lieblingsfilm, not "Lieblings Film".

questions.stem: Put the parts in order: "My brother prefers chess to football."
questions.explanation: The verb spielt is in position 2, lieber and the preferred thing follow it, and the als part goes at the end: Mein Bruder spielt lieber Schach als Fußball.

questions.stem: Match each word to what it means in Germany.
choices: Quiet time usually from 22 to 6 Uhr
Quiet time often from 13 to 15 Uhr in house rules
The rules of a block of flats
The training plan of a club
questions.explanation: Night quiet is the firm rule (usually 22 to 6). Midday quiet is common but depends on the town and the house rules. Sundays are days of rest all day. The Hausordnung is a building's house rules.

questions.stem: Which statement about shopping on a Sunday in Germany is true?
choices: All shops are closed, even at stations and airports.
Most shops are closed, but bakeries may open for a few hours and shops at big stations stay open.
Shops open only in the afternoon.
questions.explanation: Sundays are protected days of rest, so most shops are closed. Bakeries may open for a few hours, and shops at large stations, airports and petrol stations stay open; details depend on the state.

questions.stem: House rules: "Fahrräder ___ man nicht im Treppenhaus parken." Type the right form of "dürfen".
questions.explanation: The subject is man (Fahrräder is the object, put first for emphasis), so the verb takes the er form: darf.

questions.stem: Your neighbour asks: "Kann ich um 23 Uhr Klavier spielen?" The house rules say "Von 22 bis 6 Uhr ist Nachtruhe." What do you answer?
choices: Nein, da muss man nicht Klavier spielen.
Ja, da soll man Klavier spielen.
Nein, da darf man nicht Klavier spielen.
questions.explanation: 23 Uhr is during the night quiet time, so playing is forbidden: nicht dürfen. "Muss man nicht" would only mean it isn't necessary.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Mittagsruhe (midday quiet) is correct?
choices: It is a national law from 12 to 14 Uhr everywhere.
It depends on the town and the house rules; 13 to 15 Uhr is common.
It means shops close for lunch.
questions.explanation: Unlike the night quiet and the Sunday rest, the Mittagsruhe is not a general law. Many house rules set it, often from 13 to 15 Uhr.

questions.stem: Jana writes: "Am liebsten singe ich, aber Tennis macht auch Spaß." What does Jana like doing most?
questions.explanation: Am liebsten = most of all, so singing is her top choice. Tennis is also fun (macht auch Spaß), but it comes second.

questions.stem: "I prefer tea to coffee": "Ich trinke lieber Tee ___ Kaffee." Type the missing word.
questions.explanation: After lieber, "than" is als: lieber Tee als Kaffee.

questions.stem: Which public holiday is the only one fixed by national law in Germany?
questions.explanation: The Day of German Unity was set by the Unification Treaty of 1990. All the other public holidays, even those that apply everywhere, are set by the 16 states.

questions.stem: Which of these are public holidays in every German state? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Labour Day, the Day of German Unity and Easter Monday are among the nine nationwide holidays. Christmas Eve and New Year's Eve are not public holidays; shops just close early.

questions.stem: Which day of the German year is each numbered calendar page?

image.alt: Six numbered calendar pages: 1. Mai with a flower, 3. Oktober with the German flag, 11. November with a paper lantern, 6. Dezember with a boot full of sweets, 24. Dezember with a Christmas tree, and 31. Dezember with fireworks.

questions.explanation: 1 May is Labour Day, 3 October the Day of German Unity, 11 November St Martin's Day (lanterns), 6 December St Nicholas' Day (sweets in a boot), 24 December Christmas Eve and 31 December New Year's Eve. Easter Monday has no fixed date.

questions.stem: When do most families in Germany open their Christmas presents?
questions.explanation: The Bescherung is usually on the evening of Heiligabend, 24 December. On 6 December children get small sweets from the Nikolaus.

questions.stem: "vom 24. bis zum 26. Dezember" is read "vom vierundzwanzigsten bis zum ___ Dezember." Type the ordinal as a word.
questions.explanation: 26 is above 19, so add -ste: sechsundzwanzigste. After zum the ending is -en: bis zum sechsundzwanzigsten.

questions.stem: A letter begins "Berlin, den 3. Oktober". It is read "Berlin, den ___ Oktober." Type the ordinal as a word.
questions.explanation: After den (accusative) the ordinal takes -en: den dritten Oktober. Only der gives -e.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Die Ferien dauern vom erste bis zum vierzehnte August.
Die Ferien dauern von der erste bis der vierzehnte August.
Die Ferien dauern vom ersten bis zur vierzehnten August.
Die Ferien dauern vom ersten bis zum vierzehnten August.
questions.explanation: A date range is vom … bis zum …, and both ordinals end in -en: vom ersten bis zum vierzehnten. "Zur" is for feminine nouns; months are masculine.

questions.stem: Match each greeting to when you say it.
questions.explanation: Guten Rutsch (a good "slide" into the new year) is said before midnight on 31 December; Frohes neues Jahr from New Year's Day on. There is no fixed greeting for 3 October.

questions.stem: Starting in November, put these days in the order they come.
questions.explanation: Sankt Martin is 11 November, Nikolaustag 6 December, Heiligabend 24 December, Silvester 31 December and Neujahr 1 January.

questions.stem: Ostern 2027 ist am 28. März. Wann ist Ostermontag?
questions.explanation: Easter Monday is the day after Easter Sunday: 29 March, am neunundzwanzigsten März (29 is above 19, so -ste, plus -n after am).

questions.stem: Your German colleague's birthday is tomorrow. What do many Germans avoid doing today?
questions.explanation: Many people think it brings bad luck to congratulate someone before the birthday. It is a superstition, but waiting for the day itself is the safe choice.

questions.stem: Which statement about Karneval and Fasching is true?
choices: Fasching is a public holiday in every state.
Karneval is celebrated only in Austria.
Fasching is the usual word in Bavaria and Austria; Karneval in the Rhineland.
questions.explanation: They are names for the same season (Mainz and the south-west also say Fastnacht). Its high point is in February or early March, with parades on Rosenmontag, which is not a public holiday.

questions.stem: A sign says "Weihnachtsmarkt: 27.11. bis 23.12." How do you read it?
choices: vom siebenundzwanzigsten November bis zum dreiundzwanzigsten Dezember
vom siebenundzwanzigsten Dezember bis zum dreiundzwanzigsten November
vom siebenundzwanzigste November bis zum dreiundzwanzigste Dezember
von siebenundzwanzig November bis dreiundzwanzig Dezember
questions.explanation: Day first, then month: 27.11. is 27 November. A range is vom … bis zum …, with -en on both ordinals. The third choice forgets the -n; the last uses plain numbers instead of ordinals.

questions.stem: Complete: "Heute ist der ___ Mai." (1.)
questions.explanation: After der the ordinal ends in -e: der erste Mai. -en comes after am, vom, zum and den.

questions.stem: You tell a friend to read the text. Write the du imperative of "lesen": "___ bitte den Text!" (Give only the verb.)
questions.explanation: Start from the du form: du liest. Drop du, and because the stem ends in s, drop only the -t: lies. The e to ie change stays. "Les" and "Lese" are common mistakes; the standard du imperative is Lies!

questions.stem: Put the words in order to make a polite instruction: "Turn left at the traffic lights!"
questions.explanation: In the Sie imperative the verb comes first and Sie second: Biegen Sie … Abbiegen is separable, so the prefix ab goes to the very end: Biegen Sie an der Ampel links ab!

questions.stem: Match each verb to its du imperative.
questions.explanation: Start from the du form and drop du and -st: du nimmst → Nimm! (e to i stays), du fährst → Fahr! (a to ä verbs lose the umlaut), du wartest → Warte! (the e before -st stays), du liest → Lies! Sein is irregular: Sei! Nehm! ignores the stem change, and Fähr! keeps an umlaut that the imperative drops.

questions.stem: Which are correct imperatives? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Nimm den Bus! (du), Gehen Sie geradeaus! (Sie) and Seid bitte leise! (ihr, from sein) are all correct. Fähr langsam! is wrong because a to ä verbs drop the umlaut: Fahr langsam! Abbiegen Sie links! is wrong because the separable prefix goes to the end: Biegen Sie links ab!

questions.stem: Name the numbered places in this town centre.

image.alt: A small town centre with a main street crossing a side street and a river with a bridge on the right. There is a church with a tower, a building with an envelope sign, a park with trees, a round H sign on the pavement, traffic lights, a building with a euro sign, a building with a large A and the bridge. Six places are numbered.

questions.explanation: The building with a tower and a cross is die Kirche (church); the envelope marks die Post (post office); the round H sign is die Haltestelle (bus or tram stop); the euro sign marks die Bank; the big A is the sign of a German die Apotheke (pharmacy); and the road over the river is die Brücke (bridge). There is no hospital or museum in the picture.

questions.stem: Write the missing article: "Wir fahren mit ___ Straßenbahn zum Zoo."
questions.explanation: Mit always takes the dative, and Straßenbahn is feminine (die Straßenbahn). The feminine dative article is der: mit der Straßenbahn. Die would be nominative or accusative; dem is for masculine and neuter nouns.

questions.stem: Match each preposition and article to its short form.
questions.explanation: zu dem → zum (zum Bahnhof), zu der → zur (zur Post), von dem → vom (vom Hotel), bei dem → beim (beim Arzt). Im is the short form of in dem (lesson 19), and mit dem has no standard short form.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "Do I have to change in Munich?"
questions.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the conjugated verb, here the modal muss. The subject ich follows, and the infinitive umsteigen goes to the end (the sentence bracket): Muss ich in München umsteigen?

questions.stem: Which prepositions always take the dative? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Mit, seit and bei are three of the seven prepositions that always take the dative (aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu). Für, ohne and durch always take the accusative (lesson 16): für dich, ohne den Koffer, durch die Stadt.

questions.stem: Name the numbered things in this station scene.

image.alt: A station scene: a plane in the sky, a long train on a track next to a platform with a number 3 sign, a suitcase and a timetable board on the platform, and in the street below a tram under an overhead wire, a bus and a taxi. Six things are numbered.

questions.explanation: Der Zug (train) stands on das Gleis (the track, also the platform number). On the platform is der Koffer (suitcase). In the street, the vehicle on rails with a pole up to the overhead wire is die Straßenbahn (tram); then come der Bus and das Taxi. The U-Bahn runs underground, and there is no bicycle in the picture.

questions.stem: A friend asks: "Wohin fährst du im Sommer?" You're going to Switzerland. Which answer is correct?
questions.explanation: Countries with an article, like die Schweiz, take in + accusative: in die Schweiz. Nach is only for cities and countries without an article (nach Österreich), so nach die Schweiz and nach Schweiz are wrong. Zur is for people and places such as zur Post, not for countries.

questions.stem: Write the missing article: "Die Lampe ist über ___ Tisch."
questions.explanation: The sentence says where the lamp is (Wo?), so über takes the dative. Tisch is masculine (der Tisch), and the masculine dative article is dem: über dem Tisch. Den would be the accusative, used only for movement (Wohin?).

questions.stem: Name the numbered rooms in this floor plan.

image.alt: A floor plan of a flat. Top row: a room with a stove, a fridge and a round table; a room with a bath, a toilet and a basin; a room with a double bed and a wardrobe. A hallway runs across the middle. Below it a large room with a sofa and a coffee table, and outside it a platform with a railing. Five places are numbered.

questions.explanation: The stove and fridge show die Küche (kitchen); the bath and toilet das Bad (bathroom); the double bed das Schlafzimmer (bedroom); the sofa das Wohnzimmer (living room); and the platform with a railing outside is der Balkon (balcony). There is no garden or staircase in this flat.

questions.stem: Wo ist der Ball? Choose the preposition for each numbered picture.

image.alt: Eight small pictures of a ball and a box: the ball on top of a box; under a table; on the floor beside a box; floating above a box; inside an open box; peeking out over the back of a box; on the floor in front of a box, covering part of it; between two boxes. Six pictures are numbered.

questions.explanation: The ball is auf dem Karton (on top), unter dem Tisch (under), neben dem Karton (beside), im Karton (inside the open box), hinter dem Karton (only its top shows behind the box) and zwischen den Kartons (between two boxes). An is for touching a vertical surface, such as a picture an der Wand.

questions.stem: "Ich finde ___ schön." Match each noun to the pronoun that replaces it.
questions.explanation: The pronoun takes the gender of the noun, and here it is a direct object (accusative). Only the masculine changes: der Schrank → ihn. Die Lampe → sie, das Sofa → es, and the plural die Stühle → sie. Er is the subject form, and den is an article, not a pronoun.

questions.stem: Which sentences correctly say where something is? Select all that apply.
choices: Das Foto ist an der Wand.
Das Buch ist auf den Tisch.
Die Katze ist unter dem Bett.
questions.explanation: Location (Wo?) needs the dative: an der Wand, unter dem Bett, im Kühlschrank (in dem). Auf den Tisch and in die Küche are accusative, which is for movement; for location say auf dem Tisch and in der Küche.

questions.stem: You ask a friend to help you and your brother. Write the missing pronoun: "Kannst du ___ bitte helfen?"
questions.explanation: Helfen takes the dative, and "us" in the dative is uns (the same form as the accusative). Mich or mir would mean only you.

questions.stem: Match each subject pronoun to its dative form.
questions.explanation: The dative pronouns: ich → mir, du → dir, er → ihm, sie (she) → ihr, Sie → Ihnen (Wie geht es Ihnen?). Mich and dich are the accusative forms.

questions.stem: Put the words in order, starting with the time phrase: "I've had a temperature since yesterday."
questions.explanation: The time phrase seit gestern comes first, so the verb habe stays in position 2 and the subject ich comes right after it (inversion): Seit gestern habe ich Fieber. Seit + present tense is how German says "have had since".

questions.stem: Which sentences correctly say how you feel? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Mir geht es nicht gut, Mir ist kalt and Ich habe Kopfschmerzen are correct. Feelings take the dative mir, not mich, so Mich geht es gut is wrong. Füße is plural, so the verb is tun: Meine Füße tun weh.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of the body.

image.alt: A person standing, seen from the front, with a head, face, ears, neck, arms, hands, belly, legs and feet. Six parts are numbered.

questions.explanation: From the top: der Kopf (head), das Ohr (ear), der Arm (arm), die Hand (hand), der Bauch (stomach, belly) and der Fuß (foot). The back (der Rücken) can't be seen from the front, and no tooth (der Zahn) is numbered.

questions.stem: Look at the board. You want to go to Munich. From which platform does your train leave today?

image.alt: A departure board headed Abfahrt. 08:04 S 3 Flughafen Gleis 2. 08:12 RE 7 Köln Hbf Gleis 5, note +10. 08:20 ICE 591 München Hbf Gleis 7, note heute Gleis 8. 08:31 RB 42 Bonn Gleis 4, note fällt aus. 08:45 IC 2013 Berlin Hbf Gleis 9.

questions.explanation: The ICE to München Hbf is planned for Gleis 7, but the Hinweis column says heute Gleis 8: today it leaves from platform 8. The note always beats the printed platform.

questions.stem: Look at the board again. Which train is cancelled?

image.alt: A departure board headed Abfahrt. 08:04 S 3 Flughafen Gleis 2. 08:12 RE 7 Köln Hbf Gleis 5, note +10. 08:20 ICE 591 München Hbf Gleis 7, note heute Gleis 8. 08:31 RB 42 Bonn Gleis 4, note fällt aus. 08:45 IC 2013 Berlin Hbf Gleis 9.

questions.explanation: Fällt aus (from ausfallen) means the train is cancelled: that's the RB 42 to Bonn. The RE 7 runs about 10 minutes late (+10), and the ICE runs but from another platform.

questions.stem: The RE 7 to Köln is planned for 08:12, and the note says +10. At about what time should it leave? Write the time on the 24-hour clock, like 08:12.
questions.explanation: +10 means about 10 minutes late (10 Minuten Verspätung): 08:12 + 10 minutes = 08:22. The train still runs; it is not cancelled.

questions.stem: On a board or ticket you see "Hbf". What does it stand for?
questions.explanation: Hbf is short for Hauptbahnhof, the main station of a town (Köln Hbf, München Hbf). People always say the full word. A Haltestelle is a bus or tram stop.

questions.stem: You have a Deutschlandticket. Which train can you NOT take with it?
questions.explanation: The Deutschlandticket covers local and regional transport: buses, trams, U-Bahn, S-Bahn, RE and RB. Long-distance trains such as the ICE, IC and EC need a separate ticket.

questions.stem: Your paper ticket says "Bitte entwerten". Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: You stamp it in a small machine before the trip.
If an inspector finds it unstamped, it counts as no ticket.
Entwerten means to throw the ticket away.
questions.explanation: Entwerten means to validate or stamp a ticket. A ticket that says Bitte entwerten is not valid until it is stamped, so an unstamped one counts as riding without a ticket. It has nothing to do with throwing the ticket away.

questions.stem: Match each sign to its meaning.
questions.explanation: Eingang is the way in, Ausgang the way out, Notausgang the emergency exit (die Not, need or emergency), and Vorsicht! warns you to be careful. Arrival is die Ankunft and departure die Abfahrt.

questions.stem: Match each verb to the noun made from it.
questions.explanation: -fahren gives -fahrt (feminine): die Abfahrt. -steigen gives -stieg (masculine): der Ausstieg. -gehen gives -gang (masculine): der Eingang. Ankommen gives die Ankunft, a word to learn as it is. Die Aussteigung doesn't exist, and Abfahrt is feminine, not der Abfahrt.

questions.stem: Write the noun with its article: einsteigen → ___ (getting on, the way on).
questions.explanation: Like aussteigen → der Ausstieg, einsteigen gives der Einstieg: -steigen verbs make masculine nouns in -stieg. You see it on doors and in announcements: Einstieg vorne (get on at the front).

questions.stem: On the train you hear: "Nächster Halt: Rathaus. Ausstieg in Fahrtrichtung rechts." What does it tell you?
choices: Change trains at the town hall.
Get on at the front of the train.
Stay on the train until the last stop.
The next stop is Rathaus; get off on the right.
questions.explanation: Nächster Halt = next stop (Rathaus, town hall). Ausstieg (from aussteigen) in Fahrtrichtung rechts = getting off on the right-hand side in the direction of travel. Nothing is said about changing trains.

questions.stem: How do you say "the S 1 towards the airport"?
questions.explanation: "Towards" is Richtung + place (or in Richtung + place): die S 1 Richtung Flughafen. Nach and zur don't go with Richtung, and für means "for".

questions.stem: In Zurich someone says: "Ein Billett nach Bern, bitte." What do they want?
choices: a seat on the tram to Bern
questions.explanation: In Switzerland das Billett is the usual word for a ticket (standard German: die Fahrkarte). Other Swiss words: der Perron (platform) and das Tram (tram).

questions.stem: Your paper ticket says "Bitte entwerten", and you have to change trains in Köln. Put the steps of your trip in order.
choices: Buy the ticket at the Fahrkartenautomat
questions.explanation: You need the ticket before you can stamp it, and a ticket that says Bitte entwerten must be stamped before the trip. Then einsteigen (get on), umsteigen in Köln (change) and finally aussteigen (get off).

questions.stem: In the text "Mein erster Tag in Hamburg", why doesn't the writer stamp the ticket?
choices: There is no machine at the station.
The day ticket is already valid.
The U-Bahn is free in Hamburg.
questions.explanation: The text says: Sie ist schon gültig, ich muss sie nicht entwerten (It's already valid; I don't have to stamp it). Many tickets from machines and apps are valid straight away.

questions.stem: Which article goes with "Ausgang"?
questions.explanation: Nouns in -gang from gehen are masculine: der Ausgang, der Eingang. (Den would be the masculine accusative: Ich suche den Ausgang.)

questions.stem: Read the ad: "2-Zi.-Whg., EG, 54 m², KM 590 €, NK 160 €, zzgl. Strom." How much is the Warmmiete?
questions.explanation: Warmmiete = Kaltmiete + Nebenkosten = 590 € + 160 € = 750 € a month. Zzgl. Strom (plus electricity) means electricity is extra on top. 590 € is only the cold rent; 430 € comes from subtracting instead of adding.

questions.stem: An ad says: "KM 640 €, NK 190 €, Kaution 3 KM". How much is the deposit in euros? Give only the number, without a thousands separator.
questions.explanation: Kaution 3 KM means three times the Kaltmiete: 3 × 640 € = 1920 €. The Nebenkosten don't count; three times the warm rent (830 €) would be 2490 €, which is wrong. In Germany the law limits the deposit to three months' cold rent.

questions.stem: What does an ad for a "3-Zimmer-Wohnung" (3 ZKB) offer?
choices: three rooms in total, including the kitchen
three bedrooms and a living room
three rooms plus a kitchen and a bathroom
three rooms and a kitchen, but no bathroom
questions.explanation: ZKB = Zimmer, Küche, Bad. The rooms never include the kitchen, the bathroom or the hallway, so 3 ZKB is three rooms plus a kitchen and a bathroom. The three rooms might be a living room and two bedrooms.

questions.stem: Match each ad abbreviation to its meaning.
questions.explanation: EBK = Einbauküche (fitted kitchen), DG = Dachgeschoss (attic floor), möbl. = möbliert (furnished), zzgl. = zuzüglich (plus, not included). Including is inkl. (inklusive), and the ground floor is EG (Erdgeschoss).

questions.stem: Name the numbered floors of this building.

image.alt: A cut-open block of flats: a room below the ground, the floor at street level with the front door, two floors above it and a floor under the roof. Five floors are numbered.

questions.explanation: Below the ground is der Keller (cellar). The street level with the front door is das Erdgeschoss (EG), floor zero. Above it come der erste Stock (1. OG) and der zweite Stock (2. OG), and under the roof das Dachgeschoss (DG).

questions.stem: Your new flat is "im 2. OG". Which floor is that in American English?
questions.explanation: German counts from the Erdgeschoss (floor zero), so 2. OG is two floors above the ground floor: the third level, which Americans call the third floor (British English: the second floor).

questions.stem: Which of these are part of the Nebenkosten? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Nebenkosten are the additional costs of the building: water, rubbish collection, cleaning, the caretaker, insurance and often heating. The Kaltmiete is the rent for the flat itself, and the Kaution is a deposit you pay once and get back when you move out.

questions.stem: "das Haus" + "der Schlüssel": which article goes with "Hausschlüssel"?
questions.explanation: The last part of a compound decides the gender: a house key is a kind of key (der Schlüssel), so der Hausschlüssel. Das comes from wrongly taking the gender of the first part.

questions.stem: Write the article: "___ Dachgeschosswohnung" (a flat on the attic floor).
questions.explanation: Read from the end: the last part is Wohnung, which is feminine (die Wohnung), so the whole word is die Dachgeschosswohnung. Das Dachgeschoss only says what kind of flat.

questions.stem: Put the words in order: "From when is the flat available?"
questions.explanation: A W-question starts with the question word (here ab wann), then the verb ist in position 2, then the subject die Wohnung, and the adjective frei at the end: Ab wann ist die Wohnung frei?

questions.stem: You want to know how much the rent is. Which question is correct?
choices: Wie viel ist die Miete hoch?
questions.explanation: A rent is hoch or niedrig, so you ask Wie hoch ist die Miete? Die Miete is singular, so the verb is ist (Wie hoch sind … is for the plural Nebenkosten). Wie groß asks about size, and Wie viel … hoch mixes two questions.

questions.stem: In the phone call, Herr Brandt says: "Die Nebenkosten sind 210 Euro mit Heizung. Strom kommt noch dazu." What does Sara pay on top of the rent and the 210 euros?
questions.explanation: Heating is already in the Nebenkosten (mit Heizung). Strom kommt noch dazu means electricity comes on top, usually with its own contract.

questions.stem: Why is it worth mentioning "EBK" in a German flat ad?
choices: Many rental flats in Germany come without a kitchen.
The kitchen is counted as a room.
A fitted kitchen makes the deposit smaller.
It means the flat is on the ground floor.
questions.explanation: Many German rental flats come without a kitchen, and tenants often bring their own. EBK (Einbauküche) tells you a fitted kitchen is included. The kitchen is never counted as a room, and EG, not EBK, is the ground floor.

questions.stem: A flat has 60 m² and a Kaltmiete of 690 €. What is the cold rent per square metre?
questions.explanation: Divide the cold rent by the size: 690 € ÷ 60 m² = 11,50 € per square metre (in German written with a comma). 13,80 comes from dividing by 50, and 1,15 and 115 have the decimal point in the wrong place.

questions.stem: Type the past participle of the separable verb "anrufen" (to phone): "Hast du deine Mutter ___?"
questions.explanation: In a separable verb, ge- goes between the prefix and the stem: an + ge + rufen = "angerufen", written as one word. "Rufen" is a strong verb, so the participle ends in -en, not -t ("angeruft" is wrong).

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask: "What did you (plural) do at the weekend?"
questions.explanation: "Was habt ihr am Wochenende gemacht?" The question word comes first, haben second (habt for ihr), the subject right after it, and the participle last. Everything else goes inside the bracket.

questions.stem: Match each verb to its past participle.
questions.explanation: besuchen → besucht (inseparable be-, so no ge-); einkaufen → eingekauft (separable: -ge- after the prefix); trinken → getrunken (strong: ge- … -en with a new vowel); wissen → gewusst (mixed); studieren → studiert (-ieren verbs have no ge-). "Gebesucht" and "gestudiert" are the classic mistakes.

questions.stem: Which past participles are spelled correctly? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Verkauft" (ver- blocks ge-), "angerufen" (separable an-, strong rufen) and "verloren" (ver-, strong) are right. "Gestudiert" is wrong because -ieren verbs take no ge- (studiert). "Gebringt" is wrong because bringen is a mixed verb: gebracht.

questions.stem: Today is Thursday. Name the numbered days and the numbered week.

image.alt: A strip of twelve days: Monday to Sunday of one week, then Monday to Friday of the next week, which is labeled "diese Woche". Thursday of this week is shaded as today. The first week and four days of this week are numbered.

questions.explanation: The whole week before this one is "letzte Woche". Counting back from today (Thursday): Wednesday is "gestern" (yesterday) and Tuesday is "vorgestern" (the day before yesterday). Thursday is "heute", and Friday is "morgen" (tomorrow).

questions.stem: Complete with the perfect of "aufstehen" (to get up): "Er ___ heute um sechs ___."
questions.explanation: "Aufstehen" is a change of state, so it takes sein: "ist" for er. It is separable and strong, so -ge- goes after the prefix and the participle ends in -en: "aufgestanden". Full sentence: "Er ist heute um sechs aufgestanden."

questions.stem: Match each verb to its perfect form (er/sie/es).
questions.explanation: Fliegen (movement), ankommen (movement) and bleiben (one of the three special verbs) take sein. Treffen and schreiben have an accusative object (jemanden treffen, einen Brief schreiben) and take haben.

questions.stem: Which verbs form the perfect with sein? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: "Ist passiert" and "ist geblieben" are the special cases you learn by heart; "ist angekommen" is movement to a place. "Besuchen" and "kaufen" have an accusative object (hat besucht, hat gekauft), and "schlafen" is neither movement nor change (hat geschlafen).

questions.stem: Name the numbered places in this landscape.

image.alt: A landscape: two mountains with snowy peaks, a lake surrounded by green land, a few houses and a church, a strip of sand, the sea reaching to the horizon, and a small island with a palm tree. Six places are numbered.

questions.explanation: 1 is a mountain (der Berg). 2 is water surrounded by land, a lake: der See (masculine). 5 is the open sea reaching to the horizon: das Meer (neuter). 3 is a village (das Dorf), 4 the sandy beach (der Strand), and 6 a small island (die Insel). There is no river or park in the picture.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask: "When did you (plural) get home?"
questions.explanation: "Wann seid ihr nach Hause gekommen?" The question word first, then the auxiliary (kommen is movement, so sein: seid for ihr), the subject, the rest, and the participle last.

questions.stem: Put the parts in order: "I'm not coming today, because I'm ill."
questions.explanation: "Ich komme heute nicht, denn ich bin krank." Denn stands in position 0, so the sentence after it keeps normal order: subject (ich) in position 1, verb (bin) in position 2. "Denn bin ich krank" and "denn ich krank bin" are both wrong.

questions.stem: Type the missing conjunction: "Das ist kein Tee, ___ Kaffee." (That isn't tea, it's coffee.)
questions.explanation: After a negative (kein, nicht), the correction is introduced by "sondern". "Aber" would be wrong here, because it doesn't replace the first idea.

questions.stem: Match each person you are writing to with the right opening.
questions.explanation: Liebe/Lieber and geehrte/geehrter follow the person: -e for a woman (Liebe Anna, Sehr geehrte Frau Weber), -er for a man (Lieber Tom, Sehr geehrter Herr Klein). Friends get Liebe/Lieber; people you call Sie get Sehr geehrte/geehrter; if you don't know a name, write "Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,".

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.
Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich krank bin.
Ich bin krank. Deshalb komme ich nicht.
Er kommt nicht heute, sondern morgen.
Das Zimmer ist klein, sondern hell.
questions.explanation: After denn the word order stays normal (ich bin krank). Deshalb takes position 1, so the verb comes straight after it (Deshalb komme ich). Sondern needs a negative before it: "nicht heute, sondern morgen" is right, but "klein, sondern hell" has no negative, so it needs aber.

questions.stem: Lukas has filled in this form, but six field names are missing. Name each numbered field.

image.alt: A course registration form. The first row says Vorname: Lukas. The next rows have no field names; their answers are Berger, 02.11.2001, Graz, österreichisch, verheiratet and a handwritten signature. The six empty field names are numbered.

questions.explanation: Berger is the surname (Familienname); 02.11.2001 is a date of birth (Geburtsdatum: 2 November 2001); Graz is a city, so it is the place of birth (Geburtsort); österreichisch (Austrian) is a nationality (Staatsangehörigkeit); verheiratet (married) is a marital status (Familienstand); the handwriting is the signature (Unterschrift).

questions.stem: Put the CEFR levels in order, from the first level to the highest.
questions.explanation: The six levels run A1, A2 (basic user), B1, B2 (independent user), C1, C2 (proficient user). This course takes you to A1; the next step is A2.

questions.stem: Match each part of the Goethe A1 exam with what it tests.
choices: Short conversations, phone messages and announcements
Signs, notes, short e-mails and small ads
A form and a short message of about 30 words
Introducing yourself and asking questions in a small group
A long essay about a book
questions.explanation: Hören is listening, Lesen reading, Schreiben writing (a form plus a message of about 30 words), and Sprechen speaking, in a small group. There is no essay at A1.

questions.stem: Type the missing word: "Hast du ___ Zeit für die Prüfung?" (Do you have enough time for the exam?)
questions.explanation: "Genug" means "enough". It never changes its form and usually comes before the noun: genug Zeit, genug Geld.

questions.stem: Which statements about the Goethe-Zertifikat A1: Start Deutsch 1 are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The writing part includes filling in a form.
In the speaking part you get 30 minutes to prepare alone.
Hören, Lesen and Schreiben are written in one block.
questions.explanation: The exam has 100 points and you need 60 (not 50) to pass. Schreiben has a form and a short message. Hören, Lesen and Schreiben form one written block of about 65 minutes; Sprechen is a separate group exam with no preparation time.

questions.stem: Type the missing word: "Ist ___ da?" — "Nein, hier ist niemand." (Is anybody there?)
