questions.explanation: "Jemand" means "somebody, anybody"; its opposite is "niemand" (nobody). Like etwas and nichts, they come in pairs.

questions.stem: Complete: "Ich ___ gestern nicht kommen, denn ich war krank."
questions.explanation: The simple past of können drops the umlaut and adds -te: "konnte", with no ending for ich. "Könnte" (with umlaut) is the subjunctive, "could / would be able to", not the past. "Kann" is present, and "konntet" is the ihr form.

questions.stem: Which form completes "Wir ___ lange warten." (We had to wait a long time.)?
questions.explanation: müssen → muss- + te, plus -n for wir: "mussten". "Müssten" keeps the umlaut (that means "would have to"), "musstet" is the ihr form, and "gemusst" is a participle, which doesn't go with an infinitive like warten.

questions.stem: Type the past of "wollen": "Früher ___ ich Lehrerin werden." (I used to want to be a teacher.)
questions.explanation: wollen → wollte, with no ending for ich. The infinitive "werden" stays at the end of the sentence.

questions.stem: Type the past of "müssen" for du: "___ du gestern arbeiten?" (Did you have to work yesterday?)
questions.explanation: müssen → muss- + te, plus -st for du: "Musstest du gestern arbeiten?" In a yes/no question the modal comes first and the infinitive stays at the end.

questions.stem: What does "Es gab keinen Kaffee." mean?
questions.explanation: "Es gab" is the simple past of "es gibt" (there is / there are), so "Es gab keinen Kaffee" means "There was no coffee." It is followed by the accusative, like es gibt.

questions.stem: Put the words in order to ask: "Why didn't you want to come along?"
questions.explanation: "Warum wolltest du nicht mitkommen?" The question word first, the modal second (wolltest for du), the subject, nicht, and the infinitive at the end. A separable verb stays in one piece when it is an infinitive.

questions.stem: Match each modal verb to its simple past (ich form).
questions.explanation: All of them drop the umlaut and add -te; mögen also changes g to ch (mochte). "Könnte" and "müsste" keep the umlaut: they are subjunctive forms (could / would have to), not the past.

questions.stem: Which sentences are correct German? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: After a time word the verb comes next (Gestern musste ich), so "Gestern ich musste" is wrong. "Ich habe nicht schlafen gekonnt" is wrong: with an infinitive, the perfect of a modal would be the double infinitive (habe … schlafen können), but "konnte" is what people say. "Konntet" is the ihr form, so it can't go with er.

questions.stem: Read: "Am Samstag wollten wir ans Meer fahren. Aber das Auto war kaputt, und es gab keinen Zug. Wir mussten zu Hause bleiben. Wir haben einen Film gesehen." What did they do on Saturday?
choices: They took the train to the sea.
They stayed at home and watched a film.
questions.explanation: They wanted (wollten) to go to the sea, but the car was broken and there was no train, so they had to stay at home (mussten zu Hause bleiben) and watched a film (haben einen Film gesehen). "Wollten" only tells you the plan, not what happened.

questions.stem: How do Germans usually say "I had to work" in conversation?
questions.explanation: With modal verbs the simple past is the normal choice in speech: "Ich musste arbeiten." The perfect of a modal with an infinitive needs a double infinitive (Ich habe arbeiten müssen), which is correct but less common; the other three options are not correct German.

questions.stem: What does "Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?" mean?
choices: Were you able to help me?
Did you have to help me?
questions.explanation: "Könnten" with an umlaut is the subjunctive, used for polite requests: "Could you help me, please?" The past "were you able to" would be "Konnten Sie …" without the umlaut.

questions.stem: Put the sentences of this story in a logical order.
choices: Ich bin schnell zur Haltestelle gelaufen.
questions.explanation: The alarm clock didn't ring, so I woke up too late. Then I ran to the bus stop, but the bus had already gone, so I had to wait twenty minutes. Each event causes the next one.

questions.stem: Type the missing word: "Gestern ___ es keine Brötchen in der Bäckerei." (Yesterday there were no rolls at the bakery.)
questions.explanation: "Es gibt" in the past is "es gab", and it is the same for one thing or many: es gab keine Brötchen.

questions.stem: What does "Früher durfte ich nicht allein in die Stadt fahren." mean?
choices: I didn't want to go into town alone.
I couldn't find the way into town alone.
I wasn't allowed to go into town alone.
I shouldn't go into town alone.
questions.explanation: "Durfte" is the past of dürfen (may, to be allowed to): "I wasn't allowed to go into town alone." "Didn't want to" would be wollte, "couldn't" konnte, and "shouldn't" sollte.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this formal letter.

image.alt: A formal German letter from Paul Novak in Bremen to Frau Berger at a language school. Six parts are numbered: the address at the top left, the address below it, the place and date on the right, a bold line, the opening line and the closing line. A signature and a typed name follow at the bottom.

questions.explanation: 1 is the sender's address (Absender: Paul Novak, who signs the letter), 2 the recipient's (Empfänger: Frau Berger). 3 is the place and date (Bremen, 12. Mai 2026), 4 the bold subject line (Betreff), 5 the salutation (Anrede: Sehr geehrte Frau Berger,), and 6 the closing (Grußformel: Mit freundlichen Grüßen). The signature below the closing is not numbered, and a stamp goes on the envelope, not in the letter.

questions.stem: You are writing to your landlord, Herr Schmidt, for the first time. Which opening is correct?
questions.explanation: For a man the ending is -er: "Sehr geehrter Herr Schmidt,". "Geehrte" is for a woman, "Herrn" is the wrong form after the opening, and "Liebe" would need -r for a man (Lieber Herr Schmidt), which is also too familiar for a first letter.

questions.stem: You are writing to Frau Roth, whom you address with Sie. Which sentences are written correctly? Select all that apply.
choices: Ich freue mich auf Ihre Nachricht.
questions.explanation: The polite Sie and its forms (Ihre, Ihnen) always have a capital letter. With a small letter, "sie" means "they" and "ihre" means "her" or "their", so "Können sie mir helfen?" asks whether they can help, and "ihre Antwort" is her or their answer.

questions.stem: Match each greeting with where and how it is used.
choices: Northern Germany, at any time of day
Bavaria and Austria, informal, for hello and goodbye
Southern Germany and Austria, a polite hello
Only in the morning, everywhere in Germany
questions.explanation: Moin is northern and is used all day, not only in the morning. Servus is the informal hello and goodbye of Bavaria and Austria. Grüezi is the Swiss polite greeting, and Grüß Gott the polite greeting of southern Germany and Austria.

questions.stem: Make the request formal. Informal: "Kannst du mir die Hausaufgabe schicken?" Formal: "___ Sie mir die Hausaufgabe schicken?"
questions.explanation: With Sie the verb takes the -en form: "Können Sie mir die Hausaufgabe schicken?"

questions.stem: Complete the formal closing: "Mit freundlichen ___"
questions.explanation: "Mit freundlichen Grüßen" is the standard formal closing, with no comma after it. In Switzerland it is written "Grüssen".

questions.stem: Put these parts of a formal letter in order, from top to bottom.
questions.explanation: The bold subject line (Betreff) comes first, then the salutation (Sehr geehrte …,), the text, the closing (Mit freundlichen Grüßen) and the signature.

questions.stem: An e-mail starts "Liebe Frau Weber,". Which form of address should the rest of the e-mail use?
choices: Sie, because she is addressed with her surname
ihr, because it is a letter
Sie, but written with a small s
questions.explanation: "Liebe Frau Weber" is friendly, but Frau or Herr + surname goes with Sie, and Sie is always written with a capital S. Du goes with a first name (Liebe Anna).

questions.stem: You are thanking your friend Lisa: "Danke für ___ Postkarte!" Which word fits?
questions.explanation: Lisa is a friend, so the du form: dein. "Postkarte" is feminine (die Postkarte), so it takes -e: "deine Postkarte". "Ihre" would be the formal Sie form, and "ihre" means "her" or "their".

questions.stem: Traditionally, who offers to switch from Sie to du?
choices: The older or more senior person
questions.explanation: By tradition the older person, or the one in the higher position, offers du (Wollen wir uns duzen?). It is a custom, not a rule, and many young people, clubs and companies use du from the start; if unsure, use Sie.

questions.stem: Read the postcard: "Liebe Oma, viele Grüße von der Insel Rügen! Wir sind am Samstag angekommen. Das Wetter war leider schlecht, aber gestern hat die Sonne geschienen, und wir waren am Strand. Am Freitag fahren wir zurück. Dein Max" What was the weather like yesterday?
choices: It was bad, so they stayed inside.
questions.explanation: "Gestern hat die Sonne geschienen" means "yesterday the sun was shining", and they went to the beach. The weather was bad before that ("war leider schlecht").

questions.stem: When do you write "Hallo zusammen,"?
choices: To a group of people, for example your course
At the end of a formal letter
questions.explanation: "Zusammen" means "together", so "Hallo zusammen" greets everyone in a group at once: a course, a team, a club.

questions.stem: Which place and date line is written the German way?
questions.explanation: German puts the day first, with a full stop because it is an ordinal number (read: zwölfter Mai), and no comma before the year: "Bremen, 12. Mai 2026".

cards.back: Register your address (sich anmelden) at the Bürgeramt within two weeks of moving in (Germany). Austria: within three days (Meldezettel).

cards.front: What do you bring to the Anmeldung?
cards.back: Passport or ID card, the Wohnungsgeberbestätigung from your landlord, and the Anmeldeformular, filled in and signed.
The certificate of registration you get at the Bürgeramt. Banks and employers may ask for it.
Your 11-digit tax ID, sent by post a few weeks after your first registration. Your employer needs it: keep the letter.
The broadcasting fee: one fee per household, TV or no TV. Flatmates share it.

cards.front: Scanning a formal letter: four questions
cards.back: Who? (Absender) What? (Betreff) When and where? (numbers) What must I do? (Bitte … and imperatives)
Address on the envelope: Herrn Lukas Brandt. Greeting: Sehr geehrter Herr Brandt,
zum Beispiel (for example) / das heißt (that is) / und so weiter (and so on). Read abbreviations aloud as full words.
circa (about) / gegebenenfalls (if necessary) / unter anderem (among other things) / beziehungsweise (or; respectively)
possibly, perhaps (NOT "eventually"): Ich komme eventuell später. — I may come later.

cards.front: Ihr / Ihre with a capital I
cards.back: your (formal, from Sie): Ihre Anmeldung = your registration. Small ihr = her, their, or you (plural).
The house rules in the stairwell: quiet hours (Ruhezeiten), no bikes in the stairwell, sort the rubbish, lock the front door at night.
Night: about 22 to 6 or 7 Uhr; often a midday rest (13 to 15 Uhr); Sundays and public holidays all day. Rules vary by building and town.
We ask for your understanding / thank you for your understanding (set phrase on notices).
Everything else first, infinitive last, no du/Sie: Bitte Tür schließen! Nicht rauchen! Separable verbs stay joined: Bitte einsteigen!
Infinitive commands are for signs, announcements and recipes. To a person, use the imperative: Schließ bitte die Tür! / Schließen Sie bitte die Tür!

cards.front: Wo? or Wohin? with in, an, auf …
cards.back: Wo? (location) + dative: in der Tonne, im Keller. Wohin? (movement) + accusative: in die Tonne, in den Keller, ins Treppenhaus.
gelb: packaging (plastic, metal); blau: paper; Biotonne (often brown): food and garden waste; Restmüll (grey/black): everything else. Colours vary by town.
In the Glascontainer on the street, by colour: Weißglas, Grünglas, Braunglas (blue goes with green). Only on working days (Mon–Sat), during the day; never on Sundays or holidays.
A deposit: 25 cents on single-use bottles and cans with the logo, usually 8 or 15 cents on reusable (Mehrweg) bottles. Return them to the Pfandautomat for a Pfandbon.
ich werfe, du wirfst, er wirft, wir werfen, ihr werft, sie werfen (e → i)
Written stories, novels and fairy tales: simple past (er ging). Speaking: perfect (er ist gegangen), except war, hatte and the modals.

cards.front: Weak verbs in the simple past
cards.back: stem + -te: sagte, machte, fragte; -t/-d stems add -e-: arbeitete. Plural: sie sagten.

cards.front: Strong verbs in the simple past
cards.back: New vowel, no ending for ich and er/sie/es: ging, kam, sah, lief, fand, saß. Plural: sie gingen.
Infinitive, simple past, past participle: gehen, ging, gegangen; kommen, kam, gekommen; sehen, sah, gesehen. Learn them together.

cards.front: Finding the infinitive of a simple past form
cards.back: -te / -ten? Weak: fragte → fragen. Short, new vowel? Strong: compare the participle or English (fand / found → finden).
lief, sprang, fiel, flog; perfect with sein: ist gelaufen, ist gesprungen, ist gefallen, ist geflogen
Jacob (1785–1863) and Wilhelm (1786–1859), born in Hanau. Kinder- und Hausmärchen from 1812.
A donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster scare robbers out of a house in the forest and stay there. They never reach Bremen. (In the Grimms' collection from 1819.)

cards.front: How fairy tales begin and end
cards.back: Es war einmal … (once upon a time) … und wenn sie nicht gestorben sind, dann leben sie noch heute.
rooster / hen (chicken)
Have a nice evening (after work)! / Have a nice weekend! Answer: Danke, gleichfalls!
Cosiness, comfort, warmth, good company and no hurry. Wir machen es uns gemütlich. — We're making ourselves comfortable.
A regulars' table in a Kneipe (pub) for a group that meets there regularly; also any regular get-together (Sprachstammtisch).
A small garden rented through a club (Kleingartenverein), about 900,000 in Germany. Named after the Leipzig doctor Moritz Schreber; first club 1864.
At most 400 m²; a simple Laube of at most 24 m², not for living in; part of the garden for fruit and vegetables (about a third).
1. Drop a final -e. 2. Usually umlaut a, o, u, au. 3. Add -chen (or -lein): die Blume → das Blümchen, das Haus → das Häuschen.
Always das: der Hund → das Hündchen. Plural looks the same: das Brötchen, die Brötchen.
Same meaning. -lein is older, more poetic and southern, and usual after -ch: das Büchlein.
Often a friendly feeling, not just smallness: ein Tässchen Kaffee, ein Gläschen Wein, mein Schätzchen.

cards.front: Diminutives that are words of their own
cards.back: das Mädchen (girl), das Märchen (fairy tale), das Brötchen (roll), das Kaninchen (rabbit), das Eichhörnchen (squirrel), ein bisschen (a little)
Swabian -le (das Häusle), Swiss -li (das Müesli), Bavarian and Austrian -erl / -l (das Sackerl). All neuter.
Häus-chen: s, then the soft ch of ich. Not "sch". Also Gläs-chen, Täss-chen.
A stressed vowel that ends its syllable is usually long: Na-me, ha-ben, le-ben.

cards.front: Short everyday words with one final consonant
cards.back: das, was, es, in, mit, an, um, bis, man, hat: all short. But der, wir, mir are long.
Its longer form Ta-ge has an open syllable, so the a is long in Tag too (also Weg, gut).
The weak unstressed e of bitte, Name, -en: like the a in "about". Never silent.
Vocalic r: a short "uh"-like vowel, no consonant r.
A small catch before a word or word part starting with a vowel: ein | Ei, Spiegel | ei, ver | eisen.
ver-reisen (to go on a trip): r sound. ver | eisen (to ice over): glottal stop, no r.
pf = p + f (Apfel); chs = ks (sechs); ng has no g (Finger); -tion = tsion, stressed (Information).
English v: Klavier, Universität, November. In old German words v = f: Vater, vier.
Statements fall, W-questions usually fall, yes/no questions rise.
ss after a short vowel (dass, Fluss, muss), ß after a long vowel or diphthong (Straße, heißen).
SS is usual (STRASSE); since 2017 a capital ẞ is also allowed (STRAẞE). Switzerland writes ss everywhere.

cards.front: Where is German an official language?
cards.back: Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Belgium (east) and South Tyrol (Italy).
German is the only official language.
Standard German. "High" means the higher-lying middle and south of the area, not better German.
Everyday spoken dialects in German-speaking Switzerland; writing and news use Swiss Standard German.
Several standards: Jänner (Austria) for Januar, Velo (Switzerland) for Fahrrad, Strasse (Switzerland) for Straße.
Hello in northern Germany, at any time of day.
Informal hi AND bye in Bavaria and Austria.
Swiss hello: Grüezi (polite, Sie), Hoi (informal).
Hi to one person you say du to (south, Austria). Not for Sie.
To say du / Sie to someone. Stems end in -z: du duzt, du siezt.
Usually the older or more senior person: Wir können gern du sagen. Accept and stay with du.
ihr if you would say du to each person; Sie if you would say Sie.
plus, minus, mal, geteilt durch. "Equals" = ist (or ist gleich).
Multiplication with a dot (6 · 7), division with a colon (20 : 4).
Consonant + n stem adds e: du rechnest, er zeichnet, er öffnet.
After r, l or a silent h, the n needs no e: du lernst, du wohnst.
Capitalized and feminine: die Eins, eine Fünf, die Sieben (also bus lines: Ich nehme die Fünf).
1 sehr gut, 2 gut, 3 befriedigend, 4 ausreichend, 5 mangelhaft, 6 ungenügend. 1–4 pass.
1 Sehr gut to 5 Nicht genügend; 4 Genügend is the lowest pass.
6 is best, 1 worst, 4 is the pass mark; half grades like 5.5 are common.
The thumb (der Daumen). Two = thumb + index finger.
Has a bar across it, because a German 1 has a long upstroke.
Writing a number with its digits swapped (52 for fünfundzwanzig). Say important numbers digit by digit.

cards.front: das Mädchen: which gender, and why?
cards.back: Neuter, because "little" forms in -chen are always neuter. Textbook pronoun: es (Das Mädchen heißt Lea. Es ist zehn.); sie is common in speech.

cards.front: die Person, der Mensch, das Kind: does the article change with the person?
cards.back: No. The article belongs to the word: die Person and der Mensch for everyone, das Kind for every child.

cards.front: Female job title: the main rule
cards.back: Add -in: der Lehrer → die Lehrerin. Some words also take an umlaut: der Arzt → die Ärztin, der Koch → die Köchin.

cards.front: Female job title for a word in -e (der Kollege)
cards.back: Drop the -e, add -in: die Kollegin. Likewise der Kunde → die Kundin.

cards.front: Female job title for a word in -mann (der Kaufmann)
cards.back: -mann becomes -frau: die Kauffrau, die Feuerwehrfrau. A mixed group: die Kaufleute, die Feuerwehrleute.

cards.front: Plural of a job title in -in
cards.back: Add -nen (double n): die Lehrerinnen, die Ärztinnen, die Köchinnen.
The masculine form used for a mixed group or any person: die Lehrer. Traditional and very common; critics say it makes readers think of men.
Both forms named: Lehrerinnen und Lehrer, Liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen. Accepted everywhere: the safe choice for letters and exams.
Gender star, colon, underscore: signs meant to include everyone, read with a short break before -innen. The older capital I names women and men. None is part of official spelling (decision of 2023).
die Lehrkräfte (teaching staff), die Studierenden (those studying), das Team.
männlich, weiblich, divers: male, female, diverse. The job is open to everyone.
die Lehrerinnen = female teachers only. Lehrer*innen = teachers of every gender.
Stiefvater, Stiefmutter: your parent's new husband or wife. Halbbruder, Halbschwester: you share one parent.
getrennt = separated (no longer living together); geschieden = divorced.
der Zwilling (die Zwillinge) = twin, masculine for girls too; das Einzelkind = only child.

cards.front: Twin sister in German, and why die?
cards.back: die Zwillingsschwester: Zwilling + linking s + Schwester. The last part (die Schwester) decides the gender.

cards.front: Onkel, Tante, Cousin, Cousine, Neffe, Nichte, Enkel, Enkelin
cards.back: uncle, aunt, cousin (m), cousin (f), nephew, niece, grandson, granddaughter.
first name, last name (= Familienname on forms), nickname.

cards.front: Müller, Schmidt, Schneider: where do these surnames come from?
cards.back: Old job titles: miller, smith, tailor. Müller is the most common surname in Germany, Schmidt the second.
Annas Bruder: name + -s, no apostrophe, no article. In speech also: der Bruder von Anna.
Max' Schwester, Jonas' Hund: names ending in s, ss, ß, x or z take only an apostrophe. Or: die Schwester von Max, der Hund von Jonas.
A shared surname, each keeps their own, or both use a double name (Müller-Schmidt). Children can get a double name from both parents.
I'd like … (the most polite way to order). Takes the accusative: Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.
ich hätte, du hättest, er/sie/es hätte, wir/sie/Sie hätten … gern
Noch einen Kaffee, bitte! (noch + accusative article)
Ich möchte keinen Kaffee mehr, danke. (kein … mehr)
Frühstück; Mittagessen (often the warm meal); Kaffee und Kuchen (afternoon, especially Sundays); Abendbrot (cold supper with bread)
Enjoy your meal! Answer: Danke, gleichfalls!
Literally "mealtime": a lunchtime greeting between colleagues at work.
Ich bin satt. (Not: Ich bin voll, which can mean "I'm drunk".)

cards.front: Regional words for the bread roll
cards.back: Brötchen (standard, north and centre), Semmel (Bavaria, Austria, Saxony), Schrippe (Berlin), Weck/Weckle (southwest), Rundstück (Hamburg)
Erdapfel = Kartoffel, Paradeiser = Tomate, Schlagobers = Sahne, Topfen = Quark, Semmel = Brötchen
Keep the change. Said when you hand over money that already includes the tip.

cards.front: How to tip in a German café
cards.back: Round up or add about 5–10 %, and tell the server the total you want to pay (Acht Euro vierzig, bitte) instead of leaving coins on the table.
every Monday, every evening, every night (small letter, -s). am Montag = on (one) Monday.
No preposition: jeden Tag, nächsten Montag, diese Woche, den ganzen Tag, nächstes Jahr

cards.front: next week / next Monday / next year
cards.back: nächste Woche / nächsten Montag / nächstes Jahr
Wie lange dauert das? – Es dauert eine Stunde / einen Tag / zwei Wochen. (accusative, no für)

cards.front: around eight / shortly after eight / eight on the dot
cards.back: gegen acht / kurz nach acht / Punkt acht
immer → meistens → oft → manchmal → selten → nie

cards.front: once a week / twice a day
cards.back: einmal pro Woche (einmal die Woche) / zweimal am Tag

cards.front: Two time phrases in one sentence
cards.back: General before specific: morgen um acht, am Freitag gegen sieben. Time usually before place.
open / closed / a restaurant's or café's weekly closing day (Montag Ruhetag)
Montag bis Freitag von acht bis achtzehn Uhr
Most are closed (rules set by each state); bakeries may open a few hours, and shops at stations, airports and petrol stations stay open.
A club or association. e. V. = eingetragener Verein, a club in the official register: TC Rotbuche e. V.

cards.front: Saying you are in a club
cards.back: im Verein: Ich spiele im Verein Fußball. Meine Tochter singt im Chor.

cards.front: How many clubs does Germany have?
cards.back: About 629,000 registered clubs (ZiviZ, March 2026); about 86,000 sports clubs with about 29.3 million memberships (DOSB, 2025).
Night quiet time, usually 22 to 6 Uhr (state and local rules). Von 22 bis 6 Uhr darf man keine laute Musik hören.
Midday quiet time, often 13 to 15 Uhr. Not a general law: it depends on the town and the house rules (Hausordnung).

cards.front: Sundays and public holidays in Germany
cards.back: Protected days of rest (Sonntagsruhe): most shops closed, no noisy work such as mowing the lawn. Bakeries may open a few hours; station and airport shops stay open.
man + modal (er form): Hier darf man nicht …, man muss …, man soll … Fahrräder darf man nicht im Treppenhaus parken.
favourite …, written as one word: der Lieblingsfilm, die Lieblingsfarbe, das Lieblingsessen. Gender from the last noun.
meine: die Farbe → die Lieblingsfarbe (feminine), so the possessive takes -e.
prefer … to …: Ich trinke lieber Tee als Kaffee. lieber right after the verb, the als part at the end.

cards.front: gar nicht gern → nicht so gern → gern → sehr gern → lieber → am liebsten
cards.back: not at all → not really → like → really like → prefer → like most of all.

cards.front: Public holidays in all German states
cards.back: Nine: Neujahr, Karfreitag, Ostermontag, Tag der Arbeit (1.5.), Christi Himmelfahrt, Pfingstmontag, Tag der Deutschen Einheit (3.10.), 25. and 26. Dezember. The states set the rest.
3 October: reunification of East and West Germany in 1990. The only public holiday fixed by national law (Unification Treaty).
Heiligabend (24.12.), Silvester (31.12.), Rosenmontag, Sankt Martin (11.11.), Nikolaustag (6.12.).

cards.front: When are Christmas presents opened in Germany?
cards.back: Usually on the evening of 24 December, Heiligabend (die Bescherung).

cards.front: Guten Rutsch! or Frohes neues Jahr!?
cards.back: Guten Rutsch! before New Year (until midnight on 31.12.); Frohes neues Jahr! from 1 January on.

Same season, different regions: Karneval in Köln and Düsseldorf, Fasching in Bavaria and Austria, Fastnacht in Mainz and the south-west. Usually in February, some years early March. Parades on Rosenmontag.
Many Germans consider it bad luck (a superstition). Wait for the day: Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!

cards.front: Easter and the holidays counted from it
cards.back: Easter Sunday: between 22 March and 25 April. Good Friday 2 days before; Ascension Day 39 days after (a Thursday); Whit Monday 50 days after.
der + -e: der dritte Mai. am, vom, zum, den + -en: am dritten, vom dritten, bis zum dritten, den dritten Mai.
vom ersten bis zum vierzehnten August (written vom 1. bis zum 14. August, or 1.–14.8.).

cards.front: Date at the top of a letter
cards.back: Hamburg, den 6. Dezember 2026 (den sechsten). Modern letters often leave out den: Hamburg, 06.12.2026.

cards.front: ICE, IC/EC, RE, RB, S, U: which are long-distance trains?
cards.back: ICE (Intercity-Express) and IC/EC (Intercity, Eurocity). RE (Regional-Express) and RB (Regionalbahn) are regional; S is the S-Bahn and U the U-Bahn.

cards.front: The five columns of a departure board
cards.back: Zeit (time), Zug (train), Richtung (direction, last stop), Gleis (platform), Hinweis (note). Always read the Hinweis.
About 10 minutes late (10 Minuten Verspätung).
The train is cancelled (ausfallen). Not the same as fährt ab (leaves).
Today from platform 8: a platform change. The note beats the platform printed in the Gleis column.
Stamp (validate) the ticket in the small machine before the trip. An unstamped ticket counts as no ticket.

cards.front: Riding without a valid ticket in Germany: what happens?
cards.back: You pay an extra fare, usually 60 euros. Informally this is called schwarzfahren.
A monthly subscription for local and regional transport in all of Germany (bus, tram, U-Bahn, S-Bahn, RE, RB), but not ICE, IC or EC trains.

cards.front: Swiss words: das Billett, der Perron, das Tram
cards.back: Ticket, platform, tram (standard German: die Fahrkarte, der Bahnsteig, die Straßenbahn).
Nouns made from verbs instead of full sentences, on signs and in announcements: Nächster Halt: Hauptbahnhof. Ausstieg links.
-fahrt nouns are feminine (die Abfahrt, die Einfahrt); -stieg and -gang nouns are masculine (der Ausstieg, der Einstieg, der Eingang, der Ausgang).
die Abfahrt = departure (ab = away, from abfahren); die Ankunft = arrival (from ankommen).

cards.front: How do you say "towards the airport"?
cards.back: Richtung Flughafen, or in Richtung Flughafen. Not nach Richtung.
3 Zimmer, Küche, Bad: three rooms plus a kitchen and a bathroom. Kitchen, bathroom and hallway are never counted as rooms.
Kaltmiete (rent without bills), Nebenkosten (additional costs), Warmmiete (rent with bills). KM + NK = WM.

cards.front: What is usually not in the Warmmiete?
cards.back: Electricity (der Strom): you usually have your own contract with an electricity company.
At most three months' Kaltmiete (cold rent, not warm rent); tenants may pay it in three parts.
Einbauküche: a fitted kitchen is included. Many German rental flats come without a kitchen.
Erdgeschoss (ground floor), erstes Obergeschoss (one floor up, im ersten Stock), Dachgeschoss (attic floor). The cellar is der Keller.
The third floor: two floors above the ground floor (British: the second floor).
inklusive = including; zuzüglich = plus, not including. NK 210 € inkl. Heizung: heating is included.
Wie hoch ist die Miete? Wie hoch sind die Nebenkosten? (Rent is hoch or niedrig; Nebenkosten is plural.)

cards.front: Is the flat still available? From when?
cards.back: Ist die Wohnung noch frei? Ab wann ist die Wohnung frei? (ab sofort = available now)

cards.front: Reading a long compound like die Dachgeschosswohnung
cards.back: Start at the end: Wohnung (so it is feminine), then what kind: Dachgeschoss (Dach + Geschoss). A flat on the attic floor.

cards.front: das Haus, der Schlüssel: what is the gender of Hausschlüssel?
cards.back: der Hausschlüssel: the last part decides the gender and the plural (die Hausschlüssel).

cards.front: Simple past of a modal verb: how is it built?
cards.back: Drop the umlaut and add -te: können → konnte, müssen → musste, dürfen → durfte. wollen → wollte, sollen → sollte.
ich konnte, du konntest, er/sie/es konnte, wir konnten, ihr konntet, sie/Sie konnten (ich = er, no ending)
mochte (g becomes ch): Ich mochte den Film. — I liked the film.
There is no past of möchte. Use wollte: Ich wollte einen Kaffee.
konnte = could, was able to (past). könnte = could, would be able to (subjunctive, polite): Könnten Sie mir helfen?

cards.front: "I had to work" in spoken German
cards.back: Ich musste arbeiten. (The perfect, Ich habe arbeiten müssen, is a double infinitive: correct but less common.)

cards.front: Word order with a modal in the past
cards.back: Same bracket as in the present: modal in position 2, infinitive at the end. Gestern musste ich lange arbeiten.
there was / there were (past of es gibt), + accusative: Es gab keinen Bus.

cards.front: Other simple past forms common in speech
cards.back: war, hatte, the modals (konnte, musste…), es gab, ich wusste, ich dachte

cards.front: The three parts of a story in the past
cards.back: Setting (war, hatte, modals) → events (perfect with zuerst, dann, plötzlich) → end (endlich, zum Schluss)

cards.front: Parts of a formal German letter, top to bottom
cards.back: Absender, Empfänger, Ort und Datum, Betreff, Anrede, Text, Grußformel, Unterschrift

cards.front: Date line in a German letter
cards.back: Bremen, 12. Mai 2026 (day first, full stop after the day; older style: Bremen, den 12. Mai 2026)
The subject line: short and in bold; the word Betreff itself is usually left out in letters. In an e-mail, the subject field.
Sehr geehrte/r … → Liebe/r Frau/Herr … → Hallo Frau/Herr … → Liebe/r or Hallo + first name

cards.front: Liebe Frau Weber: du or Sie?
cards.back: Sie. As a rule, Frau/Herr + surname goes with Sie; a first name goes with du.
Mit freundlichen Grüßen → Freundliche Grüße → Viele Grüße → Liebe Grüße (LG only in text messages; avoid MfG)
Sie, Ihnen, Ihr always capital. du, dein, ihr, euer: small, but may be capitalized in letters.
Traditionally the older or more senior person. If unsure, use Sie.
Moin: hi in northern Germany (any time of day). Servus: informal hi/bye in Bavaria and Austria. Grüezi: polite hello in Switzerland.
Dein Max (from a man or boy), Deine Mira (from a woman or girl)

glossary.definition: A letter or sound made with the mouth open and the air flowing freely: a, e, i, o, u, plus ä, ö, ü in German. Every German vowel can be long (Tag, sie) or short (Stadt, bitte), and the length can change the meaning of a word.
A sound made by partly or fully blocking the air with the lips, tongue or throat, such as b, k, s or ch. In German, a vowel before a double consonant (ll, mm, ss, tt) is usually short: Hallo, kommen.

The two dots over a, o or u (ä, ö, ü), which change the vowel's sound. They are part of the spelling: schon (already) and schön (beautiful) are different words. Write ae, oe, ue only if you cannot type the real letters.

Two vowel sounds that glide together in one syllable. German has three: ei/ai (as in eye: nein), eu/äu (as in boy: Deutschland), au (as in cow: Frau). Note that ie is not a diphthong but a long ee sound.
The rule that b, d and g at the end of a word or syllable are pronounced like p, t and k: Tag sounds like "tahk", und like "oont". The spelling stays the same.

The syllable said more strongly than the others. German words are usually stressed on the first syllable (DAN-ke), except after prefixes such as be-, ent-, ver- (ver-STE-hen), in verbs ending in -ieren (stu-DIE-ren) and in many borrowed words (Ad-RES-se).

A word for a person, place, thing or idea: Name, Stadt, Wort. In German every noun starts with a capital letter and has a gender, shown by its article der, die or das, so learn each noun with its article.
The friendly way of addressing someone, with du (one person) or ihr (two or more). Used with friends, family, children, and among students and young people. Goes with first names.

The polite way of addressing someone, with Sie (always capitalized), for one or more people. Used with adults you don't know, staff in shops and offices, and anyone you call Herr or Frau. The verb form is the same as the infinitive: Sie wohnen, Sie heißen (except Sie sind).
A word for an action or state, such as wohnen (to live), kommen (to come) or sein (to be). In a German sentence the verb changes its ending to match the subject: ich wohne, du wohnst.
The basic form of a verb, the one listed in a dictionary. German infinitives end in -en or -n: machen, arbeiten, sein. Remove the -en to find the stem.
The person or thing that does the action of the verb, or that the sentence is about: in Ich wohne in Berlin, the subject is ich. The verb ending must match the subject.

A question that starts with a question word such as wer (who), wie (how), wo (where), woher (where from), was (what), warum (why) or wann (when). The verb comes second, straight after the question word: Wo wohnst du?

A short word that stands for a person or thing. The German subject pronouns are ich (I), du (you, informal), er/sie/es (he/she/it), wir (we), ihr (you, informal plural), sie (they) and Sie (you, formal).

To give a verb the form that matches its subject, usually by adding an ending to the stem: lernen becomes ich lerne, du lernst, er lernt, wir lernen, ihr lernt, sie lernen. The full set of forms is the verb's conjugation.
The part of a verb left when you remove the infinitive ending -en (or -n): mach- from machen, arbeit- from arbeiten. Endings are added to the stem.

The letters added to a stem to show who does the action. The regular present-tense endings are -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en (ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie). Stems ending in -t or -d add an e: du arbeitest.
The verb form for things happening now, in general, or (with a time word) in the future. One German form covers English "I play", "I am playing" and "I do play": ich spiele.
A sentence that tells something rather than asking or ordering: Ich wohne in Köln. In a German statement the conjugated verb is always the second element.

The rule that the conjugated verb is the second element of a German statement. If something other than the subject comes first (a time word, a place), the subject moves to just after the verb: Heute arbeite ich, not Heute ich arbeite.
A question that can be answered with ja or nein. In German the conjugated verb comes first and the subject second, with no helper verb like English "do": Wohnst du hier? (Do you live here?)

The group a German noun belongs to: masculine, feminine or neuter. It is a property of the word, not of the thing, and it decides the form of articles and possessives (der Tisch, die Lampe, das Buch). Learn every noun with its article.
One of the three German genders. Masculine nouns take der and ein in the nominative: der Stuhl, ein Stuhl.
One of the three German genders. Feminine nouns take die and eine: die Tür, eine Tür. Nouns ending in -ung, -heit, -keit and -ion, and words for female people in -in (die Lehrerin), are feminine.
One of the three German genders. Neuter nouns take das and ein: das Buch, ein Buch. Nouns ending in -chen and -lein are always neuter.
The word for "the". In the nominative it is der (masculine), die (feminine), das (neuter) and die (all plurals).
The word for "a" or "an": ein for masculine and neuter nouns, eine for feminine nouns (nominative). It has no plural form.

The form of a noun for more than one. All German plurals take the article die, but the ending varies (die Tische, die Bücher, die Lampen, die Handys, die Schlüssel), so learn each plural with the noun.
A noun made by joining two or more words: die Handynummer = das Handy + die Nummer. The last part decides the gender and the plural.

A word that says whose something is: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, Ihr. The owner chooses the word; the noun that follows chooses the ending, which is the same as for ein (meine Mutter, mein Vater, meine Eltern).
The case of the subject, the person or thing doing the action or being described: Der Tisch ist neu. It is the form you find in dictionaries.

The form of an article, pronoun or noun that shows its job in the sentence. German has four cases: nominative (subject), accusative (direct object), dative (indirect object, after some prepositions) and genitive.
A verb whose stem vowel changes in the du and er/sie/es forms of the present tense, while the endings stay regular: sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht; fahren → du fährst, er fährt.
A word that describes a noun: groß, neu, rot. After sein an adjective has no ending (Die Lampe ist neu); before a noun it takes endings, which you learn at A2.
Saying that something is not so. German uses kein to negate nouns that would have ein or no article, and nicht for everything else (verbs, adjectives, nouns with der/die/das or a possessive).
kein, the negative form of ein: "not a", "no", "not any". It takes the same endings as ein and also has a plural: kein Hund, keine Katze, kein Buch, keine Kinder.
A small word that adds a shade of meaning or attitude rather than content, such as doch (yes, contradicting a negative), ja or mal. Particles are very common in spoken German.

The case of the direct object: the person or thing the verb acts on. In German only the masculine article changes: der becomes den, ein becomes einen, kein becomes keinen (Ich trinke einen Kaffee). Feminine, neuter and plural forms are the same as in the nominative.
The person or thing that the action of the verb is done to. In "I eat the apple" the apple is the direct object. In German the direct object is in the accusative: Ich esse den Apfel.
A word that points to a particular thing, like English this or that. German dieser (this, that) takes the same endings as der, die, das: dieser, diese, dieses, masculine accusative diesen.
An adverb that says how often something happens: immer (always), oft (often), manchmal (sometimes), nie (never). It usually comes right after the verb: Ich trinke oft Tee.

A verb with a stressed prefix that splits off in a main clause: the conjugated verb stays in second place and the prefix goes to the end. aufstehen: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf. In the infinitive the verb stays in one piece: Ich möchte einkaufen.
The small front part of a separable verb, such as auf, an, ein, mit, ab or fern. It carries the stress (AUFstehen) and moves to the end of a main clause: Ich rufe meine Mutter an.

Putting the subject after the verb. In a German statement the verb is always the second element, so when something else comes first, such as a time phrase, the subject follows the verb: Am Montag arbeite ich.
The form used to compare two things or options ("more", "-er", "rather"). The comparative of gern is lieber: Ich trinke lieber Tee (I prefer tea).
The form that says something is the most or the best of all. The superlative of gern is am liebsten: Am liebsten lese ich (most of all I like reading).

A verb that adds ability, wish, obligation or permission to another verb: können, wollen, mögen/möchten, müssen, dürfen, sollen. The modal is conjugated and stands in position 2; the other verb goes to the end in the infinitive, without zu: Ich kann schwimmen. The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending (ich kann, er kann), except möchte (ich möchte, er möchte).

The German pattern in which the verb is split into two parts: the conjugated verb in position 2 and the rest of the verb (an infinitive, a separable prefix, later a past participle) at the end, with everything else in between. Ich will am Samstag eine Party feiern. Ich stehe um sieben auf.
A pronoun that does not refer to a particular person or thing. Man means people in general (English one, you or they) and always takes the er/sie/es form of the verb: Hier darf man nicht rauchen.

A number that gives a position in a row: first, second, third. In German 1–19 add -te (zweite, vierte) and 20 and up add -ste (zwanzigste); erste, dritte, siebte and achte are irregular. Written with a full stop: der 3. Oktober (der dritte Oktober), am 3. Oktober (am dritten Oktober).
A verb used only with the placeholder subject es, which does not refer to anything, like English "it" in "it is raining". Weather verbs are impersonal: es regnet, es schneit.

A preposition that is always followed by the accusative case. At A1: für (for), ohne (without), durch (through) and um (at a time, around). Only masculine articles change: für den Vater, durch einen Park.

The verb form for telling or asking someone to do something. German has one for each kind of "you", always with the verb first: du (Geh! Nimm!), ihr (Geht! Nehmt!) and Sie (Gehen Sie! Nehmen Sie!). The du form is the present-tense du form without du and its -st ending; the Sie form keeps Sie. Add bitte to sound polite.

The third German case, after the nominative and accusative. It is used after the prepositions aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, after in, an, auf and similar prepositions when they say where something is, and for the indirect object (the person who receives something). Articles: dem/einem (masculine and neuter), der/einer (feminine), den (plural, and the noun adds -n).

A preposition and an article fused into one word: zum (zu dem), zur (zu der), vom (von dem), beim (bei dem), im (in dem), am (an dem), ins (in das). The short forms are the normal ones in speech and writing.

One of nine prepositions (in, an, auf, unter, über, neben, zwischen, hinter, vor) that take the dative for location (Wo? Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch) and the accusative for movement to a place (Wohin? Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch). At A1 you mainly need the location use.
A personal pronoun used as the direct object: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie. Only mich, dich, ihn, uns and euch differ from the subject forms. Example: Verstehen Sie mich?

A personal pronoun in the dative: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, ihm, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen. Used after dative prepositions (mit mir), with verbs like helfen (Kannst du mir helfen?), in set phrases (Wie geht es dir? Mir ist kalt) and for the indirect object.

The person who receives something or to whom something is done, as in "Give me the book", where me is the indirect object and the book is the direct object. In German the indirect object is in the dative: Gib mir das Buch.

The main past tense of spoken German, made of a present-tense form of haben or sein (the auxiliary, in position 2) and a past participle at the end of the sentence: Ich habe gegessen, Wir sind gefahren. It translates both "I ate" and "I have eaten".

A helper verb that combines with another verb to form a tense. In the German perfect the auxiliary is haben or sein; it takes the person ending and stands in position 2, while the main verb goes to the end as a participle.

The form of a verb used in the perfect tense, placed at the end of the sentence. It never changes its ending. Most have ge- at the front and end in -t (gemacht) or -en (gesehen); separable verbs put -ge- after the prefix (eingekauft), and verbs in -ieren or with an inseparable prefix have no ge- (studiert, besucht).
A regular verb whose stem stays the same in all forms. Its past participle is ge- + stem + -t: machen → gemacht, kaufen → gekauft, arbeiten → gearbeitet. Most German verbs are weak.
A verb whose past participle ends in -en, often with a changed vowel: sehen → gesehen, trinken → getrunken, schreiben → geschrieben. Strong participles have to be learned with the verb.
A verb that changes its vowel like a strong verb but ends in -t like a weak verb in the past participle. At A1: bringen → gebracht, denken → gedacht, kennen → gekannt, wissen → gewusst.

A prefix that always stays attached to its verb and is never stressed, such as be-, ver-, er-, ent- and ge-. Verbs with an inseparable prefix take no ge- in the past participle: besuchen → besucht, verlieren → verloren, erzählen → erzählt.

A one-word past tense, used mainly in writing. In spoken German you need it at A1 only for sein and haben, where it is more common than the perfect: ich war, du warst (was, were); ich hatte, du hattest (had).

A word that joins words or sentences. The coordinating conjunctions und, oder, aber, denn and sondern stand in position zero and do not change the word order of the sentence after them: Ich bleibe hier, denn ich bin müde.

The slot in front of a sentence where und, oder, aber, denn and sondern stand. A word there does not count as position 1, so the next element is position 1 and the verb is still in position 2: …, aber heute habe ich Zeit.

A short form of a word or phrase. Most are read aloud as the full words and written with a full stop: z. B. = zum Beispiel, usw. = und so weiter, ca. = circa. A few, like PLZ or ICE, are said letter by letter and have no full stop.

An order given with just the infinitive at the end, with no du or Sie: Bitte Tür schließen! Nicht rauchen! Used on notices, in announcements and in recipes, not face to face. A separable verb stays in one piece: Bitte einsteigen!

The three forms you learn for each strong or irregular verb: the infinitive, the simple past and the past participle, e.g. gehen, ging, gegangen; sehen, sah, gesehen. Together they let you build every tense.

A noun made "little" (and often friendlier) with the ending -chen or -lein, usually with an umlaut and without a final -e: das Haus → das Häuschen, die Katze → das Kätzchen. Diminutives are always neuter, and the plural looks the same: die Brötchen.

A syllable that ends in a vowel, such as the first syllable of Na-me or ha-ben. A stressed vowel in an open syllable is usually long. A syllable that ends in a consonant (Stadt, Wort) is closed, and its vowel is often short.
The weak, relaxed vowel of an unstressed e, as in bitte, Name or the ending -en; it sounds like the a in English "about". A final e in German is never silent: it is a schwa.

The r that turns into a vowel-like sound after a vowel, especially in the ending -er: Lehrer, aber, oder end in a short sound close to the u in English "but", and der, wir, hier end in a short "uh" glide. No consonant r is heard.

A brief closing of the throat, like the break in English "uh-oh". In careful standard German of Germany, a word or word part that starts with a vowel usually begins with one: ein | Ei, Spiegel | ei, ver | eisen. It is often softer or missing in the south, Austria and Switzerland.
Two words that differ in only one sound, such as bitte and bitter, Wein and Wien, or schon and schön. Practising minimal pairs trains you to hear and make the difference.

A word taken from another language, such as Klavier, Information, Handy or Universität. Loanwords often keep some of their original pronunciation and stress: v sounds like English v in Klavier, and -tion is stressed in Information.
The rise and fall of the voice across a sentence. In German, statements and W-questions usually fall at the end (Wo wohnst du?), and yes/no questions usually rise (Wohnst du in Berlin?).

The reform of German spelling agreed in 1996 by Germany, Austria and Switzerland, taught in schools from 1998 and revised in 2004 and 2006. Its best-known rule: ss after a short vowel (dass, Fluss, muss; formerly daß, Fluß, muß) and ß after a long vowel or diphthong (Straße, heißen).
A language a state uses for its laws, offices and schools. German is an official language in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg and Belgium, and in South Tyrol in Italy.

The form of German used in writing, schools, news and between people from different regions, and the form you learn in this course. Its German name Hochdeutsch ("High German") refers to the higher-lying middle and south of the German-speaking area, not to quality.

A regional form of a language with its own sounds, words and some grammar, such as Bavarian, Swabian or Low German (Plattdeutsch, which many linguists count as a language of its own). Many German speakers use a dialect at home and standard German at work or with people from elsewhere.

The family of German dialects spoken in everyday life by German-speaking Swiss people of every background. In writing, at school and in the news they use Swiss Standard German, which learners also speak in Switzerland.

A language with more than one standard form. German has standards in Germany, Austria and Switzerland that differ in some words (Januar / Jänner, Fahrrad / Velo), spellings (Straße / Strasse) and sounds. All of them are correct where they are used.
A number used for counting: eins, zwei, drei, zwanzig. Compare the ordinal numbers (erste, zweite) used for dates and order.

A number used as a noun to name a digit, a school grade or a bus line. It is capitalized and always feminine: die Eins, eine Fünf, die Sieben. Ich habe eine Eins in Mathe means I got the top grade (in Germany) in maths.
The comma German uses where English uses a decimal point: 2,5 is two point five, said zwei Komma fünf. A point (or a small space) separates thousands: 1.000.

Using the masculine form of a word for people of any gender, or for a mixed group: die Lehrer for male and female teachers together. It is the traditional usage and still very common; critics say it makes readers think of men first.
Naming both the female and the male form of a word for people: Lehrerinnen und Lehrer, Liebe Kolleginnen und Kollegen, Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren. It is accepted in every kind of text.

Ways of writing and speaking about people that include more than the masculine form: paired forms (Lehrerinnen und Lehrer), neutral words (die Lehrkräfte, die Studierenden) and signs such as the gender star (Lehrer*innen). How far to use it is debated in German-speaking countries.

The asterisk in forms like Lehrer*innen, meant to include women, men and people who are neither. Similar signs are the colon (Lehrer:innen) and the underscore (Lehrer_innen); the older capital I (LehrerInnen) was made to name women and men. Read aloud with a short break before -innen. The Council for German Orthography decided in 2023 not to make these signs part of official spelling.

The fourth German case. At A1 you need only one use of it: -s after a name to say whose something is, with no apostrophe and no article: Annas Bruder (Anna's brother). Names ending in s, ss, ß, x or z take only an apostrophe: Max' Schwester. In speech von + name is common: der Bruder von Anna.
An s that joins the two parts of some compound nouns without adding meaning: der Zwilling + die Schwester = die Zwillingsschwester; die Geburt + der Tag = der Geburtstag.

A word or form that is normal in one region but not everywhere, such as die Semmel (Bavaria, Austria) or die Schrippe (Berlin) for the bread roll das Brötchen. Regional variants are correct where they are used; the standard word is understood everywhere.

The "would" form of a verb, used for wishes and polite requests. At A1 you meet it in two fixed forms: ich hätte gern (from haben) and ich möchte (from mögen), both meaning "I would like": Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee.

A time phrase in the accusative with no preposition. It is used with jeder, nächster, dieser and ganz (jeden Tag, nächsten Montag, diese Woche, den ganzen Tag) and to say how long something lasts (Der Kurs dauert einen Tag). Only the masculine changes: den, einen, jeden, nächsten.

An adverb that says when something happens, such as heute, morgen or jetzt. Adverbs made from days and parts of the day with -s, such as montags, abends or nachts, mean "regularly, every Monday / evening / night" and are written with a small letter.

A piece added to the front of a word to change its meaning. Lieblings- in front of a noun means "favourite": der Film → der Lieblingsfilm. Verbs have separable prefixes (auf-, mit-) and inseparable prefixes (be-, ver-).

The short ending (-e, -en and others) an adjective takes in front of a noun; it depends on the word before it and on the case. Ordinal numbers in dates take these endings too: der dritte Mai (-e after der), but am, vom, bis zum and den dritten Mai (-en). The full system comes at A2.

Writing with nouns made from verbs instead of full sentences, as on signs, boards and announcements: die Abfahrt (from abfahren), die Ankunft (from ankommen), der Ausstieg (from aussteigen), der Eingang (from eingehen). Nächster Halt: Hauptbahnhof. Ausstieg links. -fahrt nouns are feminine; -stieg and -gang nouns are masculine.

Two infinitives together at the end of a sentence, as in the perfect of a modal verb: Ich habe arbeiten müssen (I had to work). It is correct but heavy, so in speech Germans usually use the simple past of the modal instead: Ich musste arbeiten.

How formal a text or a way of speaking is. In German letters and e-mails the register shows in the opening (Sehr geehrte … / Liebe … / Hallo …), the closing (Mit freundlichen Grüßen … Liebe Grüße) and the choice of Sie or du.
The opening line of a letter or e-mail, followed by a comma: Sehr geehrte Frau Berger, / Liebe Anna, / Hallo zusammen,. The text after it starts with a small letter.
The closing words of a letter or e-mail, before your name, with no comma after them: Mit freundlichen Grüßen (formal), Viele Grüße (neutral), Liebe Grüße (warm).

references.title: Articles, possessives and cases
references.body:
## Which case?

| Case | Job in the sentence | Typical triggers | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | subject; after *sein* | who/what does it? | *Der Hund schläft.* — The dog is sleeping. |
| Accusative | direct object | *haben, möchten, es gibt*; *für, ohne, durch, um* | *Ich habe einen Hund.* — I have a dog. |
| Dative | indirect object; after some prepositions | *mit, zu, nach, von, aus, bei, seit*; location with *in, an, auf* … | *Ich fahre mit dem Bus.* — I'm going by bus. |

Only masculine changes between nominative and accusative. In the dative everything changes,
and plural nouns add *-n* if they don't already end in *-n* or *-s* (*mit den Kindern*, but
*mit den Fotos*).

## Definite article: the

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | der | die | das | die |
| Accusative | den | die | das | die |
| Dative | dem | der | dem | den (+ -n) |

## Indefinite article: a / an

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | ein | eine | ein | — |
| Accusative | einen | eine | ein | — |
| Dative | einem | einer | einem | — |

## Negative article: kein (not a, no)

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | kein | keine | kein | keine |
| Accusative | keinen | keine | kein | keine |
| Dative | keinem | keiner | keinem | keinen (+ -n) |

Use *kein* where you would say *ein* or no article: *Das ist kein Kuli. Ich habe keine Zeit.*
Use *nicht* for everything else.

## Possessive articles

Choose the word by the owner:

| Owner | Possessive | English |
|---|---|---|
| ich | mein | my |
| du | dein | your (informal, one person) |
| er / es | sein | his / its |
| sie (she) | ihr | her |
| wir | unser | our |
| ihr (you all) | euer | your (informal, several people) |
| sie (they) | ihr | their |
| Sie | Ihr | your (formal) |

Then add the ending for the noun that follows. The endings are the same as for *kein*:

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nominative | mein | meine | mein | meine |
| Accusative | meinen | meine | mein | meine |
| Dative | meinem | meiner | meinem | meinen (+ -n) |

Examples with other possessives: *unser Sohn, unsere Tochter, unseren Sohn (acc.), unserem
Sohn (dat.)*. *euer* drops its second *e* before an ending: *eure Tochter, euren Sohn, eurem
Sohn*.

## Gender hints

Always learn the article with the noun; these endings help you check.

| Ending or group | Gender | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ie | feminine | die Zeitung, die Universität, die Information, die Familie |
| -in (female person) | feminine | die Lehrerin, die Ärztin |
| -e | usually feminine | die Lampe, die Tasche — but der Name, der Käse |
| -chen, -lein | neuter | das Mädchen, das Brötchen |
| -ment, -um | usually neuter | das Medikament, das Museum, das Zentrum |
| -er (person or machine) | usually masculine | der Lehrer, der Computer — but das Fenster |
| -ismus, -ling | masculine | der Tourismus, der Frühling |
| days, months, seasons | masculine | der Montag, der Mai, der Sommer |
| compound nouns | gender of the last part | das Haus + die Tür = die Haustür |

## Plural patterns

| Pattern | Typical nouns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| -e | many masculine and neuter | der Tisch → die Tische; das Heft → die Hefte |
| ¨ + -e | many masculine | der Stuhl → die Stühle; der Sohn → die Söhne |
| -er | short neuter nouns | das Kind → die Kinder |
| ¨ + -er | short neuter nouns, some masculine | das Buch → die Bücher; der Mann → die Männer |
| -n / -en | most feminine nouns | die Lampe → die Lampen; die Tür → die Türen |
| -nen | feminine nouns in -in | die Lehrerin → die Lehrerinnen |
| -s | loanwords, words ending in a vowel (not -e) | das Handy → die Handys; das Foto → die Fotos |
| no ending | masculine/neuter in -er, -el, -en | der Schlüssel → die Schlüssel; das Fenster → die Fenster |
| ¨ only | some masculine/feminine in -er | der Vater → die Väter; die Mutter → die Mütter |

All plurals take *die* in the nominative and accusative, *den* in the dative.

## Personal pronouns by case

| Nominative | Accusative | Dative | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | mich | mir | I / me |
| du | dich | dir | you (informal, one person) |
| er | ihn | ihm | he / him (also "it" for masculine nouns) |
| sie | sie | ihr | she / her (also "it" for feminine nouns) |
| es | es | ihm | it |
| wir | uns | uns | we / us |
| ihr | euch | euch | you (informal, several people) |
| sie | sie | ihnen | they / them |
| Sie | Sie | Ihnen | you (formal) |

Pronouns follow the noun's grammatical gender, even for things: *Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist
schön.* — The table is new. It's beautiful.

## Short forms (preposition + article)

| Long | Short | Example |
|---|---|---|
| in dem | im | *im Büro* — in the office |
| an dem | am | *am Montag* — on Monday |
| zu dem | zum | *zum Bahnhof* — to the station |
| zu der | zur | *zur Schule* — to school |
| von dem | vom | *vom Arzt* — from the doctor |
| bei dem | beim | *beim Arzt* — at the doctor's |
| in das | ins | *ins Kino* — to the cinema |

references.title: Modal verbs and the sentence bracket
references.body:
## Present tense forms

| | können | wollen | mögen | möchten | müssen | dürfen | sollen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | kann | will | mag | möchte | muss | darf | soll |
| du | kannst | willst | magst | möchtest | musst | darfst | sollst |
| er/sie/es/man | kann | will | mag | möchte | muss | darf | soll |
| wir | können | wollen | mögen | möchten | müssen | dürfen | sollen |
| ihr | könnt | wollt | mögt | möchtet | müsst | dürft | sollt |
| sie/Sie | können | wollen | mögen | möchten | müssen | dürfen | sollen |

Patterns:

- ich and er/sie/es are identical and have no ending: *ich kann, er kann* (*möchte* keeps its
  *-e*: *ich möchte, er möchte*).
- The singular has its own vowel (*können → kann*, *dürfen → darf*, *müssen → muss*,
  *wollen → will*, *mögen → mag*); *sollen* keeps its vowel.
- The plural is regular and built from the infinitive: *wir müssen, ihr müsst*.
- *möchte* is the polite "would like" form of *mögen*; at A1 it is used like a verb of its own.

## Meanings

| Verb | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *können* | can, be able to; be possible | *Ich kann schwimmen.* — I can swim. |
| *wollen* | want (to); plan to | *Wir wollen im Sommer reisen.* — We want to travel in summer. |
| *mögen* | like (mostly + noun) | *Ich mag Tee.* — I like tea. |
| *möchten* | would like (to), polite | *Ich möchte bitte zahlen.* — I'd like to pay, please. |
| *müssen* | must, have to | *Du musst pünktlich sein.* — You have to be on time. |
| *dürfen* | may, be allowed to | *Darf ich hier parken?* — May I park here? |
| *sollen* | should, be supposed to (someone else wants it) | *Soll ich helfen?* — Shall I help? |

- *will* is direct, *möchte* is polite. *Ich will* means "I want", never "I will".
- For liking an activity, use *gern*: *Ich tanze gern* (not usually *Ich mag tanzen*).
- *können* with a language needs no second verb: *Ich kann Deutsch.*

## nicht müssen vs nicht dürfen

| German | Meaning | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Du musst nicht warten.* | it isn't necessary | You don't have to wait. |
| *Du darfst nicht warten.* | it is forbidden | You mustn't wait. / You're not allowed to wait. |
| *Man muss hier nicht bezahlen.* | free, no need to pay | You don't need to pay here. |
| *Man darf hier nicht rauchen.* | smoking is forbidden | You mustn't smoke here. |

English "must not" = German *nicht dürfen*. German *nicht müssen* = English "don't have to".

## man + modal verb for rules

*Man* (one, people in general) takes the er/sie/es form: *man kann, man muss, man darf, man
soll*.

- *Hier darf man parken.* — You're allowed to park here.
- *Im Kurs muss man pünktlich sein.* — You have to be on time in the course.

## The sentence bracket

The conjugated modal verb stands in position 2; the second verb goes to the end in the
infinitive, without *zu*. Everything else goes in between.

| Position 1 | Position 2 | middle | end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ich | kann | sehr gut | kochen. |
| Am Samstag | wollen | wir eine Party | feiern. |
| Hier | darf | man nicht | rauchen. |
| Was | möchtest | du | trinken? |
| | Musst | du heute | arbeiten? |

- Statements: modal in position 2, even after a time phrase (*Am Samstag wollen wir …*).
- W-questions: question word, then modal: *Was möchtest du trinken?*
- Yes/no questions: modal first: *Musst du heute arbeiten?*
- *nicht* normally goes directly before the infinitive: *Ich kann heute nicht kommen.*

## Separable verbs

Without a modal, a separable verb is itself a bracket: the stem in position 2, the prefix at
the end. With a modal, the infinitive at the end is written as one word again.

| Without a modal | With a modal |
|---|---|
| *Ich stehe um sieben auf.* | *Ich muss um sieben aufstehen.* |
| *Kommst du mit?* | *Willst du mitkommen?* |
| *Er lädt seine Freunde ein.* | *Er möchte seine Freunde einladen.* |
| *Wir füllen das Formular aus.* | *Wir sollen das Formular ausfüllen.* |
| *Sie ruft ihre Mutter an.* | *Sie kann ihre Mutter morgen anrufen.* |

Inseparable verbs such as *unterschreiben* never split: *Sie unterschreibt hier.* — *Sie muss
hier unterschreiben.*

## Polite requests and offers

| Pattern | Example |
|---|---|
| *Kann ich …?* | *Kann ich hier warten?* — Can I wait here? |
| *Darf ich …?* (more polite) | *Darf ich das Fenster öffnen?* — May I open the window? |
| *Können Sie …?* | *Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?* — Could you spell that, please? |
| *Soll ich …?* (offer) | *Soll ich die Tür schließen?* — Shall I close the door? |
| *Ich möchte …* | *Ich möchte einen Termin.* — I'd like an appointment. |

references.title: Numbers, prices, dates and time
references.body:
## Numbers 0–20

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 *null* | 6 *sechs* | 11 *elf* | 16 *sechzehn* |
| 1 *eins* | 7 *sieben* | 12 *zwölf* | 17 *siebzehn* |
| 2 *zwei* (*zwo*) | 8 *acht* | 13 *dreizehn* | 18 *achtzehn* |
| 3 *drei* | 9 *neun* | 14 *vierzehn* | 19 *neunzehn* |
| 4 *vier* | 10 *zehn* | 15 *fünfzehn* | 20 *zwanzig* |
| 5 *fünf* | | | |

13–19 are the unit + *zehn*. Two lose letters: *sechzehn* (not sechszehn), *siebzehn* (not siebenzehn). *zwo* is used on the phone and in announcements so it isn't confused with *drei*.

## Tens and 21–99

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 10 *zehn* | 40 *vierzig* | 70 *siebzig* |
| 20 *zwanzig* | 50 *fünfzig* | 80 *achtzig* |
| 30 *dreißig* | 60 *sechzig* | 90 *neunzig* |

Tens end in *-zig*, except *dreißig* (with *ß*). From 21 to 99 the unit comes first, joined by *und*, all in one word:

| Number | German | Literally |
|---|---|---|
| 21 | *einundzwanzig* | one-and-twenty |
| 34 | *vierunddreißig* | four-and-thirty |
| 57 | *siebenundfünfzig* | seven-and-fifty |
| 66 | *sechsundsechzig* | six-and-sixty |
| 99 | *neunundneunzig* | nine-and-ninety |

*eins* becomes *ein-* before *und*: *einundzwanzig*. *sechs* and *sieben* keep their full form before *und* (*sechsundsechzig, siebenundsiebzig*) but shorten in *sechzig* and *siebzig*.

## Hundreds, thousands, a million

| Number | German |
|---|---|
| 100 | *hundert* / *einhundert* |
| 101 | *hunderteins* |
| 115 | *hundertfünfzehn* |
| 199 | *hundertneunundneunzig* |
| 200 | *zweihundert* |
| 486 | *vierhundertsechsundachtzig* |
| 1.000 | *tausend* / *eintausend* |
| 1.001 | *tausendeins* |
| 2.750 | *zweitausendsiebenhundertfünfzig* |
| 10.000 | *zehntausend* |
| 65.000 | *fünfundsechzigtausend* |
| 100.000 | *hunderttausend* |
| 1.000.000 | *eine Million* |
| 2.500.000 | *zwei Komma fünf Millionen* / *zweieinhalb Millionen* |

Pattern: thousands + hundreds + (units *und* tens). Everything below a million is written as one word. *die Million* is a noun: *eine Million, zwei Millionen*.

## Writing numbers

| German | English | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *1.000* or *1 000* | 1,000 | one thousand |
| *2,5* | 2.5 | two point five, said *zwei Komma fünf* |
| *0,75 l* | 0.75 l | three quarters of a litre |

A point (or a space) groups thousands; a comma marks decimals.

## Prices

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| *1,00 €* | *ein Euro* |
| *2,50 €* | *zwei Euro fünfzig* |
| *9,99 €* | *neun Euro neunundneunzig* |
| *0,60 €* | *sechzig Cent* |
| *15,05 €* | *fünfzehn Euro fünf* |
| *1.200,00 €* | *tausendzweihundert Euro* or *zwölfhundert Euro* |

- No plural after a number: *zehn Euro, fünfzig Cent*.
- No *und* and no *Cent* in the middle: *zwei Euro fünfzig*.
- Questions: *Was kostet …? / Wie viel kostet …?* (one thing), *Was kosten …?* (several). The total: *Das macht 12,40 €.*
- Quantities have no "of": *ein Kilo Äpfel, 200 Gramm Käse, ein Liter Milch, eine Flasche Wasser*. *Kilo, Gramm, Liter, Stück* stay singular after numbers (*zwei Kilo*); *Flasche, Packung* take the plural (*zwei Flaschen*).

## Ordinal numbers and dates

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. *erste* | 6. *sechste* | 11. *elfte* | 20. *zwanzigste* |
| 2. *zweite* | 7. *siebte* | 12. *zwölfte* | 21. *einundzwanzigste* |
| 3. *dritte* | 8. *achte* | 13. *dreizehnte* | 30. *dreißigste* |
| 4. *vierte* | 9. *neunte* | 16. *sechzehnte* | 31. *einunddreißigste* |
| 5. *fünfte* | 10. *zehnte* | 19. *neunzehnte* | 100. *hundertste* |

- 1–19: number + *-te*. Irregular: *erste, dritte, siebte, achte* (*achte* has only one *t*).
- From 20: number + *-ste*.
- In writing, an ordinal is a number with a point: *der 3. Mai* = *der dritte Mai*.

| Use | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| What's the date? | *der* + ordinal + *-e* | *Heute ist der 1. Juli.* (*der erste Juli*) |
| On which day? | *am* + ordinal + *-en* | *am 1. Juli* (*am ersten Juli*) |
| Written date | day. month. year | *01.07.2026* or *1. Juli 2026* |

Questions: *Welches Datum ist heute?* / *Der Wievielte ist heute?* — What's the date today? *Wann hast du Geburtstag? — Am 12. März.*

Years are read in hundreds up to 1999, and as thousands from 2000:

| Year | Said |
|---|---|
| 1989 | *neunzehnhundertneunundachtzig* |
| 2000 | *zweitausend* |
| 2026 | *zweitausendsechsundzwanzig* |

Say *2026* or *im Jahr 2026*, never *in 2026*.

## Clock time

Questions: *Wie spät ist es?* / *Wie viel Uhr ist es?* Answer: *Es ist …*. At what time? *Um wie viel Uhr …? / Wann …? — Um …*

### Official (24-hour)

Hours + *Uhr* + minutes. Used for timetables, opening hours, appointments, radio and TV.

| Written | Said |
|---|---|
| 6:00 | *sechs Uhr* |
| 9:10 | *neun Uhr zehn* |
| 13:30 | *dreizehn Uhr dreißig* |
| 17:45 | *siebzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig* |
| 0:05 | *null Uhr fünf* |

### Informal (12-hour)

| Time | Said | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 8:00 | *acht (Uhr)* | |
| 8:05 | *fünf nach acht* | *nach* = past |
| 8:15 | *Viertel nach acht* | regional: *viertel neun* |
| 8:20 | *zwanzig nach acht* | also *zehn vor halb neun* |
| 8:25 | *fünf vor halb neun* | |
| 8:30 | *halb neun* | half way to nine |
| 8:35 | *fünf nach halb neun* | |
| 8:40 | *zwanzig vor neun* | also *zehn nach halb neun* |
| 8:45 | *Viertel vor neun* | regional: *drei viertel neun* |
| 8:55 | *fünf vor neun* | *vor* = to |
| 1:00 | *ein Uhr* / *eins* | never *eins Uhr* |
| 12:00 | *zwölf Uhr* | *Mittag* (noon), *Mitternacht* (midnight) |

*halb* always points to the next hour: *halb drei* = 2:30. Add *morgens, nachmittags, abends* if needed: *um acht Uhr abends* (8 p.m.).

*die Uhr* = o'clock (no plural in times); *die Stunde* = an hour of time: *Es ist zwei Uhr* vs *Ich warte zwei Stunden*.

## Days of the week

All masculine: *der Montag*.

| German | Short | English |
|---|---|---|
| *Montag* | Mo | Monday |
| *Dienstag* | Di | Tuesday |
| *Mittwoch* | Mi | Wednesday |
| *Donnerstag* | Do | Thursday |
| *Freitag* | Fr | Friday |
| *Samstag* (north also *Sonnabend*) | Sa | Saturday |
| *Sonntag* | So | Sunday |

*das Wochenende* = Saturday and Sunday. With *-s* and a small letter a day means "every": *montags* = on Mondays.

## Parts of the day

| German | Roughly | "in the …" | "every …" |
|---|---|---|---|
| *der Morgen* | 5–9 | *am Morgen* | *morgens* |
| *der Vormittag* | 9–12 | *am Vormittag* | *vormittags* |
| *der Mittag* | 12–14 | *am Mittag* | *mittags* |
| *der Nachmittag* | 14–18 | *am Nachmittag* | *nachmittags* |
| *der Abend* | 18–23 | *am Abend* | *abends* |
| *die Nacht* | 23–5 | *in der Nacht* | *nachts* |

| Today | Yesterday | Tomorrow |
|---|---|---|
| *heute Morgen* | *gestern Morgen* | *morgen früh* |
| *heute Nachmittag* | *gestern Nachmittag* | *morgen Nachmittag* |
| *heute Abend* | *gestern Abend* | *morgen Abend* |

*morgen* (small) = tomorrow; *der Morgen* (capital) = the morning. Tomorrow morning is *morgen früh*.

## Months and seasons

All masculine: *der Januar*, *der Sommer*.

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *Januar* (Austria: *Jänner*) | *April* | *Juli* | *Oktober* |
| *Februar* | *Mai* | *August* | *November* |
| *März* | *Juni* | *September* | *Dezember* |

| Season | German |
|---|---|
| spring | *der Frühling* |
| summer | *der Sommer* |
| autumn, fall | *der Herbst* |
| winter | *der Winter* |

On the phone people sometimes say *Juno* and *Julei* to keep *Juni* and *Juli* apart.

## Time prepositions

| Preposition | With | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| *um* | clock times | *um 8 Uhr, um halb drei* |
| *am* | days, dates, parts of the day, the weekend | *am Montag, am 3. Mai, am Abend, am Wochenende* |
| *in der* | the night | *in der Nacht* |
| *im* | months, seasons | *im Mai, im Sommer* |
| *von … bis* | a period from start to end | *von 9 bis 17 Uhr, von Montag bis Freitag* |
| *bis* | an end point | *bis morgen, bis acht Uhr* |
| no preposition | years | *2026* or *im Jahr 2026* |

Question words: *Wann?* (when?), *Um wie viel Uhr?* (at what time?), *Wie lange?* (how long?), *Wie oft?* (how often?).

How often: *immer* (always) – *oft* (often) – *manchmal* (sometimes) – *nie* (never).

references.title: The perfect tense
references.body:
## How to form it

Perfect = present tense of *haben* or *sein* (position 2) + past participle (end of the
sentence).

| | with haben | with sein |
|---|---|---|
| ich | habe … gemacht | bin … gefahren |
| du | hast … gemacht | bist … gefahren |
| er/sie/es | hat … gemacht | ist … gefahren |
| wir | haben … gemacht | sind … gefahren |
| ihr | habt … gemacht | seid … gefahren |
| sie/Sie | haben … gemacht | sind … gefahren |

- Statement: *Ich habe gestern Fußball gespielt.*
- Time phrase first: *Gestern habe ich Fußball gespielt.*
- Yes/no question: *Hast du gestern Fußball gespielt?*
- W-question: *Wann bist du nach Hause gekommen?*
- Modal verbs are not used in the perfect at A1; their past forms (*ich konnte, ich musste*) come at A2.

## haben or sein?

| use sein | examples |
|---|---|
| movement from one place to another | *gehen, kommen, fahren, fliegen, laufen, reisen, wandern, schwimmen* |
| a change of state | *aufstehen, werden, aufwachen, einschlafen* |
| three special verbs | *sein, bleiben, passieren* |

Everything else uses *haben*, including every verb with an accusative object (*einen Film
sehen*, *ein Buch kaufen*). *Fahren* with an object takes *haben*: *Ich habe das Auto
gefahren.*

## Participle patterns

| pattern | rule | examples |
|---|---|---|
| weak (regular) | ge- + stem + -t | machen → gemacht, kaufen → gekauft, hören → gehört |
| stem ends in -t/-d | ge- + stem + -et | arbeiten → gearbeitet, warten → gewartet, antworten → geantwortet |
| strong (irregular) | ge- + stem + -en, vowel often changes | sehen → gesehen, trinken → getrunken, schreiben → geschrieben |
| mixed | ge- + changed stem + -t | bringen → gebracht, denken → gedacht, kennen → gekannt, wissen → gewusst |
| separable | prefix + ge + participle | einkaufen → eingekauft, anrufen → angerufen, aufstehen → aufgestanden |
| -ieren | no ge-, ends in -t | studieren → studiert, fotografieren → fotografiert |
| inseparable prefix (be-, ver-, er-, ent-, ge-) | no ge- | besuchen → besucht, verstehen → verstanden, erzählen → erzählt |

## Irregular and sein verbs at A1

Regular *haben* verbs are not listed. *Sein* verbs are marked by *ist* in the last column.

| infinitive | er/sie/es (present) | perfect |
|---|---|---|
| abbiegen | biegt ab | ist abgebogen |
| abfahren | fährt ab | ist abgefahren |
| anfangen | fängt an | hat angefangen |
| ankommen | kommt an | ist angekommen |
| anrufen | ruft an | hat angerufen |
| aufstehen | steht auf | ist aufgestanden |
| aussteigen | steigt aus | ist ausgestiegen |
| bekommen | bekommt | hat bekommen |
| bestehen | besteht | hat bestanden |
| bleiben | bleibt | ist geblieben |
| bringen | bringt | hat gebracht |
| denken | denkt | hat gedacht |
| einladen | lädt ein | hat eingeladen |
| einsteigen | steigt ein | ist eingestiegen |
| essen | isst | hat gegessen |
| fahren | fährt | ist gefahren |
| fernsehen | sieht fern | hat ferngesehen |
| finden | findet | hat gefunden |
| fliegen | fliegt | ist geflogen |
| geben | gibt | hat gegeben |
| gehen | geht | ist gegangen |
| haben | hat | hat gehabt |
| heißen | heißt | hat geheißen |
| helfen | hilft | hat geholfen |
| kennen | kennt | hat gekannt |
| kommen | kommt | ist gekommen |
| laufen | läuft | ist gelaufen |
| lesen | liest | hat gelesen |
| mitkommen | kommt mit | ist mitgekommen |
| mögen | mag | hat gemocht |
| nehmen | nimmt | hat genommen |
| passieren | passiert | ist passiert |
| reisen | reist | ist gereist |
| schlafen | schläft | hat geschlafen |
| schließen | schließt | hat geschlossen |
| schreiben | schreibt | hat geschrieben |
| schwimmen | schwimmt | ist geschwommen |
| sehen | sieht | hat gesehen |
| sein | ist | ist gewesen |
| singen | singt | hat gesungen |
| sprechen | spricht | hat gesprochen |
| treffen | trifft | hat getroffen |
| trinken | trinkt | hat getrunken |
| umsteigen | steigt um | ist umgestiegen |
| umziehen | zieht um | ist umgezogen |
| unterschreiben | unterschreibt | hat unterschrieben |
| vergessen | vergisst | hat vergessen |
| verlieren | verliert | hat verloren |
| verstehen | versteht | hat verstanden |
| wandern | wandert | ist gewandert |
| waschen | wäscht | hat gewaschen |
| wehtun | tut weh | hat wehgetan |
| werden | wird | ist geworden |
| wissen | weiß | hat gewusst |
| zurückkommen | kommt zurück | ist zurückgekommen |

*Schwimmen* can also take *haben* when it means the activity rather than going somewhere
(*Ich habe eine Stunde geschwommen*); *ist geschwommen* is always correct.

## war and hatte

With *sein* and *haben* the simple past is more common than the perfect.

| | sein | haben |
|---|---|---|
| ich | war | hatte |
| du | warst | hattest |
| er/sie/es | war | hatte |
| wir | waren | hatten |
| ihr | wart | hattet |
| sie/Sie | waren | hatten |

references.title: Prepositions and the imperative
references.body:
## Articles after prepositions

| | masculine | feminine | neuter | plural |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| accusative | *den / einen* | *die / eine* | *das / ein* | *die / –* |
| dative | *dem / einem* | *der / einer* | *dem / einem* | *den / –* (noun + *-n*) |

Possessives and *kein* take the same endings: *für meinen Vater*, *mit meiner Mutter*, *ohne
mein Handy*, *mit meinen Kindern*, *keinem*, *keiner*.

## Prepositions with the accusative

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *durch* | through | *durch den Park* — through the park |
| *für* | for | *für meinen Bruder* — for my brother |
| *gegen* | against | *gegen die Wand* — against the wall |
| *ohne* | without | *ohne einen Koffer* — without a suitcase |
| *um* | around; at (clock time) | *um die Ecke* — round the corner; *um 8 Uhr* — at 8 |

## Prepositions with the dative

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| *aus* | out of, from (origin) | *aus dem Haus* — out of the house; *aus der Schweiz* — from Switzerland |
| *bei* | at (someone's place, a company), near | *bei meinen Eltern* — at my parents' |
| *mit* | with, by (transport) | *mit dem Zug* — by train |
| *nach* | to (cities, countries); after | *nach Wien* — to Vienna; *nach dem Essen* — after the meal |
| *seit* | since, for (up to now) | *seit einem Jahr* — for a year |
| *von* | from, of | *von der Arbeit* — from work |
| *zu* | to (people, places) | *zum Arzt* — to the doctor |
| *gegenüber* | opposite | *gegenüber der Post* — opposite the post office |

*Seit* + present tense: *Ich wohne seit 2020 hier.* — I've lived here since 2020.

| Where to? (*Wohin?*) | Where? (*Wo?*) | Where from? (*Woher?*) |
|---|---|---|
| *zum Arzt* | *beim Arzt* | *vom Arzt* |
| *zu Anna* | *bei Anna* | *von Anna* |
| *nach Berlin* | *in Berlin* | *aus Berlin* |
| *nach Hause* | *zu Hause* | *von zu Hause* |

## Two-way prepositions: location with Wo? + dative

| Preposition | Meaning | Example (*Wo?* + dative) |
|---|---|---|
| *in* | in, inside | *im Bad, in der Küche* |
| *an* | on (a wall), at, by | *an der Wand, am Fenster* |
| *auf* | on (top of) | *auf dem Tisch* |
| *unter* | under | *unter dem Bett* |
| *über* | above, over | *über dem Sofa* |
| *neben* | next to | *neben der Tür* |
